translations.an10.13:1: “There are, monks, these ten fetters. What ten? The five lower fetters and the five higher fetters. What are the five lower fetters? Identity view, doubt, grasping at habits and observances, sensual desire, and ill will—these are the five lower fetters.
translations.an10.15:1: “Monks, whatever sentient beings there are—whether footless or two-footed, four-footed or many-footed, with form or formless, percipient or non-percipient, or neither percipient nor non-percipient—the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, declares them to be foremost among them; so too, monks, whatever skillful qualities there are, they all have heedfulness as their root, converge on heedfulness, and heedfulness is declared to be their foremost.
translations.an10.15:2: “Suppose, monks, there were various footprints of jungle animals. All of them would fit within the footprint of an elephant, and the elephant’s footprint would be declared to be the foremost among them on account of its size; so too, monks, whatever skillful qualities there are, they all have heedfulness as their root, converge on heedfulness, and heedfulness is declared to be their foremost.
translations.an10.15:3: “Suppose, monks, there were all the rafters of a gabled house. They would all slope towards the peak, meet at the peak, and converge on the peak, and the peak would be declared to be their foremost; so too, monks, whatever skillful qualities there are, they all have heedfulness as their root, converge on heedfulness, and heedfulness is declared to be their foremost.
translations.an10.15:7: “Suppose, monks, there were various petty kings. They would all be vassals of a wheel-turning monarch, and the wheel-turning monarch would be declared to be their foremost; so too, monks ….
translations.an10.15:8: “Suppose, monks, there were the radiance of all the stars. They would not amount to a sixteenth part of the moon’s radiance, and the moon’s radiance would be declared to be their foremost; so too, monks ….
translations.an10.15:9: “Suppose, monks, in the last month of the rainy season, at harvest time, when the sky is clear and cloudless, the sun rising in the sky dispels all the darkness in the sky and shines, blazes, and radiates; so too, monks ….
translations.an10.17:1: “Live, monks, with a protector, not without a protector. One who lives without a protector, monks, lives in suffering. There are these ten qualities that are a protector. What ten? Here, monks, a monk is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest fault, and training in the rules of training. In that a monk is virtuous … and trains in the rules of training, this too is a quality that is a protector.
translations.an10.17:2: “Furthermore, monks, a monk is learned, remembering and retaining what he has learned; those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings as these he is well-learned in, has remembered well, has practiced well with speech, has thought about well, and has penetrated well by view. In that a monk is learned … and has penetrated well by view, this too is a quality that is a protector.
translations.an10.17:3: “Furthermore, monks, a monk has good friends, good companions, and good associates. In that a monk has good friends, good companions, and good associates, this too is a quality that is a protector.
translations.an10.18:10: “Furthermore, monks, a monk is mindful, possessing supreme mindfulness and discernment, remembering and recalling what was done and said long ago. Thinking, ‘This monk is mindful, possessing supreme mindfulness and discernment, remembering and recalling what was done and said long ago,’ the senior monks do not need to admonish or instruct him, nor do the middle monks … nor do the new monks need to admonish or instruct him. For one who is compassionate towards the seniors, the middling, and the new, growth in skillful qualities is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that is a protector.
translations.an10.18:11: “Furthermore, monks, a monk is wise, possessing wisdom regarding arising and passing away, noble, penetrating, leading to the right destruction of suffering. Thinking, ‘This monk is wise, possessing wisdom regarding arising and passing away, noble, penetrating, leading to the right destruction of suffering,’ the senior monks do not need to admonish or instruct him, nor do the middle monks … nor do the new monks need to admonish or instruct him. For one who is compassionate towards the seniors … decline. This too is a quality that is a protector.
translations.an10.18:2: “Live, monks, with a protector, not without a protector. One who lives without a protector, monks, lives in suffering. There are these ten qualities that are a protector. What ten? Here, monks, a monk is virtuous … and trains in the rules of training. Thinking, ‘This monk is virtuous, dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest fault, and trains in the rules of training,’ the senior monks do not need to admonish or instruct him, nor do the middle monks … nor do the new monks need to admonish or instruct him. For one who is compassionate towards the seniors, the middling, and the new, growth in skillful qualities is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that is a protector.
translations.an10.18:4: “Furthermore, monks, a monk has good friends, good companions, and good associates. Thinking, ‘This monk has good friends, good companions, and good associates,’ the senior monks do not need to admonish or instruct him, nor do the middle monks … nor do the new monks need to admonish or instruct him. For one who is compassionate towards the seniors, the middling, and the new, growth in skillful qualities is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that is a protector.
translations.an10.18:5: “Furthermore, monks, a monk is easy to speak to, possessing qualities that make him easy to speak to, patient, and receptive to instruction. Thinking, ‘This monk is easy to speak to, possessing qualities that make him easy to speak to, patient, and receptive to instruction,’ the senior monks do not need to admonish or instruct him, nor do the middle monks … nor do the new monks need to admonish or instruct him. For one who is compassionate towards the seniors, the middling, and the new, growth in skillful qualities is to be expected, not decline. This too is a quality that is a protector.
translations.an10.18:6: Furthermore, monks, a monk is skilled and tireless in whatever duties there are to be done for their fellow monks, endowed with the means for investigating them, capable of doing and arranging them. The elder monks think that this monk should be admonished and instructed: ‘This monk is skilled and tireless in whatever duties there are to be done for their fellow monks, endowed with the means for investigating them, capable of doing and arranging them.’ The middle monks … the new monks also think that he should be admonished and instructed. For him who is pitied by the elders, pitied by the middle monks, and pitied by the new monks, growth is to be expected in skillful qualities, not decline. This too is a protective factor.
translations.an10.18:7: Furthermore, monks, a monk is fond of Dhamma, delights in it, and takes great pleasure in the higher Dhamma and discipline. The elder monks think that this monk should be admonished and instructed: ‘This monk is fond of Dhamma, delights in it, and takes great pleasure in the higher Dhamma and discipline.’ The middle monks … the new monks also think that he should be admonished and instructed. For him who is pitied by the elders, pitied by the middle monks, and pitied by the new monks, growth is to be expected in skillful qualities, not decline. This too is a protective factor.
translations.an10.18:8: Furthermore, monks, a monk lives with energy aroused for the abandoning of unskillful qualities and the attainment of skillful qualities; he is strong, firm in exertion, not shirking the burden of skillful qualities. The elder monks think that this monk should be admonished and instructed: ‘This monk lives with energy aroused for the abandoning of unskillful qualities and the attainment of skillful qualities; he is strong, firm in exertion, not shirking the burden of skillful qualities.’ The middle monks … the new monks also think that he should be admonished and instructed. For him who is pitied by the elders, pitied by the middle monks, and pitied by the new monks, growth is to be expected in skillful qualities, not decline. This too is a protective factor.
translations.an10.18:9: Furthermore, monks, a monk is content with any kind of robe, alms food, lodging, and medicines and provisions for the sick. The elder monks think that this monk should be admonished and instructed: ‘This monk is content with any kind of robe, alms food, lodging, and medicines and provisions for the sick.’ The middle monks … the new monks also think that he should be admonished and instructed. For him who is pitied by the elders, pitied by the middle monks, and pitied by the new monks, growth is to be expected in skillful qualities, not decline. This too is a protective factor.
translations.an10.20:1: At one time the Buddha was staying among the Kurus at Kammāsadhamma, a market town of the Kurus. There the Buddha addressed the monks ….
translations.an10.20:10: And how, monks, is a monk calmed in bodily formation? Here, monks, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which has neither pleasure nor pain, and mindfulness purified by equanimity. In this way, monks, a monk is calmed in bodily formation.
translations.an10.20:11: And how, monks, is a monk well liberated in mind? Here, monks, a monk’s mind is liberated from lust, liberated from hatred, and liberated from delusion. In this way, monks, a monk is well liberated in mind.
translations.an10.20:2: “These ten, monks, are noble dwellings, which noble ones have dwelt in, do dwell in, and will dwell in. What ten? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned the five hindrances, possesses the six factors, has a single protection, is guarded on four sides, is one who has cut off individual truths, has abandoned craving, has uncorrupted thought, is calmed in bodily formation, is well liberated in mind, and is well liberated in wisdom.
translations.an10.20:3: And how, monks, has a monk abandoned the five hindrances? Here, monks, a monk’s sensual desire is abandoned, ill will is abandoned, sloth and torpor are abandoned, restlessness and remorse are abandoned, and doubt is abandoned. In this way, monks, a monk has abandoned the five hindrances.
translations.an10.20:4: And how, monks, does a monk possess the six factors? Here, monks, a monk, seeing a form with the eye, is neither pleased nor displeased, but dwells with equanimity, mindful and fully aware. Hearing a sound with the ear … smelling an odor with the nose … tasting a flavor with the tongue … touching a tactile object with the body … knowing a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is neither pleased nor displeased, but dwells with equanimity, mindful and fully aware. In this way, monks, a monk possesses the six factors.
translations.an10.20:5: And how, monks, is a monk of single protection? Here, monks, a monk is endowed with a mind that has a single protection. In this way, monks, a monk is of single protection.
translations.an10.20:6: And how, monks, is a monk guarded on four sides? Here, monks, a monk practices, tolerates, avoids, and removes based on a reckoning. In this way, monks, a monk is guarded on four sides.
translations.an10.20:7: And how, monks, is a monk one who has cut off individual truths? Here, monks, whatever various individual truths there are of wandering ascetics and brahmins—such as: ‘The world is eternal’ or ‘The world is not eternal’; ‘The world is finite’ or ‘The world is infinite’; ‘The soul and the body are the same’ or ‘The soul is one thing and the body another’; ‘The Tathāgata exists after death’ or ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death’ or ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’ or ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’—all these are cut off, uprooted, removed, abandoned, and given up. In this way, monks, a monk is one who has cut off individual truths.
translations.an10.20:8: And how, monks, has a monk abandoned craving? Here, monks, a monk’s craving for sensual pleasures is abandoned, craving for existence is abandoned, and craving for the holy life has subsided. In this way, monks, a monk has abandoned craving.
translations.an10.20:9: And how, monks, does a monk have uncorrupted thought? Here, monks, a monk’s sensual thought is abandoned, ill will thought is abandoned, and cruel thought is abandoned. In this way, monks, a monk has uncorrupted thought.
translations.an10.24:1: At one time Venerable Mahācunda was staying among the Cetis at Sahajāti. There Venerable Mahācunda addressed the monks: “Friends, monks.” “Friend,” those monks replied to Venerable Mahācunda. Venerable Mahācunda said this:
translations.an10.24:10: Suppose, friend, a person, being wealthy, speaks of wealth; being rich, speaks of riches; being affluent, speaks of affluence. When some occasion for gaining wealth arises, they would be able to acquire wealth, grain, silver, or gold. Then they would know him thus: ‘This venerable, being wealthy, speaks of wealth; being rich, speaks of riches; being affluent, speaks of affluence. Why is that? Because this venerable, when some occasion for gaining wealth arises, is able to acquire wealth, grain, silver, or gold.’
translations.an10.24:2: “When a monk speaks of knowledge, friend, saying: ‘I know this teaching, I see this teaching.’ If, friend, greed overcomes that monk and stands, hatred … delusion … anger … resentment … contempt … spite … stinginess … wicked envy … wicked desire overcomes him and stands, he should be understood thus: ‘This venerable does not understand as it really is; if he understood as it really is, greed would not arise; yet greed overcomes this venerable and stands. This venerable does not understand as it really is; if he understood as it really is, hatred would not arise … delusion … anger … resentment … contempt … spite … stinginess … wicked envy … wicked desire would not arise, yet wicked desire overcomes this venerable and stands.’
translations.an10.24:3: When a monk speaks of development, friend, saying: ‘I am developed in body, developed in virtue, developed in mind, developed in wisdom.’ If, friend, greed overcomes that monk and stands, hatred … delusion … anger … resentment … contempt … spite … stinginess … wicked envy … wicked desire overcomes him and stands, he should be understood thus: ‘This venerable does not understand as it really is; if he understood as it really is, greed would not arise; yet greed overcomes this venerable and stands. This venerable does not understand as it really is; if he understood as it really is, hatred would not arise … delusion … anger … resentment … contempt … spite … stinginess … wicked envy … wicked desire would not arise, yet wicked desire overcomes this venerable and stands.’
translations.an10.24:5: Suppose, friend, a person, being poor, speaks of wealth; being poor, speaks of riches; being destitute, speaks of affluence. When some occasion for gaining wealth arises, they would not be able to acquire wealth, grain, silver, or gold. Then they would know him thus: ‘This venerable, being poor, speaks of wealth; being poor, speaks of riches; being destitute, speaks of affluence. Why is that? Because this venerable, when some occasion for gaining wealth arises, is not able to acquire wealth, grain, silver, or gold.’
translations.an10.24:9: When a monk speaks of knowledge, friend, and speaks of development, saying: ‘I know this teaching, I see this teaching; I am developed in body, developed in virtue, developed in mind, developed in wisdom.’ If, friend, greed does not overcome that monk and stand, hatred … delusion … anger … resentment … contempt … spite … stinginess … wicked envy … wicked desire does not overcome him and stand, he should be understood thus: ‘This venerable understands as it really is; because he understands as it really is, greed does not arise; and greed does not overcome this venerable and stand. This venerable understands as it really is; because he understands as it really is, hatred does not arise … delusion … anger … resentment … contempt … spite … stinginess … wicked envy … wicked desire does not arise, and wicked desire does not overcome this venerable and stand.’
translations.an10.29:1: “Monks, as far as the Kāsi and Kosala countries extend, as far as the domain of King Pasenadi of Kosala extends, King Pasenadi of Kosala is the chief there. But, monks, even in King Pasenadi of Kosala there is change other than what is appropriate, there is alteration. Seeing this, monks, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that too. Becoming disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate towards the foremost, and even more so towards the inferior.
translations.an10.29:10: Perceiving formless internally, alone, one sees forms externally—blue, blue-colored, of blue appearance, blue radiance. Just as a blue flower is blue, blue-colored, of blue appearance, blue radiance; or just as that Benares cloth is smooth on both sides, blue, blue-colored, of blue appearance, blue radiance; so too, perceiving formless internally, alone, one sees forms externally—blue, blue-colored, of blue appearance, blue radiance; thinking ‘I know and see having overcome them,’ thus one perceives. This is the fifth base of mastery.
translations.an10.29:11: Perceiving formless internally, alone, one sees forms externally—yellow, yellow-colored, of yellow appearance, yellow radiance. Just as a yellow flower is yellow, yellow-colored, of yellow appearance, yellow radiance; or just as that Benares cloth is smooth on both sides, yellow, yellow-colored, of yellow appearance, yellow radiance; so too, perceiving formless internally, alone, one sees forms externally—yellow, yellow-colored, of yellow appearance, yellow radiance; thinking ‘I know and see having overcome them,’ thus one perceives. This is the sixth base of mastery.
translations.an10.29:12: Internally perceiving the formless, a single person sees externally forms that are red, of red color, red in appearance, red in radiance. Just as a bandhujīvaka flower is red, of red color, red in appearance, red in radiance, or just as that Benares cloth is double-sided, red, of red color, red in appearance, red in radiance; so too, internally perceiving the formless, a single person sees externally forms that are red, of red color, red in appearance, red in radiance; perceiving, ‘I know and see having overcome them,’ they have such perception. This is the seventh base of mastery.
translations.an10.29:13: Internally perceiving the formless, a single person sees externally forms that are white, of white color, white in appearance, white in radiance. Just as the morning star is white, of white color, white in appearance, white in radiance, or just as that Benares cloth is double-sided, white, of white color, white in appearance, white in radiance; so too, internally perceiving the formless, a single person sees externally forms that are white, of white color, white in appearance, white in radiance; perceiving, ‘I know and see having overcome them,’ they have such perception. This is the eighth base of mastery. These, monks, are the eight bases of mastery.
translations.an10.29:14: The foremost, monks, of these eight bases of mastery is this: internally perceiving the formless, a single person sees externally forms that are white, of white color, white in appearance, white in radiance; perceiving, ‘I know and see having overcome them,’ they have such perception. There are beings, monks, who have such perception. Even for those beings who have such perception, there is change, alteration, and decay. Seeing thus, the learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with that too. Being disillusioned, they become dispassionate at the top, and even more so in what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:15: There are these four practices, monks. What four? Painful practice with slow direct knowledge, painful practice with quick direct knowledge, pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge, pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge—these are the four practices, monks.
translations.an10.29:16: The foremost, monks, of these four practices is the pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge. There are beings, monks, who practice in this way. Even for those beings who practice in this way, there is change, alteration, and decay. Seeing thus, the learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with that too. Being disillusioned, they become dispassionate at the top, and even more so in what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:17: There are these four perceptions, monks. What four? One perceives the limited, one perceives the exalted, one perceives the immeasurable, one perceives the base of nothingness as ‘there is nothing’—these are the four perceptions, monks.
translations.an10.29:18: The foremost, monks, of these four perceptions is this: one perceives the base of nothingness as ‘there is nothing’. There are beings, monks, who have such perception. Even for those beings who have such perception, there is change, alteration, and decay. Seeing thus, the learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with that too. Being disillusioned, they become dispassionate at the top, and even more so in what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:2: Monks, as far as the moon and sun revolve, shining and radiating, there is a thousandfold world. In that thousandfold world there are a thousand moons, a thousand suns, a thousand Mount Sinerus, a thousand Jambudīpas, a thousand Aparagoyānas, a thousand Uttarakurus, a thousand Pubbavidehas, four thousand great oceans, four thousand great kings, a thousand Four Great Kings, a thousand Thirty-three Gods, a thousand Yāmas, a thousand Tusitas, a thousand Nimmānaratīs, a thousand Paranimmitavasavattīs, and a thousand Brahmā worlds. Monks, as far as the thousandfold world extends, Mahābrahmā is reckoned as the foremost there. Even for Mahābrahmā, monks, there is change, alteration, and decay. Seeing thus, the learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with that too. Being disillusioned, they become dispassionate at the top, and even more so in what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:20: There are some ascetics and brahmins, monks, who proclaim ultimate purity. The foremost, monks, of those proclaiming ultimate purity is this: having entirely passed beyond the base of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Knowing that, realizing it, they teach the Dhamma. There are beings, monks, who speak thus. Even for those beings who speak thus, there is change, alteration, and decay. Seeing thus, the learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with that too. Being disillusioned, they become dispassionate at the top, and even more so in what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:3: There comes a time, monks, when this world evolves. When the world evolves, monks, beings mostly become radiant-evolving. There they are mind-made, feeding on bliss, self-luminous, traveling through the air, abiding in glory, for a long period, a very long time. When the world evolves, monks, the radiant gods are reckoned as the foremost. Even for the radiant gods, monks, there is change, alteration, and decay. Seeing thus, the learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with that too. Being disillusioned, they become dispassionate at the top, and even more so in what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:4: There are these ten kasina bases, monks. What ten? One perceives the earth kasina above, below, across, undivided, immeasurable; one perceives the water kasina … one perceives the fire kasina … one perceives the air kasina … one perceives the blue kasina … one perceives the yellow kasina … one perceives the red kasina … one perceives the white kasina … one perceives the space kasina … one perceives the consciousness kasina above, below, across, undivided, immeasurable. These, monks, are the ten kasina bases.
translations.an10.29:5: Foremost, monks, among these ten kasina bases is the consciousness kasina, where one perceives above, below, across, without a division, limitless. There are, monks, beings with such perception. There is, monks, for beings with such perception a change and a transformation. Seeing thus, monks, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with that too. Being disillusioned, passion fades in the beginning, and in the end too.
translations.an10.29:6: There are, monks, eight bases of mastery. What are the eight? Perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally, limited, beautiful and ugly; thinking 'I know them, I see them having mastered them', one has such perception. This is the first base of mastery.
translations.an10.29:7: Perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally, limitless, beautiful and ugly; thinking 'I know them, I see them having mastered them', one has such perception. This is the second base of mastery.
translations.an10.29:8: Perceiving no form internally, one sees forms externally, limited, beautiful and ugly; thinking 'I know them, I see them having mastered them', one has such perception. This is the third base of mastery.
translations.an10.29:9: Perceiving no form internally, one sees forms externally, limitless, beautiful and ugly; thinking 'I know them, I see them having mastered them', one has such perception. This is the fourth base of mastery.
translations.an10.51:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks.' 'Venerable sir,' they replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an10.51:3: And how, monks, is a monk skilled in the exposition of his own mind? Suppose, monks, a woman or man, young, youthful, fond of ornaments, examining their own face in a clear, bright mirror or a bowl of clear water. If they see a speck of dirt or a blemish there, they make an effort to remove that speck of dirt or blemish. But if they do not see a speck of dirt or a blemish there, they are glad about it, with fulfilled intention: 'What a gain for me, how clean I am!' So too, monks, a monk's review is very helpful for skillful qualities: 'Do I often dwell with covetousness, or do I often dwell without covetousness? Do I often dwell with a mind of ill will, or do I often dwell without ill will? Do I often dwell with sloth and torpor, or have I overcome sloth and torpor? Do I often dwell with restlessness, or do I often dwell without restlessness? Do I often dwell with doubt, or have I gone beyond doubt? Do I often dwell with anger, or do I often dwell without anger? Do I often dwell with a corrupt mind, or do I often dwell with an uncorrupt mind? Do I often dwell with aroused energy, or do I often dwell with unaroused energy? Do I often dwell with laziness, or do I often dwell with aroused energy? Do I often dwell without concentration, or do I often dwell with concentration?'
translations.an10.51:4: If, monks, while reviewing, a monk knows this: 'I often dwell with covetousness, with a mind of ill will, with sloth and torpor, with restlessness, with doubt, with anger, with a corrupt mind, with aroused energy, with laziness, without concentration,' then that monk should generate extreme desire, effort, endeavor, struggle, persistence, mindfulness, and discernment to abandon those same bad, unskillful qualities. Suppose, monks, a cloth or head were on fire. To extinguish that cloth or head, one would generate extreme desire, effort, endeavor, struggle, persistence, mindfulness, and discernment. So too, that monk should generate extreme desire, effort, endeavor, struggle, persistence, mindfulness, and discernment to abandon those same bad, unskillful qualities.
translations.an10.54:2: And how, monks, is a monk skilled in the exposition of his own mind? Suppose, monks, a woman or man, young, youthful, fond of ornaments, examining their own face in a clear, bright mirror or a bowl of clear water. If they see a speck of dirt or a blemish there, they make an effort to remove that speck of dirt or blemish. But if they do not see a speck of dirt or a blemish there, they are glad about it, with fulfilled intention: 'What a gain for me, how clean I am!' So too, monks, a monk's review is very helpful for skillful qualities: 'Have I attained internal serenity of mind, or have I not attained internal serenity of mind? Have I attained the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena, or have I not attained the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena?'
translations.an10.54:5: But if, monks, while reviewing, a monk knows this: 'I have not attained internal serenity of mind, I have not attained the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena,' then that monk should generate extreme desire, effort, endeavor, struggle, persistence, mindfulness, and discernment to attain those same skillful qualities. Suppose, monks, a cloth or head were on fire. To extinguish that cloth or head, one would generate extreme desire, effort, endeavor, struggle, persistence, mindfulness, and discernment. So too, that monk should generate extreme desire, effort, endeavor, struggle, persistence, mindfulness, and discernment to attain those same skillful qualities. By and by he attains internal serenity of mind and the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena.
translations.an10.54:6: But if, monks, while reviewing, a monk knows this: 'I have attained internal serenity of mind, I have attained the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena,' then that monk should make an effort based on those same skillful qualities for the further destruction of the taints.
translations.an10.58:1: “If, monks, wanderers of other sects were to ask: ‘What is the root of all phenomena, what is their origin, what is their arising, what is their resort, what is their establishment, what is their authority, what is their superior, what is their essence, what is their culmination, what is their consummation?’—thus asked, how would you answer those wanderers of other sects?” “Our root, venerable sir, is the Blessed One; our guide is the Blessed One; our refuge is the Blessed One. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would explain the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will retain it.”
translations.an10.58:2: “Then listen, monks, and pay close attention; I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an10.59:1: “Therefore, monks, you should train thus: ‘Our mind will be practiced in accordance with the going forth; arisen unwholesome states will not take hold of our mind; our mind will be practiced in the perception of impermanence, practiced in the perception of not-self, practiced in the perception of foulness, practiced in the perception of danger, practiced in the perception of that perception after knowing the evenness and unevenness of the world, practiced in the perception of that perception after knowing the existence and non-existence of the world, practiced in the perception of that perception after knowing the origination and passing away of the world, practiced in the perception of abandoning, practiced in the perception of dispassion, practiced in the perception of cessation.’—Thus, monks, should you train.
translations.an10.60:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's park. At that time Venerable Girimānanda was sick, afflicted, and gravely ill. Then Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and bowed to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:
translations.an10.60:10: “And what, Ānanda, is the perception of cessation? Here, Ānanda, a monk gone to the forest or to the root of a tree or to an empty hut reflects thus: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, cessation, Nibbāna.’ This is called, Ānanda, the perception of cessation.
translations.an10.60:11: “And what, Ānanda, is the perception of non-delight in the whole world? Here, Ānanda, a monk lives having abandoned the underlying tendencies to clinging, mental standpoints, adherence, and latent tendencies in the world, without grasping. This is called, Ānanda, the perception of non-delight in the whole world.
translations.an10.60:12: “And what, Ānanda, is the perception of non-desire for all formations? Here, Ānanda, a monk is wearied, disgusted, and repelled by all formations. This is called, Ānanda, the perception of non-desire for all formations.
translations.an10.60:13: “And what, Ānanda, is mindfulness of breathing? Here, Ānanda, a monk gone to the forest or to the root of a tree or to an empty hut sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him, ever mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out. Breathing in long, he discerns, ‘I am breathing in long’; or breathing out long, he discerns, ‘I am breathing out long.’ Breathing in short, he discerns, ‘I am breathing in short’; or breathing out short, he discerns, ‘I am breathing out short.’ He trains thus, ‘I will breathe in experiencing the whole body’; he trains thus, ‘I will breathe out experiencing the whole body.’ He trains thus, ‘I will breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation’; he trains thus, ‘I will breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation.’ He trains thus, ‘I will breathe in experiencing rapture’; he trains thus, ‘I will breathe out experiencing rapture.’ He trains thus, ‘I will breathe in experiencing pleasure’; he trains thus, ‘I will breathe out experiencing pleasure.’ He trains thus, ‘I will breathe in experiencing mental formations’; he trains thus, ‘I will breathe out experiencing mental formations.’ He trains thus, ‘I will breathe in tranquilizing mental formations’; he trains thus, ‘I will breathe out tranquilizing mental formations.’ He trains thus, ‘I will breathe in experiencing the mind’; he trains thus, ‘I will breathe out experiencing the mind.’ Gladdening the mind… satisfying the mind… steadying the mind… releasing the mind… He trains thus, ‘I will breathe in contemplating impermanence’; he trains thus, ‘I will breathe out contemplating impermanence.’ He trains thus, ‘I will breathe in contemplating dispassion’; he trains thus, ‘I will breathe out contemplating dispassion.’ He trains thus, ‘I will breathe in contemplating cessation’; he trains thus, ‘I will breathe out contemplating cessation.’ He trains thus, ‘I will breathe in contemplating relinquishment’; he trains thus, ‘I will breathe out contemplating relinquishment.’ This is called, Ānanda, mindfulness of breathing.
translations.an10.60:14: “If you, Ānanda, were to teach these ten perceptions to the monk Girimānanda, there is a possibility that the monk Girimānanda, having heard these ten perceptions, his illness might subside right there.”
translations.an10.60:2: “Venerable sir, Venerable Girimānanda is sick, afflicted, and gravely ill. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would visit Venerable Girimānanda out of compassion.” “If you, Ānanda, were to teach ten perceptions to the monk Girimānanda, there is a possibility that the monk Girimānanda, having heard these ten perceptions, his illness might subside right there.
translations.an10.60:3: “What ten? The perception of impermanence, the perception of not-self, the perception of foulness, the perception of danger, the perception of abandoning, the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation, the perception of non-delight in the whole world, the perception of non-desire for all formations, and mindfulness of breathing.
translations.an10.60:4: “And what, Ānanda, is the perception of impermanence? Here, Ānanda, a monk gone to the forest or to the root of a tree or to an empty hut reflects thus: ‘Form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, mental formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent.’ Thus he dwells contemplating impermanence in these five aggregates subject to clinging. This is called, Ānanda, the perception of impermanence.
translations.an10.60:5: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of not-self? Here, Ānanda, a monk—gone to the wilderness or to the foot of a tree or to an empty dwelling—reflects thus: ‘The eye is not-self, forms are not-self, the ear is not-self, sounds are not-self, the nose is not-self, odors are not-self, the tongue is not-self, flavors are not-self, the body is not-self, touches are not-self, the mind is not-self, phenomena are not-self.’ Thus he dwells contemplating not-self in these six internal and external sense bases. This is called, Ānanda, the perception of not-self.
translations.an10.60:6: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of foulness? Here, Ānanda, a monk reflects on this very body from the soles of the feet up and from the crown of the head down, enclosed by skin and full of various impurities: ‘In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, membranes, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, snot, synovial fluid, urine.’ Thus he dwells contemplating foulness in this body. This is called, Ānanda, the perception of foulness.
translations.an10.60:7: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of danger? Here, Ānanda, a monk—gone to the wilderness or to the foot of a tree or to an empty dwelling—reflects thus: ‘This body is much afflicted and much exposed to danger. In this body various diseases arise, namely: eye disease, ear disease, nose disease, tongue disease, body disease, head disease, ear disease, mouth disease, tooth disease, cough, asthma, catarrh, fever, aging, stomach ailment, fainting, cholera, plague, tumors, leprosy, boils, eczema, itch, scabies, cracked skin, bleeding, diabetes, hemorrhoids, hernia, diseases arising from bile, diseases arising from phlegm, diseases arising from wind, diseases arising from their combination, changes due to climate, irregular behavior, injuries, and the result of kamma; cold, heat, hunger, thirst, defecation, and urination.’ Thus he dwells contemplating danger in this body. This is called, Ānanda, the perception of danger.
translations.an10.60:8: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of abandoning? Here, Ānanda, a monk does not tolerate a sensual thought that has arisen; he abandons it, dispels it, destroys it, and makes it non-existent. He does not tolerate a thought of ill will that has arisen; he abandons it, dispels it, destroys it, and makes it non-existent. He does not tolerate a thought of cruelty that has arisen; he abandons it, dispels it, destroys it, and makes it non-existent. He does not tolerate evil unwholesome states that have arisen; he abandons them, dispels them, destroys them, and makes them non-existent. This is called, Ānanda, the perception of abandoning.
translations.an10.61:1: “Monks, an earlier point of ignorance cannot be discerned such that: ‘Before this, ignorance did not exist, and afterwards it came into being.’ But it can be discerned that: ‘With this as condition, ignorance exists.’
translations.an10.61:2: I say, monks, that ignorance has a nutriment, not that it is without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for ignorance? It should be said: ‘The five hindrances.’ I say, monks, that the five hindrances have a nutriment, not that they are without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the five hindrances? It should be said: ‘The three kinds of misconduct.’ I say, monks, that the three kinds of misconduct have a nutriment, not that they are without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the three kinds of misconduct? It should be said: ‘Lack of restraint of the faculties.’ I say, monks, that lack of restraint of the faculties has a nutriment, not that it is without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for lack of restraint of the faculties? It should be said: ‘Lack of mindfulness and full awareness.’ I say, monks, that lack of mindfulness and full awareness has a nutriment, not that it is without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for lack of mindfulness and full awareness? It should be said: ‘Unwise attention.’ I say, monks, that unwise attention has a nutriment, not that it is without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for unwise attention? It should be said: ‘Lack of faith.’ I say, monks, that lack of faith has a nutriment, not that it is without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for lack of faith? It should be said: ‘Listening to the wrong teaching.’ I say, monks, that listening to the wrong teaching has a nutriment, not that it is without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for listening to the wrong teaching? It should be said: ‘Association with bad persons.’
translations.an10.61:3: Thus, monks, association with bad persons fulfills listening to the wrong teaching; listening to the wrong teaching fulfills lack of faith; lack of faith fulfills unwise attention; unwise attention fulfills lack of mindfulness and full awareness; lack of mindfulness and full awareness fulfills lack of restraint of the faculties; lack of restraint of the faculties fulfills the three kinds of misconduct; the three kinds of misconduct fulfill the five hindrances; the five hindrances fulfill ignorance; thus there is nutriment for this ignorance, and thus it is fulfilled.
translations.an10.61:4: Suppose, monks, there is a mountain slope with large boulders and clefts. When heavy rain falls, the water flows down the slope and fills the clefts and crevices of the mountain slope. The clefts and crevices being full fill the small streams. The small streams being full fill the large streams. The large streams being full fill the great rivers. The great rivers being full fill the great ocean, the sea. Thus there is nutriment for this great ocean, the sea, and thus it is fulfilled.
translations.an10.61:7: Thus, monks, association with good persons fulfills listening to the true teaching; listening to the true teaching fulfills faith; faith fulfills wise attention; wise attention fulfills mindfulness and full awareness; mindfulness and full awareness fulfill restraint of the faculties; restraint of the faculties fulfills the three kinds of good conduct; the three kinds of good conduct fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness; the four foundations of mindfulness fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment; the seven factors of enlightenment fulfill true knowledge and liberation; thus there is nutriment for this true knowledge and liberation, and thus it is fulfilled.
translations.an10.7:1: Then Venerable Ānanda approached Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Sāriputta. After exchanging courteous and friendly greetings, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Ānanda said to Venerable Sāriputta:
translations.an10.7:2: “Is it possible, friend Sāriputta, for a monk to attain such a concentration that he would not perceive earth as earth, nor water as water, nor fire as fire, nor air as air, nor the base of infinite space as the base of infinite space, nor the base of infinite consciousness as the base of infinite consciousness, nor the base of nothingness as the base of nothingness, nor the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor this world as this world, nor the other world as the other world; yet he would still be perceiving?”
translations.an10.7:4: “But how, friend Sāriputta, could it be possible for a monk to attain such a concentration that he would not perceive earth as earth … yet he would still be perceiving?” “Once, friend Ānanda, I was living right here in Sāvatthī in the Dark Forest. There I attained such a concentration that I did not perceive earth as earth, nor water as water, nor fire as fire, nor air as air, nor the base of infinite space as the base of infinite space, nor the base of infinite consciousness as the base of infinite consciousness, nor the base of nothingness as the base of nothingness, nor the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor this world as this world, nor the other world as the other world; yet I was still perceiving.”
translations.an3.10:1: “Possessed of three qualities, monks, a person, without abandoning three stains, is cast into hell just as a stone is cast into water. What three? They are immoral, and the stain of immorality is not abandoned in them; they are envious, and the stain of envy is not abandoned in them; they are stingy, and the stain of stinginess is not abandoned in them. Possessed of these three qualities, monks, a person, without abandoning these three stains, is cast into hell just as a stone is cast into water.
translations.an3.12:5: Furthermore, monks, in whatever region a monk understands suffering as it really is, the origin of suffering as it really is, the cessation of suffering as it really is, and the way leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is. This, monks, is the second refuge for a monk for life.
translations.an3.15:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. There the Buddha addressed the monks: “Monks.” “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Buddha. The Buddha said this:
translations.an3.15:2: “In the past, monks, there was a king named Sācetana. Then, monks, King Sācetana addressed a wheelwright: ‘My good wheelwright, in six months there will be a battle. Can you, my good wheelwright, make me a new pair of wheels?’ ‘I can, your majesty,’ the wheelwright replied to King Sācetana. Then, monks, the wheelwright finished one wheel in six months and four years. Then, monks, King Sācetana addressed the wheelwright: ‘My good wheelwright, in six days there will be a battle. Is the new pair of wheels finished?’ ‘By these six months and four years, your majesty, one wheel is finished.’ ‘But can you, my good wheelwright, finish the second wheel in these six days?’ ‘I can, your majesty.’ Then, monks, the wheelwright finished the second wheel in six days, and taking the new pair of wheels approached King Sācetana; approaching, he said to King Sācetana: ‘Your new pair of wheels is finished, your majesty.’ ‘As for this wheel of yours, my good wheelwright, finished in six months and four years, and this wheel finished in six days, what is the difference between them? I see no difference between them.’ ‘There is a difference, your majesty. Let your majesty see the difference.’
translations.an3.15:3: Then, monks, the wheelwright set the wheel that was finished in six days spinning. Spinning, it went as far as the range of its construction, then wobbling it fell to the ground. But he set the wheel that was finished in six months and four years spinning. Spinning, it went as far as the range of its construction, and I think it stayed steady.
translations.an3.15:5: Perhaps you think, monks: ‘That wheelwright at that time must have been someone else.’ It should not be seen thus, monks. I was that wheelwright at that time. At that time, monks, I was skilled in the cracks of wood, the defects of wood, and the joints of wood. But now, monks, I am an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One, skilled in the cracks of body, the defects of body, and the joints of body, skilled in the cracks of speech, the defects of speech, and the joints of speech, skilled in the cracks of mind, the defects of mind, and the joints of mind. Of whatever monk or nun, monks, the crack of body is not abandoned, the defect of body, the joint of body; the crack of speech is not abandoned, the defect of speech, the joint of speech; the crack of mind is not abandoned, the defect of mind, the joint of mind; they, monks, fall from this Dhamma and Vinaya, just like that wheel finished in six days.
translations.an3.15:6: Of whatever monk or nun, monks, the crack of body is abandoned, the defect of body, the joint of body; the crack of speech is abandoned, the defect of speech, the joint of speech; the crack of mind is abandoned, the defect of mind, the joint of mind; they, monks, stand firm in this Dhamma and Vinaya, just like that wheel finished in six months and four years.
translations.an3.1:3: Thus, monks, the fool is full of danger, the wise is free from danger. The fool is full of calamity, the wise is free from calamity. The fool is full of peril, the wise is free from peril. There is no danger for the wise, monks, no calamity for the wise, no peril for the wise.
translations.an3.20:1: “Possessed of three factors, mendicants, a merchant soon attains greatness and growth in wealth. What three? Here, mendicants, a merchant is far-sighted, capable, and has resources. And how, mendicants, is a merchant far-sighted? Here, mendicants, a merchant knows merchandise: ‘This merchandise is made like this, sells like this, the capital will be this much, the profit will be this much.’ In this way, mendicants, a merchant is far-sighted.
translations.an3.20:2: And how, mendicants, is a merchant capable? Here, mendicants, a merchant is skilled in buying and selling merchandise. In this way, mendicants, a merchant is capable.
translations.an3.20:3: And how, mendicants, is a merchant one who has resources? Here, mendicants, those householders or householders’ sons who are wealthy and with great riches know of him: ‘This merchant is far-sighted and capable, able to support wife and children, and to give to us from time to time.’ They pour wealth upon him: ‘Here, good merchant, having made wealth, support wife and children, and give to us from time to time.’ In this way, mendicants, a merchant is one who has resources. Possessed of these three factors, mendicants, a merchant soon attains greatness and growth in wealth.
translations.an3.20:4: So too, mendicants, possessed of three qualities, a monk soon attains greatness and growth in skillful qualities. What three? Here, mendicants, a monk is far-sighted, capable, and has resources. And how, mendicants, is a monk far-sighted? Here, mendicants, a monk understands as it actually is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.’ In this way, mendicants, a monk is far-sighted.
translations.an3.20:5: And how, mendicants, is a monk capable? Here, mendicants, a monk dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unskillful qualities, for the attainment of skillful qualities, steadfast, firm in effort, not neglecting the practice of skillful qualities. In this way, mendicants, a monk is capable.
translations.an3.22:1: “There are these three types of sick people found in the world. What three? Here, mendicants, a certain sick person, whether getting suitable food or not getting suitable food, whether getting suitable medicine or not getting suitable medicine, whether getting a suitable attendant or not getting a suitable attendant, does not recover from that illness.
translations.an3.22:3: Here, however, mendicants, a certain sick person, getting suitable food and not not getting it, getting suitable medicine and not not getting it, getting a suitable attendant and not not getting it, recovers from that illness.
translations.an3.22:4: Whereas, mendicants, that sick person who, getting suitable food and not not getting it, getting suitable medicine and not not getting it, getting a suitable attendant and not not getting it, recovers from that illness—because of that sick person, the sick-person’s allowance is allowed, the sick-person’s medicine is allowed, the sick-person’s attendant is allowed. And because of that sick person, other sick people should also be attended to. These are the three types of sick people found in the world.
translations.an3.22:5: So too, mendicants, there are these three types of people found in the world who are like the sick. What three? Here, mendicants, a certain person, whether getting to see the Tathāgata or not getting to see the Tathāgata, whether getting to hear the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata or not getting to hear the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, does not enter the sure course with regard to skillful qualities, rightness.
translations.an3.22:6: Here, however, mendicants, a certain person, whether getting to see the Tathāgata or not getting to see the Tathāgata, whether getting to hear the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata or not getting to hear the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, enters the sure course with regard to skillful qualities, rightness.
translations.an3.24:1: “There are these three types of people who are of great service to a person. What three? The person, mendicants, depending on whom a person goes for refuge to the Buddha, goes for refuge to the Dhamma, goes for refuge to the Saṅgha; this person, mendicants, is of great service to that person.
translations.an3.24:2: Again, mendicants, the person depending on whom a person understands as it actually is: ‘This is suffering’; understands as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; understands as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; understands as it actually is: ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’; this person, mendicants, is of great service to that person.
translations.an3.24:3: Again, mendicants, the person depending on whom a person, with the destruction of the taints, realizes in this very life the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, dwells in it; this person, mendicants, is of great service to that person. These are the three types of people who are of great service to a person.
translations.an3.2:1: “A fool, mendicants, is marked by his deeds, a wise person is marked by his deeds, and wisdom is adorned by conduct. A fool possessed of three qualities should be known. What three? By bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. A fool possessed of these three qualities should be known.
translations.an3.2:2: A wise person possessed of three qualities should be known. What three? By bodily good conduct, verbal good conduct, and mental good conduct. A wise person possessed of these three qualities should be known.
translations.an3.30:4: A man with inverted wisdom, a fool, unperceptive; Even if he goes often to the presence of monks.
translations.an3.30:5: At the beginning of the talk, in the middle, and at the end he is the same; He is not able to learn, for wisdom is not found in him.
translations.an3.30:6: A man with high wisdom, he is called better than this; Even if he goes often to the presence of monks.
translations.an3.30:8: A man of extensive wisdom, he is called better than these; Even if he goes often to the presence of monks.
translations.an3.32:4: “Here, Ānanda, a monk has this thought: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime—that is, the stilling of all fabrications, the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the ending of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.’ It is possible, Ānanda, that a monk might attain such a state of concentration that in this very conscious body there would be no underlying tendency to conceit ‘I am,’ and externally regarding all signs there would be no underlying tendency to conceit ‘I am’; and that he would attain and dwell in that deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom where there is no underlying tendency to conceit ‘I am.’
translations.an3.33:1: Then Venerable Sāriputta approached the Buddha, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and the Buddha said to him: “Sāriputta, I could teach the Dhamma in brief; I could teach the Dhamma in detail; I could teach the Dhamma both in brief and in detail; but there are few who understand it.” “Now is the time, Blessed One, now is the time, Sugata, for the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma in brief, in detail, or both in brief and in detail. There will be those who understand the Dhamma.”
translations.an3.33:2: “Therefore, Sāriputta, you should train yourselves thus: ‘In this very conscious body there will be no underlying tendency to conceit ‘I am,’ and externally regarding all signs there will be no underlying tendency to conceit ‘I am,’ and I will attain and dwell in that deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom where there is no underlying tendency to conceit ‘I am.’ Thus, Sāriputta, should you train.
translations.an3.33:3: When, Sāriputta, a monk has no underlying tendency to conceit ‘I am’ in this very conscious body, and externally regarding all signs there is no underlying tendency to conceit ‘I am,’ and he attains and dwells in that deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom where there is no underlying tendency to conceit ‘I am’; this is called, Sāriputta: ‘A monk has cut off craving, broken the fetter, and by realizing conceit made an end of suffering.’ And it was with reference to this that I spoke in the ‘Questions of the Rising’ in the Parāyana:
translations.an3.33:4: ‘The abandoning of perceptions of sensual desire, and of both kinds of bad moods; the removal of dullness and drowsiness, and the blocking of restlessness and remorse.
translations.an3.34:1: “There are, monks, three origins for the arising of actions. What three? Greed is an origin for the arising of actions, hate is an origin for the arising of actions, delusion is an origin for the arising of actions.
translations.an3.34:10: Any action, monks, originated from non-delusion, born of non-delusion, caused by non-delusion, arising from non-delusion—with the vanishing of delusion that action is abandoned, its root destroyed, made like a palm stump, deprived of conditions, not destined for future arising.
translations.an3.34:11: Suppose, monks, there were seeds that were whole and undamaged, not spoiled by wind or heat, fertile, and well-buried. A man would burn them with fire. Having burned them with fire, he would reduce them to ashes. Having reduced them to ashes, he would winnow them away in a strong wind or float them away in a swift-flowing river. Those seeds, monks, would thus be destroyed at the root, made like a palm stump, deprived of conditions, not destined for future arising. So too, monks, any action originated from non-greed, born of non-greed, caused by non-greed, arising from non-greed—with the vanishing of greed that action is abandoned, its root destroyed, made like a palm stump, deprived of conditions, not destined for future arising.
translations.an3.34:13: Born of greed and born of hate, and born of delusion as well; whatever action was done by that, whether little or much; that is experienced right here, there is no other ground.
translations.an3.34:2: Any action, monks, originated from greed, born of greed, caused by greed, arising from greed—wherever that individual is reborn, that action ripens there. Wherever that action ripens, there he experiences its fruit, either in this very life, or in the next life, or in some subsequent existence.
translations.an3.34:5: Suppose, monks, there were seeds that were whole and undamaged, not spoiled by wind or heat, fertile, and well-buried in good soil. The rain god would provide rain in due season. Those seeds, monks, would thus grow, increase, and flourish. So too, monks, any action originated from greed, born of greed, caused by greed, arising from greed—wherever that individual is reborn, that action ripens there. Wherever that action ripens, there he experiences its fruit, either in this very life, or in the next life, or in some subsequent existence.
translations.an3.34:6: Any action originated from hate … any action originated from delusion, born of delusion, caused by delusion, arising from delusion—wherever that individual is reborn, that action ripens there. Wherever that action ripens, there he experiences its fruit, either in this very life, or in the next life, or in some subsequent existence. These, monks, are the three origins for the arising of actions.
translations.an3.34:9: Any action, monks, originated from non-hate, born of non-hate, caused by non-hate, arising from non-hate—with the vanishing of hate that action is abandoned, its root destroyed, made like a palm stump, deprived of conditions, not destined for future arising.
translations.an3.35:3: “In that case, young man, I will question you about just this. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, young man? Here a householder or householder’s son has a multi-storied building plastered inside and out, draft-proof, with fastened shutters and shut windows. There is a couch spread with a long fleece cover, a white canopy, red cushions at both ends, and an oil lamp burning there. Four wives are present, charming and delightful. What do you think, young man? Would he sleep happily or not? How does it seem to you?” “He would sleep happily, sir. Of all who sleep happily in the world, he would be one of them.”
translations.an3.35:4: “What do you think, young man, would any fever born of lust, physical or mental, arise in that householder or his son’s son, by which, overwhelmed by fever born of lust, he would lie in misery?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.an3.35:8: Always the brahmin who is fully extinguished sleeps happily; He who does not cling to sensual pleasures, cooled, without attachments.
translations.an3.39:10: So I, dwelling in this way, having known the state without attachments; In health, youth, and life, whatever pride there was.
translations.an3.39:2: For me, monks, there were three palaces—one for the winter, one for the summer, and one for the rainy season. And I, monks, during the four months of the rainy season, dwelling in the rainy-season palace, waited on by female musicians, did not descend from the upper palace. But just as, monks, in the dwellings of others, coarse food mixed with bran is given to slaves, workmen, and servants, so in my father’s dwelling, fine rice and meat were given to slaves, workmen, and servants.
translations.an3.39:3: For me, monks, possessed of such power and such subtlety, it occurred to me: ‘An uneducated ordinary person, subject to old age himself, not having gone beyond old age, seeing another who is aged, feels disgust, loathing, and contempt, having surpassed himself. I too am subject to old age, not having gone beyond old age. If I, subject to old age, not having gone beyond old age, seeing another who is aged, were to feel disgust, loathing, and contempt, that would not be fitting for me.’ For me, monks, reflecting thus, whatever pride in youth there was, that was entirely abandoned.
translations.an3.39:4: An uneducated ordinary person, subject to illness himself, not having gone beyond illness, seeing another who is ill, feels disgust, loathing, and contempt, having surpassed himself: ‘I too am subject to illness, not having gone beyond illness. If I, subject to illness, not having gone beyond illness, seeing another who is ill, were to feel disgust, loathing, and contempt, that would not be fitting for me.’ For me, monks, reflecting thus, whatever pride in health there was, that was entirely abandoned.
translations.an3.39:5: An uneducated ordinary person, subject to death himself, not having gone beyond death, seeing another who is dead, feels disgust, loathing, and contempt, having surpassed himself: ‘I too am subject to death, not having gone beyond death. If I, subject to death, not having gone beyond death, seeing another who is dead, were to feel disgust, loathing, and contempt, that would not be fitting for me.’ For me, monks, reflecting thus, whatever pride in life there was, that was entirely abandoned.
translations.an3.39:7: A monk, monks, obsessed with pride in youth, abandoning the training, reverts to what is inferior. A monk, monks, obsessed with pride in health … A monk, monks, obsessed with pride in life, abandoning the training, reverts to what is inferior.
translations.an3.39:8: Subject to illness, subject to old age, and also subject to death; Ordinary people feel disgust, being in such a state and existing thus.
translations.an3.39:9: If I were to feel disgust, at beings in such a state; That would not be fitting for me, living in this way.
translations.an3.40:1: “There are, monks, three grounds of supremacy. What three? Self as supremacy, the world as supremacy, and the Dhamma as supremacy. And what, monks, is self as supremacy? Here, monks, a monk gone to the forest or to the root of a tree or to an empty dwelling reflects thus: ‘I have not gone forth from the home life into homelessness for the sake of robes. Not for the sake of almsfood, nor for the sake of a lodging, nor for the sake of this or that state of becoming. But I am entangled by birth, aging, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair; I am afflicted by suffering, overcome by suffering. Surely an end to this whole mass of suffering might be known. If I, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness by giving up such-and-such sensual pleasures, were to seek such-and-such sensual pleasures, that would be even more disgraceful; that would not be fitting for me.’ So he reflects: ‘My energy will be aroused, not lax; mindfulness will be established, not confused; my body will be calm, not agitated; my mind will be concentrated, one-pointed.’ Making himself the supreme, he abandons unwholesome qualities, cultivates wholesome qualities, abandons qualities with blame, cultivates qualities without blame, and looks after himself with purity. This is called, monks, self as supremacy.
translations.an3.40:3: And what, monks, is the Dhamma as supremacy? Here, monks, a monk gone to the forest or to the root of a tree or to an empty dwelling reflects thus: ‘I have not gone forth from the home life into homelessness for the sake of robes. Not for the sake of almsfood, nor for the sake of a lodging, nor for the sake of this or that state of becoming. But I am entangled by birth, aging, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair; I am afflicted by suffering, overcome by suffering. Surely an end to this whole mass of suffering might be known. The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be known by the wise for themselves. And there are my fellow monks who are dwelling knowing and seeing. If I, having gone forth in this well-expounded Dhamma and discipline, were to dwell lazy and negligent, that would not be fitting for me.’ So he reflects: ‘My energy will be aroused, not lax; mindfulness will be established, not confused; my body will be calm, not agitated; my mind will be concentrated, one-pointed.’ Making the Dhamma the supreme, he abandons unwholesome qualities, cultivates wholesome qualities, abandons qualities with blame, cultivates qualities without blame, and looks after himself with purity. This is called, monks, the Dhamma as supremacy. These are, monks, the three grounds of supremacy.
translations.an3.40:4: There is no secret in the world, for one doing bad deeds; The self knows you, man, whether true or false.
translations.an3.40:5: Good indeed, sir, is the witness, you have despised yourself; You who have evil in yourself, you conceal yourself.
translations.an3.40:6: Devas and Tathāgatas see, a fool walking unevenly in the world; Therefore, one who is self-supreme, and prudent, a meditator, and world-supreme; Dhamma-supreme and one who lives according to the Dhamma, The sage striving for truth does not decline.
translations.an3.48:1: “Great trees, mendicants, grow with three kinds of growth relying on the Himālaya, the king of mountains. What three? They grow with branches, leaves, and foliage; they grow with bark and inner bark; they grow with sapwood and heartwood. Great trees, mendicants, grow with these three kinds of growth relying on the Himālaya, the king of mountains.
translations.an3.48:2: In the same way, mendicants, the people inside grow with three kinds of growth relying on a faithful layperson. What three? They grow with faith, they grow with ethics, they grow with wisdom. The people inside, mendicants, grow with these three kinds of growth relying on a faithful layperson.
translations.an3.48:3: Like a rocky mountain, in a wilderness forest; the trees growing there rely on it.
translations.an3.51:1: Then two brahmins who were old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, one hundred and twenty years old, approached the Buddha. After exchanging greetings with the Buddha, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those brahmins said to the Buddha: “We, Master Gotama, are brahmins who are old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, one hundred and twenty years old; and we have not done what is good, wholesome, or a refuge. Advise us, Master Gotama, instruct us, Master Gotama, for what will be for our long-term welfare and happiness.”
translations.an3.51:2: “Certainly, brahmins, you are old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, one hundred and twenty years old; and you have not done what is good, wholesome, or a refuge. This world, brahmins, is overcome by old age, sickness, and death. When the world is so overcome by old age, sickness, and death, whoever here has restraint of body, restraint of speech, and restraint of mind—that is a shelter, a cave, a refuge, and support for that person.”
translations.an3.51:3: Life is swept away, limited by old age; for one overcome by old age there are no shelters. Seeing this danger in death, do meritorious deeds that bring happiness.
translations.an3.57:2: “Those who said, ‘The ascetic Gotama says: “A gift should be given to me … and not to the disciples of others, for a gift given to them has great fruit”’—they do not report my words correctly. They misrepresent me with what is false and untrue. Whoever, Vaccha, discourages others from giving a gift creates an obstacle for three, a hindrance for three. Which three? They create an obstacle to the merit of the giver, an obstacle to the gain of the recipients, and previously their own self has been struck and injured. Whoever, Vaccha, discourages others from giving a gift creates an obstacle for these three, a hindrance for these three.
translations.an3.5:1: “A fool, mendicants, should be known by three qualities. What three? They ask a question improperly, they answer a question improperly, and when another has answered a question properly, they do not approve of it with roundabout expressions, obscure words, and derived terms. A fool, mendicants, should be known by these three qualities.
translations.an3.60:1: Then the brahmin Saṅgārava approached the Buddha. After exchanging greetings with the Buddha, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the brahmin Saṅgārava said to the Buddha: “We, Master Gotama, are brahmins. We perform sacrifices and cause others to perform sacrifices. In that, Master Gotama, whoever performs a sacrifice or causes others to perform a sacrifice—all of them practice a path of merit involving many bodies, that is, the basis of the sacrifice. But whoever, Master Gotama, has gone forth from the home life into homelessness in someone’s family, tames himself, calms himself, and extinguishes himself—that person practices a path of merit involving one body, that is, the basis of going forth.”
translations.an3.60:10: Herein, brahmin, some person does not recollect based on a sign, but recollects having heard the sound of humans or non-humans or deities: ‘Your mind is thus, your mind is thus, your mind is thus.’ Even if they recollect much, it is just so, not otherwise.
translations.an3.60:11: Herein, brahmin, some person does not recollect based on a sign, nor recollects having heard the sound of humans or non-humans or deities, but recollects having heard the sound of thought-occurrence while thinking and examining: ‘Your mind is thus, your mind is thus, your mind is thus.’ Even if they recollect much, it is just so, not otherwise.
translations.an3.60:12: Herein, brahmin, some person does not recollect based on a sign, nor recollects having heard the sound of humans or non-humans or deities, nor recollects having heard the sound of thought-occurrence while thinking and examining, but, having entered into non-thinking and non-examining concentration, understands with their mind the mind of another: ‘Just as these mental formations of this person are inclined, immediately after this mind-state they will think such a thought.’ Even if they recollect much, it is just so, not otherwise. This is called the miracle of recollection.
translations.an3.60:13: And what, brahmin, is the miracle of instruction? Herein, brahmin, some person instructs thus: ‘Think in this way, do not think in this way; pay attention in this way, do not pay attention in this way; abandon this, enter upon and dwell in this.’ This is called the miracle of instruction. These, brahmin, are the three miracles. Of these three miracles, brahmin, which miracle pleases you, which is more excellent and sublime?”
translations.an3.60:14: “Therein, Master Gotama, regarding the miracle of psychic power … even up to the Brahmā world, he wields power with the body—this miracle, Master Gotama, whoever makes it, only they experience it; whoever makes it, it belongs only to them. This miracle of yours, Master Gotama, seems like an illusion or a magical trick.
translations.an3.52:4: Thus is the world ablaze, with old age and death; Like a reed cut down, what is given is well-removed.
translations.an3.60:16: And as for this miracle, Master Gotama, that someone instructs thus: 'Think in this way, do not think in that way; pay attention in this way, do not pay attention in that way; abandon this, dwell having attained this.' This miracle alone, Master Gotama, is pleasing to me, more excellent and sublime than these three miracles.
translations.an3.60:17: It is wonderful, Master Gotama, it is marvelous, Master Gotama. How well-spoken is this by Master Gotama, that we, being endowed with these three miracles, will rely on Master Gotama. For Master Gotama experiences manifold kinds of superhuman power ... even up to the world of Brahmā he wields power with his body. For Master Gotama, with his mind concentrated and free from applied and sustained thought, understands the mind of another: 'Thus are the mental formations of this good person directed, immediately after this thought he will apply his mind to that thought.' For Master Gotama instructs thus: 'Think in this way, do not think in that way; pay attention in this way, do not pay attention in that way; abandon this, dwell having attained this.'
translations.an3.60:18: Indeed, brahmin, I have spoken to you after drawing near and addressing you; but I will explain it to you. For I, brahmin, experience manifold kinds of superhuman power ... even up to the world of Brahmā I wield power with my body. For I, brahmin, with my mind concentrated and free from applied and sustained thought, understand the mind of another: 'Thus are the mental formations of this good person directed, immediately after this thought he will apply his mind to that thought.' For I, brahmin, instruct thus: 'Think in this way, do not think in that way; pay attention in this way, do not pay attention in that way; abandon this, dwell having attained this.'
translations.an3.60:19: But is there, Master Gotama, even a single monk other than Master Gotama who is endowed with these three miracles? There is not, brahmin, only one hundred, nor two hundred, nor three hundred, nor four hundred, nor five hundred, but rather more, the monks who are endowed with these three miracles. But where, Master Gotama, are those monks dwelling now? In this very Sangha of monks, brahmin.
translations.an3.60:2: Then, brahmin, I will ask you a question about this. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, brahmin, here a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, a Sublime One, knower of worlds, incomparable trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One. He says thus: 'This is the path, this is the practice, that having practiced it I realized the unexcelled goal of the holy life by my own direct knowledge and proclaimed it; come, you also practice in this way, that having practiced it you too, realizing the unexcelled goal of the holy life by your own direct knowledge, will dwell having attained it.' In this way the Teacher teaches the Dhamma, and others practice for that goal, and there are many hundreds, many thousands, many hundreds of thousands.
translations.an3.60:3: What do you think, brahmin, when this is the case, is the practice of meritfulness for one person or for many persons, that is, the going forth? In this case, Master Gotama, when this is the case, the practice of meritfulness is for many persons, that is, the going forth.
translations.an3.60:4: When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the brahmin Saṅgārava: Of these two practices of yours, brahmin, which practice is pleasing to you, requiring less effort, less striving, bearing great fruit, great benefit? When this was said, the brahmin Saṅgārava said to the Venerable Ānanda: Just as Master Gotama, so too Master Ānanda. These are my objects of respect, these are my objects of praise.
translations.an3.60:5: For a second time the Venerable Ānanda said to the brahmin Saṅgārava: I am not asking you, brahmin, in this way: 'What are your objects of respect, what are your objects of praise?' But I am asking you, brahmin, in this way: 'Of these two practices of yours, brahmin, which practice is pleasing to you, requiring less effort, less striving, bearing great fruit, great benefit?' For a second time the brahmin Saṅgārava said to the Venerable Ānanda: Just as Master Gotama, so too Master Ānanda. These are my objects of respect, these are my objects of praise.
translations.an3.60:7: Then it occurred to the Blessed One: For a third time the brahmin Saṅgārava, asked a question by Ānanda in accordance with the Dhamma, is hesitating and not answering. Why should I not release him? Then the Blessed One said to the brahmin Saṅgārava: What was the conversation, brahmin, that arose among the king's men sitting together in the royal palace? This was the conversation, Master Gotama, that arose among the king's men sitting together in the royal palace: 'Formerly there were fewer monks and more who displayed superhuman powers; now there are more monks and fewer who will display superhuman powers.' This was the conversation, Master Gotama, that arose among the king's men sitting together in the royal palace.
translations.an3.60:8: There are these three miracles, brahmin. What three? The miracle of psychic power, the miracle of telepathy, the miracle of instruction. And what is the miracle of psychic power, brahmin?
