Here, brahmin, a certain one experiences manifold kinds of superhuman power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain as if through space; he dives in and out of the earth as if in water; he walks on water without sinking as if on earth; sitting cross-legged he flies through the air like a winged bird; with his hand he touches and strokes the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; he exercises mastery with his body even as far as the world of Brahmā. This is called the miracle of psychic power, brahmin.
translations.an3.60:9: And what, brahmin, is the miracle of declaration? Here, brahmin, someone declares by a sign: 'Your mind is like this, your mind is like this, your mind is like this.' Even though they declare much, it is just so, not otherwise.
translations.an3.61:13: Monks, I have taught the four noble truths—ungrasped, unstained, without reproach, not criticized by ascetics and brahmins, wise men. Thus has it been said. And for what reason was this said? Dependent on the six elements, monks, there occurs the descent into the womb. With the occurrence of descent, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling. While feeling, monks, I proclaim this is suffering, I proclaim this is the origin of suffering, I proclaim this is the cessation of suffering, I proclaim this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.an3.61:14: And what, monks, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, (...) death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair are suffering; association with the disliked is suffering, separation from the liked is suffering, not getting what one wants is suffering. In short, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering. This, monks, is called the noble truth of suffering.
translations.an3.61:15: And what, monks, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? With ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, becoming; with becoming as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
translations.an3.61:16: And what, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? With the fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, the cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, the cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, the cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, the cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, the cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, the cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, the cessation of becoming; with the cessation of becoming, the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease. Thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
translations.an3.61:3: But, monks, when going back to what was done before, there is no desire or effort: 'This should be done, this should not be done.' And since what should be done and what should not be done is not found in reality and truth, while living with unguarded mindfulness, there is no personal, genuine teaching of an ascetic. This, monks, is my first genuine refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who hold such views and see in such a way.
translations.an3.61:8: Monks, there are these three realms of speculation which, when examined, investigated, and discussed by the wise, even after going to the far side, result in inaction.
translations.an3.61:9: Monks, I have taught the Dhamma—ungrasped, unstained, without reproach, not criticized by ascetics and brahmins, wise men. And what, monks, is the Dhamma I have taught—ungrasped, unstained, without reproach, not criticized by ascetics and brahmins, wise men? 'These six elements,' monks, is the Dhamma I have taught—ungrasped, unstained, without reproach, not criticized by ascetics and brahmins, wise men. 'These six contact bases,' monks, is the Dhamma I have taught—ungrasped, unstained, without reproach, not criticized by ascetics and brahmins, wise men. 'These eighteen mental volitions,' monks, is the Dhamma I have taught—ungrasped, unstained, without reproach, not criticized by ascetics and brahmins, wise men. 'These four noble truths,' monks, is the Dhamma I have taught—ungrasped, unstained, without reproach, not criticized by ascetics and brahmins, wise men.
translations.an3.62:1: Monks, an uninformed ordinary person speaks of three terrors involving mother and child. What three? There comes a time, monks, when a great fire blazes up. When a great fire blazes up, monks, villages burn, towns burn, cities burn. While villages are burning, towns are burning, cities are burning, there the mother does not find the child, nor the child the mother. This, monks, is the first terror involving mother and child that an uninformed ordinary person speaks of.
translations.an3.62:2: Again, monks, there comes a time when a great storm arises. When a great storm arises, monks, a great flood of water arises. When a great flood of water arises, monks, villages are swept away, towns are swept away, cities are swept away. While villages are being swept away, towns are being swept away, cities are being swept away, there the mother does not find the child, nor the child the mother. This, monks, is the second terror involving mother and child that an uninformed ordinary person speaks of.
translations.an3.62:3: Again, monks, there comes a time when there is terror, a disturbance in the wilderness, and districts are raided by bandits. When there is terror, monks, a disturbance in the wilderness, and districts are being raided by bandits, there the mother does not find the child, nor the child the mother. This, monks, is the third terror involving mother and child that an uninformed ordinary person speaks of. Monks, an uninformed ordinary person speaks of these three terrors involving mother and child.
translations.an4.24:5: If I were to say, 'Monks, I know that and I do not know that,' it would be a falsehood for me.
translations.an4.24:7: Thus, monks, the Tathāgata, having seen, sees what is to be seen; he does not misconstrue what is seen, nor what is not seen, nor what is to be seen, nor the seer. Having heard, he hears what is to be heard; he does not misconstrue what is heard, nor what is not heard, nor what is to be heard, nor the hearer. Having sensed, he senses what is to be sensed; he does not misconstrue what is sensed, nor what is not sensed, nor what is to be sensed, nor the senser. Having known, he knows what is to be known; he does not misconstrue what is known, nor what is not known, nor what is to be known, nor the knower. Thus, monks, the Tathāgata is such with regard to phenomena that are seen, heard, sensed, and known. I say: 'There is no other such one more excellent or sublime than that such one.'
translations.an4.24:8: Whatever is seen, heard, or sensed,  And clung to as true by others;  Not among those self-controlled ones,  Would one speak truth or lie to another.
translations.an4.28:1: “Monks, there are four noble lineages—ancient, traditional, original, uncorrupted, uncorrupted from the beginning, not corrupted now, nor will they be corrupted; they are not objected to by wise ascetics and brahmins. What four? Here, monks, a monk is content with any kind of robe; he is a speaker of praise regarding contentment with any kind of robe, and he does not resort to unsuitable begging for the sake of robes. If he does not get a robe, he does not worry; if he gets a robe, he uses it without being attached, infatuated, or enslaved, perceiving the danger and possessing the wisdom of escape. And with that contentment with any kind of robe, he neither praises himself nor disparages others. Whoever is skilled, lazy-less, aware, and contemplative there is called, monks, a monk standing in the ancient original noble lineage.
translations.an4.28:4: Furthermore, monks, a monk is devoted to development, delighting in development, devoted to abandoning, delighting in abandoning; and with that devotion to development and delight in development, devotion to abandoning and delight in abandoning, he neither praises himself nor disparages others. Whoever is skilled, lazy-less, aware, and contemplative there is called, monks, a monk standing in the ancient original noble lineage. These, monks, are the four noble lineages—ancient, traditional, original, uncorrupted, uncorrupted from the beginning, not corrupted now, nor will they be corrupted; they are not objected to by wise ascetics and brahmins.
translations.an4.28:5: And, monks, a monk endowed with these four noble lineages, even if he dwells in the eastern direction, he endures only his own dissatisfaction, not that dissatisfaction endures him; even if he dwells in the western direction, he endures only his own dissatisfaction, not that dissatisfaction endures him; even if he dwells in the northern direction, he endures only his own dissatisfaction, not that dissatisfaction endures him; even if he dwells in the southern direction, he endures only his own dissatisfaction, not that dissatisfaction endures him. For what reason? Because the wise one, monks, endures dissatisfaction.
translations.an4.28:6: Dissatisfaction does not endure the wise one,  nor does the wise one endure dissatisfaction;  The wise one endures dissatisfaction,  for the wise one is one who endures dissatisfaction.
translations.an4.31:1: “Monks, there are four wheels, possessed of which the four-wheel turns for gods and humans, and possessed of which gods and humans soon attain greatness and expansion in wealth. What four? Suitable region, association with good people, self-righteous resolve, and past merit done— These, monks, are the four wheels, possessed of which the four-wheel turns for gods and humans, and possessed of which gods and humans soon attain greatness and expansion in wealth.
translations.an4.32:1: “Monks, there are four bases of sympathy. What four? Giving, kind speech, beneficial action, impartiality— These, monks, are the four bases of sympathy.
translations.an4.32:2: Giving and kind speech,  and beneficial action here;  Impartiality in the Dhamma,  here and there as appropriate;  These are the sympathies in the world,  like the linchpin of a chariot.
translations.an4.32:3: If these sympathies were not,  mothers would not do for children,  Nor would fathers for children,  obtain honor or respect.
translations.an4.33:1: “Monks, the lion, king of beasts, in the evening leaves his lair. Having left his lair, he stretches himself. Having stretched himself, he looks around in all four directions. Having looked around in all four directions, he utters his lion's roar three times. Having uttered his lion's roar three times, he goes to his feeding ground. Those animals, monks, who are of the animal kingdom and hear the sound of the lion, king of beasts, roaring, mostly fall into fear, dread, and terror. They enter a hole with a hole, water with water, forest with forest; those with wings take to the sky. Those royal elephants, monks, bound in villages, towns, and royal capitals with strong bonds and fetters, also break those bonds, scattering them, and fleeing in fear, voiding urine and excrement, wherever they go. Thus powerful, monks, is the lion, king of beasts, among animals of the animal kingdom, thus mighty, thus influential.
translations.an4.33:2: So too, monks, when a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, Fully Enlightened One, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed, he teaches the Dhamma:  'This is identity, this is the origin of identity, this is the cessation of identity, this is the way leading to the cessation of identity.' Those gods, monks, who are long-lived, beautiful, abundant in happiness, dwelling in high palaces for a long time, hearing the Dhamma teaching of the Tathāgata, mostly fall into fear, dread, and terror:  'It seems we are impermanent, though we thought ourselves permanent; it seems we are impermanent, though we thought ourselves permanent; it seems we are non-eternal, though we thought ourselves eternal. We, it seems, are impermanent, non-eternal, included in identity.' Thus powerful, monks, is the Tathāgata in the world with its gods, thus mighty, thus influential.
translations.an4.33:3: When the Buddha, having realized,  set rolling the Dhamma wheel,  For the world with its gods,  the teacher without equal.
translations.an4.33:4: The cessation of identity and  the arising of identity;  The noble eightfold path,  leading to the subsiding of suffering.
translations.an4.34:1: “There are these four kinds of supreme confidence, monks. What four? Insofar as there are beings—footless, two-footed, four-footed, many-footed; having form or formless; percipient or non-percipient or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient—the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, is declared to be the foremost among them. Those, monks, who have confidence in the Buddha have confidence in the foremost. And for those who have confidence in the foremost, the result is foremost.
translations.an4.34:2: Insofar as there are conditioned phenomena, the noble eightfold path is declared to be the foremost among them. Those, monks, who have confidence in the noble eightfold path have confidence in the foremost. And for those who have confidence in the foremost, the result is foremost.
translations.an4.34:3: Insofar as there are phenomena, conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared to be the foremost among them—that is, the subduing of intoxication, the destroying of thirst, the uprooting of attachment, the cutting off of the round, the extinction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. Those, monks, who have confidence in the Dhamma of dispassion have confidence in the foremost. And for those who have confidence in the foremost, the result is foremost.
translations.an4.34:4: Insofar as there are communities or groups, the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is declared to be the foremost among them—that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight kinds of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Those, monks, who have confidence in the Saṅgha have confidence in the foremost. And for those who have confidence in the foremost, the result is foremost. These, monks, are the four kinds of supreme confidence.
translations.an4.34:5: For those who are devoted to the supreme, knowing the supreme Dhamma; devoted to the Buddha, the unsurpassed worthy of offerings.
translations.an4.34:6: Devoted to the Dhamma, the happiness of dispassion and peace; devoted to the Saṅgha, the unsurpassed field of merit.
translations.an4.34:7: Giving a gift to the supreme, supreme merit grows; supreme life, complexion, honor, fame, happiness, and strength.
translations.an4.35:1: At one time the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground. Then Vassakāra the Brahmin, the chief minister of Magadha, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. After exchanging courteous and friendly talk, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Vassakāro the Brahmin, the chief minister of Magadha, said this to the Blessed One:
translations.an4.35:2: “We, Master Gotama, declare a great wise man to be endowed with four qualities. What four? Here, Master Gotama, he is learned; he knows the meaning of whatever teaching he has learned: ‘This is the meaning of this teaching, this is the meaning of that teaching.’ He is mindful, remembering and recalling what was done and said long ago. And he is skilled and diligent in the tasks of a householder, possessed of investigation into how to manage and carry them out. We, Master Gotama, declare a great wise man to be endowed with these four qualities. If it is fitting for me to approve, let Master Gotama approve; if it is fitting for me to criticize, let Master Gotama criticize.”
translations.an4.35:6: He who knows the release from the snare of death for all beings; the good for gods and humans, the true Dhamma he has explained; which, having seen and heard, many people delight in.
translations.an4.36:1: At one time the Blessed One was traveling along the road between Ukkaṭṭha and Setabya. Doṇa the Brahmin was also traveling along the road between Ukkaṭṭha and Setabya. Doṇa the Brahmin saw the wheel marks on the Blessed One’s feet: thousand-spoked, complete with rims and hubs, fully adorned in all details. Seeing them, it occurred to him: “It is wonderful, sir, it is marvelous, sir. These will not be the footprints of a human being.” Then the Blessed One left the road and sat at the root of a certain tree, having crossed his legs, held his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him. Then Doṇa the Brahmin, following the Blessed One’s footprints, saw the Blessed One sitting at the root of a certain tree—pleasing, inspiring, with subdued senses, with subdued mind, having attained the utmost control and tranquility, tamed, guarded, with controlled senses, a naga. Seeing him, he approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
translations.an4.36:2: “Will the sir be a god?” “I will not be a god, Brahmin.” “Will the sir be a Gandhabba?” “I will not be a Gandhabba, Brahmin.” “Will the sir be a Yakkha?” “I will not be a Yakkha, Brahmin.” “Will the sir be a human?” “I will not be a human, Brahmin.”
translations.an4.36:4: “If, Brahmin, I were to become a god because my taints were not fully destroyed, then my taints would be destroyed, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more in the future. If, Brahmin, I were to become a Gandhabba because my taints were not fully destroyed … a Yakkha … a human, then my taints would be destroyed, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more in the future. Just as, Brahmin, a blue lotus, or a pink lotus, or a white lotus, born in the water, grown in the water, rising above the water, stands unsoiled by the water; so too, I, born in the world, grown in the world, having overcome the world, dwell unsoiled by the world. Recognize me as a Buddha, Brahmin.”
translations.an4.37:1: “Endowed with four qualities, monks, a monk is incapable of decline, and is face to face with Nibbāna. What four? Here, monks, a monk is virtuous, he guards the sense doors, he is moderate in eating, he is devoted to wakefulness.
translations.an4.37:2: How is a monk endowed with virtue? Here, monks, a monk is virtuous, he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest fault, and undertaking the training rules. Thus, monks, a monk is endowed with virtue.
translations.an4.37:3: And how, monks, is a monk guarded at the sense doors? Here, monks, a monk, seeing a form with the eye, does not grasp at its signs or features. Since, if he left the eye faculty unguarded, evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might invade, he practices restraint; he guards the eye faculty; he undertakes the restraint of the eye faculty. Hearing a sound with the ear … Smelling a smell with the nose … Tasting a flavor with the tongue … Touching a tactile object with the body … Knowing a mental phenomenon with the mind, he does not grasp at its signs or features. Since, if he left the mind faculty unguarded, evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might invade, he practices restraint; he guards the mind faculty; he undertakes the restraint of the mind faculty. In this way, monks, a monk is guarded at the sense doors.
translations.an4.37:4: And how, monks, is a monk moderate in eating? Here, monks, a monk reflects carefully and eats food: ‘Not for amusement, not for intoxication, not for adornment, not for beautification; only for the maintenance and nourishment of this body, for keeping it unharmed, for supporting the holy life. Thus I will put an end to old feelings and not produce new feelings, and I will live blamelessly and at ease.’ In this way, monks, a monk is moderate in eating.
translations.an4.37:5: And how, monks, is a monk devoted to wakefulness? Here, monks, a monk during the day purifies his mind of obstructive states by walking and sitting; in the first part of the night he purifies his mind of obstructive states by walking and sitting; in the middle part of the night he lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture, with one foot on top of the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, after giving attention to the thought of rising; in the last part of the night, after rising, he purifies his mind of obstructive states by walking and sitting. In this way, monks, a monk is devoted to wakefulness. Endowed with these four factors, monks, a monk is incapable of decline and is close to Nibbāna.
translations.an4.37:6: A monk established in virtue, restrained at the senses; moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness.
translations.an4.37:7: Living thus ardent, by day and night untiring; developing wholesome states, for the attainment of security from bondage.
translations.an4.38:1: “A monk, monks, who has abandoned individual views, whose search is free from desire, whose bodily formations are tranquil, and who has withdrawn—is called such. And how, monks, is a monk one who has abandoned individual views? Here, monks, whatever various individual views of ascetics and brahmins there are—such as: ‘The world is eternal,’ or ‘The world is not eternal,’ or ‘The world is finite,’ or ‘The world is infinite,’ or ‘The soul and the body are the same,’ or ‘The soul is one thing and the body another,’ or ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’—all those are abandoned, cut off, uprooted, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and are no longer subject to future arising. In this way, monks, a monk is one who has abandoned individual views.
translations.an4.38:4: And how, monks, is a monk withdrawn? Here, monks, a monk’s conceit ‘I am’ is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and is no longer subject to future arising. In this way, monks, a monk is withdrawn. A monk, monks, who has abandoned individual views, whose search is free from desire, whose bodily formations are tranquil, and who has withdrawn—is called such.
translations.an4.38:5: Craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for the holy life; this grasping at truths, and the accumulation of views.
translations.an4.38:6: For one detached from all lust, freed from the destruction of craving; having abandoned craving, the accumulation of views is destroyed.
translations.an4.52:1: “There are, monks, these four streams of merit, streams of what is skillful, nutriments of happiness, conducive to heaven, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven, conducive to what is desirable, pleasing, beneficial, and happy. What four? Here, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with confirmed confidence in the Buddha: ‘That Blessed One is an Arahant, fully enlightened, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’ This is the first stream of merit, stream of what is skillful, nutriment of happiness, conducive to heaven, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven, conducive to what is desirable, pleasing, beneficial, and happy.
translations.an4.52:2: Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with confirmed confidence in the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally known by the wise.’ This is the second stream of merit, stream of what is skillful, nutriment of happiness, conducive to heaven, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven, conducive to what is desirable, pleasing, beneficial, and happy.
translations.an4.52:3: Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, the straight way, the true way, the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight kinds of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.’ This is the third stream of merit, stream of what is skillful, nutriment of happiness, conducive to heaven, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven, conducive to what is desirable, pleasing, beneficial, and happy.
translations.an4.52:4: Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with virtues that are appealing to the noble ones: unbroken, flawless, unblemished, unmixed, liberating, praised by the wise, conducive to concentration. This is the fourth stream of merit, stream of what is skillful, nutriment of happiness, conducive to heaven, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven, conducive to what is desirable, pleasing, beneficial, and happy. These, monks, are the four streams of merit, streams of what is skillful, nutriments of happiness, conducive to heaven, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven, conducive to what is desirable, pleasing, beneficial, and happy.
translations.an4.52:5: Whose confidence in the Tathāgata is immovable, well established; and whose virtue is good, appealing to the noble ones, praised.
translations.an4.52:6: Whoever has confidence in the Saṅgha and a straightforward view; they are called not poor, and their life is not in vain.
translations.an4.53:1: At one time the Buddha was traveling along the road between Madhurā and Verañjā. Many householders and householders’ wives were also traveling along the road between Madhurā and Verañjā. Then the Buddha, leaving the road, sat down at the root of a certain tree. The householders and householders’ wives saw the Buddha sitting at the root of a certain tree. Seeing him, they approached the Buddha; having approached, they bowed down to the Buddha and sat down to one side. When they were seated to one side, the Buddha said to them:
translations.an4.53:10: Both are faithful and skilled in speech, restrained and living righteously; they become a couple, speaking kindly to one another.
translations.an4.53:11: Their wealth becomes abundant, ease and comfort arise; enemies become displeased, of both who are of equal virtue.
translations.an4.53:2: “There are these four kinds of living together, householders. What four? A wretch lives with a wretch, a wretch lives with a goddess, a god lives with a wretch, a god lives with a goddess.
translations.an4.53:3: How does a wretch live with a wretch? Here, householders, the husband is a killer of living beings, a taker of what is not given, a misconducter in sensual pleasures, a liar, a drinker of intoxicants, of unvirtuous conduct, of bad character, with a mind defiled by stinginess, dwelling at home, abusive and insulting to ascetics and brahmins; and his wife is also a killer of living beings, a taker of what is not given, a misconducter in sensual pleasures, a liar, a drinker of intoxicants, of unvirtuous conduct, of bad character, with a mind defiled by stinginess, dwelling at home, abusive and insulting to ascetics and brahmins. In this way, householders, a wretch lives with a wretch.
translations.an4.53:8: The husband is of unvirtuous conduct, stingy and insulting; the wife is of virtuous conduct, skilled in speech and free from stinginess; she, a goddess, lives with her husband, a wretch.
translations.an4.53:9: The husband is of virtuous conduct, skilled in speech and free from stinginess; the wife is of unvirtuous conduct, stingy and insulting; she, a wretch, lives with her husband, a god.
translations.an4.5:1: “There are these four kinds of people found existing in the world, monks. What four? One who goes with the flow, one who goes against the flow, one who stands fast, and one who has crossed over, gone beyond, and stands on dry land, a brahmin. Who is the one who goes with the flow, monks? Here, monks, a certain person indulges in sensual pleasures and does bad deeds. This is called the one who goes with the flow, monks.
translations.an4.5:2: Who is the one who goes against the flow, monks? Here, monks, a certain person does not indulge in sensual pleasures and does not do bad deeds; while suffering with pain and displeasure, weeping with a tearful face, he lives the complete and pure holy life. This is called the one who goes against the flow, monks.
translations.an4.5:3: Who is the one who stands fast, monks? Here, monks, a certain person, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, is spontaneously born, there he attains final Nibbāna without returning from that world. This is called the one who stands fast, monks.
translations.an4.5:4: Who is the person who has crossed over, gone beyond, and stands on dry land, a brahmin? Here, monks, a certain person, with the destruction of the taints, realizes the taintless mind liberation and wisdom liberation for himself in this very life, and having entered into it, dwells in it. This is called the person who has crossed over, gone beyond, and stands on dry land, a brahmin. These, monks, are the four kinds of people found existing in the world.
translations.an4.5:5: Whoever here are people unrestrained in sensual pleasures, not free from lust here, enjoyers of sensual pleasures; they go again and again to birth and aging, overcome by craving, going with the flow.
translations.an4.5:6: Therefore, a wise person, established in mindfulness here, not frequenting sensual pleasures and bad things, should abandon sensual pleasures even with pain; such a person is called one who goes against the flow.
translations.an4.5:7: Whoever has abandoned the five defilements, a sekha with complete training, of concentrated mind and controlled faculties, that person is called one who stands fast.
translations.an4.62:2: “There are these four kinds of happiness to be obtained by a householder, an enjoyer of sensual pleasures, at the proper time, on the proper occasion. What four? The happiness of having, the happiness of enjoyment, the happiness of debtlessness, the happiness of blamelessness.
translations.an4.62:3: What is the happiness of having? Here, householder, a son of good family has wealth obtained by energetic striving, amassed by strength of arm, earned by sweat, righteous and righteously gained. He reflects, ‘I have wealth obtained by energetic striving, amassed by strength of arm, earned by sweat, righteous and righteously gained,’ and he obtains happiness, he obtains gladness. This is called the happiness of having.
translations.an4.62:5: What is the happiness of debtlessness? Here, householder, a son of good family owes no debt to anyone, whether little or much. He reflects, ‘I owe no debt to anyone, whether little or much,’ and he obtains happiness, he obtains gladness. This is called the happiness of debtlessness.
translations.an4.62:6: What is the happiness of blamelessness? Here, householder, a noble disciple is possessed of blameless bodily conduct, possessed of blameless verbal conduct, possessed of blameless mental conduct. He reflects, ‘I am possessed of blameless bodily conduct, possessed of blameless verbal conduct, possessed of blameless mental conduct,’ and he obtains happiness, he obtains gladness. This is called the happiness of blamelessness. These, householder, are the four kinds of happiness to be obtained by a householder, an enjoyer of sensual pleasures, at the proper time, on the proper occasion.
translations.an4.62:7: Knowing the happiness of debtlessness, and then the happiness of having as supreme; a mortal enjoys the happiness of enjoyment, then wisdom looks on.
translations.an5.23:1: “There are these five impurities of gold, by which gold when affected is neither malleable nor workable nor radiant, but brittle, and does not properly fit the work. What five? Iron, copper, tin, lead, and zinc—these are the five impurities of gold, by which gold when affected is neither malleable nor workable nor radiant, but brittle, and does not properly fit the work. But when gold is freed from these five impurities, then it is malleable, workable, radiant, and not brittle, and properly fits the work. Whatever kind of ornament he wishes to fashion—whether a finger-ring, an earring, a necklace, or a gold garland—he achieves that purpose.
translations.an5.23:2: So too, there are these five impurities of the mind, by which the mind when affected is neither malleable nor workable nor radiant, but brittle, and does not properly concentrate for the destruction of the taints. What five? Sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt—these are the five impurities of the mind, by which the mind when affected is neither malleable nor workable nor radiant, but brittle, and does not properly concentrate for the destruction of the taints. But when the mind is freed from these five impurities, then it is malleable, workable, radiant, and not brittle, and properly concentrates for the destruction of the taints. To whatever state realizable by direct knowledge the mind is bent for the realization of direct knowledge, he achieves the capacity to witness it in every single base.
translations.an5.23:3: If he wishes: ‘May I wield the various kinds of spiritual power—having been one, may I become many; having been many, may I become one; may I appear and vanish; may I go unhindered through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; may I dive in and out of the earth as if in water; may I walk on water without sinking as if on land; may I travel cross-legged in the sky like a bird; may I touch and stroke with my hand the sun and moon, mighty and powerful as they are; may I exercise mastery with the body as far as the Brahmā world,’ he achieves the capacity to witness it in every single base.
translations.an5.23:4: If he wishes: ‘May I hear with the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, both kinds of sounds, divine and human, whether far or near,’ he achieves the capacity to witness it in every single base.
translations.an5.23:5: If he wishes: ‘May I understand the minds of other beings and other persons, having encompassed them with my own mind. I may understand a mind with lust as a mind with lust, a mind free from lust as a mind free from lust, a mind with hate as a mind with hate, a mind free from hate as a mind free from hate, a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion, a mind free from delusion as a mind free from delusion, a constricted mind as a constricted mind, a scattered mind as a scattered mind, an expanded mind as an expanded mind, an unexpanded mind as an unexpanded mind, a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind, an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind, a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind, an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind, a liberated mind as a liberated mind, an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind,’ he achieves the capacity to witness it in every single base.
translations.an5.25:1: “Supported by five factors, right view has the fruit of mind-release and the benefits of mind-release, and it has the fruit of wisdom-release and the benefits of wisdom-release.
translations.an5.26:1: “There are these five bases of deliverance. When a bhikkhu dwells heedful, ardent, and resolute, in them his unliberated mind is liberated, his uneliminated taints are eliminated, and the unsurpassed security from bondage not yet attained is attained.
translations.an5.26:3: Furthermore, it is not the Teacher who teaches the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, nor a respected fellow monk in the holy life, but he himself expounds the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard and learned it. As he expounds the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard and learned it, he becomes one who experiences the meaning and the Dhamma in that Dhamma. Because he experiences the meaning and the Dhamma, joy arises. In one who is joyful, rapture arises. In one whose mind is filled with rapture, the body becomes tranquil. When the body is tranquil, one experiences pleasure. In one who experiences pleasure, the mind becomes concentrated. This is the second base of deliverance. When a bhikkhu dwells heedful, ardent, and resolute, in it his unliberated mind is liberated, his uneliminated taints are eliminated, and the unsurpassed security from bondage not yet attained is attained.
translations.an5.26:4: Furthermore, it is not the Teacher who teaches the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, nor a respected fellow monk in the holy life, nor does he himself expound the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard and learned it, but he himself recites the Dhamma in detail as he has heard and learned it. As he recites the Dhamma in detail as he has heard and learned it, he becomes one who experiences the meaning and the Dhamma in that Dhamma. Because he experiences the meaning and the Dhamma, joy arises. In one who is joyful, rapture arises. In one whose mind is filled with rapture, the body becomes tranquil. When the body is tranquil, one experiences pleasure. In one who experiences pleasure, the mind becomes concentrated. This is the third base of deliverance. When a bhikkhu dwells heedful, ardent, and resolute, in it his unliberated mind is liberated, his uneliminated taints are eliminated, and the unsurpassed security from bondage not yet attained is attained.
translations.an5.26:6: Furthermore, monks, a monk does not teach the Dhamma to others in detail as learned and mastered, nor does he recite the Dhamma in detail as learned and mastered, nor does he examine the Dhamma in detail as learned and mastered with his mind, thinking and pondering over it; but he has well-grasped, well-attended to, well-held, and well-penetrated with wisdom a certain meditation subject. As he has well-grasped, well-attended to, well-held, and well-penetrated with wisdom a certain meditation subject, he experiences both the meaning and the Dhamma in that Dhamma. As he experiences the meaning and the Dhamma, rapture arises. When he is rapturous, joy arises. When joyful, his body becomes tranquil. When his body is tranquil, he experiences pleasure. When pleasurable, his mind becomes concentrated. This, monks, is the fifth liberation base where, when a monk lives heedful, ardent, and resolute, his mind is liberated either without clinging, or the taints are destroyed so that they come to an end, or he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage that has not been attained before.
translations.an5.27:1: “Develop concentration, monks, that is limitless, prudent, and mindful. When concentration is developed that is limitless, prudent, and mindful, five knowledges arise personally. What five? The knowledge arises personally: ‘This concentration is pleasant in the present life and yields pleasure in the future life’; the knowledge arises personally: ‘This concentration is noble and taintless’; the knowledge arises personally: ‘This concentration is not frequented by ordinary people’; the knowledge arises personally: ‘This concentration is peaceful, sublime, attained through tranquility, has unity of mind, and is not attained by forceful restraint’; the knowledge arises personally: ‘I enter this concentration mindfully and emerge from it mindfully.’
translations.an5.28:1: “I will teach the development of the noble right concentration with its five factors, monks. Listen to that, attend closely, and I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an5.28:10: Suppose, monks, there was a royal chariot yoked to thoroughbreds, standing at the four main crossroads on level ground, with its goad and reins ready. A skilled trainer, expert in handling horses, having mounted it, taking the reins with the left hand and the goad with the right hand, would drive it wherever he wanted and however he wanted. In the same way, monks, when a monk has developed and cultivated the noble right concentration with its five factors, he inclines his mind towards whatever state conducive to direct knowledge he wishes to realize; he achieves the ability to witness it in that very state, at the very basis.
translations.an5.28:15: If he wishes: ‘May I understand beings passing away and reappearing according to their actions with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human,’ he achieves the ability to witness it in that very state, at the very basis.
translations.an5.28:7: When, monks, a monk has developed and cultivated the noble right concentration with its five factors in this way, he inclines his mind towards whatever state conducive to direct knowledge he wishes to realize; he achieves the ability to witness it in that very state, at the very basis.
translations.an5.28:8: Suppose, monks, a water pot was placed on a level stand, full to the brim with water, so that a crow could drink from it. If a strong man were to tilt it in whatever direction, would the water flow out?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “In the same way, monks, when a monk has developed and cultivated the noble right concentration with its five factors in this way, he inclines his mind towards whatever state conducive to direct knowledge he wishes to realize; he achieves the ability to witness it in that very state, at the very basis.
translations.an5.28:9: Suppose, monks, there was a lotus pond with blue, white, or red lotuses born in the water, grown in the water, not rising above the water, thriving in the water. If a strong man were to pull them out in whatever direction, would they be broken off?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “In the same way, monks, when a monk has developed and cultivated the noble right concentration with its five factors in this way, he inclines his mind towards whatever state conducive to direct knowledge he wishes to realize; he achieves the ability to witness it in that very state, at the very basis.
translations.an5.2:1: “There are these five powers of a trainee, monks. What five? The power of faith, the power of conscience, the power of fear of wrongdoing, the power of energy, the power of wisdom.
translations.an5.2:2: And what, monks, is the power of faith? Here, monks, a noble disciple is faithful; he has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’ This is called the power of faith.
translations.an5.2:3: And what, monks, is the power of conscience? Here, monks, a noble disciple has conscience; he is ashamed of bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; he is ashamed of acquiring bad, unwholesome states. This is called the power of conscience.
translations.an5.2:4: And what, monks, is the power of fear of wrongdoing? Here, monks, a noble disciple fears wrongdoing; he fears bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; he fears acquiring bad, unwholesome states. This is called the power of fear of wrongdoing.
translations.an5.2:5: And what, monks, is the power of energy? Here, monks, a noble disciple lives with energy aroused for abandoning unwholesome states and acquiring wholesome states; he is strong, firm, and unshaken in making effort in wholesome states. This is called the power of energy.
translations.an5.2:6: And what, monks, is the power of wisdom? Here, monks, a noble disciple is wise; he possesses the wisdom that sees into the rise and fall, the noble penetrative wisdom that leads to the complete destruction of suffering. This is called the power of wisdom. These, monks, are the five powers of a trainee.
translations.an5.30:1: Thus I have heard. At one time the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosala country with a large Sangha of bhikkhus when he arrived at a Brahmin village named Icchānaṅgala. There the Blessed One stayed in the Icchānaṅgala forest grove. The Brahmin householders of Icchānaṅgala heard: 'The ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans, who went forth from the Sakyan clan, has arrived at Icchānaṅgala and is staying in the Icchānaṅgala forest grove. Concerning that Blessed One Gotama, a good report has been spread about: "That Blessed One is an Arahant, a fully enlightened Buddha, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, the knower of worlds, the incomparable leader of persons to be tamed, the teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed." He has realized by his own direct knowledge this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, its generations with their ascetics and Brahmins, its gods and humans, and he makes it known. He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals a perfectly complete and pure spiritual life. It is good to see such Arahants.' Then the Brahmin householders of Icchānaṅgala, taking a large amount of solid and soft food at the end of that night, approached the Icchānaṅgala forest grove; having approached, they stood outside the doorway making a loud noise.
translations.an5.30:3: 'May the Blessed One accept, venerable sir, may the Sugata accept; it is time, venerable sir, for the Blessed One to accept. Wherever the Blessed One goes now, the Brahmin householders will go in that direction, both villages and towns. Just as, venerable sir, when heavy rain falls, the water flows according to the slope; so too, venerable sir, wherever the Blessed One goes now, the Brahmin householders will go in that direction, both villages and towns. Why is that? Because, venerable sir, of the Blessed One's virtue and wisdom.'
translations.an5.31:1: At one time ... the Blessed One was staying in the Jeta Grove in Anāthapiṇḍika's park. Then Princess Sumanā, surrounded by five hundred chariots and five hundred princesses, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, she sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Princess Sumanā said this to the Blessed One:
translations.an5.31:10: So too, a person of virtue, a faithful man; Surpasses all the stingy in the world by generosity.
translations.an5.31:11: Like a cloud in the sky, adorned with a wreath of lightning; Filling the low and high places, watering the earth.
translations.an5.31:12: Thus endowed with vision, a disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One; The wise man surpasses the stingy in five ways.
translations.an5.31:2: 'Here, venerable sir, there are two disciples of the Blessed One, equal in faith, equal in virtue, equal in wisdom—one is a giver, one is a non-giver. When, with the breakup of the body, after death, they would be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. But would there be a difference between them, venerable sir, when they have become gods?'
translations.an5.31:3: 'There would be, Sumanā,' the Blessed One said. 'The giver, Sumanā, having become a god, surpasses that non-giver in five ways—with divine life span, divine beauty, divine pleasure, divine fame, and divine sovereignty. The giver, Sumanā, having become a god, surpasses that non-giver in these five ways.'
translations.an5.31:4: 'But if they, venerable sir, pass away from there and come back to this state, would there be a difference between them, venerable sir, when they have become humans?' 'There would be, Sumanā,' the Blessed One said. 'The giver, Sumanā, having become a human, surpasses that non-giver in five ways—with human life span, human beauty, human pleasure, human fame, and human sovereignty. The giver, Sumanā, having become a human, surpasses that non-giver in these five ways.'
translations.an5.31:5: 'But if they both, venerable sir, go forth from the home life into homelessness, would there be a difference between them, venerable sir, when they have gone forth?' 'There would be, Sumanā,' the Blessed One said. 'The giver, Sumanā, having gone forth, surpasses that non-giver in five ways—he uses robes that are mostly invited and little uninvited, almsfood that is mostly invited and little uninvited, lodging that is mostly invited and little uninvited, and requisites for medicine and cure for the sick that are mostly invited and little uninvited. With whom he lives, the fellow practitioners, they mostly conduct themselves towards him with agreeable bodily action and little disagreeable, with agreeable verbal action and little disagreeable, with agreeable mental action and little disagreeable; they mostly offer agreeable gifts and little disagreeable. The giver, Sumanā, having gone forth, surpasses that non-giver in these five ways.'
translations.an5.31:6: 'But if they both, venerable sir, attain Arahantship, would there be a difference between them, venerable sir, when they have attained Arahantship?' 'Herein, Sumanā, I do not see any difference, that is, in liberation from liberation.'
translations.an5.31:9: 'Like the moon, pure, moving in the sky; Surpasses all the stars in the world by its radiance.'
translations.an5.34:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Then General Sīha approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, General Sīha said this to the Blessed One: 'Is it possible, venerable sir, for the Blessed One to point out a visible fruit of giving?'
translations.an5.34:2: 'It is possible, Sīha,' the Blessed One said. 'A giver, Sīha, a donor is dear and pleasing to many people. Whatever, Sīha, a giver, a donor is dear and pleasing to many people, this too is a visible fruit of giving.'
translations.an5.34:8: A giver is dear, many associate with him; He acquires a good reputation and his fame grows; Unconceited, he mingles with the assembly; The man without stinginess is confident.
translations.an5.34:9: Therefore the wise give gifts, having removed the stain of stinginess, seeking happiness; They stand for a long time in the heavenly worlds, Delighting in the company of gods.
translations.an5.36:1: “There are these five timely gifts. What five? One gives a gift to a traveler; one gives a gift to one who is about to travel; one gives a gift to a sick person; one gives a gift in time of famine; one first establishes new grain and new fruit among those of virtue. These are the five timely gifts.”
translations.an5.36:2: The wise give at the proper time, those who know what is suitable and are free from stinginess; Given at the right time to the noble ones, to those who are upright and of such nature.
translations.an5.36:3: His mind is clear and bright, the donation is abundant; Those who rejoice therein or perform a duty; By that the donation is not deficient, they too are sharers in the merit.
translations.an5.37:1: “When giving food, monks, the giver gives five things to the recipients. What five? He gives life, he gives beauty, he gives happiness, he gives strength, he gives quick-wittedness. Having given life, he is a sharer in life, divine or human; having given beauty, he is a sharer in beauty, divine or human; having given happiness, he is a sharer in happiness, divine or human; having given strength, he is a sharer in strength, divine or human; having given quick-wittedness, he is a sharer in quick-wittedness, divine or human. When giving food, monks, the giver gives these five things to the recipients.”
translations.an5.37:2: A giver of life and strength, wise, a giver of beauty and quick-wittedness; The intelligent giver of happiness, he himself attains happiness.
translations.an5.38:2: Suppose, monks, there is a great banyan tree at a crossroads in a good village, a shelter for birds all around; so too, monks, a faithful son of a good family is a shelter for many people—for monks, nuns, male lay followers, and female lay followers.
translations.an5.38:3: With branches, leaves, and fruits, standing like a great mountain; With roots and full of fruit, it stands as a shelter for birds.
translations.an5.38:4: In a pleasant abode, birds resort to it; Those seeking shade and shade go there, fruit-eaters and eaters of fruit.
translations.an5.38:5: So too a person of virtue, a faithful man; Living in a cool place, resolute, calm, with soft branches.
translations.an5.38:6: Free from lust, free from hate, free from delusion, taintless; Fields of merit in the world, they resort to such a man.
translations.an5.41:1: At one time the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One; having approached and bowed to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. While the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to him: “There are these five uses of wealth, householder. What five? Here, householder, a noble disciple uses wealth earned by energetic striving, amassed by strength of arm, earned by sweat, righteous, righteously gained to make himself happy and cheerful, to maintain himself rightly in happiness; he makes his mother and father happy and cheerful, to maintain them rightly in happiness; he makes his wife, children, slaves, workers, and servants happy and cheerful, to maintain them rightly in happiness. This is the first use of wealth.
translations.an5.41:4: Furthermore, householder, a noble disciple uses wealth earned by energetic striving, amassed by strength of arm, earned by sweat, righteous, righteously gained to make five offerings. An offering to relatives, an offering to guests, an offering to departed ancestors, an offering to the king, an offering to the deities—this is the fourth use of wealth.
translations.an5.41:5: Furthermore, householder, a noble disciple uses wealth earned by energetic striving, amassed by strength of arm, earned by sweat, righteous, righteously gained to establish an exalted offering to those ascetics and brahmins who abstain from negligence, are settled in patience and gentleness, taming themselves, calming themselves, liberating themselves. In such ascetics and brahmins he establishes an exalted offering conducive to heaven, resulting in happiness, conducive to heavenly rebirth. This is the fifth use of wealth. These are the five uses of wealth.
translations.an5.41:6: If, householder, for a noble disciple making these five uses of wealth, his wealth declines, he thinks thus: ‘Indeed, I used the wealth as it should be used, and my wealth has declined.’ He has no regret. If, householder, for a noble disciple making these five uses of wealth, his wealth increases, he thinks thus: ‘Indeed, I used the wealth as it should be used, and my wealth has increased.’ He has no regret in either case.
translations.an5.41:7: Wealth has been enjoyed, food has been eaten, I have passed through calamities; Exalted offerings have been given, and the five offerings made; Virtuous ones are supported, those restrained in the holy life.
translations.an5.41:8: Whatever wealth a wise man living at home might wish for, That purpose of mine has been attained, done without regret.
translations.an5.43:1: Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One; having approached and bowed to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. While the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to him:
translations.an5.43:4: It is not fit, householder, for a noble disciple who desires long life to pray for long life or to delight in it or to make it a cause for long life. A noble disciple who desires long life should practice the conduct conducive to long life. Having practiced the conduct conducive to long life, he will attain long life. He will obtain life, divine or human.
translations.an5.43:5: It is not fit, householder, for a noble disciple who desires beauty to pray for beauty or to delight in it or to make it a cause for beauty. A noble disciple who desires beauty should practice the conduct conducive to beauty. Having practiced the conduct conducive to beauty, he will attain beauty. He will obtain beauty, divine or human.
translations.an5.43:6: It is not fit, householder, for a noble disciple who desires happiness to pray for happiness or to delight in it or to make it a cause for happiness. A noble disciple who desires happiness should practice the conduct conducive to happiness. Having practiced the conduct conducive to happiness, he will attain happiness. He will obtain happiness, divine or human.
translations.an8.13:1: “Possessed of eight factors, monks, a royal thoroughbred steed is worthy of a king, fit to serve a king, reckoned as a limb of the king. What eight? Here, monks, a royal thoroughbred steed is well-born on both sides— on the mother’s side and on the father’s side. He is born in the same region where other fine thoroughbred steeds are born. Whatever food is given to him— whether hard or dry— he eats it carefully, without scattering. He is disgusted at voiding excrement or urine or dropping them. He is easy to keep and pleasant to live with, and does not startle other horses. Whatever deceptions, tricks, ruses, or deviousness he has, these are made known to the charioteer as they actually are. The charioteer strives to turn him away from them. He is strong. He arouses the thought: ‘Let other horses pull or not pull; I will pull here.’ When he goes, he goes on a straight path. He is enduring, able to set up strength until the end of life and death. Possessed of these eight factors, monks, a royal thoroughbred steed is worthy of a king, fit to serve a king, reckoned as a limb of the king.
translations.an8.14:1: “I will teach you, monks, the eight faults of a horse and the eight faults of a horse, and the eight faults of a person and the eight faults of a person. Listen to that, attend closely, I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an8.14:2: “What are the eight, monks, faults of a horse and the eight faults of a horse? Here, monks, when a certain horse with a fault is told ‘Giddyup’, being struck and urged by the charioteer, he retreats backward, pushing the chariot behind him. Such, monks, is a certain horse with a fault. This is the first fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:3: Again, monks, when a certain horse with a fault is told ‘Giddyup’, being struck and urged by the charioteer, he leaps backward, breaks the pole, snaps the yoke. Such, monks, is a certain horse with a fault. This is the second fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:4: Again, monks, when a certain horse with a fault is told ‘Giddyup’, being struck and urged by the charioteer, he pushes against the shaft of the chariot with his shoulder and crushes the charioteer. Such, monks, is a certain horse with a fault. This is the third fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:5: Again, monks, when a certain horse with a fault is told ‘Giddyup’, being struck and urged by the charioteer, he seizes the bridle and makes the chariot tip over. Such, monks, is a certain horse with a fault. This is the fourth fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:6: Again, monks, when a certain horse with a fault is told ‘Giddyup’, being struck and urged by the charioteer, he leaps forward and tramples the front legs. Such, monks, is a certain horse with a fault. This is the fifth fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:7: Again, monks, when a certain horse with a fault is told ‘Giddyup’, being struck and urged by the charioteer, without taking hold of the charioteer or the goad-stick, he smashes the mouth-guard with his teeth and goes wherever he wants. Such, monks, is a certain horse with a fault. This is the sixth fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:8: Again, monks, when a certain horse with a fault is told ‘Giddyup’, being struck and urged by the charioteer, he neither goes forward nor goes back, but stands there like a stump. Such, monks, is a certain horse with a fault. This is the seventh fault of a horse.
translations.an8.14:9: Again, monks, when a certain horse with a fault is told ‘Giddyup’, being struck and urged by the charioteer, gathering the front legs and gathering the hind legs, he sits down right there on all four legs. Such, monks, is a certain horse with a fault. This is the eighth fault of a horse. These are the eight, monks, faults of a horse and the eight faults of a horse.
translations.an8.19:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling near Verañjā at the root of the Naleru fig tree. Then the Asura king Pahārāda approached the Blessed One; having approached and bowed down to the Blessed One, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Asura king Pahārāda was addressed by the Blessed One thus:
translations.an8.22:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Vajjians in Hatthigāma. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma is possessed of eight wonderful and marvelous factors.” This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One rose from his seat and entered the dwelling.
translations.an8.22:10: If, venerable sir, I were to pass away first, it would not be wonderful if the Blessed One were to declare of me: ‘There is no fetter by which the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma is bound that would cause him to return to this world.’ This is the eighth wonderful and marvelous factor found in me.
translations.an8.22:11: These are the eight wonderful and marvelous factors found in me. But I do not know: ‘With which eight wonderful and marvelous factors I was declared by the Blessed One.’”
translations.an8.22:12: Then that monk, having taken almsfood at the residence of the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma, rose from his seat and departed. Then that monk, having returned from almsround after the meal, approached the Blessed One; having approached and bowed down to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that monk reported to the Blessed One all the conversation that had taken place with the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma.
translations.an8.22:2: Then a certain monk, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, approached the residence of the householder Ugga the elephant trainer; having approached, he sat down on the appointed seat. Then the householder Ugga the elephant trainer approached that monk; having approached, he paid homage to that monk and sat down to one side. While he was sitting to one side, that monk said this to the householder Ugga the elephant trainer: 'You are endowed with eight wonderful and marvelous things that have been proclaimed by the Blessed One. What are these eight wonderful and marvelous things that you are endowed with that have been proclaimed by the Blessed One?'
translations.an8.22:3: 'I do not know, venerable sir, what the eight wonderful and marvelous things are that I am endowed with that have been proclaimed by the Blessed One. But, venerable sir, there are eight wonderful and marvelous things that I am aware of; listen to that, pay close attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, householder,' said that monk, responding to the householder Ugga the elephant trainer. The householder Ugga the elephant trainer said this: 'When, venerable sir, I was walking in the elephant forest and saw the Blessed One from afar for the first time; at the sight of the Blessed One, my mind became serene, and intoxication with liquor was abandoned. This is the first wonderful and marvelous thing that I am aware of.'
translations.an8.22:4: Then I, venerable sir, with a confident mind, attended upon the Blessed One. The Blessed One spoke to me step by step, that is to say—talk on giving, talk on virtue, talk on heaven; he explained the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the advantages of renunciation. When the Blessed One knew that my mind was ready, receptive, free from hindrances, enthusiastic, and confident, then he explained the teaching special to the Buddhas—suffering, origin, cessation, and the path. Just as a clean cloth free of stains would properly absorb dye; so too, in me right there on that seat, the dustless, stainless Dhamma eye arose: 'Whatever is subject to origination, all that is subject to cessation.' So I, venerable sir, having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, plunged into the Dhamma, crossed over doubt, freed from uncertainty, attained self-confidence, independent of others in the Teacher's instruction, went for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha right there, and undertook the five training rules of the holy life. This is the second wonderful and marvelous thing that I am aware of.
translations.an8.22:5: I had, venerable sir, four young wives. Then I, venerable sir, approached those wives; having approached, I said this to those wives: 'I have undertaken the five training rules of the holy life. Let whoever wishes enjoy pleasures here and do meritorious deeds, or go to her own relatives. Or if there is a desire for a husband, to whom shall I give you?' When this was said, the eldest wife, venerable sir, said this to me: 'Give me to a man of such and such a name, master's son.' Then I, venerable sir, having invited that man, took the wife by the left hand and took the water-pot by the right hand and poured the water for that man. But while giving away the young wife, venerable sir, I did not perceive any change of mind. This is the third wonderful and marvelous thing that I am aware of.
translations.an8.22:6: There are, venerable sir, wealth in my family. And they are undivided with those of virtue and good character. This is the fourth wonderful and marvelous thing that I am aware of.
translations.an8.22:7: When I, venerable sir, attend upon a monk; I attend upon him carefully, not carelessly. If that venerable one teaches the Dhamma; I listen carefully, not carelessly. If that venerable one does not teach the Dhamma, I teach the Dhamma to him. This is the fifth wonderful and marvelous thing that I am aware of.
translations.an8.22:8: It is not wonderful, venerable sir, that when the Sangha is invited, deities approach and announce: 'Such and such a monk is both-ways liberated, such and such is liberated by wisdom, such and such is a body-witness, such and such is a attainer-of-view, such and such is liberated by faith, such and such is a Dhamma-follower, such and such is a faith-follower, such and such is virtuous and of good character, such and such is immoral and of bad character.' But while waiting upon the Sangha, venerable sir, I do not perceive a mind arising thus: 'I will give little to this one, much to that one.' Then I, venerable sir, give with an equal mind. This is the sixth wonderful and marvelous thing that I am aware of.
translations.an8.22:9: It is not wonderful, venerable sir, that deities approach me and announce: 'The Dhamma is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One.' When this was said, I, venerable sir, said this to those deities: 'You might speak thus or you might not speak thus, but the Dhamma is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One.' But I, venerable sir, do not perceive an uplift of mind because of that: 'Deities are approaching me, or I am conversing with deities.' This is the seventh wonderful and marvelous thing that I am aware of.
translations.an8.23:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava shrine. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks, you should remember Hatthaka of Āḷavī as endowed with seven wonderful and marvelous things. What seven? Hatthaka of Āḷavī is faithful, monks; Hatthaka of Āḷavī is virtuous, monks; Hatthaka of Āḷavī has a sense of shame, monks; Hatthaka of Āḷavī has a sense of dread, monks; Hatthaka of Āḷavī is learned, monks; Hatthaka of Āḷavī is generous, monks; Hatthaka of Āḷavī is wise, monks—monks, you should remember Hatthaka of Āḷavī as endowed with these seven wonderful and marvelous things.' This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One rose from his seat and entered the dwelling.
translations.an8.23:2: Then a certain monk, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, approached the residence of Hatthaka of Āḷavī; having approached, he sat down on the appointed seat. Then Hatthaka of Āḷavī approached that monk; having approached, he paid homage to that monk and sat down to one side. While he was sitting to one side, that monk said this to Hatthaka of Āḷavī:
translations.an8.23:3: “You, friend, are endowed with seven wonderful and marvelous qualities declared by the Blessed One. What seven? ‘Hatthaka Āḷavaka is faithful; virtuous … ashamed … afraid of wrongdoing … learned … generous … wise, monks, Hatthaka Āḷavaka.’ You, friend, are endowed with these seven wonderful and marvelous qualities declared by the Blessed One.” “Has there been, sir, no layperson wearing white clothes?” “There has not been, friend, any layperson wearing white clothes.” “It is good, sir, that there has been no layperson wearing white clothes.”
translations.an8.23:4: Then that monk, having taken alms-food at Hatthaka Āḷavaka’s residence, rose from his seat and departed. Then that monk, after returning from alms-round, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. While sitting to one side, that monk said to the Blessed One:
translations.an8.24:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying near Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava shrine. Then Hatthaka Āḷavaka, surrounded by five hundred lay followers, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. While Hatthaka Āḷavaka was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to him: “Hatthaka, this is a large assembly. But how, Hatthaka, do you bring this large assembly together?” “Sir, with regard to the four bases of sympathy taught by the Blessed One, I bring this large assembly together. Sir, as I know: ‘This person should be won over by giving,’ I win them over by giving; as I know: ‘This person should be won over by kind speech,’ I win them over by kind speech; as I know: ‘This person should be won over by beneficial conduct,’ I win them over by beneficial conduct; as I know: ‘This person should be won over by impartiality,’ I win them over by impartiality. But, sir, there are families with wealth. They do not think that a poor person should be listened to in the same way.” “Good, good, Hatthaka. It is fitting, Hatthaka, that you bring a large assembly together in this way. For whoever in the past, Hatthaka, brought a large assembly together, they all did so with just these four bases of sympathy. Whoever in the future, Hatthaka, will bring a large assembly together, they all will do so with just these four bases of sympathy. Whoever now, Hatthaka, brings a large assembly together, they all do so with just these four bases of sympathy.”
translations.an8.26:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove. Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. While sitting to one side, Jīvaka Komārabhacca said to the Blessed One: “Sir, how is a lay follower defined?” “When, Jīvaka, one has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha; in this way, Jīvaka, a lay follower is defined.”
translations.an8.26:2: “But how, sir, is a lay follower virtuous?” “When, Jīvaka, a lay follower abstains from killing living beings … from intoxicating drinks and drugs that cause heedlessness; in this way, Jīvaka, a lay follower is virtuous.”
translations.an8.26:3: “But how, sir, is a lay follower practicing for his own benefit, but not for the benefit of another?” “When, Jīvaka, a lay follower is himself accomplished in faith, but does not urge another to accomplish faith … is himself practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, knowing the meaning and the Dhamma, but does not urge another to practice in accordance with the Dhamma. In this way, Jīvaka, a lay follower is practicing for his own benefit, but not for the benefit of another.”
translations.an8.28:5: Furthermore, sir, the four establishments of mindfulness of a monk with taints destroyed are developed and cultivated. Whatever, sir, are the four establishments of mindfulness of a monk with taints destroyed that are developed and cultivated, this too, sir, is a strength of a monk with taints destroyed, relying on which strength a monk with taints destroyed declares the destruction of the taints: ‘My taints are destroyed.’
translations.an8.28:6: Furthermore, sir, the four bases of power of a monk with taints destroyed are developed and cultivated … the five faculties are developed and cultivated … the seven factors of enlightenment are developed and cultivated … the noble eightfold path is developed and cultivated. Whatever, sir, is the noble eightfold path of a monk with taints destroyed that is developed and cultivated, this too, sir, is a strength of a monk with taints destroyed, relying on which strength a monk with taints destroyed declares the destruction of the taints: ‘My taints are destroyed.’
translations.an8.2:1: “Monks, there are these eight causes, eight conditions for the initial wisdom of the holy life not to be obtained, for obtaining it, for obtaining it to increase, to expand, to develop, and to fulfill. What eight? Here, monks, a monk lives relying on the teacher or on a certain fellow monk in the training who inspires strong shame and dread in him, and for whom there is affection and respect. This, monks, is the first cause, the first condition for the initial wisdom of the holy life not to be obtained, for obtaining it, for obtaining it to increase, to expand, to develop, and to fulfill.
translations.an8.2:11: ‘That venerable, having heard that Dhamma, makes it manifest in two ways—by bodily manifestation and by mental manifestation. Surely that venerable knows and sees.’ This Dhamma also conduces to affection, respect, development, sameness, and oneness.
translations.an8.2:15: ‘That venerable has gone to the Saṅgha and is not a maker of quarrels, a maker of strife. He speaks Dhamma in common or asks questions of another, and does not despise the noble silence. Surely that venerable knows and sees.’ This Dhamma also conduces to affection, respect, development, sameness, and oneness.
translations.an8.2:2: Dwelling relying on the Teacher, they approach a certain fellow monk who is worthy of respect, in whom strong conscientiousness and concern, as well as affection and respect, are established. From time to time they approach and question and interrogate him: ‘What is this, sir? What is the meaning of this?’ Those venerables explain it to him without holding back, they make clear what was not clear, and they dispel doubt in many states that are doubtful and questionable. This is the second cause and condition for the attainment of the initial wisdom of the holy life, for the increase, expansion, fulfillment, and completion of it once it has been attained.
translations.an8.2:4: They are virtuous, they dwell restrained by the Pātimokkha, they are perfect in conduct and resort, they see fear in the slightest fault, and they train in the rules of training they have undertaken. This is the fourth cause and condition for the attainment of the initial wisdom of the holy life, for the increase, expansion, fulfillment, and completion of it once it has been attained.
translations.an8.2:5: They are learned, they remember and retain what they have learned. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the complete and purified holy life—such teachings are well learned by them, well retained by verbal recitation, well examined mentally, and well penetrated by view. This is the fifth cause and condition for the attainment of the initial wisdom of the holy life, for the increase, expansion, fulfillment, and completion of it once it has been attained.
translations.an8.2:6: They dwell with aroused energy for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the attainment of wholesome states; they are strong, firm in exertion, not shirking the burden of wholesome states. This is the sixth cause and condition for the attainment of the initial wisdom of the holy life, for the increase, expansion, fulfillment, and completion of it once it has been attained.
translations.an8.2:7: They go to the Saṅgha and do not engage in quarrelsome talk; they speak either on the Dhamma or ask questions, and they do not regret the noble silence. This is the seventh cause and condition for the attainment of the initial wisdom of the holy life, for the increase, expansion, fulfillment, and completion of it once it has been attained.
translations.an8.2:8: They dwell contemplating rise and fall in the five aggregates subject to clinging: ‘Thus is material form, thus is the arising of material form, thus is the passing away of material form; thus is feeling, thus is the arising of feeling, thus is the passing away of feeling; thus is perception … thus are volitional formations … thus is consciousness, thus is the arising of consciousness, thus is the passing away of consciousness.’ This is the eighth cause and condition for the attainment of the initial wisdom of the holy life, for the increase, expansion, fulfillment, and completion of it once it has been attained.
translations.an8.2:9: Then their fellow monks reflect on them thus: ‘This venerable dwells relying on the Teacher or on a certain fellow monk who is worthy of respect, in whom strong conscientiousness and concern, as well as affection and respect, are established. Surely this venerable knows and sees.’ This Dhamma also conduces to affection, respect, development, sameness, and unity.
translations.an8.30:1: At one time the Buddha was staying among the Bhaggas at Suṁsumāragiri in the Deer Park at Bhesakalāvana. At that time Venerable Anuruddha was staying among the Cetis at the Eastern Bamboo Park.
