Then, while Venerable Anuruddha was in private retreat, this reflection arose in his mind: “This Dhamma is for one with few desires, not for one with many desires; this Dhamma is for one who is content, not for one who is discontent; this Dhamma is for one who is secluded, not for one who is fond of company; this Dhamma is for one with aroused energy, not for one who is lazy; this Dhamma is for one with established mindfulness, not for one with muddled mindfulness; this Dhamma is for one with concentrated mind, not for one with unconcentrated mind; this Dhamma is for one with wisdom, not for one with little wisdom.”
translations.an8.30:10: When you, Anuruddha, reflect on these eight thoughts of a great person and obtain these four jhānas—proceedings of mind, comfortable dwellings in the here and now—at will, without difficulty, without trouble, then for you, Anuruddha, it will be like a householder or a householder’s son with a gabled chamber plastered inside and out, draft-free, with shutters fastened, and windows shut; so too will your dwelling at the root of a tree be while you live content, finding pleasure that is without anxiety, for a comfortable abiding and for the attainment of Nibbāna.
translations.an8.30:11: When you, Anuruddha, reflect on these eight thoughts of a great person and obtain these four jhānas—proceedings of mind, comfortable dwellings in the here and now—at will, without difficulty, without trouble, then for you, Anuruddha, it will be like a householder or a householder’s son with a couch spread with a long fleece cover, a white cover, a flower-embroidered cover, or a cover of antelope skin, with a canopy above and red pillows at both ends; so too will your bed of grass or leaves be while you live content, finding pleasure that is without anxiety, for a comfortable abiding and for the attainment of Nibbāna.
translations.an8.30:12: When you, Anuruddha, reflect on these eight thoughts of a great person and obtain these four jhānas—proceedings of mind, comfortable dwellings in the here and now—at will, without difficulty, without trouble, then for you, Anuruddha, it will be like a householder or a householder’s son with various kinds of medicines, that is to say—ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses; so too will your medicine of urine and feces be while you live content, finding pleasure that is without anxiety, for a comfortable abiding and for the attainment of Nibbāna. Therefore, Anuruddha, you should spend the remaining rains residence right here among the Cetis at the Eastern Bamboo Park.” “Yes, sir,” Venerable Anuruddha replied to the Buddha.
translations.an8.30:13: Then the Buddha, having advised Venerable Anuruddha with this admonition—just as a strong man might extend his flexed arm or flex his extended arm; in just this way—disappeared from among the Cetis at the Cātumā shrine and appeared in the Bhagga country, on the Sumasāgala mountain, in the Deer Park at Bhesakalāvana. The Buddha sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Buddha addressed the monks: “I will teach you the eight thoughts of a great person, monks; listen to it …pe… What are the eight thoughts of a great person, monks? This Dhamma is for one with few desires, monks, not for one with many desires; this Dhamma is for one who is content, monks, not for one who is discontent; this Dhamma is for one who loves solitude, monks, not for one who delights in company; this Dhamma is for one who has aroused energy, monks, not for one who is lazy; this Dhamma is for one who has established mindfulness, monks, not for one whose mindfulness is confused; this Dhamma is for one who is concentrated, monks, not for one who is not concentrated; this Dhamma is for one who is wise, monks, not for one who is unwise; this Dhamma is for one who delights in non-proliferation and is a lover of non-proliferation, monks, not for one who delights in proliferation and is a lover of proliferation.
translations.an8.30:2: Then the Buddha, knowing the reflection of Venerable Anuruddha’s mind—just as a strong man might extend his flexed arm or flex his extended arm; in just this way—disappeared from the Bhagga country, on the Sumasāgala mountain, in the Deer Park at Bhesakalāvana and appeared in front of Venerable Anuruddha among the Cetis at the Cātumā shrine. The Buddha sat down on the prepared seat. Venerable Anuruddha also, having bowed to the Buddha, sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Buddha said this to Venerable Anuruddha:
translations.an8.30:22: Then Venerable Anuruddha, having spent the rainy residence there among the Cetis at the Cātumā shrine, dwelt there. Then Venerable Anuruddha, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, before long—realizing for himself with direct knowledge the supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness—entered upon and dwelt in that goal. He understood: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of existence.” And Venerable Anuruddha became one of the Arahants. Then Venerable Anuruddha, having attained Arahantship at that time, recited these verses:
translations.an8.30:23: “Knowing my thought,  the unsurpassed teacher in the world;  With a mind-made body,  he approached by psychic power.
translations.an8.30:24: As my thought was,  he taught something further;  The Buddha, a lover of non-proliferation,  taught non-proliferation.
translations.an8.30:3: “Good, good, Anuruddha. It is good of you, Anuruddha, that you thought this thought of a great person: ‘This Dhamma is for one with few desires, not for one with many desires; this Dhamma is for one who is content, not for one who is discontent; this Dhamma is for one who loves solitude, not for one who delights in company; this Dhamma is for one who has aroused energy, not for one who is lazy; this Dhamma is for one who has established mindfulness, not for one whose mindfulness is confused; this Dhamma is for one who is concentrated, not for one who is not concentrated; this Dhamma is for one who is wise, not for one who is unwise.’ Therefore, Anuruddha, you should also think this eighth thought of a great person: ‘This Dhamma is for one who delights in non-proliferation and is a lover of non-proliferation, not for one who delights in proliferation and is a lover of proliferation.’
translations.an8.30:4: When you, Anuruddha, think these eight thoughts of a great person, then you, Anuruddha, will desire as much as to enter upon and dwell in the first jhāna, which is secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, with applied and sustained thought, and with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
translations.an8.30:5: When you, Anuruddha, think these eight thoughts of a great person, then you, Anuruddha, will desire as much as to enter upon and dwell in the second jhāna, which has the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, with inner confidence and unification of mind, without applied and sustained thought, and with rapture and pleasure born of concentration.
translations.an8.30:6: When you, Anuruddha, think these eight thoughts of a great person, then you, Anuruddha, will desire as much as to enter upon and dwell in the third jhāna, with the fading away of rapture, dwelling equanimous, mindful and clearly aware, experiencing pleasure with the body, about which the noble ones declare: ‘Equanimous and mindful, one dwells pleasantly.’
translations.an8.30:7: When you, Anuruddha, think these eight thoughts of a great person, then you, Anuruddha, will desire as much as to enter upon and dwell in the fourth jhāna, which has neither pleasure nor pain, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, and with equanimity and mindfulness purified.
translations.an8.39:1: “There are these eight, monks, floods of merit, floods of skillfulness, nutriments of happiness, conducive to a good destination, with happiness as their fruit, conducive to heaven; they conduce to what is desirable, lovely, agreeable, to welfare and happiness. What are the eight? Here, monks, a noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Buddha. This is the first flood of merit, monks, flood of skillfulness, nutriment of happiness, conducive to a good destination, with happiness as its fruit, conducive to heaven; it conduces to what is desirable, lovely, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.
translations.an8.39:2: Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Dhamma. This is the second flood of merit, monks …pe… it conduces to what is desirable, lovely, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.
translations.an8.39:3: Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha. This, monks, is the third stream of merit, stream of skillfulness, nutriment of happiness, conducive to good fortune, resulting in happiness, conducive to heaven; it conduces to what is desirable, lovely, agreeable, to welfare and happiness. There are these five great gifts, primeval, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, not adulterated in the past; they are not adulterated, will not be adulterated, and are not criticized by ascetics and brahmins. What five? Here, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned the killing of living beings, abstains from killing living beings. Having abstained from killing living beings, monks, the noble disciple gives freedom from danger, freedom from hostility, freedom from oppression to limitless beings. Having given freedom from danger, freedom from hostility, freedom from oppression to limitless beings, he is a sharer in limitless freedom from danger, freedom from hostility, freedom from oppression. This, monks, is the first gift, great gift, primeval, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, not adulterated in the past; it is not adulterated, will not be adulterated, and is not criticized by ascetics and brahmins. This, monks, is the fourth stream of merit, stream of skillfulness, nutriment of happiness, conducive to good fortune, resulting in happiness, conducive to heaven; it conduces to what is desirable, lovely, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.
translations.an8.39:7: having abandoned the use of intoxicants that cause heedlessness, abstains from the use of intoxicants that cause heedlessness. Having abstained from the use of intoxicants that cause heedlessness, monks, the noble disciple gives freedom from danger, freedom from hostility, freedom from oppression to limitless beings. Having given freedom from danger, freedom from hostility, freedom from oppression to limitless beings, he is a sharer in limitless freedom from danger, freedom from hostility, freedom from oppression. This, monks, is the fifth gift, great gift, primeval, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, not adulterated in the past; it is not adulterated, will not be adulterated, and is not criticized by ascetics and brahmins. This, monks, is the eighth stream of merit, stream of skillfulness, nutriment of happiness, conducive to good fortune, resulting in happiness, conducive to heaven; it conduces to what is desirable, lovely, agreeable, to welfare and happiness.
translations.an8.40:1: “The killing of living beings, monks, when practiced, developed, and cultivated, conduces to hell, to the animal womb, to the realm of ghosts. The chief result of the killing of living beings, when one has become a human, is short life.
translations.an8.40:2: Taking what is not given, monks, when practiced, developed, and cultivated, conduces to hell, to the animal womb, to the realm of ghosts. The chief result of taking what is not given, when one has become a human, is loss of wealth.
translations.an8.40:3: Sexual misconduct, monks, when practiced, developed, and cultivated, conduces to hell, to the animal womb, to the realm of ghosts. The chief result of sexual misconduct, when one has become a human, is rivalry and resentment.
translations.an8.40:4: False speech, monks, when practiced, developed, and cultivated, conduces to hell, to the animal womb, to the realm of ghosts. The chief result of false speech, when one has become a human, is being accused of lying.
translations.an8.40:5: Divisive speech, monks, when practiced, developed, and cultivated, conduces to hell, to the animal womb, to the realm of ghosts. The chief result of divisive speech, when one has become a human, is the breaking of friendships.
translations.an8.40:6: Harsh speech, monks, when practiced, developed, and cultivated, conduces to hell, to the animal womb, to the realm of ghosts. The chief result of harsh speech, when one has become a human, is an unappealing voice.
translations.an8.40:7: Idle chatter, monks, when practiced, developed, and cultivated, conduces to hell, to the animal womb, to the realm of ghosts. The chief result of idle chatter, when one has become a human, is speech that is not worth taking up.
translations.an8.6:2: For an unlearned ordinary person, monks, gain arises and loss arises; fame arises and disrepute arises; blame arises and praise arises; pleasure arises and pain arises. For a learned noble disciple too, monks, gain arises and loss arises; fame arises and disrepute arises; blame arises and praise arises; pleasure arises and pain arises. What then, monks, is the distinction, the disparity, the difference between the learned noble disciple and the unlearned ordinary person?” “Our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, take refuge in the Blessed One. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would explain the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it.”
translations.an8.6:4: His mind stands encompassed by gain, it stands encompassed by loss, it stands encompassed by fame, it stands encompassed by disrepute, it stands encompassed by blame, it stands encompassed by praise, it stands encompassed by pleasure, it stands encompassed by pain. He is upset by gain that has arisen, and is upset by loss; he is upset by fame that has arisen, and is upset by disrepute; he is upset by praise that has arisen, and is upset by blame; he is upset by pleasure that has arisen, and is upset by pain. Being thus overwhelmed by compliance and resistance, he is not freed from birth, aging, and death; from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. I say he is not freed from suffering.
translations.an8.6:7: Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain; these conditions among people are impermanent, impermanent, and subject to change.
translations.an8.6:8: Knowing this, the mindful wise one reflects on conditions subject to change; desirable conditions do not disturb his mind, nor does resentment arise from undesirable conditions.
translations.an8.7:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had departed. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants regarding Devadatta: “It’s good, mendicants, that a mendicant should review their own downfall from time to time. It’s good, mendicants, that a mendicant should review another’s downfall from time to time. It’s good, mendicants, that a mendicant should review their own success from time to time. It’s good, mendicants, that a mendicant should review another’s success from time to time. Overcome by eight bad qualities, with a mind dominated by them, Devadatta is headed for a place of loss, to the bad destination, to the underworld, bound for hell.
translations.an8.7:2: What eight? Overcome by gain, with a mind dominated by it, Devadatta is headed for a place of loss, to the bad destination, to the underworld, bound for hell. Overcome by loss, mendicants … Overcome by fame, mendicants … Overcome by disgrace, mendicants … Overcome by honor, mendicants … Overcome by lack of honor, mendicants … Overcome by bad ambition, mendicants … Overcome by bad friends, with a mind dominated by them, Devadatta is headed for a place of loss, to the bad destination, to the underworld, bound for hell. It is by these eight bad qualities that Devadatta is overcome, with a mind dominated by them, and is headed for a place of loss, to the bad destination, to the underworld, bound for hell.
translations.an8.7:3: It’s good, mendicants, that a mendicant should live having overcome gain when it has arisen, having overcome loss when it has arisen … having overcome fame when it has arisen … having overcome disgrace when it has arisen … having overcome honor when it has arisen … having overcome lack of honor when it has arisen … having overcome bad ambition when it has arisen … having overcome bad friends when it has arisen.
translations.an8.8:4: Then Sakka, lord of gods, vanished in the realm of the Thirty-Three and reappeared in the Mahisavana, in the Bamboo Grove, in front of Venerable Uttara. Then Sakka, lord of gods, approached Venerable Uttara, bowed, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of gods, said to Venerable Uttara:
translations.an8.8:5: “Is it true, sir, that Venerable Uttara taught the mendicants this Dhamma: ‘It’s appropriate, friends, that a mendicant should review their own downfall from time to time, it’s appropriate, friends, that a mendicant should review another’s downfall … their own success … another’s success from time to time’?” “Yes, lord of gods.” “Is this Venerable Uttara’s own insight, or the words of the Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha?” “Then I will give you a simile, lord of gods. For by means of a simile some intelligent people understand the meaning of what is said.
translations.an8.8:6: Suppose, lord of gods, there was a great pile of grain near a village or town. A large crowd of people would carry off the grain—in baskets, bags, and in the fold of their arms. If someone, approaching that large crowd, were to ask: ‘Where did you carry this grain from?’ how would that large crowd answer correctly?” “‘We carried it from that great pile of grain,’ is how that large crowd would answer correctly, sir.” “So too, lord of gods, whatever is well spoken is all the word of the Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha. Relying on that, we and others speak.
translations.an8.8:7: “It’s amazing, sir, it’s incredible, how well spoken this is by Venerable Uttara: ‘Whatever is well spoken is all the word of the Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha. Relying on that, we and others speak.’ There is one occasion, sir Uttara, when the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had departed. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants regarding Devadatta:
translations.mn108:1: Thus I have heard. At one time Venerable Ānanda was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrel sanctuary, not long after the Buddha had passed away.
translations.mn108:13: “There are, brahmin, ten inspiring qualities explained by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha. When these qualities are found in us, we now honor, respect, esteem, and venerate them; and having honored, respected, esteemed, and venerated them, we live relying on them. What ten?
translations.mn108:14: It’s when a mendicant is ethical, restrained in the code of conduct, conducting themselves well and seeking alms in suitable places. They see danger in the slightest fault and keep the rules they’ve undertaken.
translations.mn108:15: They’re very learned, remembering and retaining what they’ve learned. These teachings are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased, describing a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure. They are very learned in such teachings, remembering them, reciting them, mentally scrutinizing them, and understanding them with right view.
translations.mn108:17: They get the four absorptions—blissful meditations in the present life that belong to the higher mind—whenever they want, without trouble or difficulty.
translations.mn108:18: They wield the many kinds of psychic power: multiplying themselves and becoming one again; appearing and vanishing; going unhindered through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; diving in and out of the earth as if it were water; walking on water as if it were earth; flying cross-legged through the sky like a bird; touching and stroking with the hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful. They control their body as far as the Brahmā realm.
translations.mn108:19: With the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, they hear both kinds of sounds, divine and human, whether near or far.
translations.mn108:2: Now at that time King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha was preparing to invade the kingdom of King Pajjota.
translations.mn108:20: They understand the minds of other beings and other people. They understand a mind with lust as a mind with lust. They understand a mind free from lust as a mind free from lust. They understand a mind with hate as a mind with hate. They understand a mind free from hate as a mind free from hate. They understand a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion. They understand a mind free from delusion as a mind free from delusion. They understand a constricted mind as a constricted mind. They understand a scattered mind as a scattered mind. They understand an expanded mind as an expanded mind. They understand an unexpanded mind as an unexpanded mind. They understand a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind. They understand an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind. They understand a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind. They understand an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind. They understand a liberated mind as a liberated mind. They understand an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind.
translations.mn108:23: With the destruction of the taints, realizing for themselves with direct knowledge the taintless liberation of mind and liberation of wisdom in this very life, they enter and dwell in it. These, brahmin, are the ten inspiring qualities taught by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the perfectly enlightened Buddha. Where these qualities are present, we today honor, respect, esteem, and revere; having honored and respected, we live depending on them.
translations.mn108:25: Then Vassakāra the brahmin, the chief minister of Magadha, said to Venerable Ānanda: “Where, sir Ānanda, does he live at present?” “I live, brahmin, at the Bamboo Grove at present.” “Is the Bamboo Grove, sir Ānanda, pleasant and quiet, free from noise, suitable for seclusion, and conducive to retreat?” “Indeed, brahmin, the Bamboo Grove is pleasant and quiet, free from noise, suitable for seclusion, and conducive to retreat, just as it is for guardians like you.” “Indeed, sir Ānanda, the Bamboo Grove is pleasant and quiet, free from noise, suitable for seclusion, and conducive to retreat, just as it is for meditators like you who are skilled in meditation. You are meditators and skilled in meditation. Once, sir Ānanda, at a certain time, that Master Gotama was living at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall. Then, sir Ānanda, I approached the Great Wood, the Gabled Hall, where that Master Gotama was. There that Master Gotama spoke on meditation in many ways. That Master Gotama was a meditator and skilled in meditation. And that Master Gotama praised all meditation.”
translations.mn108:28: “It seems, sir Ānanda, that that Master Gotama criticized meditation and praised it. Come then, sir Ānanda, let us go; we have much to do and many tasks.” “Go, brahmin, at the time you think fit.” Then Vassakāra the brahmin, the chief minister of Magadha, having approved and rejoiced in what Venerable Ānanda said, rose from his seat and departed.
translations.mn108:3: Then Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and outer robe, entered Rājagaha for alms. Then it occurred to Venerable Ānanda: “It is too early to go for alms in Rājagaha. Why should I not go to the workplace of the brahmin Gopaka-Moggallāna, to where the brahmin Gopaka-Moggallāna is?”
translations.mn108:4: Then Venerable Ānanda went to the workplace of the brahmin Gopaka-Moggallāna, to where the brahmin Gopaka-Moggallāna was. The brahmin Gopaka-Moggallāna saw Venerable Ānanda coming from afar. Seeing him, he said to Venerable Ānanda: “Come, sir Ānanda. Welcome to sir Ānanda. It is a long time since sir Ānanda has made this opportunity to come here. Please sit, sir Ānanda, this seat is prepared.” Venerable Ānanda sat down on the prepared seat. The brahmin Gopaka-Moggallāna also took a low seat and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the brahmin Gopaka-Moggallāna said to Venerable Ānanda:
translations.mn108:5: “Is there, sir Ānanda, even a single monk who is endowed with all those qualities in every way, with which qualities that Master Gotama was an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha?” “There is not, brahmin, even a single monk who is endowed with all those qualities in every way, with which qualities the Blessed One was an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha. For the Blessed One was the producer of the unarisen path, the bringer-into-being of the unarisen path, the declarer of the undeclared path; he was the knower of the path, the one who understood the path, the one who was skilled in the path. And his disciples now live following the path, endowed afterwards.”
translations.mn108:7: “Is there, sir Ānanda, even a single monk appointed by that Master Gotama saying: ‘He will be your refuge after my passing,’ whom you might follow now?” “There is not, brahmin, even a single monk appointed by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, saying: ‘He will be your refuge after my passing,’ whom we might follow now.”
translations.mn108:9: “Then, sir Ānanda, since there is no single refuge, what is the reason for the unity?” “We are not, brahmin, without a refuge; we have a refuge, brahmin; we have the Dhamma as a refuge.”
translations.mn117:10: There, monks, right view comes first. And how, monks, does right view come first? One understands wrong intention as wrong intention, right intention as right intention; this is one's right view.
translations.mn117:11: And what, monks, is wrong intention? Intention of sensual desire, intention of ill will, intention of cruelty— this, monks, is wrong intention.
translations.mn117:12: And what, monks, is right intention? I speak of right intention in two ways, monks: there is right intention that is tainted, conducive to merit, and a condition for rebirth; and there is right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, and a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:13: And what, monks, is right intention that is tainted, conducive to merit, and a condition for rebirth? Intention of renunciation, intention of non-ill will, intention of non-cruelty: this, monks, is right intention that is tainted, conducive to merit, and a condition for rebirth.
translations.mn117:14: And what, monks, is right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, and a factor of the path? The thought, applied thought, intention, absorption, sustained application, and mental conformation of one who is developing the noble path, whose mind is noble and taintless, and who is endowed with the noble path—this, monks, is right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, and a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:15: They strive to abandon wrong intention and to enter upon right intention; this is their right effort. They mindfully abandon wrong intention, and mindfully enter upon and dwell in right intention; this is their right mindfulness. Thus these three factors surround and circle right intention, that is to say, right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.
translations.mn117:16: In this, monks, right view comes first. And how, monks, does right view come first? They understand wrong speech as wrong speech, and right speech as right speech; this is their right view.
translations.mn117:18: And what, monks, is right speech? I speak of right speech in two ways, monks: there is right speech that is tainted, conducive to merit, and a condition for rebirth; and there is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, and a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:19: And what, monks, is right speech that is tainted, conducive to merit, and a condition for rebirth? Abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from idle chatter—this, monks, is right speech that is tainted, conducive to merit, and a condition for rebirth.
translations.mn117:2: “I will teach you, monks, the noble right concentration with its supports and its requisites. Listen to that, attend closely, and I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn117:20: And what, monks, is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, and a factor of the path? The avoidance, abstention, restraint, and abstinence from the four kinds of verbal misconduct of one who is developing the noble path, whose mind is noble and taintless, and who is endowed with the noble path—this, monks, is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, and a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:22: In this, monks, right view comes first. And how, monks, does right view come first? They understand wrong action as wrong action, and right action as right action; this is their right view.
translations.mn117:24: And what, monks, is right action? I speak of right action in two ways, monks: there is right action that is tainted, conducive to merit, and a condition for rebirth; and there is right action that is noble, taintless, supramundane, and a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:25: And what, monks, is right action that is tainted, conducive to merit, and a condition for rebirth? Abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct—this, monks, is right action that is tainted, conducive to merit, and a condition for rebirth.
translations.mn117:28: In this, monks, right view comes first. And how, monks, does right view come first? They understand wrong livelihood as wrong livelihood, and right livelihood as right livelihood; this is their right view.
translations.mn117:29: And what, monks, is wrong livelihood? Scheming, persuading, hinting, belittling, and pursuing gain with gain—this, monks, is wrong livelihood.
translations.mn117:30: And what, monks, is right livelihood? I speak of right livelihood in two ways, monks: there is right livelihood that is tainted, conducive to merit, and a condition for rebirth; and there is right livelihood that is noble, taintless, supramundane, and a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:31: And what, monks, is right livelihood that is tainted, conducive to merit, and a condition for rebirth? Here, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, makes a living by right livelihood—this, monks, is right livelihood that is tainted, conducive to merit, and a condition for rebirth.
translations.mn117:34: In this, monks, right view comes first. And how, monks, does right view come first? For one with right view, monks, right intention springs up; for one with right intention, right speech springs up; for one with right speech, right action springs up; for one with right action, right livelihood springs up; for one with right livelihood, right effort springs up; for one with right effort, right mindfulness springs up; for one with right mindfulness, right concentration springs up; for one with right concentration, right knowledge springs up; for one with right knowledge, right liberation springs up. Thus, monks, the one in training is endowed with eight factors, the Arahant is endowed with ten factors. And for that one too, by right knowledge, many unwholesome states vanish and reach full development.
translations.mn117:35: In this, monks, right view comes first. And how, monks, does right view come first? For one with right view, monks, wrong view is dried up. And those many unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong view are also dried up for them. Conditioned by right view, many wholesome states reach full development. For one with right intention, monks, wrong intention is dried up … for one with right speech, monks, wrong speech is dried up … for one with right action, monks, wrong action is dried up … for one with right livelihood, monks, wrong livelihood is dried up … for one with right effort, monks, wrong effort is dried up … for one with right mindfulness, monks, wrong mindfulness is dried up … for one with right concentration, monks, wrong concentration is dried up … for one with right knowledge, monks, wrong knowledge is dried up … for one with right liberation, monks, wrong liberation is dried up. And those many unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong liberation are also dried up for them. Conditioned by right liberation, many wholesome states reach full development.
translations.mn117:36: Thus, monks, there are twenty factors of the wholesome side and twenty factors of the unwholesome side—the forty-fourfold exposition of Dhamma has been set rolling and cannot be stopped by any ascetic or brahmin, any deva or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world.
translations.mn117:4: Here, monks, right view comes first. And how, monks, does right view come first? One understands wrong view as wrong view, and right view as right view—that is one’s right view.
translations.mn117:5: And what, monks, is wrong view? ‘There is nothing given, nothing sacrificed, nothing offered; there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no beings who are spontaneously born; there are no ascetics or brahmins in the world who have realized by their own direct knowledge and declare this world and the other world’—this, monks, is wrong view.
translations.mn117:6: And what, monks, is right view? I speak of two kinds of right view, monks: there is right view that is tainted, meritorious, ripening in attachment; and there is noble right view that is taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:7: And what, monks, is right view that is tainted, meritorious, ripening in attachment? ‘There is what is given, what is sacrificed, what is offered; there is fruit and result of good and bad actions; there is this world, there is the other world; there is mother, there is father; there are beings who are spontaneously born; there are ascetics and brahmins in the world who have realized by their own direct knowledge and declare this world and the other world’—this, monks, is right view that is tainted, meritorious, ripening in attachment.
translations.mn117:8: And what, monks, is noble right view that is taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? The wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the investigation-of-dhammas enlightenment factor, and the path factor of right view of one who develops the noble path, whose mind is taintless, who possesses the noble path—this is called, monks, noble right view that is taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:9: One strives to abandon wrong view and to enter upon right view; this is one’s right effort. One mindfully abandons wrong view, and mindfully enters upon and dwells in right view; this is one’s right mindfulness. Thus these three factors surround and circle right view, that is to say: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.
translations.mn118:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, the palace of Migāra’s Mother, together with a large community of elder monks—well-known, distinguished elder monks such as the Venerable Sāriputta, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, the Venerable Mahākassapa, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita, the Venerable Mahākappina, the Venerable Mahācunda, the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Revata, the Venerable Ānanda, and other well-known, distinguished elder monks.
translations.mn118:15: Mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and benefit. Mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the four establishments of mindfulness. The four establishments of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven enlightenment factors. The seven enlightenment factors, when developed and cultivated, fulfill true knowledge and liberation.
translations.mn118:17: Here, monks, a monk, gone to the forest or to the root of a tree or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him, ever mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out.
translations.mn118:18: Breathing in long, he discerns, ‘I am breathing in long’; or breathing out long, he discerns, ‘I am breathing out long’; breathing in short, he discerns, ‘I am breathing in short’; or breathing out short, he discerns, ‘I am breathing out short’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe in experiencing the whole body’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe out experiencing the whole body’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe in tranquilizing the bodily formation’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe out tranquilizing the bodily formation’.
translations.mn118:19: He trains himself, ‘I will breathe in experiencing rapture’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe out experiencing rapture’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe in experiencing pleasure’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe out experiencing pleasure’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe in experiencing the mental formation’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe out experiencing the mental formation’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe in tranquilizing the mental formation’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe out tranquilizing the mental formation’.
translations.mn118:2: At that time the elder monks were instructing and admonishing the new monks. Some elder monks were instructing and admonishing ten monks, some twenty, some thirty, some forty. And those new monks, being instructed and admonished by the elder monks, gained a distinction in both earlier and later times.
translations.mn118:20: He trains himself, ‘I will breathe in experiencing the mind’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe out experiencing the mind’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe in gladdening the mind’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe out gladdening the mind’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe in concentrating the mind’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe out concentrating the mind’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe in liberating the mind’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe out liberating the mind’.
translations.mn118:21: He trains himself, ‘I will breathe in contemplating impermanence’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe out contemplating impermanence’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe in contemplating fading away’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe out contemplating fading away’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe in contemplating cessation’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe out contemplating cessation’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe in contemplating relinquishment’; he trains himself, ‘I will breathe out contemplating relinquishment’.
translations.mn118:23: And how, monks, is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it fulfills the four establishments of mindfulness?
translations.mn118:24: At that time, monks, when a monk is breathing in long, he understands: 'I am breathing in long'; when breathing out long, he understands: 'I am breathing out long'; when breathing in short, he understands: 'I am breathing in short'; when breathing out short, he understands: 'I am breathing out short'; he trains: 'Experiencing the whole body, I will breathe in'; he trains: 'Experiencing the whole body, I will breathe out'; he trains: 'Tranquilizing the bodily formation, I will breathe in'; he trains: 'Tranquilizing the bodily formation, I will breathe out'; at that time, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world. Of these, monks, I say that one is a certain body in the body, that is to say—inhaling and exhaling. Therefore, monks, at that time a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world.
translations.mn118:25: At that time, monks, when a monk trains: 'Experiencing rapture, I will breathe in'; he trains: 'Experiencing rapture, I will breathe out'; he trains: 'Experiencing pleasure, I will breathe in'; he trains: 'Experiencing pleasure, I will breathe out'; he trains: 'Experiencing the mental formation, I will breathe in'; he trains: 'Experiencing the mental formation, I will breathe out'; he trains: 'Tranquilizing the mental formation, I will breathe in'; he trains: 'Tranquilizing the mental formation, I will breathe out'; at that time, monks, a monk dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world. Of these, monks, I say that one is a certain feeling in feelings, that is to say—careful attention to in-breathing and out-breathing. Therefore, monks, at that time a monk dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world.
translations.mn118:26: At that time, monks, when a monk trains: 'Experiencing the mind, I will breathe in'; he trains: 'Experiencing the mind, I will breathe out'; he trains: 'Gladdening the mind, I will breathe in'; he trains: 'Gladdening the mind, I will breathe out'; he trains: 'Concentrating the mind, I will breathe in'; he trains: 'Concentrating the mind, I will breathe out'; he trains: 'Liberating the mind, I will breathe in'; he trains: 'Liberating the mind, I will breathe out'; at that time, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world. I do not, monks, speak of mindfulness of breathing for one who is forgetful and not fully aware. Therefore, monks, at that time a monk dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world.
translations.mn118:27: At that time, monks, when a monk trains: 'Contemplating impermanence, I will breathe in'; he trains: 'Contemplating impermanence, I will breathe out'; he trains: 'Contemplating fading away, I will breathe in'; he trains: 'Contemplating fading away, I will breathe out'; he trains: 'Contemplating cessation, I will breathe in'; he trains: 'Contemplating cessation, I will breathe out'; he trains: 'Contemplating relinquishment, I will breathe in'; he trains: 'Contemplating relinquishment, I will breathe out'; at that time, monks, a monk dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world. Having seen with wisdom the abandoning of covetousness and displeasure, he closely looks on with equanimity. Therefore, monks, at that time a monk dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world.
translations.mn118:28: Thus developed and thus practiced, monks, mindfulness of breathing fulfills the four establishments of mindfulness.
translations.mn118:29: How developed and how practiced, monks, do the four establishments of mindfulness fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment?
translations.mn118:3: At that time the Blessed One was living in the open air surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks on the day of theuposatha, the fifteenth, on the full-moon night of the Pavāraṇā ceremony. Then the Blessed One, having surveyed the silent Saṅgha of monks, addressed the monks:
translations.mn118:30: At that time, monks, when a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world, his mindfulness is established and not lost. At that time, monks, when a monk's mindfulness is established and not lost, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness is aroused in him. He develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, and the enlightenment factor of mindfulness reaches fullness in him.
translations.mn118:31: Dwelling thus, he investigates that Dhamma with wisdom and examines it closely. At that time, monks, when a monk dwelling thus investigates that Dhamma with wisdom and examines it closely, the enlightenment factor of investigation of Dhamma is aroused in him. He develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of Dhamma, and the enlightenment factor of investigation of Dhamma reaches fullness in him.
translations.mn118:33: Rapture non-material arises in one who has aroused energy. At that time, monks, when rapture non-material arises in a monk who has aroused energy, the enlightenment factor of rapture is aroused in him. He develops the enlightenment factor of rapture, and the enlightenment factor of rapture reaches fullness in him.
translations.mn118:34: In one who is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil and the mind becomes tranquil. At that time, monks, when in a monk who is rapturous the body becomes tranquil and the mind becomes tranquil, the enlightenment factor of tranquility is aroused in him. He develops the enlightenment factor of tranquility, and the enlightenment factor of tranquility reaches fullness in him.
translations.mn118:35: When the body is tranquil and one is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. At that time, monks, when in a monk whose body is tranquil and who is happy the mind becomes concentrated, the enlightenment factor of concentration is aroused in him. He develops the enlightenment factor of concentration, and the enlightenment factor of concentration reaches fullness in him.
translations.mn118:36: They carefully examine a mind that is thus concentrated. At that time, monks, when a monk carefully examines a mind that is thus concentrated, the equanimity enlightenment factor arises in that monk, the monk develops the equanimity enlightenment factor, and the equanimity enlightenment factor in that monk reaches full development through cultivation.
translations.mn118:4: “I have undertaken this practice, monks; I have set my mind upon this practice, monks. Therefore, monks, you should make an effort for the attainment of what has not been attained, for the realization of what has not been realized, for the realization of what has not been directly known. I will stay right here in Sāvatthī for the rainy season.”
translations.mn118:40: Thus developed and thus practiced, monks, the four establishments of mindfulness fulfill the seven enlightenment factors.
translations.mn118:41: How developed and how practiced, monks, do the seven enlightenment factors fulfill knowledge and liberation?
translations.mn118:6: And those elder monks admonish and instruct the new monks even more. Some elder monks admonish and instruct ten monks, some elder monks admonish and instruct twenty monks, some elder monks admonish and instruct thirty monks, some elder monks admonish and instruct forty monks. And those new monks, being admonished and instructed by the elder monks, recognize a special excellence before and after.
translations.mn118:9: There are, monks, in this Saṅgha monks who are Arahants, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, destroyed the fetters of becoming, and are completely freed through final knowledge— monks of such a kind, monks, exist in this Saṅgha.
translations.mn11:13: In such a teaching and discipline, monks, confidence in the Teacher is not said to be right entry; confidence in the Dhamma is not said to be right entry; the fulfillment of moral conduct is not said to be right entry; friendship with fellow practitioners is not said to be right entry. Why is that? Because, monks, it is hard to understand in a teaching and discipline that is badly proclaimed, not well proclaimed, not leading to peace, not proclaimed by a Fully Enlightened One.
translations.mn11:14: The Realized One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, monks, declaring the full comprehension of all clinging, teaches the full comprehension of all clinging correctly— teaches the full comprehension of sensual clinging, the full comprehension of view clinging, the full comprehension of habit-and-ritual clinging, and the full comprehension of self-doctrine clinging.
translations.mn11:15: In such a teaching and discipline, monks, confidence in the Teacher is said to be right entry; confidence in the Dhamma is said to be right entry; the fulfillment of moral conduct is said to be right entry; friendship with fellow practitioners is said to be right entry. Why is that? Because, monks, it is easy to understand in a teaching and discipline that is well proclaimed, well proclaimed, leading to peace, conducive to peace, proclaimed by a Fully Enlightened One.
translations.mn11:2: “Here is a recluse, monks; here is a second recluse; here is a third recluse; here is a fourth recluse; there are no other recluses besides these. So, monks, roar the lion’s roar correctly.
translations.mn11:6: There are, monks, two views— the view of existence and the view of non-existence. Those recluses or brahmins, monks, who are devoted to the view of existence, who have entered upon the view of existence, who cherish the view of existence, are opposed to the view of non-existence. Those recluses or brahmins, monks, who are devoted to the view of non-existence, who have entered upon the view of non-existence, who cherish the view of non-existence, are opposed to the view of existence.
translations.mn11:7: Those recluses or brahmins, monks, who do not know as it really is the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these two views, are passionate, angry, deluded, craving, clinging, not seeing clearly, not understanding, opposed to those who see clearly, delighting in proliferation, enjoying proliferation; they do not escape from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair; I say they do not escape from suffering.
translations.mn11:9: There are, monks, four kinds of clinging. What four? Sensual clinging, view clinging, habit-and-ritual clinging, and self-doctrine clinging.
translations.mn12:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was living near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.
translations.mn12:10: Here, Sāriputta, the Realized One understands as it really is what is a condition and what is not a condition. What the Realized One understands as it really is— what is a condition and what is not a condition— this, Sāriputta, is a Realized One’s power of a Realized One. Relying on that power, the Realized One claims the bull’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the Wheel of Brahmā.
translations.mn12:19: Again, Sāriputta, with the destruction of the taints, the Realized One has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells in it. What the Realized One has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells in it— this, Sāriputta, is a Realized One’s power of a Realized One. Relying on that power, the Realized One claims the bull’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the Wheel of Brahmā.
translations.mn12:2: Now at that time Sunakkhatta the son of the Licchavis had recently left this teaching and discipline. In the assembly at Vesālī he spoke as follows: “There is no superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, in the ascetic Gotama. The ascetic Gotama teaches a Dhamma hammered out by reasoning, following inquiry, self-made. And for the sake of which that Dhamma was taught, it leads only to the destruction of reasoning, not to the complete destruction of suffering.”
translations.mn12:20: These, Sāriputta, are the ten powers of a Realized One. Possessed of these powers, the Realized One claims the bull’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the Wheel of Brahmā.
translations.mn12:22: There are, Sāriputta, four kinds of confidence of the Realized One. Possessed of these kinds of confidence, the Realized One claims the bull’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the Wheel of Brahmā. What four?
translations.mn12:23: 'While he claims to be a perfectly awakened Buddha, these teachings have not been fully understood by him.' I do not perceive any sign, Sāriputta, that any ascetic or brahmin, god or Māra, Brahmā or anyone in the world would rebuke me on this ground together with truth. Not perceiving this sign, Sāriputta, I dwell at ease, fearless, and confident.
translations.mn12:24: 'While he claims to be one with taints destroyed, these taints are not fully exhausted.' I do not perceive any sign, Sāriputta, that any ascetic or brahmin, god or Māra, Brahmā or anyone in the world would rebuke me on this ground together with truth. Not perceiving this sign, Sāriputta, I dwell at ease, fearless, and confident.
translations.mn12:25: 'Those things that are obstructive have been taught, but by practicing them one is not free from obstruction.' I do not perceive any sign, Sāriputta, that any ascetic or brahmin, god or Māra, Brahmā or anyone in the world would rebuke me on this ground together with truth. Not perceiving this sign, Sāriputta, I dwell at ease, fearless, and confident.
translations.mn12:26: 'The teaching for whose sake it was taught does not lead one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.' I do not perceive any sign, Sāriputta, that any ascetic or brahmin, god or Māra, Brahmā or anyone in the world would rebuke me on this ground together with truth. Not perceiving this sign, Sāriputta, I dwell at ease, fearless, and confident.
translations.mn12:32: There are these four origins, Sāriputta. What four? Egg-born origin, womb-born origin, moisture-born origin, and spontaneous origin.
translations.mn12:33: And what, Sāriputta, is the egg-born origin? Those beings, Sāriputta, who are born by breaking out of an egg shell—this is called, Sāriputta, the egg-born origin. And what, Sāriputta, is the womb-born origin? Those beings, Sāriputta, who are born by breaking out of a membrane—this is called, Sāriputta, the womb-born origin. And what, Sāriputta, is the moisture-born origin? Those beings, Sāriputta, who are born in rotten fish or in a corpse, or in rotten porridge, or in a sewer, or in a stagnant pool—this is called, Sāriputta, the moisture-born origin. And what, Sāriputta, is the spontaneous origin? Gods, beings in hell, some humans, and some beings in the lower realms—this is called, Sāriputta, the spontaneous origin. These, Sāriputta, are the four origins.
translations.mn12:35: There are these five destinations, Sāriputta. What five? Hell, the animal realm, the realm of ghosts, humans, and gods.
translations.mn12:36: I understand hell, Sāriputta, and the path leading to hell, and the practice leading to hell; and I understand that one who practices in that way, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a bad destination, a lower realm, in hell. I understand the animal realm, Sāriputta, and the path leading to the animal realm, and the practice leading to the animal realm; and I understand that one who practices in that way, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in the animal realm. I understand the realm of ghosts, Sāriputta, and the path leading to the realm of ghosts, and the practice leading to the realm of ghosts; and I understand that one who practices in that way, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in the realm of ghosts. I understand humans, Sāriputta, and the path leading to the human world, and the practice leading to the human world; and I understand that one who practices in that way, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn among humans. I understand gods, Sāriputta, and the path leading to the heavenly world, and the practice leading to the heavenly world; and I understand that one who practices in that way, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. I understand Nibbāna, Sāriputta, and the path leading to Nibbāna, and the practice leading to Nibbāna; and I understand that one who practices in that way, with the destruction of the taints, realizes the taintless mind liberation and wisdom liberation in this very life and enters and dwells in it.
translations.mn12:4: That Sunakkhatta, Sāriputta, is an angry foolish man. And that is his angry speech. 'I will speak disparagement,' Sāriputta, is what the foolish man Sunakkhatta says, but he actually speaks praise of the Tathāgata. That is praise, Sāriputta, of the Tathāgata if anyone were to say: 'The teaching for whose sake it was taught leads one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.'
translations.mn12:43: If anyone, Sāriputta, knowing me thus, seeing me thus, were to say: 'There is no higher human state, no distinction in knowledge and vision befitting an ascetic beyond the human state for the ascetic Gotama; the ascetic Gotama teaches a Dhamma hammered out by reasoning, following inquiry, self-originated'—that person, Sāriputta, not abandoning that speech, not abandoning that mind, not abandoning that view, would be cast into hell just as if he were to fall head first. Just as, Sāriputta, a monk of virtuous conduct, concentrated mind, and wisdom would realize another attainment in this very life; so do I declare, Sāriputta, that that person, not abandoning that speech, not abandoning that mind, not abandoning that view, would be cast into hell just as if he were to fall head first.
translations.mn12:44: I recall, Sāriputta, that I practiced the holy life endowed with four factors—I was an ascetic, a supreme ascetic; I was ragged, a supreme ragged one; I was disgusted, a supreme disgusted one; I was secluded, a supreme secluded one.
translations.mn12:46: In this regard, Sāriputta, while I was ragged, layers of dust and dirt accumulated on my body, caked on like a crust. Just as, Sāriputta, on a tinduka seed bowl layers of dust and dirt accumulate, caked on, so too, Sāriputta, layers of dust and dirt accumulated on my body, caked on like a crust. I did not then think, Sāriputta: 'Oh, if only I could rub off this dust and dirt with my hand, or if only someone else would rub off this dust and dirt with my hand.' I did not think thus, Sāriputta. This was the case, Sāriputta, while I was ragged.
translations.mn12:47: In this regard, Sāriputta, while I was disgusted, I would go forward and back fully aware, so that compassion even for a drop of water arose in me: 'Let me not harm any little living creature that has gone astray.' This was the case, Sāriputta, while I was disgusted.
translations.mn12:49: So I, Sāriputta, approaching a cattle pen with tethered cattle and no cowherds, would eat the dung of those young calves and milch cows. As long as my own urine and excrement were not exhausted, I would eat only my own urine and excrement. This was my practice of eating great filth.
translations.mn12:5: For this foolish man Sunakkhatta will not have a following of the Dhamma in me: ‘The Blessed One is an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, the knower of worlds, the incomparable trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’
translations.mn12:50: So I, Sāriputta, would dwell having entered a terrifying forest grove. In that terrifying forest grove, Sāriputta, it was terrifying—anyone without dispassion entering that forest grove would typically get goosebumps. So I, Sāriputta, would dwell in the open air at night during the cold winter nights when snow falls, and in the forest grove by day; during the last month of the hot season, I would dwell in the open air by day and in the forest grove at night. And this unprecedented verse, never heard before, occurred to me, Sāriputta: ‘Soaked and shivering, alone in the terrifying forest, naked, not sitting by a fire, the sage free from craving.’
translations.mn12:51: So I, Sāriputta, would make my bed in a charnel ground, using a skeleton for a pillow. And people, Sāriputta, would come to the charnel ground, some spitting, some urinating, some throwing dust, and even sticking twigs in my ears. But I, Sāriputta, do not recall ever arising a mind of ill will towards them. This was my practice of equanimity.
translations.mn12:52: There are, Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a view and doctrine: ‘Purification comes from food.’ They said: ‘We will live on jujube fruit.’ They ate jujube fruit, jujube powder, drank jujube water—consuming jujube in various ways. I recall, Sāriputta, eating only a single jujube fruit as food. One might think, Sāriputta: ‘The jujube fruit must have been large at that time.’ But that should not be seen in this way. The jujube fruit then was just as it is now. While I was eating only a single jujube fruit as food, my body became extremely emaciated. Just as the joints of eighty-year-old vines or bamboo joints appear knotted and gnarled, so did my limbs and joints appear knotted and gnarled due to the scantiness of food. Just as a camel’s hoof, so did my spine appear bent and crooked due to the scantiness of food. Just as the beads of a string of beads, so did my ribs project and recede due to the scantiness of food. Just as the rafters of an old, dilapidated house appear jagged and rough, so did my hair appear jagged and rough due to the scantiness of food. Just as water-bugs in deep water appear deep, sunken, and hollow, so did the pupils of my eyes appear deep, sunken, and hollow due to the scantiness of food. Just as a bitter gourd, cut raw, appears battered and shriveled by wind and sun, so did my scalp appear battered and shriveled due to the scantiness of food. So I, Sāriputta, thinking ‘I will touch my belly with my spine,’ would grasp my spine, and thinking ‘I will touch my spine with my belly,’ would grasp my belly, but due to the scantiness of food, my belly and spine did not meet. So I, Sāriputta, thinking ‘I will defecate or urinate,’ would fall over right there due to the scantiness of food. So I, Sāriputta, stroking my limbs with my hand to comfort the body, the hair, rotten at the roots, would fall from my body due to the scantiness of food.
translations.mn12:56: Even with that mode of living, that practice, that austerity, I did not reach any superior human state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. Why? Because of not realizing that noble wisdom, by which one realizes noble emancipation, the emancipation of the sage, the complete destruction of suffering.
translations.mn12:57: There are, Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a view and doctrine: ‘Purification comes from transmigration.’ But that transmigration, Sāriputta, is not easy to achieve by me who have not transmigrated in this long time, apart from the Pure Abode gods. If I were to transmigrate among the Pure Abode gods, Sāriputta, I would not return to this world.
translations.mn12:6: For this foolish man Sunakkhatta will not have a following of the Dhamma in me: ‘The Blessed One experiences various kinds of superhuman powers—having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain as if through space; he dives in and out of the earth as if in water; he walks on water without sinking as if on land; sitting cross-legged, he flies through the air like a winged bird; with his hand he touches and strokes the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; he exercises mastery with his body even as far as the Brahmā world.’
translations.mn12:60: There are, Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a view and doctrine: ‘Purification comes from sacrifice.’ But that sacrifice, Sāriputta, is not easy to perform by me who have not performed it in this long time, and indeed it is performed by a king, a wealthy nobleman, or a rich brahmin.
translations.mn12:61: There are, Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a view and doctrine: ‘Purification comes from tending the sacred fire.’ But that fire, Sāriputta, is not easy to tend by me who have not tended it in this long time, and indeed it is tended by a king, a wealthy nobleman, or a rich brahmin.
translations.mn12:62: There are, Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and view: ‘Only insofar as this person is young, a black-haired youth, in the prime of life, in the first stage of life, are they endowed with the highest wisdom and understanding. But when this person is old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, eighty or ninety or a hundred years old, then from that wisdom and understanding, it declines.’ But this, Sāriputta, should not be seen in that way. I, however, Sāriputta, am now old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, eighty years old. Here, Sāriputta, I have four disciples who are a hundred years old, living for a hundred years, endowed with the highest mindfulness, movement, and steadfastness, and with the highest wisdom and understanding. Just as, Sāriputta, a strong archer, trained, practiced, and drilled, could easily shoot a light arrow across a palm grove, so they, with great mindfulness, great movement, great steadfastness, and endowed with the highest wisdom and understanding. They might ask me a question based on the four foundations of mindfulness, and being asked, I would answer them, and they would retain what was answered, and they would not ask me a second time further. Without having eaten, drunk, chewed, or tasted; without having defecated or urinated; and without dispelling sleepiness and lethargy, the Realized One’s teaching of the Dhamma, the Realized One’s exposition of the Dhamma phrasing, and the Realized One’s readiness in answering questions would not be given up. Then those four disciples of mine, a hundred years old, living for a hundred years, after the lapse of a hundred years, might pass away. Even if you were to carry me on a cot, Sāriputta, there would be no change in the Realized One’s wisdom and understanding.
translations.mn12:7: For this too, Sāriputta, will not be a basis for the foolish man Sunakkhatta to find fault in me: ‘The Blessed One, with the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, hears both kinds of sounds—divine and human, whether far or near.’
translations.mn12:8: For this too, Sāriputta, will not be a basis for the foolish man Sunakkhatta to find fault in me: ‘The Blessed One understands the minds of other beings, other individuals; he understands a mind with lust as a mind with lust; he understands a mind free from lust as a mind free from lust; he understands a mind with hate as a mind with hate; he understands a mind free from hate as a mind free from hate; he understands a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion; he understands a mind free from delusion as a mind free from delusion; he understands a constricted mind as a constricted mind; he understands a scattered mind as a scattered mind; he understands an expanded mind as an expanded mind; he understands an unexpanded mind as an unexpanded mind; he understands a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind; he understands an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind; he understands a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind; he understands an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind; he understands a liberated mind as a liberated mind; he understands an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind.’
translations.mn12:9: There are these ten, Sāriputta, Tathāgata’s powers, which the Tathāgata, having attained and realized, claims the foremost position, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the Wheel of Brahma. What ten?
translations.mn135:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s park.
translations.mn135:13: Here, young man, a certain woman or man is not a giver of food, drink, cloth, vehicle, garlands, perfumes, unguents, bed, dwelling, or lamps to an ascetic or brahmin. With that very deed, fully accomplished and fully determined, on the breakup of the body, after death, they reappear in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, in hell. If on the breakup of the body, after death, they do not reappear in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, in hell, but if they come back to the human state, wherever they are reborn they are poor. This is the way that leads to poverty, namely: not being a giver of food, drink, cloth, vehicle, garlands, perfumes, unguents, bed, dwelling, or lamps to an ascetic or brahmin.
translations.mn135:2: Then the young man Subha, Todeyya’s son, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When they had exchanged courteous greetings, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the young man Subha, Todeyya’s son, said this to the Blessed One:
translations.mn135:20: Beings are owners of their actions, young man, heirs of their actions, born from their actions, related through their actions, and have their actions as their refuge. Action divides beings into inferior and superior.
translations.mn135:3: What is the reason, Master Gotama, what is the cause why among human beings, who are human by nature, inferiority and superiority are seen? For, Master Gotama, short-lived people are seen, long-lived people are seen; people with many illnesses are seen, people with few illnesses are seen; ugly people are seen, beautiful people are seen; people of little influence are seen, people of great influence are seen; poor people are seen, wealthy people are seen; people of low birth are seen, people of high birth are seen; foolish people are seen, wise people are seen. What is the reason, Master Gotama, what is the cause why among human beings, who are human by nature, inferiority and superiority are seen?
translations.mn135:4: Beings are owners of their actions, young man, heirs of their actions, born from their actions, related through their actions, and have their actions as their refuge. Action divides beings into inferior and superior. I do not understand in detail the meaning of this brief statement of Master Gotama, which is not explained in detail. It would be good if Master Gotama were to teach the Dhamma so that I might understand in detail the meaning of this brief statement of Master Gotama, which is not explained in detail. Then listen, young man, pay close attention, I will speak. Yes, Master, the young man Subha, Todeyya’s son, replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn135:5: “Here, young man, a certain woman or man is a killer of living beings, cruel, bloody-handed, engaged in killing and slaying, merciless to living beings. With that deed, so complete and so undertaken, on the breakup of the body, after death, they reappear in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, in hell. If they do not reappear in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, in hell on the breakup of the body, after death, but if they come back to the human state, wherever they are reborn they are short-lived. This is the course of conduct leading to short life, namely—being a killer of living beings, cruel, bloody-handed, engaged in killing and slaying, merciless to living beings.
translations.mn135:6: But here, young man, a certain woman or man, having abandoned the killing of living beings, abstains from killing living beings; having laid down the rod and the sword, scrupulous and merciful, he dwells compassionate for all living beings. With that deed, so complete and so undertaken, on the breakup of the body, after death, they reappear in a good destination, in a heavenly world. If they do not reappear in a good destination, in a heavenly world on the breakup of the body, after death, but if they come back to the human state, wherever they are reborn they are long-lived. This is the course of conduct leading to long life, namely—having abandoned the killing of living beings, abstaining from killing living beings; having laid down the rod and the sword, scrupulous and merciful, dwelling compassionate for all living beings.
translations.mn13:10: If, monks, for that clansman striving and making effort, those wealths do not accrue, he experiences sorrow, lamentation, and pain: ‘My wealth does not succeed!’ If, monks, for that clansman striving and making effort, those wealths do accrue, he experiences pain, displeasure, and distress in their protection: ‘How might kings not take my wealth, or thieves not take it, or fire not burn it, or water not carry it off, or disliked heirs not take it?’ While he is thus protecting and guarding them, kings take them, or thieves take them, or fire burns them, or water carries them off, or disliked heirs take them. He grieves, lament, and wails; beating his breast, he weeps and falls into confusion: ‘What I used to have is no more!’ This too, monks, is a danger of sensual pleasures, visible here and now, a mass of suffering, because of sensual pleasures, originating from sensual pleasures, caused by sensual pleasures, for the sake of sensual pleasures themselves.
translations.mn13:11: Again, monks, because of sensual pleasures, originating from sensual pleasures, caused by sensual pleasures, for the sake of sensual pleasures themselves, kings quarrel with kings, nobles with nobles, brahmins with brahmins, householders with householders; a mother quarrels with her child, a child with the mother; a father with his child, a child with the father; a brother with a brother, a brother with a sister; a sister with a brother; a friend with a friend. There, engaging in quarrels, brawls, and disputes, they attack one another with fists, clods, sticks, or knives. There they meet with death, or deadly pain. This too, monks, is a danger of sensual pleasures, visible here and now, a mass of suffering, because of sensual pleasures, originating from sensual pleasures, caused by sensual pleasures, for the sake of sensual pleasures themselves.
translations.mn13:12: Again, monks, because of sensual pleasures, originating from sensual pleasures, caused by sensual pleasures, for the sake of sensual pleasures themselves, having taken a sword and shield, having fitted a bow and quiver, they rush into an arrayed battle, while arrows fly thick and fast, while swords flash. There they are pierced by arrows, pierced by swords, their heads cut off by swords. There they meet with death, or deadly pain. This too, monks, is a danger of sensual pleasures, visible here and now, a mass of suffering, because of sensual pleasures, originating from sensual pleasures, caused by sensual pleasures, for the sake of sensual pleasures themselves.
translations.mn13:13: Again, monks, because of sensual pleasures, originating from sensual pleasures, caused by sensual pleasures, for the sake of sensual pleasures themselves, having taken a sword and shield, having fitted a bow and quiver, they rush into a battle of arrows, while arrows fly thick and fast, while swords flash. There they are pierced by arrows, pierced by swords, splashed with boiling oil, crushed by a pestle, their heads cut off by swords. There they meet with death, or deadly pain. This too, monks, is a danger of sensual pleasures, visible here and now, a mass of suffering, because of sensual pleasures, originating from sensual pleasures, caused by sensual pleasures, for the sake of sensual pleasures themselves.
translations.mn13:15: Again, monks, because of sensual pleasures, originating from sensual pleasures, caused by sensual pleasures, for the sake of sensual pleasures themselves, they engage in bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct. Having engaged in bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct, on the breakup of the body, after death, they reappear in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, in hell. This too, monks, is a danger of sensual pleasures, visible in the next life, a mass of suffering, because of sensual pleasures, originating from sensual pleasures, caused by sensual pleasures, for the sake of sensual pleasures themselves.
translations.mn13:16: And what, monks, is the escape from sensual pleasures? The removal of desire and lust for sensual pleasures, the abandoning of desire and lust for sensual pleasures—this is the escape from sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:17: Those ascetics or brahmins who do not understand as it actually is the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to sensual pleasures: it is impossible that they will either completely understand sensual pleasures themselves or will make others understand them in such a way that leads to the complete understanding of sensual pleasures. But those ascetics or brahmins who do understand as it actually is the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to sensual pleasures: it is possible that they will either completely understand sensual pleasures themselves or will make others understand them in such a way that leads to the complete understanding of sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:18: And what, monks, is the gratification of forms? Suppose there was a girl of the warrior caste, or the brahmin caste, or the householder caste, fifteen or sixteen years old, neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too fat, neither too dark nor too fair—is she, monks, at that time endowed with the beauty of complexion? ‘Yes, venerable sir.’ The pleasure and joy that arise dependent on that beauty of complexion—this is the gratification of forms.
translations.mn13:19: And what, monks, is the danger in material forms? Here, monks, having seen the same sister at another time—aged, decrepit, bent double, crooked, leaning on a stick, going along trembling, ill, past her prime, broken-toothed, grey-haired, wrinkled, with blotched limbs—one would think: 'The former beauty, that complexion, has vanished, the danger has become apparent.' 'Yes, venerable sir.' This too, monks, is the danger in material forms.
translations.mn13:2: Then, in the forenoon, several monks, having dressed and taken their bowls and robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Then it occurred to those monks: 'It is too early to go for alms in Sāvatthī; let us go to the park of the wanderers of other sects.' Then those monks went to the park of the wanderers of other sects; having gone, they exchanged greetings with the wanderers of other sects; having exchanged pleasant and courteous talk, they sat down to one side. When those monks were seated to one side, the wanderers of other sects said this:
