translations.mn13:20: Furthermore, monks, having seen the same sister sick, suffering, gravely ill, lying in her own filth and urine, being lifted up by others, being put to bed by others—one would think: 'The former beauty, that complexion, has vanished, the danger has become apparent.' 'Yes, venerable sir.' This too, monks, is the danger in material forms.
translations.mn13:23-28: Furthermore, monks, having seen the same sister's body cast away in a charnel ground—a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by sinews; a skeleton without flesh but smeared with blood, held together by sinews; a skeleton without flesh and blood, held together by sinews; bones scattered here and there, in different directions—a hand bone here, a foot bone there, a hip bone here, a shin bone there, a thigh bone here, a backbone here, a rib bone here, a breastbone here, an arm bone here, a neck bone here, a jaw bone here, a tooth bone here, the skull like a bowl—one would think: 'The former beauty, that complexion, has vanished, the danger has become apparent.' 'Yes, venerable sir.' This too, monks, is the danger in material forms.
translations.mn13:29: Furthermore, monks, having seen the same sister's body cast away in a charnel ground—bones white in color, the shape of shells; bones heaped up, more than a year old; bones rotten, crumbling to powder—one would think: 'The former beauty, that complexion, has vanished, the danger has become apparent.' 'Yes, venerable sir.' This too, monks, is the danger in material forms.
translations.mn13:3: 'The ascetic Gotama, friends, declares full comprehension of sensual pleasures; we too declare full comprehension of sensual pleasures. The ascetic Gotama, friends, declares full comprehension of material forms; we too declare full comprehension of material forms. The ascetic Gotama, friends, declares full comprehension of feelings; we too declare full comprehension of feelings. What then, friends, is the difference, what is the distinction, what is the diversity between the ascetic Gotama and us—that is, in teaching the Dhamma or in instruction?'
translations.mn13:4: Then those monks neither delighted in nor rejected the statement of those wanderers of other sects; neither delighting nor rejecting, they rose from their seats and left, thinking: 'We will learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One.'
translations.mn13:6: 'Monks, those wanderers of other sects who speak thus should be spoken to thus: "What then, friend, is the gratification in sensual pleasures, what is the danger, what is the escape? What is the gratification in material forms, what is the danger, what is the escape? What is the gratification in feelings, what is the danger, what is the escape?" When questioned thus, monks, those wanderers of other sects will not be able to answer and will fall into confusion. For what reason? Because that is not their domain. I do not see, monks, anyone in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, who could satisfy their minds with an explanation of these questions, other than a Tathāgata or a Tathāgata's disciple, or one who has heard it from them.'
translations.mn13:30: And what, monks, is the escape from material forms? The removal of desire and lust for material forms, the giving up of desire and lust for material forms—this is the escape from material forms.
translations.mn13:32: And what, monks, is the gratification in feelings? Here, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought and filled with the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. At that time, monks, when a monk enters and dwells in the first jhāna, he does not intend for his own affliction, nor for the affliction of others, nor for the affliction of both; he feels only feeling that is free from affliction. I say, monks, that the gratification in feelings is the highest gratification free from affliction.
translations.mn13:36: And what, monks, is the danger in feelings? That feelings are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in feelings.
translations.mn13:37: And what, monks, is the escape from feelings? The removal of desire and lust for feelings, the giving up of desire and lust for feelings—this is the escape from feelings.
translations.mn13:8: And what, monks, is the danger in sensual pleasures? Here, monks, a clansman earns a living by whatever craft—whether by counting, measuring, accounting, farming, trading, cattle-keeping, archery, service to the king, or by a craft—exposed to cold and heat, harassed by mosquitoes and flies, wind and sun, snakes and creatures, dying of hunger and thirst; this too, monks, is the danger in sensual pleasures, visible, a mass of suffering, because of sensual desire, born of sensual desire, a matter of sensual desire, for the sake of sensual pleasures themselves.
translations.mn13:9: If, monks, for that clansman so striving and striving, those riches do not succeed. He grieves, laments, wails, beating his breast, he falls into confusion: ‘My striving is in vain, my effort is fruitless.’ This too, monks, is the danger in sensual pleasures, visible, a mass of suffering, because of sensual desire, born of sensual desire, a matter of sensual desire, for the sake of sensual pleasures themselves.
translations.mn140:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was wandering in the land of the Magadhans and arrived at Rājagaha; he approached the potter Bhaggava; having approached, he said to the potter Bhaggava:
translations.mn140:12: ‘One should not be negligent in wisdom, should guard the truth, should cultivate generosity, one should train oneself in peacefulness’—thus was it said. With reference to what was this said?
translations.mn140:14: And what, monk, is the earth element? The earth element may be internal or external. And what, monk, is the internal earth element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is solid, solidified, grasped, that is to say: head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, membranes, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach, feces, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is solid, solidified, grasped—this is called, monk, the internal earth element. Now both the internal earth element and the external earth element are simply earth element. ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—this should be seen as it really is with right wisdom. Having seen it thus as it really is with right wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the earth element; the mind becomes dispassionate towards the earth element.
translations.mn140:15: And what, monk, is the water element? The water element may be internal or external. And what, monk, is the internal water element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is water, watery, grasped, that is to say: bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints, urine, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is water, watery, grasped—this is called, monk, the internal water element. Now both the internal water element and the external water element are simply water element. ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—this should be seen as it really is with right wisdom. Having seen it thus as it really is with right wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the water element; the mind becomes dispassionate towards the water element.
translations.mn140:16: And what, monk, is the fire element? The fire element may be internal or external. And what, monk, is the internal fire element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is fire, fiery, grasped, that is to say: that by which one is warmed, aged, consumed; that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is properly digested; or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is fire, fiery, grasped—this is called, monk, the internal fire element. Now both the internal fire element and the external fire element are simply fire element. ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—this should be seen as it really is with right wisdom. Having seen it thus as it really is with right wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the fire element; the mind becomes dispassionate towards the fire element.
translations.mn140:17: And what, monk, is the air element? The air element may be internal or external. And what, monk, is the internal air element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is air, airy, grasped, that is to say: winds going upwards, winds going downwards, winds in the belly, winds in the intestines, winds that course through the limbs, in-breath and out-breath; or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is air, airy, grasped—this is called, monk, the internal air element. Now both the internal air element and the external air element are simply air element. ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—this should be seen as it really is with right wisdom. Having seen it thus as it really is with right wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the air element; the mind becomes dispassionate towards the air element.
translations.mn140:18: And what, monk, is the space element? The space element may be internal or external. And what, monk, is the internal space element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is space, spatial, grasped, that is to say: the holes of the ears, the nostrils, the door of the mouth, whereby what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is swallowed; and where it remains; and whereby it passes out of the lower body; or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is space, spatial, hollow, hollowness, aperture, apertural, not touched by flesh and blood, grasped—this is called, monk, the internal space element. Now both the internal space element and the external space element are simply space element. ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—this should be seen as it really is with right wisdom. Having seen it thus as it really is with right wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the space element; the mind becomes dispassionate towards the space element.
translations.mn140:2: “If you, Bhaggava, are agreeable, let us dwell for one night in your workshop.” “I am not, sir, in a position. There is a mendicant who has come for the first night. If he agrees, dwell, sir, as you please.”
translations.mn140:20: Then, only equanimity remains, purified, bright, malleable, workable, and radiant. Suppose, monk, a skilled goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice were to prepare a furnace, heat the opening of the furnace, and take gold with tongs and place it in the opening of the furnace. Then he would blow on it from time to time, moisten it from time to time with water, and examine it from time to time. The gold would become well-refined, thoroughly refined, free of dross, free of impurities, malleable, workable, and radiant. Whatever ornament he wished to make from it—whether a gold chain, an earring, a necklace, or a gold garland—it would serve his purpose. In the same way, monk, then, only equanimity remains, purified, bright, malleable, workable, and radiant.
translations.mn140:23: If they feel a pleasant feeling, they understand: ‘This is impermanent’; they understand: ‘This is not to be indulged in’; they understand: ‘This is not to be relished’. If they feel a painful feeling, they understand: ‘This is impermanent’; they understand: ‘This is not to be indulged in’; they understand: ‘This is not to be relished’. If they feel a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, they understand: ‘This is impermanent’; they understand: ‘This is not to be indulged in’; they understand: ‘This is not to be relished’.
translations.mn140:29: ‘One should not be heedless regarding wisdom, one should guard the truth, one should foster relinquishment, one should train oneself for peace’—what was said was said because of this.
translations.mn140:3: Now at that time a clansman named Pukkusāti, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith in the Buddha, had gone to the potter’s shed for his first lodging. Then the Buddha approached the Venerable Pukkusāti; having approached, he said to the Venerable Pukkusāti: ‘If it is not disagreeable to you, monk, let us stay the night in the shed.’ ‘The shed is roomy, friend. The venerable one may stay as he wishes.’
translations.mn140:30: ‘Where one stands, perceptions do not arise; and when perceptions do not arise, one is called a sage’—this was said. What was this said in reference to?
translations.mn140:31: ‘I am,’ monk, this is a perception; ‘I am this,’ this is a perception; ‘I will be,’ this is a perception; ‘I will not be,’ this is a perception; ‘I will be material,’ this is a perception; ‘I will be immaterial,’ this is a perception; ‘I will be percipient,’ this is a perception; ‘I will be non-percipient,’ this is a perception; ‘I will be neither percipient nor non-percipient,’ this is a perception. Perception, monk, is a disease, a boil, a dart. Having gone beyond all perceptions, monk, one is called a sage. A sage, however, monk, who is at peace is not born, does not age, does not die, does not fall into agitation, and does not crave. For him, monk, there is no basis by which birth might occur; without birth, what would age? Without aging, what would die? Without dying, what would fall into agitation? Without agitation, what would crave?
translations.mn140:32: ‘Where one stands, perceptions do not arise; and when perceptions do not arise, one is called a sage’—what was said was said because of this. You, monk, should remember this brief exposition of the six elements.’
translations.mn140:33: Then the Venerable Pukkusāti thought: ‘My teacher has arrived, the Good One has arrived, the Fully Enlightened One has arrived.’ He rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, bowed with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha: ‘I have committed an offense, sir, I have done wrong, like a fool, a confused person, an unskillful person, in that I did not recognize that I should have addressed the Blessed One as a friend. May the Blessed One acknowledge my offense for me for the sake of restraint in the future.’ ‘Certainly, monk, you have committed an offense, you have done wrong, like a fool, a confused person, an unskillful person, in that you did not recognize that you should have addressed me as a friend. But since you, monk, seeing your offense as an offense, make amends according to the Dhamma, we acknowledge it. This is growth, monk, in the Noble Discipline for one who, seeing an offense as an offense, makes amends according to the Dhamma and attains restraint in the future.’
translations.mn140:34: ‘May I obtain full ordination, sir, in the presence of the Blessed One.’ ‘But do you have a full set of robes and an almsbowl, monk?’ ‘I do not have a full set of robes and an almsbowl, sir.’ ‘The Tathāgata, monk, does not ordain one without a full set of robes and an almsbowl.’
translations.mn140:35: Then the Venerable Pukkusāti, having rejoiced in and approved of the Buddha’s words, rose from his seat, bowed to the Buddha, circumambulated him with his right side towards him, and went in search of robes and an almsbowl. Then, while the Venerable Pukkusāti was going in search of robes and an almsbowl, a stray cow gored him to death.
translations.mn140:4: Then the Buddha entered the potter’s shed, prepared a grass seat in one place, and sat down cross-legged, holding his body erect and establishing mindfulness in front of him. Then the Buddha spent much of the night sitting. The Venerable Pukkusāti also spent much of the night sitting. Then it occurred to the Buddha: ‘This clansman conducts himself in a pleasing manner. Why shouldn’t I question him?’ Then the Buddha said to the Venerable Pukkusāti:
translations.mn140:5: ‘In whose name, monk, have you gone forth? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you approve of?’ ‘There is, friend, the ascetic Gotama, a Sakyan son, who went forth from a Sakyan clan. That Blessed One Gotama has such a good reputation that has spread about: “That Blessed One is an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Happy One, knower of worlds, an unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.” I have gone forth in dependence on that Blessed One. He is my teacher. I approve of that Blessed One’s Dhamma.’ ‘And where, monk, is that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, dwelling now?’ ‘There is, friend, a town called Sāvatthī in the northern countries. That Blessed One is dwelling there now, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One.’ ‘But have you, monk, seen that Blessed One before; and having seen him, would you recognize him?’ ‘I have not, friend, seen that Blessed One before; and having seen him, I would not recognize him.’
translations.mn140:6: Then it occurred to the Blessed One: 'This clansman has gone forth under me. Why should I not teach him the Dhamma?' Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Pukkusāti: 'I will teach you the Dhamma, monk. Listen to it closely and pay attention; I will speak.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' replied the venerable Pukkusāti to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn140:7: '“This person consists of six elements, six contact bases, eighteen mental examinations, and four wrong views; where they stand, perceptions do not arise; and when perceptions do not arise, they are called a sage. One should not be negligent in wisdom, should guard the truth, should cultivate giving up, and should train in peace”—this is the summary of the analysis of elements.
translations.mn146:12: '“Sisters, this simile has been made by me to explain the meaning. This is the meaning here: “inner flesh” is a term for the six internal sense bases, sisters; “outer hide” is a term for the six external sense bases, sisters; “inner sinew, inner muscle, inner bond” is a term for delight and lust, sisters; “sharp stake” is a term for noble wisdom, sisters; that noble wisdom which cuts through, breaks through, goes through and passes through within defilements, fetters, and bonds.
translations.mn146:13: There are, sisters, these seven factors of enlightenment, when developed and cultivated, lead a monk to the destruction of the taints, to the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, realized here and now through direct knowledge, and to dwelling therein. What are the seven? Here, sisters, a monk develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, resulting in letting go. He develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of states ... He develops the enlightenment factor of energy ... He develops the enlightenment factor of rapture ... He develops the enlightenment factor of tranquility ... He develops the enlightenment factor of concentration ... He develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, resulting in letting go. These, sisters, are the seven factors of enlightenment, when developed and cultivated, lead a monk to the destruction of the taints, to the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, realized here and now through direct knowledge, and to dwelling therein.”
translations.mn146:14: Then the venerable Nandaka, having advised those nuns with this admonition, dismissed them: 'Go, sisters; it is time.' Then those nuns, rejoicing and approving of what the venerable Nandaka had said, rose from their seats, bowed to the venerable Nandaka, circumambulated him to the right, and approached the Blessed One; having approached, they bowed to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, those nuns were addressed by the Blessed One: 'Go, nuns; it is time.' Then those nuns, having bowed to the Blessed One and circumambulated him to the right, departed.
translations.mn146:3: At that time, the elder monks were admonishing the nuns in a summary way. The venerable Nandaka did not wish to admonish the nuns in a summary way. Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: 'Ānanda, who is there today to admonish the nuns in a summary way?' 'Venerable sir, everyone has been asked to admonish the nuns in a summary way. But the venerable Nandaka does not wish to admonish the nuns in a summary way.'
translations.mn146:4: Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Nandaka: 'Admonish the nuns, Nandaka; instruct the nuns, Nandaka; you, brahmin, should give a Dhamma talk to the nuns.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' replied the venerable Nandaka to the Blessed One. Then, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, he entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from the alms round after the meal, he approached the King's Grove accompanied by a second monk. Those nuns saw the venerable Nandaka coming from afar. Seeing him, they prepared a seat and set out water for washing the feet. The venerable Nandaka sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, he washed his feet. Those nuns also, having bowed to the venerable Nandaka, sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the venerable Nandaka said this to those nuns:
translations.mn146:5: '“There will be a question-and-answer discussion, sisters. In that case, those who know should say “I know,” and those who do not know should not say “I do not know.” If there is any doubt or uncertainty in anyone, I should be questioned in that matter: “How is this, venerable sir? What is the meaning of this?”' 'Even by this much, venerable sir, we are pleased and confident that Master Nandaka invites us.'
translations.mn147:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Then, while the Blessed One was in seclusion and secluded, this thought arose in his mind: 'Rāhula's deliverance is ripe for the realization of the Dhamma. Why should I not lead Rāhula further to the destruction of the taints?' Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from the alms round after the meal, he addressed the venerable Rāhula: 'Take your sitting cloth, Rāhula; let us go to the Andhavana forest for the day's abiding.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' replied the venerable Rāhula to the Blessed One, and taking his sitting cloth, he followed behind the Blessed One.
translations.mn147:2: Now at that time many thousands of deities were following the Blessed One: 'Today the Blessed One will instruct the venerable Rāhula to the destruction of the taints.' Then the Blessed One, having entered the Andhavana forest, sat down at the root of a certain tree on a seat prepared. The venerable Rāhula also, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side. The Blessed One then said to the venerable Rāhula who was sitting to one side: 'What do you think, Rāhula, is the eye permanent or impermanent?' 'Impermanent, venerable sir.' 'Is what is impermanent suffering or happiness?' 'Suffering, venerable sir.' 'Is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: "This is mine, this I am, this is my self"?' 'No, venerable sir.'
translations.mn148:16: Now, monks, this is the practice that leads to the origination of identity—regarding the eye thus: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self';
translations.mn148:2: "I will teach you the Dhamma, monks, good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, with meaning and phrasing; I will reveal the holy life that is entirely complete and pure. Listen to that, attend closely, I will speak." 'Yes, venerable sir,' those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn148:22: Now, monks, this is the practice that leads to the cessation of identity—regarding the eye thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self';
translations.mn148:3: "Six internal bases are to be understood, six external bases are to be understood, six classes of consciousness are to be understood, six classes of contact are to be understood, six classes of feeling are to be understood, six classes of craving are to be understood.
translations.mn148:34: Dependent on the eye and forms, monks, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, there arises a feeling that is pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. When touched by a pleasant feeling, he does not delight in it, not welcome it, not remain holding to it. The underlying tendency to lust does not lie behind this. When touched by a painful feeling, he does not sorrow, lament, wail, beat his breast and weep, nor fall into confusion. The underlying tendency to aversion does not lie behind this. When touched by a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands it as it actually is: the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in that feeling. The underlying tendency to ignorance does not lie behind this. When he, monks, has abandoned the underlying tendency to lust regarding pleasant feelings, removed the underlying tendency to aversion regarding painful feelings, eliminated the underlying tendency to ignorance regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings, abandoned ignorance and aroused knowledge, he will, in this very life, make an end to suffering—this is possible.
translations.mn148:40: Seeing thus, monks, the learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with the eye, with forms, with eye-consciousness, with eye-contact, with feeling, with craving.
translations.mn149:11: And what, monks, are the things to be fully understood by direct knowledge? 'The five aggregates subject to clinging' should be the reply; that is, the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the mental formations aggregate subject to clinging, the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. These are the things to be fully understood by direct knowledge. And what, monks, are the things to be abandoned by direct knowledge? Ignorance and craving for existence—these are the things to be abandoned by direct knowledge. And what, monks, are the things to be developed by direct knowledge? Serenity and insight—these are the things to be developed by direct knowledge. And what, monks, are the things to be realized by direct knowledge? Knowledge and liberation—these are the things to be realized by direct knowledge.
translations.mn149:2: "I will teach you the great sixfold base. Listen to that, attend closely, I will speak." 'Yes, venerable sir,' those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn149:3: "Monks, without knowing and seeing the eye as it actually is, without knowing and seeing forms as they actually are, without knowing and seeing eye-consciousness as it actually is, without knowing and seeing eye-contact as it actually is, and without knowing and seeing that feeling which arises dependent on eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—as it actually is, one becomes infatuated with the eye, with forms, with eye-consciousness, with eye-contact, and with that feeling which arises dependent on eye-contact. Dwelling infatuated, attached, confused, contemplating gratification, the five aggregates subject to clinging grow in the future. Craving, which is productive of renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting here and there, grows for him. His bodily distresses grow, mental distresses grow; bodily torments grow, mental torments grow; bodily fevers grow, mental fevers grow. He experiences bodily suffering and mental suffering.
translations.mn149:8: Dwelling infatuated, attached, confused, contemplating gratification, the five aggregates subject to clinging grow in the future. Craving, which is productive of renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting here and there, grows for him. His bodily distresses grow, mental distresses grow; bodily torments grow, mental torments grow; bodily fevers grow, mental fevers grow. He experiences bodily suffering and mental suffering.
translations.mn149:9: Knowing and seeing the eye as it actually is, knowing and seeing forms as they actually are, knowing and seeing eye-consciousness as it actually is, knowing and seeing eye-contact as it actually is, and knowing and seeing that feeling which arises dependent on eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—as it actually is, one is not infatuated with the eye, forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, or that feeling which arises dependent on eye-contact. For one who is not infatuated, not attached, not deluded, and who dwells perceiving danger, the five aggregates subject to clinging diminish in the future. Craving, which is a producer of renewed becoming, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting here and there, is abandoned for him. Physical restlessness is abandoned for him, mental restlessness is abandoned; physical torment is abandoned, mental torment is abandoned; physical fever is abandoned, mental fever is abandoned. He experiences bodily pleasure and mental pleasure.
translations.mn19:11: Whatever a monk frequently thinks about and ponders upon, that becomes the inclination of his mind. If a monk frequently thinks about and ponders upon thoughts of renunciation, he has abandoned thoughts of sensual desire, made thoughts of renunciation abundant, and his mind inclines to thoughts of renunciation. If he frequently thinks about and ponders upon thoughts of non-ill will... If he frequently thinks about and ponders upon thoughts of non-cruelty, he has abandoned thoughts of cruelty, made thoughts of non-cruelty abundant, and his mind inclines to thoughts of non-cruelty.
translations.mn19:12: Suppose, monks, in the last month of the hot season, when all the crops have been gathered into the village, a cowherd were to watch over the cows. While staying at the root of a tree or in the open air, he would simply be mindful: 'These are the cows.' So too, for me, mindfulness was established: 'These are the teachings.'
translations.mn19:13: My energy was roused, monks, and was not slack; mindfulness was established and not lost; my body was tranquil and not agitated; my mind was concentrated and one-pointed.
translations.mn19:14: I, monks, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, entered upon and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
translations.mn19:24: This was the third knowledge attained by me in the last watch of the night, monks. Ignorance was destroyed and knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed and light arose—as happens for one who is ardent, resolute, and mindful.
translations.mn19:25: Suppose, monks, there is a great pit of mire in a forest wilderness. A large herd of deer would depend on it for dwelling. Then a man might come along who wants their harm, wants their misfortune, wants their unhappiness. If the path for them were safe, comfortable, and pleasant, he would block that path, open up a false path, set up a dangerous place, and place a decoy. In that way, monks, that large herd of deer would later meet with harm and suffering. Then, monks, another man might come along who wants their welfare, wants their happiness, wants their safety. If the path for them were safe, comfortable, and pleasant, he would open up that path, block the false path, remove the dangerous place, and do away with the decoy. In that way, monks, that large herd of deer would later grow, increase, and flourish.
translations.mn19:26: This simile, monks, I have made to convey the meaning. If the meaning here is this: 'A great pit of mire'—this is a designation for sensual pleasures. 'A large herd of deer'—this is a designation for beings. 'A man who wants harm, misfortune, and unhappiness'—this is a designation for Māra, the Evil One. 'A false path'—this is a designation for the eightfold wrong path, namely: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration. 'A dangerous place'—this is a designation for delight and lust. 'A decoy'—this is a designation for ignorance. 'A man who wants welfare, happiness, and safety'—this is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. 'A path that is safe, comfortable, and pleasant'—this is a designation for the noble eightfold path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. Thus, monks, I have opened up the safe, comfortable, and pleasant path, blocked the false path, removed the dangerous place, and done away with the decoy.
translations.mn19:3: While I dwelt thus heedless, ardent, and resolute, monks, a thought of sensual desire arose in me. I understood thus: 'This thought of sensual desire has arisen in me. It leads to my own affliction, to others' affliction, to the affliction of both; it obstructs wisdom, causes trouble, and does not lead to Nibbāna.' As I considered that it leads to my own affliction, monks, it faded away. As I considered that it leads to others' affliction, it faded away. As I considered that it leads to the affliction of both, it faded away. As I considered that it obstructs wisdom, causes trouble, and does not lead to Nibbāna, it faded away. Whenever a thought of sensual desire arose, monks, I simply abandoned it, dispelled it, wiped it out, and did away with it.
translations.mn19:6: Whatever a monk frequently thinks about and ponders upon, that becomes the inclination of his mind. If a monk frequently thinks about and ponders upon thoughts of sensual desire, he has abandoned thoughts of renunciation, made thoughts of sensual desire abundant, and his mind inclines to thoughts of sensual desire. If he frequently thinks about and ponders upon thoughts of ill will... If he frequently thinks about and ponders upon thoughts of cruelty, he has abandoned thoughts of non-cruelty, made thoughts of cruelty abundant, and his mind inclines to thoughts of cruelty.
translations.mn19:7: Suppose, monks, a cowherd were guarding cows in the last month of the rainy season, in the autumn, when the crops are thick. He would strike them with a stick from time to time, turn them back, hem them in, and corral them. Why is that? Because that cowherd, monks, sees that from that cause comes death, bondage, or reproach. So too, monks, I saw the drawback, danger, and defilement of unwholesome states, and the benefit of renunciation as a cleansing factor for wholesome states.
translations.mn19:8: As I dwelt thus heedful, ardent, and resolute, monks, a thought of renunciation arose in me. I understood it thus: ‘This thought of renunciation has arisen in me. It does not lead to my own affliction, nor to the affliction of others, nor to the affliction of both; it aids wisdom, does not cause obstacles, and leads to Nibbāna.’ If I were to attend to that thought, monks, even by night or by day, I would not perceive any danger on that account. If I were to attend to that thought, monks, even by day or by night, I would not perceive any danger on that account. If I were to attend to that thought, monks, both day and night, I would not perceive any danger on that account. But as I attended to it and pondered it for a long time, my body became weary. When the body was weary, my mind became disturbed. And when the mind was disturbed, it drew far from concentration. So I steadied, settled, unified, and concentrated my mind internally. Why? ‘So that my mind would not be disturbed.’
translations.mn1:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was living at Ukkatthā in the Subhaga Forest at the root of a sāla tree. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks.” “Venerable sir,” those monks replied. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn1:10: They perceive Brahmā as Brahmā; having perceived Brahmā as Brahmā, they conceive it as Brahmā, they conceive it in Brahmā, they conceive it as belonging to Brahmā, they conceive it as ‘mine’, they delight in Brahmā. Why is that? I say that it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:11: They perceive the Radiant Gods as Radiant Gods; having perceived the Radiant Gods as Radiant Gods, they conceive them as Radiant Gods, they conceive them in Radiant Gods, they conceive them as belonging to Radiant Gods, they conceive them as ‘mine’, they delight in Radiant Gods. Why is that? I say that it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:123: That monk too, monks, who is an arahant, with taints destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached the true goal, destroyed the fetters of becoming, and is completely liberated through final knowledge— he too directly knows earth as earth; having directly known earth as earth, he does not conceive it as earth, he does not conceive it in earth, he does not conceive it as belonging to earth, he does not conceive it as ‘mine’, he does not delight in earth. Why is that? Because delusion has been destroyed; because he is free from delusion.
translations.mn1:13: They perceive the Fruitful Gods as Fruitful Gods; having perceived the Fruitful Gods as Fruitful Gods, they conceive them as Fruitful Gods, they conceive them in Fruitful Gods, they conceive them as belonging to Fruitful Gods, they conceive them as ‘mine’, they delight in Fruitful Gods. Why is that? I say that it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:14: They perceive the Conquerors as Conquerors; having perceived the Conquerors as Conquerors, they conceive them as Conquerors, they conceive them in Conquerors, they conceive them as belonging to Conquerors, they conceive them as ‘mine’, they delight in Conquerors. Why is that? I say that it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:147: The Tathāgata too, monks, an arahant, fully enlightened, directly knows earth as earth; having directly known earth as earth, he does not conceive it as earth, he does not conceive it in earth, he does not conceive it as belonging to earth, he does not conceive it as ‘mine’, he does not delight in earth. Why is that? I say that it is fully understood in the case of the Tathāgata.
translations.mn1:171: The Tathāgata too, monks, an arahant, fully enlightened, directly knows earth as earth; having directly known earth as earth, he does not conceive it as earth, he does not conceive it in earth, he does not conceive it as belonging to earth, he does not conceive it as ‘mine’, he does not delight in earth. Why is that? ‘Craving is the root of suffering’— knowing this, ‘that is birth, the coming-to-be of what is, old age and death’. Therefore, monks, I say that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to the unexcelled right self-awakening through the destruction of craving, the fading away of craving, the cessation of craving, the giving up and relinquishing of craving.
translations.mn1:19: They perceive the seen as the seen; having perceived the seen as the seen, they conceive it as the seen, they conceive it in the seen, they conceive it as belonging to the seen, they conceive it as ‘mine’, they delight in the seen. Why is that? I say that it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:2: “I will teach you the exposition of the root of all things, monks. Listen to that, attend closely, and I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn1:20: They perceive the heard as the heard; having perceived the heard as the heard, they conceive it as the heard, they conceive it in the heard, they conceive it as belonging to the heard, they conceive it as ‘mine’, they delight in the heard. Why is that? I say that it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:22: They perceive the sensed as the sensed; having perceived the sensed as the sensed, they conceive it as the sensed, they conceive it in the sensed, they conceive it as belonging to the sensed, they conceive it as ‘mine’, they delight in the sensed. Why is that? I say that it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:23: They perceive oneness as oneness; having perceived oneness as oneness, they conceive it as oneness, they conceive it in oneness, they conceive it as belonging to oneness, they conceive it as ‘mine’, they delight in oneness. Why is that? I say that it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:24: They perceive diversity as diversity; having perceived diversity as diversity, they conceive it as diversity, they conceive it in diversity, they conceive it as belonging to diversity, they conceive it as ‘mine’, they delight in diversity. Why is that? I say that it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:25: They perceive the all as the all; having perceived the all as the all, they conceive it as the all, they conceive it in the all, they conceive it as belonging to the all, they conceive it as ‘mine’, they delight in the all. Why is that? I say that it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:27: That monk too, monks, who is a learner, not yet attained to the goal, aspiring to the unexcelled security from bondage, directly knows earth as earth; having directly known earth as earth, he does not conceive it as earth, he does not conceive it in earth, he does not conceive it as belonging to earth, he does not conceive it as ‘mine’, he does not delight in earth. Why is that? I say that it is to be fully understood.
translations.mn1:3: “Here, bhikkhus, an untaught ordinary person, who has not seen the noble ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, untrained in the Dhamma of the noble ones, who has not seen the good persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the good persons, untrained in the Dhamma of the good persons— perceives earth as earth; having perceived earth as earth, he conceives [of] earth, he conceives [in] earth, he conceives [from] earth, he conceives 'earth is mine', he delights in earth.  Why is that?  I say that it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:4: He perceives water as water; having perceived water as water, he conceives [of] water, he conceives [in] water, he conceives [from] water, he conceives 'water is mine', he delights in water.  Why is that?  I say that it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:5: He perceives fire as fire; having perceived fire as fire, he conceives [of] fire, he conceives [in] fire, he conceives [from] fire, he conceives 'fire is mine', he delights in fire.  Why is that?  I say that it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:51: That bhikkhu too, bhikkhus, who is an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached the true goal, destroyed the fetters of becoming, and is completely liberated through final knowledge— he too perceives earth as earth; having directly known earth as earth, he does not conceive [of] earth, he does not conceive [in] earth, he does not conceive [from] earth, he does not conceive 'earth is mine', he does not delight in earth.  Why is that?  I say that it is fully understood.
translations.mn1:7: He perceives beings as beings; having perceived beings as beings, he conceives [of] beings, he conceives [in] beings, he conceives [from] beings, he conceives 'beings are mine', he delights in beings.  Why is that?  I say that it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:8: He perceives gods as gods; having perceived gods as gods, he conceives [of] gods, he conceives [in] gods, he conceives [from] gods, he conceives 'gods are mine', he delights in gods.  Why is that?  I say that it is not fully understood.
translations.mn1:9: He perceives Brahmā as Brahmā; having perceived Brahmā as Brahmā, he conceives [of] Brahmā, he conceives [in] Brahmā, he conceives [from] Brahmā, he conceives 'Brahmā is mine', he delights in Brahmā.  Why is that?  I say that it is not fully understood.
translations.mn20:2: “A bhikkhu who is devoted to higher mind, bhikkhus, should attend to five signs from time to time.  What five?
translations.mn22:12: Therefore, bhikkhus, you should understand the meaning of what I have said, and you should remember it.  But of what I have said whose meaning you should not understand, I should be questioned about that, or those learned bhikkhus.
translations.mn22:14: I have taught you the Dhamma, bhikkhus, by the simile of a raft; for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping.  You, understanding the simile of the raft, should let go even the Dhammas, to say nothing of what is not Dhamma.
translations.mn22:18: When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One:  “Is there, venerable sir, anxiety when there is something external?”  “There is, bhikkhu,” the Blessed One said.  “Here, bhikkhu, it occurs to a certain person:  ‘It was for me, but it is not for me now; if only it were for me, I would get it.’  He sorrows, laments, grieves, beats his breast, and becomes distraught.  Thus, bhikkhu, there is anxiety when there is something external.”
translations.mn22:19: “Is there, venerable sir, no anxiety when there is something external?”  “There is, bhikkhu,” the Blessed One said.  “Here, bhikkhu, it does not occur to a certain person:  ‘It was for me, but it is not for me now; if only it were for me, I would get it.’  He does not sorrow, he does not lament, he does not grieve, he does not beat his breast, and he does not become distraught.  Thus, bhikkhu, there is no anxiety when there is something external.”
translations.mn22:20: “Is there, venerable sir, anxiety when there is something internal?”  “There is, bhikkhu,” the Blessed One said.  “Here, bhikkhu, a certain person has this view:  ‘This world is the self; after death I will be permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change; I will stay the same for eternity.’  He hears the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata teaching the Dhamma for the uprooting of all speculative views, for the ending of all mental fermentations, for the abandoning of all attachments, for the destruction of craving, for dispassion, for cessation, for Nibbāna.  Then he thinks:  ‘I will be annihilated, I will be destroyed, I will be no more.’  He sorrows, laments, grieves, beats his breast, and becomes distraught.  Thus, bhikkhu, there is anxiety when there is something internal.”
translations.mn22:23: Take, bhikkhus, that clinging to self which, when clung to, would not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair.  Do you see, bhikkhus, that clinging to self which, when clung to, would not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair?”  “No, venerable sir.”  “Good, bhikkhus. I too, bhikkhus, do not see that clinging to self which, when clung to, would not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair.
translations.mn22:24: Take, bhikkhus, that dependence on view which, when depended upon, would not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair.  Do you see, bhikkhus, that dependence on view which, when depended upon, would not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair?”  “No, venerable sir.”  “Good, bhikkhus. I too, bhikkhus, do not see that dependence on view which, when depended upon, would not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair.
translations.mn22:25: When there is self, bhikkhus, would there be [the thought] 'my self'?”  “Yes, venerable sir.”  “When there is what belongs to self, bhikkhus, would there be [the thought] 'I am'?”  “Yes, venerable sir.”  “Since self and what belongs to self are not found in reality and truth, and that speculative view— 'This world is the self; after death I will be permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change; I will stay the same for eternity'— is this not, bhikkhus, entirely a doctrine of fools?”  “What else could it be, venerable sir? It is entirely, venerable sir, a doctrine of fools.”
translations.mn22:27: “Therefore, bhikkhus, whatever form—past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—should all be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Whatever feeling … whatever perception … whatever formations … whatever consciousness—past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—should all be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’
translations.mn22:28: Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple grows disillusioned with form, with feeling, with perception, with formations, with consciousness.
translations.mn22:29: Being disillusioned, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated; when liberated, there is the knowledge: ‘I am liberated.’ One understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.’
translations.mn22:30: This is called, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has thrown off the crossbar, who has destroyed the corral, who has pulled up the post, who has broken the barrier, a noble one with the banner lowered, the burden deposited, the fetter undone.
translations.mn22:31: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has thrown off the crossbar? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s ignorance has been abandoned, its root destroyed, made like a palm stump, deprived of conditions, not to arise in the future. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu is one who has thrown off the crossbar.
translations.mn22:32: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has destroyed the corral? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s round of rebirth in the lower realms has been abandoned, its root destroyed, made like a palm stump, deprived of conditions, not to arise in the future. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu is one who has destroyed the corral.
translations.mn22:33: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has pulled up the post? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s craving has been abandoned, its root destroyed, made like a palm stump, deprived of conditions, not to arise in the future. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu is one who has pulled up the post.
translations.mn22:34: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has broken the barrier? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s five lower fetters have been abandoned, their roots destroyed, made like palm stumps, deprived of conditions, not to arise in the future. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu is one who has broken the barrier.
translations.mn22:35: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu a noble one with the banner lowered, the burden deposited, the fetter undone? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s conceit ‘I am’ has been abandoned, its root destroyed, made like a palm stump, deprived of conditions, not to arise in the future. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu is a noble one with the banner lowered, the burden deposited, the fetter undone.
translations.mn22:38: If, bhikkhus, others honor, respect, revere, and venerate the Tathāgata, on that occasion the Tathāgata does not feel delight, pleasure, or elation of mind. If, bhikkhus, others honor, respect, revere, and venerate the Tathāgata, on that occasion the Tathāgata thinks thus: ‘For what was formerly understood, causes of that sort are being produced.’
translations.mn22:39: Therefore, bhikkhus, if others should abuse, insult, annoy, and harass you, you should not harbor ill will, annoyance, or resentment of mind there. Therefore, bhikkhus, if others should honor, respect, revere, and venerate you, you should not feel delight, pleasure, or elation of mind there. Therefore, bhikkhus, if others should honor, respect, revere, and venerate you, you should think thus: ‘For what was formerly understood, causes of that sort are being produced.’
translations.mn22:40: Therefore, bhikkhus, abandon what is not yours; having abandoned it, it will be for your welfare and happiness for a long time.
translations.mn22:42: So, bhikkhus, the Dhamma has been well proclaimed by me—revealed, uncovered, stripped of the patchwork. In this Dhamma that has been well proclaimed by me—revealed, uncovered, stripped of the patchwork—for those bhikkhus who are arahants, taintless, possessing the holy life, having done what had to be done, laid down the burden, attained the goal, destroyed the fetters of becoming, and are liberated by right knowledge, there is no future round of rebirth to be indicated.
translations.mn22:43: So, bhikkhus, the Dhamma has been well proclaimed by me—revealed, uncovered, stripped of the patchwork. In this Dhamma that has been well proclaimed by me—revealed, uncovered, stripped of the patchwork—for those bhikkhus whose five lower fetters have been abandoned, all of them are spontaneously born, there they become fully extinguished, not liable to return from that world.
translations.mn22:44: So, bhikkhus, the Dhamma has been well proclaimed by me—revealed, uncovered, stripped of the patchwork. In this Dhamma that has been well proclaimed by me—revealed, uncovered, stripped of the patchwork—for those bhikkhus whose three fetters have been abandoned, and lust, hatred, and delusion have become attenuated, all of them are once-returners who, having returned to this world only once, will make an end of suffering.
translations.mn22:45: So, bhikkhus, the Dhamma has been well proclaimed by me—revealed, uncovered, stripped of the patchwork. In this Dhamma that has been well proclaimed by me—revealed, uncovered, stripped of the patchwork—for those bhikkhus whose three fetters have been abandoned, all of them are stream-enterers, not liable to fall away, destined for enlightenment.
translations.mn22:46: So, bhikkhus, the Dhamma has been well proclaimed by me—revealed, uncovered, stripped of the patchwork. In this Dhamma that has been well proclaimed by me—revealed, uncovered, stripped of the patchwork—for those bhikkhus who are Dhamma-followers and faith-followers, all of them are destined for enlightenment.
translations.mn22:6: “From whom do you know, foolish man, that I have taught the Dhamma like this?  Have I not, foolish man, in many ways described sensual pleasures as obstructive, as obstacles?  And it is enough for you to indulge in them for your own harm.  I have said that sensual pleasures give little enjoyment and are fraught with much suffering and distress; the danger in them is greater.  I have said that sensual pleasures are like a skeleton … like a lump of meat … like a torch of dry grass … like a pit of coals … like a dream … like borrowed goods … like a fruit-bearing tree … like a slaughterhouse … like a sword stake … like a snake’s head; they give little enjoyment and are fraught with much suffering and distress; the danger in them is greater.  Yet you, foolish man, having misgrasped the teaching yourself, misrepresent us and dig a pit for yourself, and you produce much demerit.  This will lead to your harm and suffering for a long time, foolish man.”
translations.mn22:7: Then the Blessed One addressed the monks:  “What do you think, monks?  Is this monk Ariṭṭha, who was formerly a dog-leader, sweating and confused in this Dhamma and Vinaya?”  “It could be, Blessed One; but not because of this, Blessed One.”  When this was said, the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a dog-leader, sat silent, dismayed, with shoulders drooping and head down, glum, and unable to respond.  Then the Blessed One, knowing that the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a dog-leader, was sitting silent, dismayed, with shoulders drooping and head down, glum, and unable to respond, said to the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a dog-leader:  “You will surely be known, foolish man, by this very wrong view.  I will question the monks about this.”
translations.mn22:9: It is impossible, monks, that one will indulge in sensual pleasures apart from sensual pleasures, apart from the perception of sensual pleasures, and apart from thoughts of sensual pleasures—this cannot happen.
translations.mn26:10: And what, monks, should be called a state of suffering?  Wife and children, monks, are a state of suffering; male and female slaves are a state of suffering; goats and sheep are a state of suffering; fowls and pigs are a state of suffering; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are a state of suffering.  These, monks, are bases for suffering.  Here, being overwhelmed, infatuated, and bound, one who is oneself in a state of suffering seeks only that which is a state of suffering.
translations.mn26:11: And what, monks, should be called a state of defilement?  Wife and children, monks, are a state of defilement; male and female slaves are a state of defilement; goats and sheep are a state of defilement; fowls and pigs are a state of defilement; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are a state of defilement; gold and silver are a state of defilement.  These, monks, are bases for defilement.  Here, being overwhelmed, infatuated, and bound, one who is oneself in a state of defilement seeks only that which is a state of defilement.  This, monks, is the unrighteous quest.
translations.mn26:13: I too, monks, before my awakening, while I was still a bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, being myself subject to birth, sought what was likewise subject to birth; being myself subject to aging, sought what was likewise subject to aging; being myself subject to illness, sought what was likewise subject to illness; being myself subject to death, sought what was likewise subject to death; being myself subject to sorrow, sought what was likewise subject to sorrow; being myself subject to defilement, sought what was likewise subject to defilement.  Then it occurred to me:  “Why, being myself subject to birth, do I seek what is likewise subject to birth?  Being myself subject to aging … illness … death … sorrow … being myself subject to defilement, why do I seek what is likewise subject to defilement?  Suppose that, being myself subject to birth, having understood the danger in birth, I were to seek the unborn supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being myself subject to aging, having understood the danger in aging, I were to seek the ageless supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being myself subject to illness, having understood the danger in illness, I were to seek the unailing supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being myself subject to death, having understood the danger in death, I were to seek the deathless supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being myself subject to sorrow, having understood the danger in sorrow, I were to seek the sorrowless supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being myself subject to defilement, having understood the danger in defilement, I were to seek the undefiled supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna.”
translations.mn26:14: So I, monks, at a later time, while still young, with black hair, in the prime of life, despite my mother and father weeping with tearful faces, cut off my hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and went forth from the home life into homelessness.
translations.mn26:17: So I, monks, searching for what is wholesome, seeking the supreme state of sublime peace, wandering on tour gradually through Magadha, eventually arrived at Uruvelā, the market town.  There I saw a delightful stretch of land, a lovely woodland grove, a flowing river with a delightful, smooth bank, and a village nearby for support.  Then I thought:  “This delightful stretch of land, this lovely woodland grove, the flowing river with a delightful, smooth bank, and the village nearby for support—this is enough for a young man intent on striving to strive.”  So I, monks, sat down right there—thinking, “This is enough for striving.”
translations.mn26:21: Then, monks, knowing the invitation of Brahmā and having compassion for beings, I surveyed the world with the eye of a Buddha. I saw, monks, while surveying the world with the eye of a Buddha, beings with little dust and much dust, with keen faculties and dull faculties, with good qualities and bad qualities, easy to teach and hard to teach, some living seeing the danger and fault in the next world, and some not living seeing the danger and fault in the next world. Just as in a pond of blue lotuses, or white lotuses, or red lotuses, some blue lotuses, or white lotuses, or red lotuses are born in the water, grown in the water, emerging from the water, not stained by the water; so too, monks, I saw while surveying the world with the eye of a Buddha beings with little dust and much dust, with keen faculties and dull faculties, with good qualities and bad qualities, easy to teach and hard to teach, some living seeing the danger and fault in the next world, and some not living seeing the danger and fault in the next world. Then, monks, I addressed Brahmā Sahampati in verse: ‘Open are the doors of the Deathless to those with ears; Let them show their faith. I do not speak with harshness, The excellent Dhamma among humans.’ Then, monks, Brahmā Sahampati, thinking ‘The Blessed One has opened the way for teaching the Dhamma,’ paid homage to me, circumambulated me to the right, and vanished right there.
translations.mn26:25: Upaka the Ascetic saw me, monks, walking on the road between Gayā and the Bodhi tree. Seeing me, he said this: ‘Your faculties are clear, friend, your complexion is pure and bright. For whose sake have you gone forth, friend? Who is your teacher, whose Dhamma do you delight in?’ When this was said, monks, I replied to Upaka the Ascetic with verses: ‘I am the conqueror of all, the knower of all things, Unstained among all dharmas. I have abandoned all, freed from the destruction of craving, Having realized it by myself, whom could I point to? I have no teacher, No one like me is found; In the world with its devas, There is no one equal to me. For I am an Arahant in the world, I am the unsurpassed teacher; I am the only Fully Enlightened One, Cool and extinguished. I am going to the city of Kāsi, To set rolling the Wheel of Dhamma. In a world become blind, I will beat the drum of the Deathless.’ ‘As you claim, friend, you are an Arahant, an infinite conqueror.’ ‘Conquerors are indeed like me, Those who have reached the destruction of taints; Evil dhammas are conquered by me, Therefore I am a conqueror, Upaka.’ When this was said, monks, Upaka the Ascetic, shaking his head, wagging his tongue, took a side path and left.
translations.mn26:26: Then, monks, wandering by stages, I approached Benares, to the Deer Park at Isipatana, where the group of five monks were. The group of five monks saw me, monks, coming from afar. Seeing me, they arranged themselves: ‘This ascetic Gotama is coming, he is luxurious, has given up the striving, has turned back to luxury. He should not be greeted, nor stood up for; his bowl and robe should not be accepted. But a seat should be prepared, if he wishes to sit.’ However often I approached, monks, the group of five monks were unable to arrange themselves as a group. Some met me and accepted my bowl and robe, some prepared a seat, some set out water for washing the feet. But they addressed me by name and as ‘friend’.
translations.mn26:28: When this was said, monks, I said this to the group of five monks: ‘Do you know, monks, that I have not spoken like this before?’ ‘No, sir.’ ‘The Tathāgata, monks, is an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One. Listen, monks, the Deathless has been attained; I will instruct, I will teach the Dhamma. Practicing in accordance with what is instructed, before long—realizing for themselves here and now what they went forth from the lay life to the homeless life for, that highest goal of the holy life—they will dwell having attained it, having directly known it by themselves.’
translations.mn26:29: I was not able, monks, to persuade the group of five monks. I instruct two monks, monks, and three monks go for alms. What the three monks bring back from alms, we six live on. I instruct three monks, monks, and two monks go for alms. What the two monks bring back from alms, we six live on.
translations.mn26:30: Then, monks, the group of five monks, being advised and instructed by me in this way, being subject to birth, knowing the danger in being subject to birth, seeking the unborn, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna, attained the unborn, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being subject to aging, knowing the danger in being subject to aging, seeking the ageless, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna, attained the ageless, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being subject to illness … being subject to death … being subject to sorrow … being subject to defilement, knowing the danger in being subject to defilement, seeking the undefiled, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna, attained the undefiled, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna. And the knowledge and vision arose in them: ‘Our liberation is unshakable; this is the last birth; there is no more renewed existence.’
translations.mn26:31: These five, monks, are strands of sensual pleasure. What five? Visible forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and arousing passion; sounds cognizable by the ear …; odors cognizable by the nose …; flavors cognizable by the tongue …; tactile objects cognizable by the body that are wished for, desired, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and arousing passion. These, monks, are the five strands of sensual pleasure.
translations.mn26:34: Suppose, monks, a forest track. A man wandering in the forest would see an ancient forest track, an ancient road traveled by people of old. He would follow it and would see an ancient city, an ancient capital inhabited by people of old, complete with parks, groves, ponds, and ramparts, a delightful place. Then the man would inform the king or the king’s minister: ‘Sire, I should know that while wandering in the forest I saw an ancient forest track, an ancient road traveled by people of old. I followed it and saw an ancient city, an ancient capital inhabited by people of old, complete with parks, groves, ponds, and ramparts, a delightful place. Sire, rebuild that city!’ Then the king or the king’s minister would rebuild the city, and some time later it would become powerful and prosperous, well populated, filled with people, attained to growth and expansion. So too, monks, I saw an ancient path, an ancient road traveled by the fully enlightened Buddhas of the past. And what is that ancient path, that ancient road? It is just this noble eightfold path; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. I followed that path and by doing so I directly knew aging-and-death, its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation. I directly knew birth… existence… clinging… craving… feeling… contact… the six sense bases… name-and-form… consciousness… volitional formations. I directly knew volitional formations, their origin, their cessation, and the way leading to their cessation. Knowing and seeing thus, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of being, and from the taint of ignorance. When it was liberated there came the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’ I directly knew: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.’
translations.mn26:35: Furthermore, monks, a monk, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, entering upon and dwelling in the second jhana, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind without applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. This is called, monks… the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:36: Furthermore, monks, a monk, with the fading away of rapture, dwelling in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing pleasure with the body, he enters upon and dwells in the third jhana, of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, one who dwells in pleasure.’ This is called, monks… the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:37: Furthermore, monks, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and grief, he enters upon and dwells in the fourth jhana, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. This is called, monks… the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:38: Furthermore, monks, a monk, by completely surmounting the base of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite,’ he enters upon and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness. This is called, monks… the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:39: Furthermore, monks, a monk, by completely surmounting the base of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing,’ he enters upon and dwells in the base of nothingness. This is called, monks… the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:4: Then the Blessed One went to the hermitage of the Brahmin Rammaka. At that time several monks were sitting together in the hermitage of the Brahmin Rammaka engaged in a Dhamma discussion. Then the Blessed One stood at the door waiting for the conversation to end. When the Blessed One knew that the conversation had ended, he knocked on the bar. The monks opened the door for the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One entered the hermitage of the Brahmin Rammaka and sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, what was your conversation just now as you were sitting together? And what was the discussion that was interrupted?” “Sir, the conversation was about the Dhamma with you as the subject, and then the Blessed One arrived.” “Good, monks. It is fitting, monks, for you clansmen who have gone forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness, that you should sit together engaged in Dhamma discussion. When you have assembled, monks, there are two things to be done: either Dhamma discussion or noble silence.
translations.mn26:40: Furthermore, monks, a monk, by completely surmounting the base of nothingness, he enters upon and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is called, monks… the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:41: Furthermore, monks, a monk, by completely surmounting the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters upon and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. This is called, monks… the Wicked One.
translations.mn26:5: There are, monks, two searches: the noble search and the ignoble search. And what, monks, is the ignoble search? Here, monks, being oneself subject to birth, one searches for that which is subject to birth; being oneself subject to aging, one searches for that which is subject to aging; being oneself subject to illness, one searches for that which is subject to illness; being oneself subject to death, one searches for that which is subject to death; being oneself subject to sorrow, one searches for that which is subject to sorrow; being oneself subject to defilement, one searches for that which is subject to defilement.
translations.mn26:6: And what, monks, is subject to birth? Wife and children, monks, are subject to birth; male and female slaves are subject to birth; goats and sheep are subject to birth; chickens and pigs are subject to birth; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to birth; gold and silver are subject to birth. These, monks, are the supports for what is subject to birth. Here, being trapped, deluded, and overwhelmed, being oneself subject to birth, one searches for that which is subject to birth.
translations.mn27:12: A householder or a householder’s son or someone born in some other clan hears that Dhamma. On hearing the Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata. Possessing that faith, he reflects thus: ‘Household life is crowded and dusty; life gone forth is wide open. It is not easy, while living in a home, to lead the holy life utterly perfect and pure as a polished shell. Suppose I shave off my hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness.’ Then, after some time, he abandons a small or large fortune, a small or large circle of relatives; he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on ochre robes, and goes forth from the home life into homelessness.
translations.mn27:13: Having gone forth in that way, he is a monk who has entered the life of training. Having abandoned the taking of life, he abstains from taking life. He dwells with his rod laid down, his knife laid down, scrupulous, merciful, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings. Having abandoned stealing, he abstains from stealing. He takes only what is given, expecting only what is given. He dwells with a self that is purified. Having abandoned sexual misconduct, he is celibate, living aloof, abstaining from the vulgar practice of sexual intercourse. Having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false speech. He speaks the truth, holds to the truth, is firm, trustworthy, not deceptive to the world. Having abandoned divisive speech, he abstains from divisive speech. What he has heard here he does not repeat elsewhere to break up those people; what he has heard elsewhere he does not repeat here to break up these people. Thus he reconciles those who are broken and supports those who are united; he loves concord, delights in concord, enjoys concord, and speaks words that create concord. Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech. He speaks words that are gentle, pleasing to the ear, affectionate, going to the heart, polite, agreeable to many, and agreeable to many people. Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter. He speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma and the Discipline; at the right time he speaks words that are valuable, reasonable, moderate, and beneficial. He abstains from damaging seeds and plants. He eats once a day, refraining from eating at night, and abstains from eating at the wrong time. He abstains from dancing, singing, music, and seeing shows. He abstains from wearing garlands, using perfumes, and beautifying and adorning himself with cosmetics. He abstains from high and luxurious beds. He abstains from accepting gold and silver. He abstains from accepting raw grain. He abstains from accepting raw meat. He abstains from accepting women and girls. He abstains from accepting male and female slaves. He abstains from accepting goats and sheep. He abstains from accepting fowl and pigs. He abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares. He abstains from accepting fields and land. He abstains from going on errands and running messages. He abstains from buying and selling. He abstains from false weights, false measures, and false scales. He abstains from bribery, deception, and fraud. He abstains from wounding, killing, binding, brigandage, plunder, and violence.
translations.mn27:14: He is content with robes to protect the body and with almsfood to sustain the stomach. Wherever he goes, he takes only his belongings with him. Just as a bird, wherever it flies, flies with its wings as its only burden; so too the monk is content with robes to protect the body and with almsfood to sustain the stomach. Wherever he goes, he takes only his belongings with him. Possessing this noble factor of morality, he experiences within himself a bliss that is blameless.
translations.mn27:15: When he sees a form with the eye, he does not grasp at its signs or features. Since, if he left the eye faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and dejection might invade, he practices the way of its restraint, he guards the eye faculty, he undertakes the restraint of the eye faculty. When he hears a sound with the ear … When he smells an odor with the nose … When he tastes a flavor with the tongue … When he touches a tactile object with the body … When he knows a mental phenomenon with the mind, he does not grasp at its signs or features. Since, if he left the mind faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and dejection might invade, he practices the way of its restraint, he guards the mind faculty, he undertakes the restraint of the mind faculty. Possessing this noble restraint of the faculties, he experiences within himself a bliss that is unblemished.
translations.mn27:16: He acts with full awareness when going forward and returning; when looking ahead and looking away; when bending and extending his limbs; when carrying his outer robe, bowl, and upper robe; when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; when urinating and defecating; when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, speaking, and keeping silent.
translations.mn27:17: Possessing this noble factor of morality, possessing this noble contentment, possessing this noble restraint of the faculties, and possessing this noble mindfulness and full awareness, he resorts to a secluded dwelling: a forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a cave, a charnel ground, a jungle, an open space, or a heap of straw.
translations.mn27:18: After his meal, returning from his alms round, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness in front of him. Abandoning covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness. Abandoning ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind of ill will and hatred. Abandoning sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, perceiving light, mindful and fully aware; he purifies his mind of sloth and torpor. Abandoning restlessness and remorse, he dwells without restlessness; his mind is internally peaceful; he purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse. Abandoning doubt, he dwells free from doubt, without perplexity about wholesome states; he purifies his mind of doubt.
translations.mn27:19: Having abandoned these five hindrances, corruptions of the mind that weaken wisdom, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. This, too, is called the Tathāgata’s path, the Tathāgata’s service, the Tathāgata’s resort. Yet the noble disciple does not come to the conclusion: ‘The Blessed One is a Fully Enlightened One, the Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, the Blessed One’s Saṅgha of disciples is practicing well.’
translations.mn27:2: Now at that time the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi was leaving Sāvatthī during the day in a decorated carriage drawn by white horses.  Jāṇussoṇi the brahmin saw the wanderer Pilotika coming from afar.  Seeing the wanderer Pilotika coming, he said to him:  'Where indeed is Master Vacchāyano coming from during the day?'  'I am coming, sir, from the presence of the ascetic Gotama.'  'What does Master Vacchāyano think of the ascetic Gotama's wisdom and cleverness? Does he consider him wise?'  'Who am I, sir, to know the ascetic Gotama's wisdom and cleverness?  Anyone who knows the ascetic Gotama's wisdom and cleverness would be just like him.'
