'Master Vacchāyano surely praises the ascetic Gotama highly.'  'Who am I, sir, to praise the ascetic Gotama?  The Master Gotama is the best of the devas and humans, praised by the praiseworthy.'  'What benefit does Master Vacchāyano foresee that he is so devoted to the ascetic Gotama?'
translations.mn27:20: Furthermore, brahmin, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells upon the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.  This too is called, brahmin …pe…  the Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples who practice well.'
translations.mn27:21: Furthermore, brahmin, a monk, with the subsiding of rapture, dwells equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing pleasure with the body; he enters and dwells upon the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: 'Equanimous, mindful, one dwells in pleasure.'  This too is called, brahmin …pe…  the Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples who practice well.'
translations.mn27:22: Furthermore, brahmin, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, enters and dwells upon the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.  This too is called, brahmin, the Tathāgata’s footing, so called, the resort of the Tathāgata, so called, the domain of the Tathāgata, so called.  Yet the noble disciple does not conclude:  'The Blessed One is a perfectly enlightened Buddha, the Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, the Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples practices well.'
translations.mn27:3: “Suppose, sir, a skilled elephant-trainer were to enter an elephant forest.  He would see in the elephant forest a large elephant footprint, long in extent and wide across.  He would conclude:  'This is a big elephant, sir.'  So too, sir, when I saw these four footprints in the ascetic Gotama, I concluded:  'The Blessed One is a perfectly enlightened Buddha, the Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, the Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples practices well.'
translations.mn27:4: What four?  Here, sir, I see some skilled khatriyas and brahmins, clever in debating, hair-splitting in their views, walking about with their views.  They hear:  'The ascetic Gotama, sir, will visit such and such a village or town.'  They formulate a question:  'We will approach the ascetic Gotama and ask him this question.  If questioned, he answers thus, we will refute him in this way.  If questioned, he answers thus, we will refute him in that way.'  They hear:  'The ascetic Gotama, sir, has visited such and such a village or town.'  They approach the ascetic Gotama.  The ascetic Gotama instructs, urges, rouses, and encourages them with a Dhamma talk.  Instructed, urged, roused, and encouraged by the ascetic Gotama with a Dhamma talk, they do not question the ascetic Gotama, so how could they refute him?  Only the ascetic Gotama’s disciples appear.  When, sir, I saw this first footprint in the ascetic Gotama, I concluded:  'The Blessed One is a perfectly enlightened Buddha, the Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, the Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples practices well.'
translations.mn27:9: Then the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.  After exchanging courteous and friendly greetings, he sat down to one side.  Sitting to one side, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi reported to the Blessed One all the conversation he had with the wanderer Pilotika.  When this was said, the Blessed One said to the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi:  'Not only to this extent, brahmin, is the elephant-footprint simile fully detailed.  But, brahmin, listen to how the elephant-footprint simile is fully detailed, pay close attention, I will speak.'  'Yes, sir,' the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi replied to the Blessed One.  The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn28:1: Thus have I heard.  At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.  There the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the monks:  'Friends, monks.'  'Friend,' those monks replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.  The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.mn28:10: If, friend, equanimity based on skillfulness does not become established in a monk who recollects the Buddha in this way, the Dhamma in this way, and the Saṅgha in this way, he is agitated and feels a sense of urgency: ‘It is a loss for me, it is not a gain for me; it is difficult for me to obtain, it is not easy for me to obtain, that equanimity based on skillfulness does not become established in me while I recollect the Buddha in this way, the Dhamma in this way, and the Saṅgha in this way.’ Just as, friend, a young woman seeing her mother-in-law is agitated and feels a sense of urgency; so too, friend, if equanimity based on skillfulness does not become established in a monk who recollects the Buddha in this way, the Dhamma in this way, and the Saṅgha in this way, he is agitated and feels a sense of urgency: ‘It is a loss for me, it is not a gain for me; it is difficult for me to obtain, it is not easy for me to obtain, that equanimity based on skillfulness does not become established in me while I recollect the Buddha in this way, the Dhamma in this way, and the Saṅgha in this way.’ If, friend, equanimity based on skillfulness becomes established in a monk who recollects the Buddha in this way, the Dhamma in this way, and the Saṅgha in this way, he is pleased with that. To this extent, friend, a monk has done much.
translations.mn28:12: There is a time, friend, when the external water element becomes disturbed. It carries away villages, towns, cities, districts, and regions. There is a time, friend, when waters flow into the great ocean even a hundred yojanas deep, two hundred yojanas deep, three hundred yojanas deep, four hundred yojanas deep, five hundred yojanas deep, six hundred yojanas deep, or seven hundred yojanas deep. There is a time, friend, when in the great ocean there stands water seven fathoms deep, six fathoms deep, five fathoms deep, four fathoms deep, three fathoms deep, two fathoms deep, or one fathom deep. There is a time, friend, when in the great ocean there stands water seven persons deep, six persons deep, five persons deep, four persons deep, three persons deep, two persons deep, or one person deep. There is a time, friend, when in the great ocean there stands water half a person deep, knee-deep, knee-joint deep, or ankle-deep. There is a time, friend, when in the great ocean there is not even water the size of a finger-tip. For that great external water element, its impermanence will be discerned, its liability to destruction will be discerned, its liability to vanishing will be discerned, its liability to change will be discerned.
translations.mn28:13: Now, regarding this little body of clung-to craving, is there anything here that could be regarded as ‘I am’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I’? Or is it not the case here that …
translations.mn28:14: If, friend, equanimity based on skillfulness becomes established in a monk who recollects the Buddha in this way, the Dhamma in this way, and the Saṅgha in this way, he is pleased with that.
translations.mn28:17: There is a time, friend, when the external fire element becomes disturbed. It burns villages, towns, cities, districts, and regions. Having reached a delightful stretch of land, a forest, a rock, or water, it goes out without fuel. There is a time, friend, when they search for fire even with a chicken’s feather or with a piece of bark. For that great external fire element, its impermanence will be discerned, its liability to destruction will be discerned, its liability to vanishing will be discerned, its liability to change will be discerned. Now, regarding this little body of clung-to craving, is there anything here that could be regarded as ‘I am’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I’?
translations.mn28:18-20: Or is it not the case here that … if, friend, equanimity based on skillfulness becomes established in a monk who recollects the Buddha in this way, the Dhamma in this way, and the Saṅgha in this way, he is pleased with that. To this extent, friend, a monk has done much.
translations.mn28:2: “Just as, friend, whatever foot-born wild animals there are, they all converge on the elephant’s footprint, and the elephant’s footprint is declared to be the chief among them because of its size; so too, friend, whatever skillful qualities there are, they all converge on the four noble truths. Which four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn28:22: There is a time, friend, when the external air element becomes disturbed. It carries away villages, towns, cities, districts, and regions. There is a time, friend, when in the last month of the hot season they search for wind with a palm leaf or a fan, and the grasses do not wish to move. For that great external air element, its impermanence will be discerned, its liability to destruction will be discerned, its liability to vanishing will be discerned, its liability to change will be discerned. Now, regarding this little body of clung-to craving, is there anything here that could be regarded as ‘I am’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I’? Or is it not the case here that.
translations.mn28:23: If, friend, others insult, revile, anger, and harass that monk. He understands thus: ‘This painful feeling arisen in me is born from ear-contact. It is conditioned, not unconditioned. Conditioned by what? Conditioned by contact.’ He sees that contact itself is impermanent, that feeling is impermanent, that perception is impermanent, that mental formations are impermanent, that consciousness is impermanent. His mind becomes established, confident, and settled in the elements as its object.
translations.mn28:24: And if, friend, others treat that monk with what is unpleasant, unlikable, and disagreeable—with a fist, with a clod, with a stick, or with a knife—he understands it thus: ‘This is such a body that, in this very body, blows from a fist, blows from a clod, blows from a stick, and blows from a knife are experienced. For it has been said by the Blessed One in the Simile of the Saw: “Even if bandits were to sever you limb by limb with a two-handled saw, anyone who sets his mind at enmity would not be carrying out my teaching.” My energy will be roused, unslackened; mindfulness established, not confused; my body calm and not aroused; my mind concentrated and one-pointed. Let blows from a fist, blows from a clod, blows from a stick, and blows from a knife befall this very body now. For the teaching of the Buddhas is being done.’
translations.mn28:26: Suppose, friend, there were a space enclosed by stakes, creepers, grass, and clay; it would be spoken of as a space. So too, friend, there is a space enclosed by bones, sinews, flesh, and skin; it is spoken of as a form.
translations.mn28:27: When, friend, the internal eye is not intact and external forms do not come within range, and there is no corresponding attention, then there is no manifestation of the corresponding section of consciousness. When, friend, the internal eye is not intact and external forms come within range, but there is no corresponding attention, then there is no manifestation of the corresponding section of consciousness. But when, friend, the internal eye is intact and external forms come within range, and there is corresponding attention, then there is the manifestation of the corresponding section of consciousness.
translations.mn28:28: That which is actual material form is included in the material form aggregate; that which is actual feeling is included in the feeling aggregate; that which is actual perception is included in the perception aggregate; that which are actual mental formations are included in the mental formations aggregate; that which is actual consciousness is included in the consciousness aggregate. He understands thus: ‘So it is that there is an aggregation, a coming together, and a meeting together of these five aggregates subject to clinging. For it has been said by the Blessed One: “One who sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma; one who sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination.” These five aggregates subject to clinging are dependently arisen. Desire, lust, delight, and clinging regarding these five aggregates subject to clinging is the origin of suffering. The fading away and cessation of desire and lust regarding these five aggregates subject to clinging is the cessation of suffering.’ In this way, friend, a monk has done much.
translations.mn28:3: And what, friend, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair are suffering; not obtaining what one wants is suffering; in short, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering. And what, friend, are the five aggregates subject to clinging? They are: the material form aggregate, the feeling aggregate, the perception aggregate, the mental formations aggregate, the consciousness aggregate.
translations.mn28:37: When the mind is not intact and external mental phenomena do not come within range, and there is no corresponding attention, then there is no manifestation of the corresponding section of consciousness.
translations.mn28:7: There comes a time, friend, when the external water element flares up. At that time the external earth element disappears. For that external earth element, it is evident that it is of great impermanence, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to change. What of this little body of a foot long, bound by craving, that it should be ‘I’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I am’? It is not so here.
translations.mn29:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, not long after Devadatta had departed. There the Blessed One addressed the monks concerning Devadatta:
translations.mn29:3: Herein, monks, a certain clansman goes forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness, thinking: ‘I am beset by birth, aging, and death, by sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair, beset by suffering, oppressed by suffering. Perhaps an end to this whole mass of suffering will be known.’ Having gone forth thus, he generates gain, honor, and renown. He is not content with that gain, honor, and renown, nor is his aspiration fulfilled. He does not praise himself or disparage others because of that gain, honor, and renown. He does not become intoxicated, negligent, or fall into negligence because of that gain, honor, and renown. Being not negligent, he fulfills virtue. He is content with that fulfillment of virtue, and his aspiration is fulfilled. He praises himself and disparages others because of that fulfillment of virtue: ‘I am virtuous and of good character, but these other monks are immoral and of bad character.’ He becomes intoxicated, negligent, and falls into negligence because of that fulfillment of virtue. Being negligent, he lives in suffering. Suppose, monks, a man seeking heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, would pass over the heartwood of a great standing tree, pass over the sapwood, pass over the bark, and cut off the outermost wood and take it away, thinking it is heartwood. A man with good sight seeing him would say: ‘This good man does not know heartwood, does not know sapwood, does not know bark, does not know outer wood. For this good man seeking heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, passed over the heartwood of a great standing tree, passed over the sapwood, passed over the bark, and cut off the outermost wood and took it away, thinking it is heartwood; but what should have been done with heartwood, that purpose of his will not be achieved.’
translations.mn2:10: And what, mendicants, are the things that should not be attended to, and if one attends to them? When attending to such things, unarisen sensual desire arises, and arisen sensual desire increases; unarisen desire for continued existence arises, and arisen desire for continued existence increases; unarisen ignorance arises, and arisen ignorance increases—these are the things that should not be attended to, and if one attends to them. And what, mendicants, are the things that should be attended to, and if one attends to them? When attending to such things, unarisen sensual desire does not arise, and arisen sensual desire is abandoned; unarisen desire for continued existence does not arise, and arisen desire for continued existence is abandoned; unarisen ignorance does not arise, and arisen ignorance is abandoned—these are the things that should be attended to, and if one attends to them. By not attending to things that should not be attended to and by attending to things that should be attended to, unarisen taints do not arise, and arisen taints are abandoned.
translations.mn2:11: They attend wisely: ‘This is suffering’; they attend wisely: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; they attend wisely: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; they attend wisely: ‘This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering’. When they attend wisely in this way, three fetters are abandoned—identity view, doubt, and misapprehension of precepts and observances. These, mendicants, are called the taints to be abandoned by seeing.
translations.mn2:12: 2. The Taints to be Abandoned by Restraint. And what, mendicants, are the taints to be abandoned by restraint? Here, mendicants, a mendicant lives restrained by the restraint of the eye faculty. For mendicants, when living without restraint of the eye faculty, taints of vexation and fever might arise; when living restrained by the restraint of the eye faculty, such taints of vexation and fever do not occur. They live restrained by the restraint of the ear faculty … they live restrained by the restraint of the nose faculty … they live restrained by the restraint of the tongue faculty … they live restrained by the restraint of the body faculty … they live restrained by the restraint of the mind faculty. For mendicants, when living without restraint of the mind faculty, taints of vexation and fever might arise; when living restrained by the restraint of the mind faculty, such taints of vexation and fever do not occur. For mendicants, when living without restraint, taints of vexation and fever might arise; when living restrained, such taints of vexation and fever do not occur. These, mendicants, are called the taints to be abandoned by restraint.
translations.mn2:14: They use almsfood wisely reflecting: ‘Not for fun, not for indulgence, not for adornment, not for decoration, but only to maintain this body, to sustain it, to avoid harm, and to support the holy life. In this way, I will put an end to old feelings and not give rise to new feelings, and I will live blamelessly and at ease’.
translations.mn2:16: They use medicinal requisites for the cure of illness wisely reflecting: ‘Only to remove arisen painful feelings of sickness, to reach the limit of freedom from disease’.
translations.mn2:17: For mendicants, if they did not use them, taints of vexation and fever might arise; but since they use them, such taints of vexation and fever do not occur. These, mendicants, are called the taints to be abandoned by using.
translations.mn2:3: “Mendicants, I declare the destruction of the taints for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see. What does one know and see, mendicants, that I declare the destruction of the taints? Wise attention and unwise attention. When attending unwisely, mendicants, unarisen taints arise, and arisen taints increase; but when attending wisely, mendicants, unarisen taints do not arise, and arisen taints are abandoned.
translations.mn2:6: And what, mendicants, are the things that should not be attended to, and if one attends to them? When attending to such things, unarisen sensual desire arises, and arisen sensual desire increases; unarisen desire for continued existence arises, and arisen desire for continued existence increases; unarisen ignorance arises, and arisen ignorance increases—these are the things that should not be attended to, and if one attends to them. And what, mendicants, are the things that should be attended to, and if one does not attend to them? When attending to such things, unarisen sensual desire does not arise, and arisen sensual desire is abandoned; unarisen desire for continued existence does not arise, and arisen desire for continued existence is abandoned; unarisen ignorance does not arise, and arisen ignorance is abandoned—these are the things that should be attended to, and if one does not attend to them.
translations.mn2:7: By attending to things that should not be attended to and not attending to things that should be attended to, unarisen taints arise and arisen taints increase. They attend unwisely in this way: ‘Was I in the past? Was I not in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what was I in the past? Will I be in the future? Will I not be in the future? What will I be in the future? How will I be in the future? Having been what, what will I be in the future?’ Or they are perplexed about the present right here: ‘Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? Where has this being come from? Where will it go?’
translations.mn2:8: When he attends to things inappropriately in this way, one of six views arises in him. The view arises in him that ‘I have a self’ truly and really; or the view arises in him that ‘I have no self’ truly and really; or the view arises in him that ‘I perceive self with self’ truly and really; or the view arises in him that ‘I perceive non-self with self’ truly and really; or the view arises in him that ‘I perceive self with non-self’ truly and really. Or else he has such a view: ‘This very self of mine that speaks and feels here and there, experiencing the results of good and bad deeds, that very self of mine is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain just as it is for eternity.’ This is called a view, a view-habit, a view-thicket, a view-wilderness, a view-contortion, a view-fetter. Fettered by a view-fetter, monks, the uninstructed ordinary person is not freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair; I say he is not freed from suffering.
translations.mn2:9: A learned noble disciple, monks, who has seen the noble ones, is skilled in the noble doctrine, trained in the noble doctrine, who has seen the good persons, is skilled in the good doctrine, trained in the good doctrine—understands what is to be attended to and understands what is not to be attended to. Understanding what is to be attended to and understanding what is not to be attended to, he does not attend to those things that are not to be attended to, and he attends to those things that are to be attended to.
translations.mn31:10: “Good, good, Anuruddha. But is there, Anuruddha, while you dwell thus heedless, ardent, resolute, a superior human state, a distinction in knowledge and vision conducive to the noble life that has been attained and a comfortable dwelling?” “What else could there be, sir? Here we, sir, as much as we wish, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. This, sir, is our superior human state, a distinction in knowledge and vision conducive to the noble life that has been attained and a comfortable dwelling while we dwell heedless, ardent, resolute.”
translations.mn31:11-13: “Good, good, Anuruddha. But is there, Anuruddha, for the transcending of this dwelling, for the settling of this dwelling, another superior human state, a distinction in knowledge and vision conducive to the noble life that has been attained and a comfortable dwelling?” “What else could there be, sir? Here we, sir, as much as we wish, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, entering and dwelling in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and has rapture and pleasure born of concentration. For the transcending of this dwelling, for the settling of this dwelling, this is another superior human state, a distinction in knowledge and vision conducive to the noble life that has been attained and a comfortable dwelling.”
translations.mn31:14: “Good, good, Anuruddha. But is there, Anuruddha, for the transcending of this dwelling, for the settling of this dwelling, another superior human state, a distinction in knowledge and vision conducive to the noble life that has been attained and a comfortable dwelling?” “What else could there be, sir? Here we, sir, as much as we wish, dwell equanimous and mindful, and with pleasure we experience pleasure in the body; entering and dwelling in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells pleasurably.’ For the transcending of this dwelling, for the settling of this dwelling, this is another superior human state, a distinction in knowledge and vision conducive to the noble life that has been attained and a comfortable dwelling.”
translations.mn31:15: “Good, good, Anuruddha. But is there, Anuruddha, for the transcending of this dwelling, for the settling of this dwelling, another superior human state, a distinction in knowledge and vision conducive to the noble life that has been attained and a comfortable dwelling?” “What else could there be, sir? Here we, sir, as much as we wish, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and displeasure, entering and dwelling in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes mindfulness purified by equanimity. For the transcending of this dwelling, for the settling of this dwelling, this is another superior human state, a distinction in knowledge and vision conducive to the noble life that has been attained and a comfortable dwelling.”
translations.mn31:16: “Good, good, Anuruddha. But is there, Anuruddha, for the transcending of this dwelling, for the settling of this dwelling, another superior human state, a distinction in knowledge and vision conducive to the noble life that has been attained and a comfortable dwelling?” “What else could there be, sir? Here we, sir, as much as we wish, by completely transcending all perceptions of form, by the passing away of the perceptions of impingement, by not attending to perceptions of diversity, entering and dwelling in the base of infinite space, thinking: ‘Space is infinite.’ For the transcending of this dwelling, for the settling of this dwelling, this is another superior human state, a distinction in knowledge and vision conducive to the noble life that has been attained and a comfortable dwelling.”
translations.mn31:19: Then the Blessed One, having instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Nandiya, and Venerable Kimbila with a Dhamma talk, rose from his seat and departed.
translations.mn31:2: At that time Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Nandiya, and Venerable Kimbila were dwelling at the Gosiṅga Sāla forest.
translations.mn31:3: Then the Blessed One, in the late afternoon, having risen from seclusion, approached the Gosiṅga Sāla forest. The forester saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Seeing him, he said to the Blessed One: “Do not, ascetic, enter this donation. There are three young men of good family dwelling here who are fond of themselves. Do not disturb them.”
translations.mn31:4: Venerable Anuruddha heard the forester talking with the Blessed One. Having heard, he said to the forester: “Do not stop the Blessed One, friend forester. Our Teacher has arrived.” Then Venerable Anuruddha approached Venerable Nandiya and Venerable Kimbila; having approached, he said to Venerable Nandiya and Venerable Kimbila: “Come, venerables, come, venerables, our Teacher has arrived.”
translations.mn31:5: Then the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimila approached the Buddha. One received the Buddha’s robe and bowl, one prepared a seat, and one set out water for washing the feet. The Buddha sat on the prepared seat. Having sat, the Buddha washed his feet. The three venerables, having bowed to the Buddha, sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Buddha said to the Venerable Anuruddha: “I hope you are bearing up, Anuruddha, I hope you are getting by, I hope you are not worn out by almsround?” “We are bearing up, Blessed One, we are getting by, Blessed One; but we, sir, are not worn out by almsround.”
translations.mn31:6: “But I hope, Anuruddha, that you are living in harmony, appreciating one another, without quarreling, blending like milk and water, and viewing each other with kindly eyes?” “Indeed, sir, we are living in harmony, appreciating one another, without quarreling, blending like milk and water, and viewing each other with kindly eyes.” “But how, Anuruddha, do you live in harmony, appreciating one another, without quarreling, blending like milk and water, and viewing each other with kindly eyes?”
translations.mn31:9: “Indeed, sir, we dwell heedful, ardent, and resolute.” “But how do you dwell heedful, ardent, and resolute?” “Here, sir, whichever of us returns first from the village for alms prepares the seats, sets out water for drinking, and sets out the washing bowl. Whoever returns last from the village for alms, if there is leftover food and they wish, they eat; if they do not wish, they put it away where there is no creeping thing, or tip it into water. They put away the seats, put away the water for drinking, put away the washing bowl, and sweep the dwelling place. Whoever sees a water pot or a food pot or a latrine pot that is empty or dirty, they attend to it. If there is something to be done, having been invited by a second with a hand gesture, we attend to it with a hand gesture; but we, sir, do not break our speech on that account. For five years, sir, we sat together all night discussing the Dhamma. That is how, sir, we dwell heedful, ardent, and resolute.”
translations.mn36:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī in the Great Wood at the Hall with the Peaked Roof.
translations.mn36:10: “I am confident in Master Gotama. Master Gotama is developed in body and developed in mind.” “This statement of yours, Aggivessana, is spoken rashly and brought forward without proper investigation, but I will explain it to you. Since I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robe, and went forth from the home life into homelessness, there is no occasion where a pleasant feeling that has arisen keeps my mind ensnared, or a painful feeling that has arisen keeps my mind ensnared.”
translations.mn36:12: “What do you think, Aggivessana? Before my awakening, while I was still a bodhisatta, this thought occurred to me: ‘The home life is crowded and dusty; the life gone forth is like the open air. It is not easy living at home to lead the holy life utterly perfect and pure as a polished shell. Let me now shave off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robe, and go forth from the home life into homelessness.’
translations.mn36:2: Then at that time the Buddha, having dressed in the morning and taken his robe and bowl, was entering Vesālī for alms.
translations.mn36:20: “The thought occurred to me: ‘Why not clench my teeth and press my tongue against the palate, and with my mind crush, constrain, and torment my mind?’ So I clenched my teeth and pressed my tongue against the palate, and with my mind I crushed, constrained, and tormented my mind. As I did so, sweat streamed from my armpits. Just as a strong man might seize a weaker man by the head or shoulders and crush, constrain, and torment him, so did I crush, constrain, and torment my mind with my mind. As I did so, sweat streamed from my armpits. But my energy was exerted, and it was not too lax; mindfulness was established and not lost; my body, however, was aroused and uncalm because of that painful exertion. But such a painful feeling that arose did not take hold of my mind.
translations.mn36:26: “Deities, seeing me, said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is dead.’ Some deities said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not dead, he is dying.’ Some deities said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not dead, nor is he dying; the ascetic Gotama is an arahant; that is the way of an arahant.’
translations.mn36:27: “The thought occurred to me: ‘Why not practice total cessation of food?’ Then deities approached me and said: ‘Do not, good sir, practice total cessation of food. If you practice total cessation of food, we will infuse divine vitality through the pores of your skin, and you will survive by that.’ The thought occurred to me: ‘If I were to claim to have attained something I have not, and these deities were to infuse divine vitality through the pores of my skin, and I were to survive by that, that would be a lie for me.’ So I dismissed those deities, saying, ‘Enough.’
translations.mn36:28: Then I thought, Aggivessana: 'Why not eat food in little bits, little by little, whether bean soup, pea soup, lentil soup, or vetch soup?' So I, Aggivessana, ate food in little bits, little by little, whether bean soup, pea soup, lentil soup, or vetch soup. While I, Aggivessana, was eating food in little bits, little by little, whether bean soup, pea soup, lentil soup, or vetch soup, my body became extremely emaciated. Just as the joints of an eighty-year-old or a hundred-year-old person; so my limbs became like that due to eating so little. Just as a camel's footprint; so my spine became like that due to eating so little. Just as the beads of a string; so my spine protruded and was uneven due to eating so little. Just as the rafters of a dilapidated shed become jagged and rough; so my ribs became jagged and rough due to eating so little. Just as water-bubbles in a deep pool appear deep, sunken, and hard to reach; so my eye-balls appeared deep, sunken, and hard to reach in their sockets due to eating so little. Just as a bitter gourd, cut raw, is smashed and shriveled by wind and sun; so my scalp became smashed and shriveled due to eating so little. So I, Aggivessana, thinking 'I will rub my belly with my hand,' rubbed my spine; thinking 'I will rub my spine,' rubbed my belly, until my belly, Aggivessana, touched my spine due to eating so little. So I, Aggivessana, thinking 'I will defecate or urinate,' fell over right there due to eating so little. So I, Aggivessana, stroking my limbs with my hand while breathing this body. As I, Aggivessana, stroked my limbs with my hand, the rotten hairs fell from my body due to eating so little.
translations.mn36:29: People, seeing me, Aggivessana, said: 'The ascetic Gotama is black.' Some people said: 'The ascetic Gotama is not black, he is brown.' Some people said: 'The ascetic Gotama is not black, nor brown, he is golden-skinned.' Until my skin, Aggivessana, became pure, bright, and dulled due to eating so little.
translations.mn36:3: Then Saccaka the Niganthaputta, while walking and wandering in the Jhanghara Grove, approached the Great Wood, the Gabled Hall. Venerable Ananda saw Saccaka the Niganthaputta coming from afar. Seeing him, he said to the Blessed One: 'This, Blessed One, is Saccaka the Niganthaputta coming; a debater, a clever speaker, well-regarded by the multitude. He, Blessed One, is fond of disparaging the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha. It would be good, Blessed One, if the Blessed One would sit for a while out of compassion.' The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat. Then Saccaka the Niganthaputta approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and after exchanging courteous and memorable talk, he sat to one side. Sitting to one side, Saccaka the Niganthaputta said to the Blessed One:
translations.mn36:30: Then I thought, Aggivessana: 'Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past experienced painful, sharp, harsh, racking feelings due to exertion, this is the utmost, not more. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will experience painful, sharp, harsh, racking feelings due to exertion, this is the utmost, not more. Whatever ascetics or brahmins at present experience painful, sharp, harsh, racking feelings due to exertion, this is the utmost, not more. But I do not reach with this painful, racking practice any superhuman states, distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. Could there be another path to enlightenment?'
translations.mn36:32: Then I thought, Aggivessana: 'Why do I delight in that happiness which is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states?' Then I thought, Aggivessana: 'I do not delight in that happiness which is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states.'
translations.mn36:34: So I, Aggivessana, having taken solid food and regained strength, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, entered and dwelt in the first jhana, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. Even such arisen pleasant feeling, Aggivessana, did not pervade my mind and remain.
translations.mn36:38: With my mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, free from defilements, pliable, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it to the knowledge of recollection of past lives. I recollected many past lives, that is, one birth... thus with details and particulars I recollected many past lives.
translations.mn36:39: This, Aggivessana, was the first knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night; ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed, light arose; as one who is heedful, ardent, and resolute dwells. Even such arisen pleasant feeling, Aggivessana, did not pervade my mind and remain.
translations.mn36:4: “There are, Master Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins who are devoted to and engaged in the development of the body, but not the development of the mind. For they experience physical painful feeling. Formerly, Master Gotama, when affected by physical painful feeling, there will be thigh cramps, the heart will burst, hot blood will come from the mouth, and they will fall into a frenzy and mental derangement. Their mind, Master Gotama, is then of a bodily nature; it proceeds in terms of the body. Why is that? Because the mind is undeveloped. There are, Master Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins who are devoted to and engaged in the development of the mind, but not the development of the body. For they experience mental painful feeling. Formerly, Master Gotama, when affected by mental painful feeling, there will be thigh cramps, the heart will burst, hot blood will come from the mouth, and they will fall into a frenzy and mental derangement. Their body, Master Gotama, is then of a mental nature; it proceeds in terms of the mind. Why is that? Because the body is undeveloped. It occurs to me thus: ‘Master Gotama’s disciples are indeed devoted to and engaged in the development of the mind, but not the development of the body.’”
translations.mn36:40: With my mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, free from defilements, pliable, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it to the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and I understood how beings pass on according to their actions …pe…
translations.mn36:42: With my mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, free from defilements, pliable, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. I directly knew ‘This is suffering’; I directly knew ‘This is the origin of suffering’; I directly knew ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; I directly knew ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’. I directly knew ‘These are the taints’; I directly knew ‘This is the origin of the taints’; I directly knew ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; I directly knew ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints’.
translations.mn36:43: When I knew and saw thus, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of existence, and from the taint of ignorance. When it was liberated, there came the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’ I directly understood: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.’
translations.mn36:45: I recall, Aggivessana, teaching the Dhamma to an assembly of several hundred. And perhaps someone thinks: ‘The ascetic Gotama is teaching the Dhamma for my sake.’ But this, Aggivessana, should not be seen thus; the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to others merely for the sake of knowledge. So I, Aggivessana, at the end of that talk, having settled my mind internally in that same meditation subject, made it one-pointed and concentrated, so that I might dwell for the rest of my life.” “Is this, Master Gotama, a delusion of the Master Gotama, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One? Or does Master Gotama know that he sleeps during the day?”
translations.mn36:46: “I recall, Aggivessana, that in the last month of the hot season, after returning from the almsround, having spread out a fourfold robe, I lay down mindful and fully aware to sleep.” “Some ascetics and brahmins, Master Gotama, say that this is a state of delusion.” “Not merely by this, Aggivessana, is one deluded or undeluded. But, Aggivessana, listen to how one is both deluded and undeluded; attend closely, I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” replied Saccaka the Niganthaputta to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
translations.mn36:47: “Whoever, Aggivessana, has taints that are corrupting, conducive to rebirth, fearful, productive of painful results, conducive to future birth, aging, and death, and are not abandoned, him I call ‘deluded’. For when taints are not abandoned, Aggivessana, one is deluded. Whoever, Aggivessana, has taints that are corrupting, conducive to rebirth, fearful, productive of painful results, conducive to future birth, aging, and death, and are abandoned, him I call ‘undeluded’. For when taints are abandoned, Aggivessana, one is undeluded. But for the Tathāgata, Aggivessana, the taints that are corrupting, conducive to rebirth, fearful, productive of painful results, conducive to future birth, aging, and death are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising. Just as, Aggivessana, a palm tree cut off at the root is unable to grow again; so too, for the Tathāgata, Aggivessana, the taints that are corrupting, conducive to rebirth, fearful, productive of painful results, conducive to future birth, aging, and death are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising.”
translations.mn36:5: “But what, Aggivessana, have you heard about the development of the body?” “That is to say— Nando Vaccho, Kiso Saṅkicco, Makkhali Gosāla— these, Master Gotama, are naked ascetics, who practice licking their hands, not accepting food prepared for them, or food prepared for their wives, or food prepared for their servants. They do not accept food from a pot or from a pan, or from between two eating people, or from a pregnant woman, or from a nursing mother, or from a woman living with a man, or from where food is kept, or where a dog is waiting, or from flies swarming. They do not drink fish or meat, or intoxicating liquor, or fermented brew. They practice eating once a day, or once every two days …pe… or once every seven days. They sustain themselves on a single almsfood, or on two almsfoods …pe… or on seven almsfoods. They eat a meal once a day, or once every two days …pe… or once every seven days. Thus they live devoted to and engaged in a practice of taking food at intervals of up to half a month.”
translations.mn36:6: "But what about you, Aggivessana, do you torment yourself only that much?" "No, Master Gotama. Sometimes, Master Gotama, they eat morsels of food that are coarse and coarse, they eat meals that are coarse and coarse, they sleep on beds that are coarse and coarse, they drink drinks that are coarse and coarse. They take hold of strength in this body, they increase it, they fatten it." "What you, Aggivessana, abandon first and cultivate later, in this way there is the accumulation and increase of this body. But what about you, Aggivessana, have you heard of the development of the mind?" When asked this by the Blessed One, Saccaka the Niganthaputta could not reply.
translations.mn36:8: "And how, Aggivessana, is one undeveloped in body and undeveloped in mind? Here, Aggivessana, an uninformed ordinary person arises a pleasant feeling. Touched by that pleasant feeling, he becomes lustful for pleasure and attains lust for pleasure. That pleasant feeling ceases in him. With the cessation of the pleasant feeling, a painful feeling arises. Touched by that painful feeling, he sorrows, laments, wails, cries beating his breast, and becomes confused. For him, Aggivessana, both the arisen pleasant feeling and the arisen painful feeling occupy the mind because of the undeveloped nature of the body and the undeveloped nature of the mind. For whomever, Aggivessana, both the arisen pleasant feeling and the arisen painful feeling occupy the mind because of the undeveloped nature of the body and the undeveloped nature of the mind, in this way, Aggivessana, one is undeveloped in body and undeveloped in mind.
translations.mn36:9: And how, Aggivessana, is one developed in body and developed in mind? Here, Aggivessana, a well-informed noble disciple arises a pleasant feeling. Touched by that pleasant feeling, he does not become lustful for pleasure and does not attain lust for pleasure. That pleasant feeling ceases in him. With the cessation of the pleasant feeling, a painful feeling arises. Touched by that painful feeling, he does not sorrow, does not lament, does not wail, does not cry beating his breast, and does not become confused. For him, Aggivessana, neither the arisen pleasant feeling nor the arisen painful feeling occupies the mind because of the developed nature of the body and the developed nature of the mind. For whomever, Aggivessana, neither the arisen pleasant feeling nor the arisen painful feeling occupies the mind because of the developed nature of the body and the developed nature of the mind, in this way, Aggivessana, one is developed in body and developed in mind."
translations.mn38:10: "Monks, when it is said 'This is real', does doubt arise, uncertainty arises?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Monks, when it is said 'It is born from nutriment', does doubt arise, uncertainty arises?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Monks, when it is said 'That which is real, born from the cessation of nutriment, is of a nature to cease', does doubt arise, uncertainty arises?" "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.mn38:11: "Monks, when it is said 'This is real', is the doubt that has arisen abandoned by one who sees rightly with right wisdom?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Monks, when it is said 'It is born from nutriment', is the doubt that has arisen abandoned by one who sees rightly with right wisdom?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Monks, when it is said 'That which is real, born from the cessation of nutriment, is of a nature to cease', is the doubt that has arisen abandoned by one who sees rightly with right wisdom?" "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.mn38:12: "Monks, when it is said 'This is real', is this also for you freedom from doubt?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Monks, when it is said 'It is born from nutriment', is this also for you freedom from doubt?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Monks, when it is said 'That which is real, born from the cessation of nutriment, is of a nature to cease', is this also for you freedom from doubt?" "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.mn38:13: "Monks, when it is said 'This is real', is it well seen by one who sees rightly with right wisdom?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Monks, when it is said 'It is born from nutriment', is it well seen by one who sees rightly with right wisdom?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Monks, when it is said 'That which is real, born from the cessation of nutriment, is of a nature to cease', is it well seen by one who sees rightly with right wisdom?" "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.mn38:14: "Monks, if you were to cling to, rely on, treasure, and regard as 'mine' this view that is so pure and so bright, would you know that I have taught the Dhamma like a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping?" "No, venerable sir." "Monks, if you were not to cling to, rely on, treasure, and regard as 'mine' this view that is so pure and so bright, would you know that I have taught the Dhamma like a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping?" "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.mn38:15: "There are these four nutriments, monks, for the sustenance of beings that have come to be or for the assistance of those about to be born. What four? Coarse nutriment or physical nutriment, contact is the second, mental volition is the third, consciousness is the fourth.
translations.mn38:17: Thus, monks, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. In this way is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:19: "Good, monks. Thus, monks, you should also speak in this way, and I also speak in this way— When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. That is: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. In this way is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:2: Now at that time the monk Sāti, son of the Kevatta, had such a wicked view arise: 'In this way I understand the Dhamma taught by the Gracious One: that it is just this very consciousness that runs and wanders on, not another.'
translations.mn38:20: With the fading away and cessation of ignorance without remainder, there is cessation of choices; with the cessation of choices, cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the six sense fields; with the cessation of the six sense fields, cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, cessation of grasping; with the cessation of grasping, cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, ageing-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease. Thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:22: 'Good, monks. So you, monks, speak thus, and I also speak thus—when this is not, that is not; with the cessation of this, that ceases; that is—with the cessation of ignorance, there is cessation of choices; with the cessation of choices, cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the six sense fields; with the cessation of the six sense fields, cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, cessation of grasping; with the cessation of grasping, cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, ageing-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease. Thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.'
translations.mn38:23: Do you, monks, knowing thus, seeing thus, run back to the past? 'Were we in the past period? Were we not in the past period? What were we in the past period? How were we in the past period? Having been what, what were we in the past period?' 'No, venerable sir.' 'Do you, monks, knowing thus, seeing thus, run forward to the future—shall we be in the future period? Shall we not be in the future period? What shall we be in the future period? How shall we be in the future period? Having been what, what shall we be in the future period?' 'No, venerable sir.'
translations.mn38:25: 'Good, monks. You have been brought near, monks, by this visible Dhamma, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be known personally by the wise. This Dhamma is visible, monks, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be known personally by the wise—whereby what was said is said because of this.'
translations.mn38:26: Now, monks, the descent into the womb takes place through the coming together of three. Here mother and father come together, but the mother is not in season, and the gandhabba is not present; in that case the descent into the womb does not take place. Here mother and father come together, and the mother is in season, but the gandhabba is not present; in that case the descent into the womb does not take place. But when, monks, mother and father come together, and the mother is in season, and the gandhabba is present—with the coming together of these three the descent into the womb takes place.
translations.mn38:27: Then, monks, the mother carries the embryo in her womb for nine or ten months with great anxiety and as a heavy burden. Then, monks, the mother gives birth to the child after nine or ten months with great anxiety and as a heavy burden. Then, having been born, she nourishes it with her own blood. This, monks, is the blood in the Noble One's discipline, that is, mother's milk.
translations.mn38:28: That boy, monks, growing up and the faculties maturing, plays with the playthings of boys, such as toy ploughs, tip-cats, windmills, toy carts, toy bows.
translations.mn38:39: He, having abandoned these five hindrances, corruptions of the mind that weaken wisdom, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. Again, monks, a monk, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, entering and dwelling in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and has rapture and pleasure born of concentration … the third jhāna … the fourth jhāna, and dwells in it.
translations.mn38:6: Then the Gracious One addressed the monks: 'What do you think, monks? Is not this monk Sāti, son of the Kevatta, even now sweating in this Dhamma and Vinaya?' 'How could it be, venerable sir? No, venerable sir.' When this was said, the monk Sāti, son of the Kevatta, sat silent, glum, shoulders drooping, head down, withdrawn, unable to reply. Then the Gracious One, knowing that the monk Sāti, son of the Kevatta, was sitting silent, glum, shoulders drooping, head down, withdrawn, unable to reply, said to the monk Sāti, son of the Kevatta: 'You fool, you will be known by this very wicked view of yours. I will now question the monks.'
translations.mn38:7: Then the Gracious One addressed the monks: 'Do you also know the Dhamma taught by me in this way, as this monk Sāti, son of the Kevatta, having grasped it wrongly, declares it about us, cutting himself off, and producing much unwholesomeness?' 'No, venerable sir. In many ways, venerable sir, consciousness dependent on origin has been stated by the Gracious One; without a cause there is no arising of consciousness.' 'Good, good, monks. It is good that you, monks, know the Dhamma taught by me in this way. In many ways, monks, consciousness dependent on origin has been stated by me; without a cause there is no arising of consciousness.' But this monk Sāti, son of the Kevatta, having grasped it wrongly, declares it about us, cutting himself off, and producing much unwholesomeness. That will be for that fool for a long time for harm and suffering.
translations.mn38:9: “Do you see, monks, that it is ‘born’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Do you see, monks, that it is ‘born of nutriment’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Do you see, monks, that due to the cessation of nutriment, what is born ceases, is subject to cessation?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn41:1: Thus I have heard. At one time the Buddha was wandering in the Kosala country together with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus when he arrived at a Brahmin village named Sālā.
translations.mn41:10: And how, householders, is there threefold unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct in mind? Here, householders, a certain person is covetous; they covet the belongings of others: ‘Oh, may what belongs to others be mine!’ They have a mind of ill will and corrupt intentions: ‘May these beings be killed, slaughtered, annihilated, destroyed, or may they not exist!’ They hold wrong view and have a distorted perspective: ‘There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; no fruit and result of good and bad actions; there is no this world, no other world; no mother, no father; no spontaneously born beings; no ascetics and brahmins who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves, make it known.’ Thus, householders, there is threefold unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct in mind. Because of this unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct, householders, some beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in the lower realms, a bad destination, perdition, in hell.
translations.mn41:12: And how, householders, is there threefold righteous conduct and even conduct in body? Here, householders, a certain person, abandoning the taking of life, abstains from the taking of life. Having laid down the rod and the weapon, ashamed and compassionate, they dwell with concern for the welfare of all living beings. Abandoning the taking of what is not given, they abstain from taking what is not given. They do not take, with thievish intent, what belongs to others and has not been given, whether it is in the village or the wilderness. Abandoning sexual misconduct, they abstain from sexual misconduct. They do not engage in sexual intercourse with women who are protected by their mother, father, mother and father, brother, sister, relatives, or clan; those protected by Dhamma; those with a husband; those protected by the law; or even those garlanded and betrothed. Thus, householders, there is threefold righteous conduct and even conduct in body.
translations.mn41:13: And how, householders, is there fourfold righteous conduct and even conduct in speech? Here, householders, a certain person, abandoning false speech, abstains from false speech. When summoned to a council, to an assembly, to one’s relatives, to a guild, or to the royal court, and questioned as a witness thus: ‘Come, good man, tell what you know,’ not knowing, they say, ‘I do not know’; knowing, they say, ‘I know’; not seeing, they say, ‘I do not see’; seeing, they say, ‘I see.’ Thus they do not knowingly speak falsehood for their own sake, for another’s sake, or for the sake of some material gain. Abandoning divisive speech, they abstain from divisive speech. What they have heard here they do not repeat elsewhere to cause a rift among these people; what they have heard elsewhere they do not repeat here to cause a rift among those people. Thus they reconcile those who are divided and encourage those who are united; they delight in harmony, enjoy harmony, and speak words that create harmony. Abandoning harsh speech, they abstain from harsh speech. They speak words that are gentle, pleasant to the ear, lovely, reaching the heart, polite, and liked by most people. Abandoning idle chatter, they abstain from idle chatter. They speak at the right time, speak what is factual, speak about the goal, speak about the Dhamma and the discipline; their speech is profound, timely, well-reasoned, and beneficial. Thus, householders, there is fourfold righteous conduct and even conduct in speech.
translations.mn41:14: And how, householders, is there threefold righteous conduct and even conduct in mind? Here, householders, a certain person is not covetous; they do not covet the belongings of others: ‘Oh, may what belongs to others be mine!’ They have a mind without ill will and without corrupt intentions: ‘May these beings be free from enmity, affliction, and anxiety! May they live happily!’ They hold right view and have an undistorted perspective: ‘There is what is given, what is offered, what is sacrificed; there is fruit and result of good and bad actions; there is this world and the other world; there is mother and father; there are spontaneously born beings; there are ascetics and brahmins who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves, make it known.’ Thus, householders, there is threefold righteous conduct and even conduct in mind. Because of this righteous conduct and even conduct, householders, some beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.
translations.mn41:15: If a righteous and even-conducting householder should wish: ‘Oh, may I, with the breakup of the body, after death, be reborn in the company of wealthy warriors’—that is possible. For what reason? Because they are righteous and even-conducting.
translations.mn41:3: Then the Brahmin householders of Sālā approached the Buddha. Having approached, some paid homage to the Buddha and sat down to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Buddha, and after exchanging courteous and memorable conversation, sat down to one side; some raised their joined palms in reverence to the Buddha and sat down to one side; some announced their name and clan in the Buddha’s presence and sat down to one side; and some sat down to one side in silence. Having sat down to one side, the Brahmin householders of Sālā said to the Buddha:
translations.mn41:4: “What, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in the lower realms, a bad destination, perdition, in hell? And what, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world?”
translations.mn41:43: If a householder who practices right conduct and uniform conduct should wish: 'Oh, that I might dwell having realized for myself with direct knowledge the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life, and enter upon it,' there is a possibility that he might dwell having realized for himself with direct knowledge the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life, and enter upon it. For what reason? Because he is one who practices right conduct and uniform conduct.
translations.mn41:5: Because of wrong conduct and misconduct, householders, some beings, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, in hell. Because of right conduct and uniform conduct, householders, some beings, on the dissolution of the body, after death, reappear in a good destination, in a heavenly world.
translations.mn41:6: We do not know in detail the meaning of this brief statement of the Master Gotama, whose meaning has not been expounded in detail. May the Master Gotama teach the Dhamma in such a way that we might know in detail the meaning of this brief statement of the Master Gotama, whose meaning has not been expounded in detail. Then listen, householders, attend closely, I will speak. Yes, venerable sir, the Sāleyyaka brahmins and householders answered the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn41:8: And how, householders, is there threefold wrong conduct and misconduct by body? Here, householders, a certain person is a killer of living beings, cruel, bloody-handed, devoted to killing and slaying, without mercy for living beings. He is a thief. Taking what is not given, he takes by way of theft the wealth and property of others in the village or in the forest. He engages in sexual misconduct. He has intercourse with women who are protected by their mother, father, mother and father, brother, sister, relatives, or clan; with those protected by Dhamma; with those who have a husband; with those who entail a penalty, even if only with a garland of flowers. In this way, householders, there is threefold wrong conduct and misconduct by body.
translations.mn41:9: And how, householders, is there fourfold wrong conduct and misconduct by speech? Here, householders, a certain person is a false speaker. When summoned to a council, to an assembly, to his relatives' presence, to his guild, or to the royal court, and questioned as a witness thus: 'So, good man, tell what you know,' not knowing, he says, 'I know'; or knowing, he says, 'I do not know'; not seeing, he says, 'I see'; or seeing, he says, 'I do not see.' Thus he consciously speaks falsehood for his own sake, for another's sake, or for some trifling worldly gain. He is a divisive speaker. Having heard something here, he repeats it elsewhere to divide those people from these; or having heard something elsewhere, he repeats it here to divide these people from those. Thus he is one who divides those who are united and creates further division among those who are already divided. He enjoys disunity, delights in disunity, enjoys speaking words that create disunity. He is an abusive speaker. He speaks words that are harsh, cutting, offensive to others, abusive of others, provoking anger, and not conducive to concentration. He is an idle chatterer. He speaks at the wrong time, speaks what is not fact, speaks what is not beneficial, speaks what is not Dhamma, speaks what is not the Discipline. He speaks words that are worthless, at the wrong time, without reason, without a limit, and not connected with the good. In this way, householders, there is fourfold wrong conduct and misconduct by speech.
translations.mn4:20: Then it occurred to me, brahmin: 'Suppose that I, on the nights of the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth of the fortnight, were to dwell in those terrifying shrines in the forest and at the foot of trees, where the rustling of the trees sounds like the cries of peacocks. Perhaps I would see fear and dread.' So I, brahmin, at a later time, on the nights of the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth of the fortnight, dwelt in those terrifying shrines in the forest and at the foot of trees, where the rustling of the trees sounds like the cries of peacocks. While dwelling there, brahmin, a deer would approach, or a peacock would knock off a branch, or the wind would rustle the leaves. Then it occurred to me, brahmin: 'This fear and dread is now coming.' Then it occurred to me, brahmin: 'Why am I waiting for fear and dread? Suppose that I, just as fear and dread comes to me in reality, subdue that fear and dread in reality.' While I was walking, brahmin, that fear and dread came to me. Then I, brahmin, neither stood still, nor sat down, nor lay down, but kept walking back and forth until I had subdued that fear and dread. While I was standing, brahmin, that fear and dread came to me. Then I, brahmin, neither walked back and forth, nor sat down, nor lay down, but kept standing until I had subdued that fear and dread. While I was sitting, brahmin, that fear and dread came to me. Then I, brahmin, neither lay down, nor stood up, nor walked back and forth, but kept sitting until I had subdued that fear and dread. While I was lying down, brahmin, that fear and dread came to me. Then I, brahmin, neither sat up, nor stood up, nor walked back and forth, but kept lying down until I had subdued that fear and dread.
translations.mn4:22-26: But for me, brahmin, energy was aroused, it was not lax; mindfulness was established, it was not forgetful; the body was tranquil, it was not agitated; the mind was concentrated and one-pointed. So I, brahmin, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, entered upon and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, I entered upon and dwelt in the second jhāna, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind without applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, I dwelt equanimous and mindful, and I experienced pleasure with the body; I entered upon and dwelt in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, one who dwells in pleasure.’ With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and grief, I entered upon and dwelt in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.
translations.mn4:27: When my concentrated mind was thus purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, pliable, malleable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it towards knowledge of recollection of past lives. I recollected many past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of contraction, many eons of expansion, many eons of contraction and expansion: ‘There I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-term; and passing away from there, I reappeared there; and there I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life-term; and passing away from there, I reappeared here.’ Thus with their aspects and particulars I recollected many past lives.
translations.mn4:28: This was the first knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night, brahmin. Ignorance was destroyed; knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed; light arose—as I dwelt diligent, ardent, and resolute.
translations.mn4:29: When my concentrated mind was thus purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, pliable, malleable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it towards knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and I understood how beings pass on according to their actions: ‘These worthy beings who were ill-conducted in body, speech, and mind, revilers of noble ones, holding wrong view, undertaking wrong view in their actions—on the dissolution of the body, after death, have reappeared in the lower world, a bad destination, perdition, hell. But these worthy beings who were well-conducted in body, speech, and mind, not revilers of noble ones, holding right view, undertaking right view in their actions—on the dissolution of the body, after death, have reappeared in a good destination, a heavenly world.’ Thus with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and I understood how beings pass on according to their actions.
translations.mn4:3: For me too, brahmin, before my awakening, while I was still a bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, it occurred to me: ‘Wildernesses and forest groves are difficult to stay in; seclusion is hard to enjoy; it is not easy to dwell alone without distraction. The forests, I think, take away the mind of a monk who has not attained concentration.’
translations.mn4:30: This was the second knowledge attained by me in the middle watch of the night, brahmin. Ignorance was destroyed; knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed; light arose—as I dwelt diligent, ardent, and resolute.
translations.mn4:34: Perhaps it occurs to you, brahmin: ‘The ascetic Gotama is still without lust, without hate, without delusion; that is why he frequents wildernesses and forest groves.’ But this, brahmin, should not be seen in that way. I frequent wildernesses and forest groves, brahmin, seeing two benefits—seeing the bliss of a secluded dwelling in the present life, and out of compassion for later generations.
translations.mn4:4: It occurred to me: ‘Those ascetics or brahmins who are not purified in their conduct of body and who frequent wildernesses and forest groves—because of the impurity of their conduct of body, those ascetics and brahmins arouse unwholesome fear and dread. But I am not one with impure conduct of body who frequents wildernesses and forest groves; I am one with pure conduct of body. I shall be one of those noble ones with pure conduct of body who frequent wildernesses and forest groves.’ Seeing this purity of conduct of body in myself, I went even deeper into the forest to dwell.
translations.mn4:5: It occurred to me: ‘Those ascetics or brahmins who are not purified in their conduct of speech … not purified in their conduct of mind … not purified in their livelihood who frequent wildernesses and forest groves—because of the impurity of their livelihood, those ascetics and brahmins arouse unwholesome fear and dread.
translations.mn4:6: But I am not one with impure livelihood who frequents wildernesses and forest groves; I am one with pure livelihood.
translations.mn4:7: I shall be one of those noble ones with pure livelihood who frequent wildernesses and forest groves.’ Seeing this purity of livelihood in myself, I went even deeper into the forest to dwell.
translations.mn52:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood. Now at that time the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhaka had arrived at Pāṭaliputta for some business.
translations.mn54:18: Suppose, householder, there is a charcoal pit more than a man’s deep, filled with glowing coals without flame or smoke. Then a man would come, wanting to live, not wanting to die, wanting pleasure, averse to pain. Two strong men would seize him by the arms and throw him into the charcoal pit. What do you think, householder? Would that man, writhing in pain, be aware of his body?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “For what reason?” “Because, venerable sir, I see that man falling into that charcoal pit, and because of that he would die or suffer death-like pain.” “So too, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Sensual pleasures have been declared by the Blessed One to be like a charcoal pit, of much suffering, much despair, and there is more danger here.’ Seeing this as it actually is with right discernment … he develops equanimity.
translations.mn54:23: That noble disciple, relying on that very supreme equanimity-purity of mindfulness, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, sees beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate … he understands how beings pass on according to their actions.
translations.mn54:24: That noble disciple, relying on that very supreme equanimity-purity of mindfulness, realizes the destruction of the taints, and in this very life, entering and remaining in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, realizing it for himself with direct knowledge.
translations.mn60:10: Herein, householders, those ascetics and brahmins who hold such views and opinions as: ‘There is what is given … and who declare this world and the other world, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge’—it is to be expected of them that, abandoning the three unwholesome deeds of bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct, and undertaking the three wholesome deeds of bodily conduct, verbal conduct, and mental conduct, they will live accordingly. For what reason? Because those ascetics and brahmins see the danger, the drawback, and the defilement in unwholesome states, and the benefit, the cleansing aspect, of renunciation in wholesome states.
translations.mn60:12: Herein, householders, a wise man reflects thus: ‘If there is another world, then this person, on the dissolution of the body, after death, will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. But if there is no other world, then this person will still be praised here and now by the wise as a virtuous person, one of right view, who asserts that there is an afterlife. If there really is another world, then this person has made a wager on both sides—praised by the wise here and now, and after the dissolution of the body, after death, he will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Thus this sure dhamma, well-proclaimed and well-established, stands covering both sides, and there is no misfortune in the undertaking.
translations.mn60:13: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such views and opinions as: ‘There is no fault in killing, causing to kill, cutting, causing to cut, cooking, causing to cook, tormenting, causing to torment, exhausting, causing to exhaust, oppressing, causing to oppress, destroying life, taking what is not given, cutting into houses, plundering wealth, committing robbery, ambushing on the road, committing adultery, speaking lies. Even if one were to make a single lump of flesh or a single pile of flesh on this earth with a wheel edged with a razor blade, there would be no evil from that, no result of evil. Even if one were to go along the bank of the Ganges killing, causing to kill, cutting, causing to cut, cooking, causing to cook; there would be no evil from that, no result of evil. Even if one were to go along the bank of the Ganges giving, causing to give, sacrificing, causing to sacrifice; there would be no merit from that, no result of merit. There is no merit in giving, self-control, restraint, and truthfulness; there is no result of merit.’
