translations.mn60:14: Of those same ascetics and brahmins, householders, some ascetics and brahmins are opponents of those who hold such views, and they spoke thus: ‘There is fault in killing, causing to kill, cutting, causing to cut, cooking, causing to cook, tormenting, causing to torment, exhausting, causing to exhaust, oppressing, causing to oppress, destroying life, taking what is not given, cutting into houses, plundering wealth, committing robbery, ambushing on the road, committing adultery, speaking lies. Even if one were to make a single lump of flesh or a single pile of flesh on this earth with a wheel edged with a razor blade, there is evil from that, there is a result of evil. Even if one were to go along the bank of the Ganges killing, causing to kill, cutting, causing to cut, cooking, causing to cook; there is evil from that, there is a result of evil. Even if one were to go along the bank of the Ganges giving, causing to give, sacrificing, causing to sacrifice; there is merit from that, there is a result of merit. There is merit in giving, self-control, restraint, and truthfulness; there is a result of merit.’ What do you think, householders? Are those ascetics and brahmins opponents of one another?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn60:16: When there is actually an action, the view ‘There is no action’ arises in him; that is wrong view. When there is actually an action, he intends ‘There is no action’; that is wrong intention. When there is actually an action, he speaks ‘There is no action’; that is wrong speech. When there is actually an action, he says ‘There is no action’, thus opposing those Arahants who are actionists. When there is actually an action, he persuades others ‘There is no action’; that is wrong teaching. And with that wrong teaching, he praises himself and disparages others. Thus his good morality is abandoned earlier, and bad morality is established—this wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, opposition to the noble ones, wrong teaching, self-praise, and disparagement of others. In this way, many bad unwholesome states arise in him caused by wrong view.
translations.mn60:17: There, householders, a wise person reflects thus: ‘If there is no action, this person will fare well after the breakup of the body; if there is action, this person will reappear in a realm of loss, a bad destination, the lower world, hell after death. But let there be no action; let the statement of those ascetics and brahmins be true; yet this person is blameworthy in the present life to the wise—immoral, of wrong view, a denier of action.’ If there is indeed action, then this person loses on both counts—what is blameworthy in the present life to the wise, and reappearing in a realm of loss, a bad destination, the lower world, hell after death. Thus this teaching is undertaken as a blind gamble, standing on one side, missing the good place.
translations.mn60:19: For there is indeed action, and the view ‘there is action’ is right view. For there is indeed action, and the intention ‘there is action’ is right intention. For there is indeed action, and the speech ‘there is action’ is right speech. For there is indeed action, and saying ‘there is action’ does not contradict those Arahants who are proponents of action. For there is indeed action, and proclaiming ‘there is action’ to others is a proclamation of the True Dhamma. And with that proclamation of the True Dhamma, one neither praises oneself nor disparages others. Thus his former immorality is abandoned and morality is established—this right view, right intention, and right speech, not contradicted by the noble ones, a proclamation of the True Dhamma, without self-praise, without disparaging others. Thus many wholesome qualities arise for him conditioned by right view.
translations.mn60:21: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and view: ‘There is no cause or condition for the defilement of beings; without cause or condition, beings become defiled. There is no cause or condition for the purification of beings; without cause or condition, beings are purified. There is no power, no energy, no manly strength, no manly effort; all beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are powerless, without strength, subject to fate, bound by their nature, changing in the six classes of birth, experiencing pleasure and pain.’
translations.mn60:22: Of those same ascetics and brahmins, householders, some are opponents of the straight teaching. They said: ‘There is a cause and condition for the defilement of beings; with cause and condition, beings become defiled. There is a cause and condition for the purification of beings; with cause and condition, beings are purified. There is power, there is energy, there is manly strength, there is manly effort; not all beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are powerless, without strength, subject to fate, bound by their nature, changing in the six classes of birth, experiencing pleasure and pain.’ What do you think, householders, are those ascetics and brahmins opponents of each other’s straight teaching? ‘Yes, venerable sir.’
translations.mn60:29: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and view: ‘There is nothing immaterial.’
translations.mn60:30: Of those same ascetics and brahmins, householders, some are opponents of the straight teaching. They said: ‘There is something immaterial.’ What do you think, householders, are those ascetics and brahmins opponents of each other’s straight teaching? ‘Yes, venerable sir.’
translations.mn60:32: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and view: ‘There is no cessation of existence.’
translations.mn60:35: There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world, householders. What four? Here, householders, a certain person torments himself and is devoted to self-torment. Here, householders, a certain person torments others and is devoted to tormenting others. Here, householders, a certain person torments himself and is devoted to self-torment, and torments others and is devoted to tormenting others. Here, householders, a certain person neither torments himself nor is devoted to self-torment, nor torments others nor is devoted to tormenting others; he, not tormenting himself, not tormenting others, dwells in the present life free from thirst, extinguished, cooled, experiencing bliss, living with a self become brahma.
translations.mn60:36: And what kind of person, householders, torments himself and is devoted to self-torment? Here, householders, a certain person is a naked ascetic, a practice of licking the hands, not accepting food brought for them… he dwells devoted to the practice of tormenting and afflicting the body in various ways like this. This is called, householders, a person who torments himself and is devoted to self-torment.
translations.mn60:37: And what kind of person, householders, torments others and is devoted to tormenting others? Here, householders, a certain person is a butcher, a pig-slaughterer… or whatever other cruel livelihood there is. This is called, householders, a person who torments others and is devoted to tormenting others.
translations.mn60:38: And what kind of person, householders, torments himself and is devoted to self-torment, and torments others and is devoted to tormenting others? Here, householders, a certain person is a king or a khattiya ruler… they perform tasks terrified by the rod, terrified by fear, weeping with a tearful face. This is called, householders, a person who torments himself and is devoted to self-torment, and torments others and is devoted to tormenting others.
translations.mn60:39: And what kind of person, householders, neither torments himself nor is devoted to self-torment, nor torments others nor is devoted to tormenting others; he, not tormenting himself, not tormenting others, dwells in the present life free from thirst, extinguished, cooled, experiencing bliss, living with a self become brahma?
translations.mn60:4: ‘But do you, householders, have any beloved teacher in whom you have gained confidence?’ ‘We do not have, venerable sir, any beloved teacher in whom we have gained confidence.’ ‘Since you have not found a beloved teacher, this teaching should be undertaken as a blind gamble. For a teaching undertaken as a blind gamble, householders, will be for your welfare and happiness for a long time. And what, householders, is the teaching undertaken as a blind gamble?
translations.mn60:5: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and view: ‘There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; no fruit or result of good and bad actions; there is no this world, no other world; no mother, no father; no spontaneously born beings; no ascetics and brahmins who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves by direct knowledge, proclaim it.’
translations.mn60:6: Of those same ascetics and brahmins, householders, there are some who are opponents of them. They said: ‘There is something given, something offered, something sacrificed; there is fruit and result of good and bad actions; there is this world, there is another world; there is mother, there is father; there are spontaneously born beings; there are ascetics and brahmins who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves by direct knowledge, proclaim it.’ What do you think, householders: ‘Are those ascetics and brahmins opponents of one another’s views?’ ‘Yes, venerable sir.’
translations.mn63:8: Why have I not declared this, Mālukyaputta? Because it is not beneficial, it does not belong to the fundamentals of the holy life, it does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna. Therefore I have not declared it.
translations.mn64:13: Furthermore, Ānanda, a monk, by passing entirely beyond the perception of forms, by the disappearance of the perception of resistance, by non-attention to the perception of diversity, perceiving ‘Infinite space’, enters and dwells in the Base of Infinite Space. Whatever feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness arises there … he does not return to that world. This too, Ānanda, is the path, the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn64:14: Furthermore, Ānanda, a monk, by passing entirely beyond the Base of Infinite Space, perceiving ‘Infinite consciousness’, enters and dwells in the Base of Infinite Consciousness. Whatever feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness arises there … he does not return to that world. This too, Ānanda, is the path, the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn64:2: ‘Do you bear in mind, monks, the five lower fetters taught by me?’ When this was said, Venerable Mālukyaputta said to the Blessed One: ‘I, venerable sir, bear in mind the five lower fetters taught by the Blessed One.’ ‘And how, Mālukyaputta, do you bear in mind the five lower fetters taught by me?’ ‘I bear in mind, venerable sir, identity view as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I bear in mind doubt as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I bear in mind adherence to rites and rituals as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I bear in mind sensual desire as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I bear in mind ill will as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One. In this way, venerable sir, I bear in mind the five lower fetters taught by the Blessed One.’
translations.mn64:4: When this was said, Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: ‘It is time, Blessed One, it is time, Sugata, for the Blessed One to teach the five lower fetters. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will bear it in mind.’ ‘Then listen, Ānanda, attend closely, and I will speak.’ ‘Yes, venerable sir,’ Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn64:7: There is a possibility, Ānanda, that relying on that path, that practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters, one will know, see, or abandon the five lower fetters.
translations.mn64:9: And what, Ānanda, is the path, what is the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters? Here, Ānanda, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. Whatever form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness arises there, he contemplates those states as impermanent, suffering, a disease, a tumor, a barb, a calamity, an affliction, an alien, a disintegration, empty, not self. He turns his mind away from those states. Having turned his mind away from those states, he focuses it on the deathless element: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.’ Standing firm there, he realizes the destruction of the taints. If he does not realize the destruction of the taints, with that passion for the Dhamma, that delight in the Dhamma, by the destruction of the five lower fetters he becomes one who is spontaneously born, and there he attains final Nibbāna without returning from that world. This too, Ānanda, is the path, the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn6:14: If a monk, monks, should wish: ‘May I experience manifold supranormal powers—having been one, may I become many; having been many, may I become one; may I appear and vanish; may I go unhindered through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; may I dive in and out of the earth as if it were water; may I walk on water without sinking as if on land; may I sit cross-legged in the air like a bird; may I touch and stroke with my hand the sun and moon, mighty and powerful as they are; may I wield mastery with the body even as far as the Brahmā world,’ he should be one who fulfills virtue … he should develop the empty dwellings.
translations.mn6:15: If a monk, monks, should wish: ‘May I hear both sounds—divine and human, far and near—with the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human,’ they should fulfill the moralities …pe… and frequent empty dwellings.
translations.mn6:16: If a monk, monks, should wish: ‘May I understand the minds of other beings and other persons—discern a mind with lust as a mind with lust, discern a mind free from lust as a mind free from lust; discern a mind with hate as a mind with hate, discern a mind free from hate as a mind free from hate; discern a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion, discern a mind free from delusion as a mind free from delusion; discern a constricted mind as a constricted mind, discern a scattered mind as a scattered mind; discern an expanded mind as an expanded mind, discern an unexpanded mind as an unexpanded mind; discern a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind, discern an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind; discern a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind, discern an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind; discern a liberated mind as a liberated mind, discern an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind,’ they should fulfill the moralities …pe… and frequent empty dwellings.
translations.mn6:2: “Monks, dwell possessed of virtue, possessed of the Pāṭimokkha; dwell restrained by the Pāṭimokkha, possessed of conduct and resort, seeing fear in the slightest fault; train in the rules of training.
translations.mn6:3: If a monk, monks, should wish: ‘May I be dear and pleasing to my spiritual companions, respected and esteemed by them,’ they should fulfill the moralities, be internally devoted to the serenity of mind, attain the jhānas without difficulty, and possess insight, and frequent empty dwellings.
translations.mn6:6: If a monk, monks, should wish: ‘May my relatives and kin who have passed away, confident, recollect me; may that be for them a great fruit and a great benefit,’ they should fulfill the moralities, be internally devoted to the serenity of mind, attain the jhānas without difficulty, and possess insight, and frequent empty dwellings.
translations.mn6:7: If a monk, monks, should wish: ‘May I be able to endure discontent; may discontent not overcome me; may I live having overcome, having mastered any discontent that has arisen,’ they should fulfill the moralities …pe… and frequent empty dwellings.
translations.mn6:8: If a monk, monks, should wish: ‘May I be able to endure fear and dread; may fear and dread not overcome me; may I live having overcome, having mastered any fear and dread that has arisen,’ they should fulfill the moralities …pe… and frequent empty dwellings.
translations.mn6:9: If a monk, monks, should wish: ‘May I obtain without difficulty, without trouble, without difficulty the four jhānas that are mental attainments and comfortable abidings in the here and now,’ they should fulfill the moralities …pe… and frequent empty dwellings.
translations.mn70:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was wandering in the land of the Kāsis with a large Saṅgha of monks. There the Blessed One addressed the monks:
translations.mn70:11: “Because, monks, I have known, seen, understood, realized, and touched with wisdom this: ‘When such a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant is experienced, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states grow,’ therefore I say: ‘Enter upon and dwell in such a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant.’
translations.mn70:12: I do not say, monks, that all monks should do it with heedfulness; nor do I say, monks, that all monks should not do it with heedfulness. Those monks, monks, who are Arahants, with taints destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached the true goal, destroyed the fetters of becoming, and are freed by right knowledge—of such monks, monks, I say: ‘They should not do it with heedfulness.’ Why is that? Heedfulness has been done by them. They are unable to be heedless.
translations.mn70:13: But those monks, monks, who are in training, whose minds have not yet reached the goal, who aspire to the supreme security from bondage—of such monks, monks, I say: ‘They should do it with heedfulness.’ Why is that? It is only to be expected that these venerable ones, while using suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, and restraining their faculties, will realize for themselves with direct knowledge the supreme consummation of the spiritual life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness, and having realized it, will enter upon and dwell in it. Seeing this fruit of heedfulness for these monks, I say: ‘They should do it with heedfulness.’
translations.mn70:14: There are, monks, these seven persons who are noble and who exist in the world. What seven? The one liberated both ways, the one liberated by wisdom, the body-witness, the one attained to view, the one liberated by faith, the one following the Dhamma, and the one following by faith.
translations.mn70:15: And who, monks, is the person liberated both ways? Here, monks, a certain person, having passed beyond the formless liberations, dwells having touched them with his body, and having seen them with wisdom, his taints are destroyed. This person, monks, is called the one liberated both ways. Of this monk, monks, I say: ‘He should not do it with heedfulness.’ Why is that? Heedfulness has been done by him. He is unable to be heedless.
translations.mn70:17: And who, monks, is the body-witness? Here, monks, a certain person, having passed beyond the formless liberations, dwells having touched them with his body, and having seen them with wisdom, some of his taints are destroyed. This person, monks, is called the body-witness. Of this monk, monks, I say: ‘He should do it with heedfulness.’ Why is that? It is only to be expected that this venerable one, while using suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, and restraining his faculties, will realize for himself with direct knowledge the supreme consummation of the spiritual life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness, and having realized it, will enter upon and dwell in it. Seeing this fruit of heedfulness for this monk, I say: ‘He should do it with heedfulness.’
translations.mn70:2: “Monks, I eat only after having taken a meal in the evening. And, monks, when I eat only after having taken a meal in the evening, I perceive freedom from illness, lightness, strength, and comfortable living. You too, monks, should eat only after having taken a meal in the evening. And, monks, when you eat only after having taken a meal in the evening, you will perceive freedom from illness, lightness, strength, and comfortable living.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
translations.mn70:20: Who, monks, is the Dhamma-follower? Here, monks, a certain person does not, having passed over the peaceful liberations that are formless, dwell having touched them with the body. But when some of their taints are destroyed by seeing with wisdom, the teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata are accepted by them to some extent by understanding. And they possess these faculties: faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. This person, monks, is called a Dhamma-follower. I also declare of this monk that heedfulness should be made. For what reason? It is possible that this venerable one, by resorting to suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, and restraining the faculties, will realize that for which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness—the unsurpassed culmination of the holy life—having directly known and realized it for themselves in this very life. Seeing this fruit of heedlessness for this monk, I declare that heedfulness should be made.
translations.mn70:22: I do not say, monks, that the attainment of knowledge happens all at once; but rather, monks, the attainment of knowledge comes about by gradual training, gradual action, and gradual practice.
translations.mn70:23: And how, monks, does the attainment of knowledge come about by gradual training, gradual action, and gradual practice? Here, monks, having gone forth out of faith, one approaches; having approached, one pays respect; having paid respect, one lends ear; having lent ear, one hears the Dhamma; having heard the Dhamma, one memorizes it; having memorized the Dhamma, one examines the meaning of the teachings; having examined the meaning, one gains approval of the teachings; having gained approval of the teachings, desire arises; when desire has arisen, one makes an effort; having made an effort, one weighs it up; having weighed it up, one strives; being one who strives with a heart full of effort, one realizes the supreme truth with the body and, having penetrated it with wisdom, sees it.
translations.mn70:24: That faith, monks, was not; that approaching, monks, was not; that paying respect, monks, was not; that lending ear, monks, was not; that hearing the Dhamma, monks, was not; that memorizing the Dhamma, monks, was not; that examining the meaning, monks, was not; that approval of the teachings, monks, was not; that desire, monks, was not; that effort, monks, was not; that weighing up, monks, was not; that striving, monks, was not. Because of the wrong aim, monks, because of wrong practice, monks. How far, monks, have foolish men strayed from this Dhamma and Discipline.
translations.mn70:25: There is, monks, a fourfold exposition that a wise man who understands it should not take long to comprehend. Shall I teach it to you, monks, so that you might understand it?” “Who are we, venerable sir, and what are we to know the Dhamma?”
translations.mn70:26: “Even if a teacher, monks, is attached to material things, an heir of material things, dwells consorting with material things, a result of such a kind as this does not apply to him: ‘Thus it would be for us, and we should do it to him; nor would it be for us that it should not be so, and we should not do it to him.’ What then, monks, of the Tathāgata who dwells entirely free from association with material things.
translations.mn70:3: Then the Blessed One, wandering by stages in the Kasi country, eventually arrived at a market town called Kitagiri in Kasi. There the Blessed One lived in the market town of Kitagiri.
translations.mn70:4: Now at that time the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka were residents at Kitagiri. Then several monks approached the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka; having approached, they said this to the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka: “The community of monks, friends, eats only after having taken a meal in the evening. And, friends, when eating only after having taken a meal in the evening, they perceive freedom from illness, lightness, strength, and comfortable living. You too, friends, should eat only after having taken a meal in the evening. And, friends, when eating only after having taken a meal in the evening, you will perceive freedom from illness, lightness, strength, and comfortable living.” When this was said, the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka said this to those monks: “We, friends, eat both in the evening and in the morning and at the wrong time of day. When we eat both in the evening and in the morning and at the wrong time of day, we perceive freedom from illness, lightness, strength, and comfortable living. Why should we, having abandoned what is immediate, run after what is timely? We will eat both in the evening and in the morning and at the wrong time of day.”
translations.mn70:7: “Do you not know, monks, that I have taught the Dhamma like this: that for some person, when experiencing a pleasant feeling of this kind, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline; but for some person, when experiencing a pleasant feeling of this kind, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase; that for some person, when experiencing a painful feeling of this kind, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline; but for some person, when experiencing a painful feeling of this kind, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase; that for some person, when experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling of this kind, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline; but for some person, when experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling of this kind, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn75:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was living among the Kurus at a market town of the Kurus called Kammasadhamma, on a spread of straw in the Brahmin Bharadvaja's dwelling.
translations.mn75:10: “I myself, Māgaṇḍiya, formerly when living the household life, enjoyed myself supplied and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure, frequenting forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, charming, beautiful, connected with sensual pleasure, and alluring; sounds cognizable by the ear … odors cognizable by the nose … flavors cognizable by the tongue … tactile objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, charming, beautiful, connected with sensual pleasure, and alluring.  I had three palaces, Māgaṇḍiya: one for the rainy season, one for the winter, and one for the summer.  Living in the palace for the rainy season during the four months of the rainy season, entertained by female musicians, I did not go down to the lower palace.  Later, truly knowing the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of sensual pleasures, I abandoned craving for sensual pleasures, removed the fever of sensual pleasures, and dwelt inwardly with a mind freed from thirst, without craving.  I saw other beings who were not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with the fever of sensual pleasures, indulging in sensual pleasures.  I did not delight in that, nor did I find pleasure there.  For what reason?  Because that pleasure, Māgaṇḍiya, apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states—even if one were to attain a divine pleasure and stand firm therein—while amusing oneself with that pleasure, I did not delight in what is inferior, nor did I find pleasure there.
translations.mn75:12: “So too, Māgaṇḍiya, I formerly when living the household life, enjoyed myself supplied and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure, frequenting forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, charming, beautiful, connected with sensual pleasure, and alluring; sounds cognizable by the ear … odors cognizable by the nose … flavors cognizable by the tongue … tactile objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, charming, beautiful, connected with sensual pleasure, and alluring.  Later, truly knowing the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of sensual pleasures, I abandoned craving for sensual pleasures, removed the fever of sensual pleasures, and dwelt inwardly with a mind freed from thirst, without craving.  I saw other beings who were not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with the fever of sensual pleasures, indulging in sensual pleasures, and I did not delight in that, nor did I find pleasure there.  For what reason?  Because that pleasure, Māgaṇḍiya, apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states—even if one were to attain a divine pleasure and stand firm therein—while amusing oneself with that pleasure, I did not delight in what is inferior, nor did I find pleasure there.
translations.mn75:13: “Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, there was a leper, covered with sores and lesions, devoured by worms, scratching at the openings of his wounds with his nails, cauterizing his body with a burning ember.  His friends, companions, and relatives would bring him a surgeon or a physician.  That surgeon or physician would apply medicine to him.  Relying on that medicine, he would recover from his leprosy; he would be free from disease, happy, and at ease, able to go wherever he wished.  Then he would see another leper, covered with sores and lesions, devoured by worms, scratching at the openings of his wounds with his nails, cauterizing his body with a burning ember.  What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya? Would that man delight in the leprosy of that other man or in applying the burning ember?”  “No, Master Gotama.  For what reason?  Because when there is disease, Master Gotama, medicine must be applied; when there is no disease, medicine need not be applied.”
translations.mn75:16: “So too, Māgaṇḍiya, in the past, sensual pleasures were of painful contact and caused great suffering and great burning; in the future, sensual pleasures will be of painful contact and cause great suffering and great burning; and in the present, sensual pleasures are of painful contact and cause great suffering and great burning.  These beings, Māgaṇḍiya, not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with the fever of sensual pleasures, with faculties afflicted, have a distorted perception, thinking that in sensual pleasures there is happiness, even though it is of painful contact.
translations.mn75:17: “Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, there was a leper, covered with sores and lesions, devoured by worms, scratching at the openings of his wounds with his nails, cauterizing his body with a burning ember.  As that leper, covered with sores and lesions, devoured by worms, scratches at the openings of his wounds with his nails and cauterizes his body with a burning ember, those openings of his wounds become more filthy, more foul-smelling, and more putrid; yet there is some measure of satisfaction and gratification—namely, the itching of the openings of his wounds.  So too, Māgaṇḍiya, beings not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with the fever of sensual pleasures, indulge in sensual pleasures.  As these beings not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being devoured by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with the fever of sensual pleasures, indulge in sensual pleasures, their craving for sensual pleasures grows, they burn more with the fever of sensual pleasures, yet there is some measure of satisfaction and gratification—namely, dependent on the five cords of sensual pleasure.
translations.mn75:18: What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya, have you ever seen or heard of a king or a king's minister, supplied and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure, enjoying them, without abandoning craving for sensual pleasures, without removing the fever of sensual pleasures, with craving faded away internally, with a mind at peace, having lived, living, or about to live?” “No, Master Gotama.” “Good, Māgaṇḍiya. I too, Māgaṇḍiya, have never seen or heard of a king or a king's minister, supplied and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure, enjoying them, without abandoning craving for sensual pleasures, without removing the fever of sensual pleasures, with craving faded away internally, with a mind at peace, having lived, living, or about to live. But, Māgaṇḍiya, all those ascetics and brahmins who have lived, are living, or will live with craving faded away internally and with a mind at peace—having directly known the origin, passing away, gratification, danger, and escape in sensual pleasures as they really are—have abandoned craving for sensual pleasures, removed the fever of sensual pleasures, and with craving faded away internally, with a mind at peace, have lived, are living, or will live.”
translations.mn75:2: Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and outer robe, entered Kammāsadhamma for alms. Having walked for alms in Kammāsadhamma and returned from the alms round after the meal, he approached a certain forest grove for the day's abode. Having entered that forest grove, he sat down at the root of a certain tree for the day's abode.
translations.mn75:22: “Thus I am confident in Master Gotama. May Master Gotama teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might understand health and see Nibbāna.” “Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, there was a man born blind. He would not see dark blue forms, yellow forms, red forms, white forms, or crimson forms; he would not see what is even and uneven, he would not see the stars and moon and sun. His friends, colleagues, relatives, and kin would employ a surgeon or an oculist for him. That surgeon or oculist would apply medicine. Having applied that medicine, he would not produce eyes, he would not clean the eyes. What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya, would that surgeon be a remover of fatigue and distress only?” “Yes, Master Gotama.” “So too, Māgaṇḍiya, if I were to teach you the Dhamma saying: ‘This is health, this is Nibbāna,’ you would not understand health, you would not see Nibbāna. That would be my fatigue, that would be my distress.”
translations.mn75:24: So too, Māgaṇḍiya, if I were to teach you the Dhamma saying: ‘This is health, this is Nibbāna.’ You would understand health, you would see Nibbāna. With the arising of vision for you, the desire and lust regarding the five aggregates subject to clinging would be abandoned; and you would think thus: ‘For a long time I have been cheated, deceived, and bound by this mind. I, clinging to form, have clung; clinging to feeling, have clung; clinging to perception, have clung; clinging to volitional formations, have clung; clinging to consciousness, have clung. With clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be; thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.’”
translations.mn75:25: “Thus I am confident in Master Gotama. May Master Gotama teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might rise from this seat without blindness.” “Then you should associate with a good person, Māgaṇḍiya. When you, Māgaṇḍiya, associate with a good person, you will hear the true Dhamma; when you hear the true Dhamma, you will practice in accordance with the Dhamma; when you practice in accordance with the Dhamma, you will know and see for yourself—these diseases, tumors, arrows; here these diseases, tumors, arrows cease without remainder. With the cessation of my clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease; thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.”
translations.mn75:26: When this was said, the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya said to the Blessed One: “Excellent, Master Gotama, excellent, Master Gotama. Just as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, to reveal what was hidden, to show the way to one who was lost, or to hold up a lamp in the dark so that those with eyes could see forms, so has the Dhamma been explained by Master Gotama in various ways. I go for refuge to Master Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May I obtain going forth in the presence of Master Gotama, may I obtain full ordination.”
translations.mn75:27: “Anyone, Māgaṇḍiya, who was previously of another sect and desires going forth or full ordination in this Dhamma and Vinaya lives on probation for four months. At the end of four months, the bhikkhus with settled minds give him the going forth and confer full ordination as a bhikkhu. But there is a distinction in individuals.” “If, venerable sir, those previously of another sect who desire going forth or full ordination in this Dhamma and Vinaya live on probation for four months, and at the end of four months the bhikkhus with settled minds give them the going forth and confer full ordination as bhikkhus; I will live on probation for four years, and at the end of four years may the bhikkhus with settled minds give me the going forth and confer full ordination as a bhikkhu.”
translations.mn75:3: Then the wanderer Magandiya, walking and wandering in the open air, approached the Brahmin Bhāradvāja Gotta’s fire-chamber. The wanderer Magandiya saw that a grass seat had been laid out in the Brahmin Bhāradvāja Gotta’s fire-chamber. Seeing this, he said to the Brahmin Bhāradvāja Gotta: 'For whom, good Bhāradvāja, has this grass seat been laid out in the fire-chamber? I suppose it is suitable for a mendicant’s seat.'
translations.mn75:6: The Buddha heard with his divine ear, which is purified and surpasses human beings, the conversation between the Brahmin Bhāradvāja Gotta and the wanderer Magandiya. Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat and approached the Brahmin Bhāradvāja Gotta’s fire-chamber. He sat down on the prepared grass seat. Then the Brahmin Bhāradvāja Gotta approached the Buddha; he exchanged greetings with the Buddha. When the courteous and agreeable conversation was finished, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Brahmin Bhāradvāja Gotta, the Buddha said to him: 'Was there, Bhāradvāja, some conversation between you and the wanderer Magandiya about this very grass seat?' When this was said, the Brahmin Bhāradvāja Gotta, shocked and with hairs standing on end, said to the Buddha: 'This is indeed what we wished to report to Master Gotama. But then Master Gotama declared the unspoken.'
translations.mn75:7: For this conversation between the Buddha and the Brahmin Bhāradvāja Gotta had been reported. Then the wanderer Magandiya, walking and wandering in the open air, approached the Brahmin Bhāradvāja Gotta’s fire-chamber, where the Buddha was; he approached the Buddha; he exchanged greetings with the Buddha. When the courteous and agreeable conversation was finished, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Buddha said to the wanderer Magandiya:
translations.mn77:1: Thus I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground.
translations.mn77:10: There are, Udāyī, these other five qualities by which my disciples honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me, and relying on which they live. What five? Here, Udāyī, my disciples reflect on my virtue: 'The ascetic Gotama is virtuous; he is endowed with the highest moral conduct.'
translations.mn77:15: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have taught the practice to my disciples, such that those of my disciples who follow it develop the four foundations of mindfulness. Here, Udāyī, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, aware, and mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings … he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind … he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, aware, and mindful, having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world. And many of my disciples dwell having attained the final knowledge of the direct knowledges.
translations.mn77:16: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have taught the practice to my disciples, such that those of my disciples who follow it develop the four right efforts. Here, Udāyī, a monk generates desire, rouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unskillful qualities; he generates desire, rouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unskillful qualities; he generates desire, rouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen skillful qualities; he generates desire, rouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, plenitude, development, and completion of arisen skillful qualities. And many of my disciples dwell having attained the final knowledge of the direct knowledges.
translations.mn77:17: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have taught the practice to my disciples, such that those of my disciples who follow it develop the four bases of power. Here, Udāyī, a monk develops the basis of power that possesses concentration due to desire and effort of will; he develops the basis of power that possesses concentration due to energy and effort of will; he develops the basis of power that possesses concentration due to mind and effort of will; he develops the basis of power that possesses concentration due to investigation and effort of will. And many of my disciples dwell having attained the final knowledge of the direct knowledges.
translations.mn77:18: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have taught the practice to my disciples, such that those of my disciples who follow it develop the five faculties. Here, Udāyī, a monk develops the faculty of confidence, which leads to peace and awakening; he develops the faculty of energy … he develops the faculty of mindfulness … he develops the faculty of concentration … he develops the faculty of wisdom, which leads to peace and awakening. And many of my disciples dwell having attained the final knowledge of the direct knowledges.
translations.mn77:2: At that time several well-known wanderers were staying at the wanderers’ park in the Peacock’s Feeding Ground, such as Annabhāra, Varadhara, the wanderer Sakuludāyī, and other well-known wanderers.
translations.mn77:20: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have taught the practice to my disciples, such that those of my disciples who follow it develop the seven factors of enlightenment. Here, Udāyī, a monk develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, which relies on seclusion, fading away, cessation, and culminates in relinquishment; he develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena … he develops the enlightenment factor of energy … he develops the enlightenment factor of rapture … he develops the enlightenment factor of tranquility … he develops the enlightenment factor of concentration … he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity, which relies on seclusion, fading away, cessation, and culminates in relinquishment. And many of my disciples dwell having attained the final knowledge of the direct knowledges.
translations.mn77:21: Again, Udāyī, I have declared the practice for my disciples, such that my disciples, practicing in this way, develop the noble eightfold path. Here, Udāyī, a monk develops right view, develops right intention, develops right speech, develops right action, develops right livelihood, develops right effort, develops right mindfulness, develops right concentration. And in this regard, many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:22: Again, Udāyī, I have declared the practice for my disciples, such that my disciples, practicing in this way, develop the eight liberations. Perceiving forms, this is the first liberation; internally perceiving the formless, perceiving forms externally, this is the second liberation; intent on the beautiful, this is the third liberation; completely transcending the perception of forms, with the disappearance of the perception of resistance, not attending to the perception of diversity, thinking 'infinite space', entering and dwelling in the base of infinite space, this is the fourth liberation; completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking 'infinite consciousness', entering and dwelling in the base of infinite consciousness, this is the fifth liberation; completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, thinking 'there is nothing', entering and dwelling in the base of nothingness, this is the sixth liberation; completely transcending the base of nothingness, entering and dwelling in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this is the seventh liberation; completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, entering and dwelling in the cessation of perception and feeling, this is the eighth liberation. And in this regard, many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:24: Again, Udāyī, I have declared the practice for my disciples, such that my disciples, practicing in this way, develop the ten kasina bases. One perceives the earth kasina above, below, across, without obstruction, limitless; one perceives the water kasina ... one perceives the fire kasina ... one perceives the air kasina ... one perceives the blue kasina ... one perceives the yellow kasina ... one perceives the red kasina ... one perceives the white kasina ... one perceives the space kasina ... one perceives the consciousness kasina above, below, across, without obstruction, limitless. And in this regard, many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:25: Again, Udāyī, I have declared the practice for my disciples, such that my disciples, practicing in this way, develop the four jhānas. Here, Udāyī, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. He drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, so that there is no part of his whole body unpervaded by the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. Just as, Udāyī, a skilled bathman or his apprentice would sprinkle bathing powder in a metal basin, kneading it repeatedly and scattering it so that the ball of bathing powder would be saturated, moisture-laden, suffused inside and out with moisture, yet would not ooze moisture; so too, Udāyī, a monk drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, so that there is no part of his whole body unpervaded by the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
translations.mn77:26: Again, Udāyī, a monk, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, entering and dwelling in the second jhāna ... He drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and pleasure born of concentration, so that there is no part of his whole body unpervaded by the rapture and pleasure born of concentration. Just as, Udāyī, a lake with spring water welling up from below, having no inflow from east, west, north, or south, and the rain clouds from time to time do not supply a proper shower of rain; yet cool water would well up from that very lake and drench, steep, fill, and suffuse that very lake with cool water, so that there would be no part of the whole lake unpervaded by cool water; so too, Udāyī, a monk drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and pleasure born of concentration, so that there is no part of his whole body unpervaded by the rapture and pleasure born of concentration.
translations.mn77:27: Again, Udāyī, a monk, with the fading away of rapture ... entering and dwelling in the third jhāna. He drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with the pleasure divested of rapture, so that there is no part of his whole body unpervaded by the pleasure divested of rapture. Just as, Udāyī, in a pond of blue, white, or red lotuses, some lotuses, born in the water, grown in the water, rising above the water, are suffused with cool water from their roots to their tips, so that no part of those lotuses is unpervaded by cool water; so too, Udāyī, a monk drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with the pleasure divested of rapture, so that there is no part of his whole body unpervaded by the pleasure divested of rapture.
translations.mn77:28: Again, Udāyī, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes purification of mindfulness by equanimity. He sits suffusing this very body with a pure, bright mind, so that there is no part of his whole body unpervaded by the pure, bright mind. Just as, Udāyī, a man might be sitting covered from head to foot with a white cloth, so that there would be no part of his body unpervaded by the white cloth; so too, Udāyī, a monk sits suffusing this very body with a pure, bright mind, so that there is no part of his whole body unpervaded by the pure, bright mind. And in this regard, many of my disciples dwell having reached the consummation and perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:3: Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms. Then it occurred to the Blessed One: 'It is too crowded to go for alms in Rājagaha just now. Why shouldn't I go to the wanderer's park at Moranivāpa and approach the wanderer Sakuludāyī?'
translations.mn77:32: Again, Udāyī, the practice has been taught by me to the disciples, such that my disciples, practicing in this way, hear both sounds—divine and human, whether far or near—with the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human. Just as, Udāyī, a strong trumpet blast might be heard in the four directions with little difficulty; so too, Udāyī, the practice has been taught by me to the disciples, such that my disciples, practicing in this way, hear both sounds—divine and human, whether far or near—with the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human. And in this regard, many of my disciples dwell having reached the end and limit of the direct knowledges.
translations.mn77:34: Again, Udāyī, the practice has been taught by me to the disciples, such that my disciples, practicing in this way, recollect their manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of contraction, many eons of expansion, many eons of contraction and expansion: 'There I was named thus, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such food, experiencing such pleasure and pain, with such a lifespan; passing away from there, I was reborn there; there I was named thus, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such food, experiencing such pleasure and pain, with such a lifespan; passing away from there, I was reborn here.' Thus they recollect their manifold past lives with features and details. Just as, Udāyī, a man might go from his own village to another village, and from that village to yet another village; then from that village he might return to his own village; he might think: 'I went from my own village to that village, and there I stood thus, sat thus, spoke thus, and was thus silent; from that village I went to that other village, and there too I stood thus, sat thus, spoke thus, and was thus silent, and now I have returned from that village to my own village.' So too, Udāyī, the practice has been taught by me to the disciples, such that my disciples, practicing in this way, recollect their manifold past lives ... Thus they recollect their manifold past lives with features and details. And in this regard, many of my disciples dwell having reached the end and limit of the direct knowledges.
translations.mn77:35: Again, Udāyī, the practice has been taught by me to the disciples, such that my disciples, practicing in this way, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, see beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and they understand how beings pass on according to their actions: 'These beings, indeed, were endowed with bad bodily conduct, bad verbal conduct, and bad mental conduct; they were revilers of noble ones, holding wrong view, and undertaking actions based on wrong view. With the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a bad destination, a lower realm, hell. But these beings, indeed, were endowed with good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, and good mental conduct; they were not revilers of noble ones, holding right view, and undertaking actions based on right view. With the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.' Thus, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, they see beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and they understand how beings pass on according to their actions. Just as, Udāyī, there are two houses with doors. A man with good sight, standing in the middle, might see people entering and leaving the houses, walking around and wandering about; so too, Udāyī, the practice has been taught by me to the disciples, such that my disciples, practicing in this way, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, see beings passing away and being reborn ... and they understand how beings pass on according to their actions. And in this regard, many of my disciples dwell having reached the end and limit of the direct knowledges.
translations.mn77:36: Again, Udāyī, the practice has been taught by me to the disciples, such that my disciples, practicing in this way, realize for themselves with direct knowledge the taintless liberation of mind and liberation through wisdom, in this very life, and dwell having attained it through the destruction of the taints. Just as, Udāyī, there is a mountain pond with clear, limpid, unruffled water, where a man with good sight standing on the bank might see shells, gravel, and fish moving about and staying still. He would think: 'This pond is clear, limpid, and unruffled, and here are these shells, gravel, and fish moving about and staying still.' So too, Udāyī, the practice has been taught by me to the disciples, such that my disciples, practicing in this way, realize for themselves with direct knowledge the taintless liberation of mind and liberation through wisdom, in this very life, and dwell having attained it through the destruction of the taints. And in this regard, many of my disciples dwell having reached the end and limit of the direct knowledges.
translations.mn77:5: Then the Blessed One approached the wanderer Sakuludāyī. Then the wanderer Sakuludāyī said this to the Blessed One: 'Come, sir, Blessed One. Welcome, sir, Blessed One. It is a long time, sir, since the Blessed One has made this opportunity to come here. Please sit, sir, Blessed One; this seat is prepared.' The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat. The wanderer Sakuludāyī also, taking a low seat, sat to one side. Sitting to one side, the wanderer Sakuludāyī, the Blessed One said this: 'What is the topic of discussion, Udāyī, that you are currently engaged in, and what was the previous conversation that was interrupted?'
translations.mn77:7: 'In how many ways, Udāyī, do you regard me in the Dhamma, such that my disciples honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, and relying on that, they dwell?'
translations.mn77:9: “‘The ascetic Gotama eats little, and he praises eating little’—if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me with that, and having honored and respected me, were to rely on me as a support, there are, Udāyi, disciples of mine who eat even a small bowlful, even a half-bowlful, even a handful, even a half-handful. But I, Udāyi, at times eat even more than enough with this bowl. “‘The ascetic Gotama eats little, and he praises eating little’—if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me with that, and having honored and respected me, were to rely on me as a support, those disciples of mine, Udāyi, who eat even a small bowlful, even a half-bowlful, even a handful, even a half-handful, would not honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me with this Dhamma, nor having honored and respected me, rely on me as a support. “‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of robe, and he praises contentment with any kind of robe’—if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me with that, and having honored and respected me, were to rely on me as a support, there are, Udāyi, disciples of mine who are rag-robe wearers, wearers of coarse robes; they sweep up from dust heaps or from a rubbish heap or from a shop floor, make a double robe, and wear it. But I, Udāyi, at times wear laymen’s robes that are strong, hemmed with rough cloth, and not of fine linen or cotton. “‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of robe, and he praises contentment with any kind of robe’—if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me with that, and having honored and respected me, were to rely on me as a support, those disciples of mine, Udāyi, who are rag-robe wearers, wearers of coarse robes, who sweep up from dust heaps or from a rubbish heap or from a shop floor, make a double robe, and wear it, would not honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me with this Dhamma, nor having honored and respected me, rely on me as a support. “‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of almsfood, and he praises contentment with any kind of almsfood’—if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me with that, and having honored and respected me, were to rely on me as a support, there are, Udāyi, disciples of mine who are alms-goers, wandering from house to house, delighting in gleanings; they, having entered a house, do not accept even an invitation to a seat. But I, Udāyi, at times eat even on invitation, rice with various soups and sauces. “‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of almsfood, and he praises contentment with any kind of almsfood’—if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me with that, and having honored and respected me, were to rely on me as a support, those disciples of mine, Udāyi, who are alms-goers, wandering from house to house, delighting in gleanings, who, having entered a house, do not accept even an invitation to a seat, would not honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me with this Dhamma, nor having honored and respected me, rely on me as a support. “‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of lodging, and he praises contentment with any kind of lodging’—if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me with that, and having honored and respected me, were to rely on me as a support, there are, Udāyi, disciples of mine who dwell at the root of a tree or in the open air; they do not go to a roofed shelter for eight months of the year. But I, Udāyi, at times dwell even in a gabled house, with walls plastered inside and out, with shutters fastened, protected from the wind and sun. “‘The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of lodging, and he praises contentment with any kind of lodging’—if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me with that, and having honored and respected me, were to rely on me as a support, those disciples of mine, Udāyi, who dwell at the root of a tree or in the open air, who do not go to a roofed shelter for eight months of the year, would not honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me with this Dhamma, nor having honored and respected me, rely on me as a support. “‘The ascetic Gotama lives aloof from society, and he praises living aloof’—if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me with that, and having honored and respected me, were to rely on me as a support, there are, Udāyi, disciples of mine who are forest dwellers, who resort to remote lodgings in forests and groves; they come into the midst of the Sangha once a fortnight for the recitation of the Pātimokkha. But I, Udāyi, at times dwell crowded with monks, nuns, male lay followers, female lay followers, kings, king’s ministers, and followers of other sects. “‘The ascetic Gotama lives aloof from society, and he praises living aloof’—if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me with that, and having honored and respected me, were to rely on me as a support, those disciples of mine, Udāyi, who are forest dwellers, who resort to remote lodgings in forests and groves, who come into the midst of the Sangha once a fortnight for the recitation of the Pātimokkha, would not honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me with this Dhamma, nor having honored and respected me, rely on me as a support. Thus, Udāyi, my disciples do not honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me with these five things, nor having honored and respected me, rely on me as a support.
translations.mn7:11: He gains the realization of meaning, gains the realization of Dhamma, gains the delight connected with Dhamma; when delighted, rapture arises; when the mind is filled with rapture, the body becomes tranquil; when the body is tranquil, one experiences happiness; with happiness, the mind becomes concentrated.
translations.mn7:13: He dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. So above, below, across, and everywhere, and to the entire world, he dwells pervading the all-encompassing world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill will;
translations.mn7:17: He understands: ‘There is this, there is the inferior, there is the superior, and there is an escape beyond this perception.’
translations.mn7:18: When he knows and sees in this way, the mind is liberated from the taint of sensuality, the mind is liberated from the taint of existence, the mind is liberated from the taint of ignorance. When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.’ This is called, monks, a monk who has bathed without bathing.’
translations.mn7:19: Now at that time the Brahmin Sundarika Bhāradvāja was sitting not far from the Blessed One. Then Sundarika Bhāradvāja the Brahmin said to the Blessed One: “Does Master Gotama go to bathe in the Bāhukā river?” “What for, Brahmin, with the Bāhukā river? What will the Bāhukā river do?” “The Bāhukā river, Master Gotama, is approved by many people, it is considered meritorious by many people; and many people wash away bad deeds done in the Bāhukā river.”
translations.mn7:2: “Suppose, monks, a cloth were stained and dirty; and a dyer would take it to any dye-heap—whether blue or yellow or red or crimson—it would take up a bad color and not a pure one. Why is that? Because of the impurity of the cloth, monks. So too, monks, when the mind is stained, a bad destination is to be expected. Suppose, monks, a cloth were clean and bright; and a dyer would take it to any dye-heap—whether blue or yellow or red or crimson—it would take up a pure color and a good one. Why is that? Because of the purity of the cloth, monks. So too, monks, when the mind is unstained, a good destination is to be expected.
translations.mn7:20: Then the Blessed One addressed Sundarika Bhāradvāja the Brahmin in verses: “Bāhukā and Adhikakkā, Gayā and Sundarikā too; Sarassatī and Payāga, and the river Bāhumatī; A fool may bathe constantly, but of dark deeds he is not purified. What will Sundarikā do, what Payāga, what the Bāhukā river? They cannot cleanse a man who is cruel and full of treachery, for he is not purified by bad water. Pure is the offering for the pure, always is the fast of the pure; For the pure of pure deeds, the vow is always fulfilled; Bathe here, Brahmin, make yourself secure towards all beings. If you do not speak lies, if you do not harm living beings; If you do not take what is not given, having faith and not being stingy; What use is going to Gayā? Your water is Gayā itself.”
translations.mn7:3: And what, monks, are the corruptions of the mind? Greed and wrong grasp are a corruption of the mind, ill will is a corruption of the mind, anger is a corruption of the mind, resentment is a corruption of the mind, contempt is a corruption of the mind, domineering is a corruption of the mind, envy is a corruption of the mind, stinginess is a corruption of the mind, deceit is a corruption of the mind, fraud is a corruption of the mind, obstinacy is a corruption of the mind, aggression is a corruption of the mind, conceit is a corruption of the mind, arrogance is a corruption of the mind, vanity is a corruption of the mind, negligence is a corruption of the mind.
translations.mn7:6: He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma: ‘Well expounded is the Dhamma by the Blessed One, to be seen for oneself, timeless, inviting verification, relevant, to be understood by the wise for themselves.’;
translations.mn7:7: He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, the straight way, the true way, the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight kinds of individuals. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.’
translations.mn82:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was wandering in the land of the Kurus together with a large Saṅgha of monks when he arrived at a market town of the Kurus named Thullakoṭṭhika.
translations.mn82:11: Then Raṭṭhapāla’s companions approached Raṭṭhapāla’s parents; having approached, they said to Raṭṭhapāla’s parents: “Mother and father, this young man Raṭṭhapāla has lain down right there on the ground saying: ‘My death will be right here, or I will go forth.’ If you do not allow Raṭṭhapāla to go forth from the home life into homelessness, he will die right here. But if you allow Raṭṭhapāla to go forth from the home life into homelessness, even if he goes forth you will not see him. If Raṭṭhapāla does not find satisfaction in going forth from the home life into homelessness, what other course will there be for him? He will return right here. Allow Raṭṭhapāla to go forth from the home life into homelessness.” “We allow Raṭṭhapāla to go forth from the home life into homelessness, father. But his parents should be admonished by the one who has gone forth.” Then Raṭṭhapāla’s companions approached Raṭṭhapāla; having approached, they said to Raṭṭhapāla: “Get up, friend Raṭṭhapāla, you have been allowed by your parents to go forth from the home life into homelessness. But your parents should be admonished by the one who has gone forth.”
translations.mn82:12: Then Raṭṭhapāla got up, took his bowl and robe, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Raṭṭhapāla said to the Blessed One: “I have been allowed, Bhante, by my parents to go forth from the home life into homelessness. Let me go forth, Blessed One.”
translations.mn82:13: The young man Raṭṭhapāla obtained the going forth in the presence of the Blessed One, he obtained full ordination. Then the Blessed One, having lived at Thullakoṭṭhika as long as he pleased after Venerable Raṭṭhapāla had not long been fully ordained, set out for Sāvatthī by wandering. Wandering step by step, he arrived at Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One lived at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.
translations.mn82:14: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, before long—realizing for himself with direct knowledge the highest goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness—having attained it, dwelled in it. He announced: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.” Venerable Raṭṭhapāla became one of the Arahants.
translations.mn82:16: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, rising from his seat, having bowed down to the Blessed One and circumambulated him, having folded his dwelling and taking his bowl and robe, set out for Thullakoṭṭhika by wandering. Wandering step by step, he arrived at Thullakoṭṭhika. There Venerable Raṭṭhapāla lived at Thullakoṭṭhika in the Migacīra of King Korabya. Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, dressing in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, entered Thullakoṭṭhika for alms. Walking for alms in Thullakoṭṭhika with his bowl, he approached his own father's house.
translations.mn82:17: Now on that occasion Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father was having a portico built in the middle of the hall. Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father saw Venerable Raṭṭhapāla coming from a distance. Seeing him, he said: “Our dear and beloved only son has gone forth with these shaven ascetics.” Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla at his own father's house obtained neither a gift nor a refusal; he obtained only abuse instead.
translations.mn82:18: Now on that occasion Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's female cousin wanted to throw away stale sour gruel. Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said to that female cousin: “If, sister, it is something to be thrown away, put it in my bowl.” Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's female cousin, throwing the stale sour gruel into Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's bowl, took note of the mark of his hands and feet. Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's female cousin approached Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's mother; having approached, she said to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's mother: “You should know, Madam: ‘The noble master's son Raṭṭhapāla has arrived.’” “If it is true that you speak, I will give you this to do.” Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's mother approached Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father; having approached, she said to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father: “You should know, householder: ‘Raṭṭhapāla, the young man, it seems, has arrived.’”
translations.mn82:19: Now on that occasion Venerable Raṭṭhapāla was eating the stale sour gruel relying on a certain tree root. Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father approached Venerable Raṭṭhapāla; having approached, he said to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: “Is it true, dear Raṭṭhapāla, that you will eat stale sour gruel? Surely, dear Raṭṭhapāla, you must go to your own home?” “Where do we have a home, householder, for us who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness? We are homeless, householder. We went to your house, householder, and there obtained neither a gift nor a refusal; we obtained only abuse instead.” “Come, dear Raṭṭhapāla, let us go home.” “Enough, householder, my meal business for today is done.” “In that case, dear Raṭṭhapāla, consent for tomorrow's meal.” Venerable Raṭṭhapāla consented by silence.
translations.mn82:20: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father, knowing Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's consent, approached his own house; having approached, he caused a large pile of gold and silver to be made, covered it with a cloth, and addressed Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's former second wife: “Come, you wives, adorn yourselves with the ornament by which you were dear and pleasing to the young man Raṭṭhapāla before.”
translations.mn82:21: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father, at the end of that night, had excellent staple and non-staple food prepared at his own house and announced the time to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: “It is time, dear Raṭṭhapāla, the meal is ready.”
translations.mn82:22: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, dressing in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, approached his own father's house; having approached, he sat on the prepared seat. Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father uncovered that pile of gold and silver and said to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: “This, dear Raṭṭhapāla, is wealth belonging to your mother, some belonging to your father, some belonging to your grandfather. You are able, dear Raṭṭhapāla, to enjoy riches and to make merit. Come, dear Raṭṭhapāla, having turned back to the lower, enjoy riches and make merit.” “If you were to do my bidding, householder, having loaded this pile of gold and silver onto a cart and dumping it into the middle of the river Ganges, you should sink it. For what reason? For those, householder, who arise from that cause would be sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair.”
translations.mn82:23: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s former second wife, taking hold of his feet, said to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: 'What are the nymphs like, good sir, for whose sake you live the holy life?' 'We do not live the holy life, sister, for the sake of nymphs.' 'The noble master Raṭṭhapāla is addressing us as sisters.' They fainted and fell right there.
translations.mn82:24: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said to his father: 'If food is to be given, householder, give it; do not harass us.' 'Eat, dear son Raṭṭhapāla, the meal is finished.' Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father, with his own hand, satisfied and served Venerable Raṭṭhapāla with excellent hard and soft food. Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, having eaten and washed his hand and bowl, standing still, spoke these verses:
translations.mn82:26: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, having spoken these verses standing still, approached the Migacīra park of King Koravya; having approached, he sat down at the root of a certain tree for the day’s abiding.
translations.mn82:27: Then King Koravya addressed the forester: 'Clean up, good forester, the Migacīra park; let us go to see the Subhūmi.' 'Yes, your majesty,' the forester replied to King Koravya. While cleaning up the Migacīra park, he saw Venerable Raṭṭhapāla sitting at the root of a certain tree for the day’s abiding. Having seen him, he approached King Koravya; having approached, he said to King Koravya: 'The Migacīra park is clean, your majesty. There is here a young man of good family named Raṭṭhapāla, the son of the chief family in Thullakoṭṭhaka, whom you often praised; he is sitting at the root of a certain tree for the day’s abiding.' 'In that case, good forester, let the park be enough for today. We will now pay respects to the master Raṭṭhapāla himself.'
translations.mn82:28: Then King Koravya, having said 'Let all the hard and soft food prepared there be released,' harnessed fine, fine carriages, mounted a fine carriage, and with fine, fine carriages, with the majesty of a great king, went out of Thullakoṭṭhaka to see Venerable Raṭṭhapāla. Having gone as far as the ground allowed by carriage, having alighted from the carriages, he approached Venerable Raṭṭhapāla with a large crowd, increasing and increasing. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Raṭṭhapāla. Having exchanged courteous and memorable talk, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, King Koravya said to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: 'Let Master Raṭṭhapāla sit on this seat.' 'Enough, great king, you sit; I am sitting on my own seat.' King Koravya sat on the prepared seat. Having sat, King Koravya said to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla:
translations.mn82:29: 'There are these four perceptions, Master Raṭṭhapāla, possessed of which some shave off hair and beard, don ochre robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness. What four? The perception of decay, the perception of disease, the perception of property, the perception of relatives.
translations.mn82:3: Then the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhaka approached the Blessed One; having approached, some bowed down to the Blessed One and sat to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and after exchanging courteous and memorable talk, sat to one side; some, raising their joined palms in reverence to the Blessed One, sat to one side; some, announcing their name and clan in the presence of the Blessed One, sat to one side; and some sat to one side in silence. When the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhaka were sitting to one side, the Blessed One instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened them with a Dhamma talk.
translations.mn82:34: These are the four perceptions, Master Raṭṭhapāla, possessed of which some shave off hair and beard, don ochre robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness. Master Raṭṭhapāla does not have these. Knowing what, seeing what, or hearing what did Master Raṭṭhapāla go forth from the home life into homelessness?'
translations.mn82:35: 'There are, great king, four expositions of Dhamma pointed out by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, knowing which, seeing which, and hearing which I went forth from the home life into homelessness. What four?
translations.mn82:4: Now at that time a young man named Raṭṭhapāla, the son of the chief family in that very Thullakoṭṭhaka, was sitting in that assembly. Then it occurred to the young man Raṭṭhapāla: 'As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy to live the complete and pure holy life while living at home. Why should I not shave off my hair and beard, don ochre robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?'
translations.mn82:6: Then the young man Raṭṭhapāla, not long after the Thūlakotṭhisa brahmins and householders had left, approached the Blessed One; having approached and bowed down to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the young man Raṭṭhapāla said to the Blessed One: 'Sir, as far as I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy for one living at home to lead the holy life that is utterly perfect and utterly pure, like a polished shell. I wish, sir, to shave off my hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness. May I, sir, obtain going forth in the presence of the Blessed One, may I obtain full ordination. Let the Blessed One ordain me.' 'But have you, Raṭṭhapāla, obtained the permission of your mother and father to go forth from the household life into homelessness?'
