'I have not, sir, obtained the permission of my mother and father to go forth from the household life into homelessness.' 'The Tathāgata, Raṭṭhapāla, does not ordain a son without the permission of his mother and father.' 'I will do, sir, what my mother and father allow regarding going forth from the household life into homelessness.'
translations.mn95:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosala country with a large community of bhikkhus when he arrived at a brahmin village named Opāsāda. There the Blessed One stayed in the Opāsāda shrine grove in the Sāla forest to the north.
translations.mn95:10: Then the brahmin Caṅkī, together with a large group of brahmins, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. After exchanging courteous greetings and talk, he sat down to one side.
translations.mn95:11: At that time the Blessed One was sitting conversing with elderly brahmins, discussing various topics. At that time a young student named Kāpaṭika, with shaven head, sixteen years old by birth, master of the three Vedas, skilled in the phonology and glossaries of the Vedas, in legends and ancient lore, a word-grammarian, versed in cosmology and the marks of a great man, was sitting in that assembly. He interrupted the conversation of the elderly brahmins while they were discussing with the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One reproved the young student Kāpaṭika: 'Do not, Master Bhāradvāja, interrupt the conversation of the elderly brahmins while they are discussing. Wait, Master Bhāradvāja, until the conclusion of the talk.' When this was said, the brahmin Caṅkī said to the Blessed One: 'Do not, Master Gotama, reprove the young student Kāpaṭika. The young student Kāpaṭika is of good family, learned, wise, and of good speech; and the young student Kāpaṭika is able to reply to Master Gotama in this discussion.'
translations.mn95:2: At that time the brahmin Caṅkī was living in Opāsāda, a village provided with food and drinking water, a royal gift given by King Pasenadi of Kosala, a royal grant, a brahmin endowment.
translations.mn95:20: When, having examined him, he sees that he is free from the defiling mental qualities, then he places faith in him; being born of faith, he approaches him; approaching, he pays respect; paying respect, he lends ear; lending ear, he hears the Dhamma; having heard the Dhamma, he remembers it; examining the meaning of the Dhammas he has remembered, he gains a reflective acceptance of those Dhammas; when there is reflective acceptance of the Dhamma, desire arises; when desire has arisen, he makes an effort; having made an effort, he weighs it up; having weighed it up, he strives; striving, he realizes with the body the supreme truth and sees it by penetrating it with wisdom. In this way, Bhāradvāja, there is an understanding of truth; in this way truth is fully understood; and in this way we declare an understanding of truth; but there is not yet the attainment of truth.
translations.mn95:33: 'But, Master Gotama, what is the benefit of approaching? We ask Master Gotama what is the benefit of approaching.' 'Approaching, Bhāradvāja, is of great benefit. If faith did not arise, one would not approach. But because faith arises, one approaches. Therefore approaching is of great benefit.'
translations.mn95:5: At that time the brahmin Caṅkī had gone up to the upper terrace of the palace for the day's rest. The brahmin Caṅkī saw the brahmins and householders of Opāsāda coming out of the palace in crowds, in groups, facing north, approaching the Sāla forest grove. Seeing this, he addressed the steward: 'Why, steward, are the brahmins and householders of Opāsāda coming out of the palace in crowds, in groups, facing north, going to the Sāla forest grove?'
translations.mn9:11: And what, friend, is nutriment, what is the origin of nutriment, what is the cessation of nutriment, and what is the way leading to the cessation of nutriment? There are these four kinds of nutriment for the maintenance of beings that have come to be or for the support of those seeking birth. What four? Physical food, gross or subtle; contact is the second; mental volition is the third; consciousness is the fourth. The origin of craving is the origin of nutriment; the cessation of craving is the cessation of nutriment; and this noble eightfold path is the way leading to the cessation of nutriment; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.
translations.mn9:12: When, friend, a noble disciple thus understands nutriment, thus understands the origin of nutriment, thus understands the cessation of nutriment, and thus understands the way leading to the cessation of nutriment, then having abandoned the underlying tendency to lust, having removed the underlying tendency to aversion, having eradicated the underlying tendency to the view and conceit 'I am', having abandoned ignorance and generated knowledge, he here and now makes an end of suffering. In this way, friend, a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma and has arrived at this true Dhamma.
translations.mn9:15: And what, friend, is suffering, what is the origin of suffering, what is the cessation of suffering, what is the way leading to the cessation of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair are suffering; association with the disliked is suffering, separation from the liked is suffering, not getting what one wants is suffering—in short, the five aggregates affected by clinging are suffering—this is called, friend, suffering.
translations.mn9:16: And what, friend, is the origin of suffering? It is that craving which produces re-becoming, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence—this is called, friend, the origin of suffering.
translations.mn9:17: And what, friend, is the cessation of suffering? It is the fading away and cessation of that very craving, the giving it up, relinquishing, letting go, and abandoning it—this is called, friend, the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn9:18: And what, friend, is the way leading to the cessation of suffering? It is this noble eightfold path; that is, right view … right concentration—this is called, friend, the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn9:2: “‘Right view, right view,’ friend, it is said. To what extent, friend, is a noble disciple one of right view, whose view is straight, who has arrived at this true Dhamma, possessing confidence in the Dhamma?” “We have come from far away, friend, to the venerable Sāriputta’s presence to understand the meaning of this statement. It would be good if the venerable Sāriputta himself would explain the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the venerable Sāriputta, the monks will remember it.” “Then listen, friend, and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to the venerable Sāriputta. The venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.mn9:20: “It is good, friend,” those monks, delighting in and rejoicing in the venerable Sāriputta’s statement, asked the venerable Sāriputta a further question: “Is there, friend, another way by which a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is straight, who has arrived at this true Dhamma, possessing confidence in the Dhamma?”
translations.mn9:3: “When, friend, a noble disciple understands what is unwholesome and the root of the unwholesome, and understands what is wholesome and the root of the wholesome— to that extent, friend, a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is straight, who has arrived at this true Dhamma, possessing confidence in the Dhamma.
translations.mn9:4: And what, friend, is unwholesome, what is the root of the unwholesome, what is wholesome, what is the root of the wholesome? Killing living creatures is unwholesome, taking what is not given is unwholesome, sexual misconduct is unwholesome, false speech is unwholesome, divisive speech is unwholesome, harsh speech is unwholesome, idle chatter is unwholesome, covetousness is unwholesome, ill will is unwholesome, wrong view is unwholesome— this is called, friend, unwholesome.
translations.mn9:5: And what, friend, is the root of the unwholesome? Greed is the root of the unwholesome, hate is the root of the unwholesome, delusion is the root of the unwholesome— this is called, friend, the root of the unwholesome.
translations.mn9:7: And what, friend, is the root of the wholesome? Non-greed is the root of the wholesome, non-hate is the root of the wholesome, non-delusion is the root of the wholesome— this is called, friend, the root of the wholesome.
translations.mn9:70: And what, friend, is the taint, what is the origin of the taint, what is the cessation of the taint, what is the way leading to the cessation of the taint? There are, friend, three taints: the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, the taint of ignorance. With the arising of ignorance comes the arising of the taint; with the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of the taint. This noble eightfold path is the way leading to the cessation of the taint; that is, right view … right concentration.
translations.mn9:8: When, friend, a noble disciple thus understands unwholesome, thus understands the root of the unwholesome, thus understands wholesome, thus understands the root of the wholesome, having entirely abandoned the underlying tendency to lust, having removed the underlying tendency to aversion, having uprooted the underlying tendency to the view ‘I am’, having abandoned ignorance and generated knowledge, he here and now makes an end of suffering— to that extent, friend, a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is straight, who has arrived at this true Dhamma, possessing confidence in the Dhamma.
translations.sn1.10:2: “For those dwelling in the wilderness,  peaceful brahmins practicing the holy life;  Eating only a single meal,  by what is their complexion radiant?”
translations.sn1.10:3: “They do not sorrow for the past,  they do not yearn for the future;  They sustain themselves with the present,  by that their complexion is radiant.
translations.sn1.17:1: “Difficult and sharp is the ascetic life,  and it is not clear to the dull;  Where the fool is depressed,  there are many impediments there.”
translations.sn1.17:2: “How should one practice the ascetic life,  if one does not restrain the mind;  One would be depressed at every step,  following the sway of thoughts.
translations.sn1.17:3: Like a tortoise withdrawing its limbs into its shell,  A monk should withdraw his mental thoughts;  Unreliant, not harming another,  Fully extinguished, he would not blame anyone.”
translations.sn1.18:1: “Is there anyone in the world,  who is restrained by shame and fear of wrong;  Who wakes up the one who slanders,  like a fine horse in the mud?”
translations.sn1.18:2: “Those restrained by shame and fear,  who always walk mindfully;  Having reached the end of suffering,  they walk in uneven terrain like a sage.”
translations.sn1.1:1: Thus I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s park. Then a certain deity, in the far extreme of the night, her extreme radiance lighting up the entirety of Jeta’s Grove, approached the Buddha. Having approached, she paid homage to him, stood to one side, and standing there, that deity said to him: “How, sir, did you cross the flood?” “By not stopping, friend, and by not straining, I crossed the flood.” “But how, sir, did you do that by not stopping and not straining?” “When I stopped, friend, I sank; when I strained, I got swept away. So it was by not stopping and not straining that I crossed the flood.”
translations.sn1.1:2: “Long indeed have I seen  a fully extinguished brahmin;  Not stopping, not straining,  who has crossed over the attachment to the world.”
translations.sn1.1:3: The deity spoke thus. The Teacher approved. Then that deity, realizing that the Teacher approved, paid homage to the Buddha, circled him to the right, and vanished right there.
translations.sn1.20:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove. Then the Venerable Samiddhi, getting up in the last watch of the night, approached the Hot Springs to wash his limbs. Having washed his limbs at the Hot Springs and come back out, he stood in a single robe warming his limbs. Then a certain deity, in the far reach of the night, of stunning beauty, illuminating the entire Hot Springs, approached the Venerable Samiddhi; having approached, she stood in the air and addressed the Venerable Samiddhi with a verse:
translations.sn1.20:2: “You have gone forth without having been, for you do not go forth having been. Having been, go forth, monk, lest time pass you by.”
translations.sn1.20:20: “Beings with the perception of ‘inexpressible’, established in the inexpressible; Not understanding the inexpressible, they run into the bondage of death.
translations.sn1.20:21: Understanding the inexpressible, they do not conceive of a proclaimer; For that does not exist for him, by which he would be harmed; If you understand, speak, spirit.”
translations.sn1.20:22: “I do not, venerable sir, understand in detail the meaning of what the Blessed One has stated in brief. May the Blessed One teach me this matter so that I may understand in detail the meaning of what the Blessed One has stated in brief.”
translations.sn1.20:23: “Whether he is equal or superior or inferior, whoever thinks, let him argue with him; Unshaken in the three modes, ‘equal or superior’ does not exist for him; If you understand, speak, spirit.”
translations.sn1.20:25: “He has given up conceit, he has not fallen into pride; He has cut off craving here for name-and-form. That one with bonds cut, without afflictions, without hope, They did not find him searching; Whether gods or humans here or beyond, Or in the realm of the Thirty-Three in all abodes.
translations.sn1.20:3: “I do not know the time, the time is hidden and does not appear; Therefore I go forth without having been, lest time pass me by.”
translations.sn1.20:4: Then that deity, having stood on the ground, said this to the Venerable Samiddhi: “You are young, monk, gone forth, with black hair, endowed with the good fortune of youth, in the prime of life, not wearying of sensual pleasures. Enjoy, monk, human sensual pleasures; do not run after what is temporary, forsaking what is visible.”
translations.sn1.20:5: “I do not, friend, run after what is temporary, forsaking what is visible. For I, friend, run after what is visible, having forsaken what is temporary. For sensual pleasures, friend, have been declared by the Blessed One to be full of suffering, full of despair; the danger here is greater. This Dhamma is visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be realized personally by the wise.”
translations.sn1.20:6: “How, monk, are sensual pleasures declared by the Blessed One to be full of suffering, full of despair, the danger here greater? How is this Dhamma visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be realized personally by the wise?”
translations.sn1.20:7: “I, friend, am new, gone forth not long ago, only recently come to this Dhamma and Vinaya. I am not able to explain it in detail. That Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is living at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove. Approach that Blessed One and ask about this meaning. As the Blessed One explains it, you should remember it.”
translations.sn1.20:8: “That Blessed One is not easy, monk, for us to approach, surrounded by other deities of great power. If you, monk, approach that Blessed One and ask about this meaning, we too will come to hear the Dhamma.” “Yes, friend,” the Venerable Samiddhi replied to that deity. Then he approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Samiddhi said this to the Blessed One:
translations.sn1.21:2: “Like a snake with its hood spread, burning as if on the head; For the abandoning of sensual lust, a mindful monk should wander.”
translations.sn1.21:3: “Like a snake with its hood spread, burning as if on the head; For the abandoning of self-identity view, a mindful monk should wander.”
translations.sn1.25:1: “If a monk is an Arahant, one whose duty is done, With taints destroyed, bearing his last body; He might say ‘I speak’, and he might say ‘They speak of me’.”
translations.sn1.25:2: “If a monk is an Arahant, one whose duty is done, With taints destroyed, bearing his last body; He might say ‘I speak’, and he might say ‘They speak of me’; Knowing the convention in the world, He would speak merely by convention.”
translations.sn1.25:3: “If a monk is an Arahant, one whose duty is done, With taints destroyed, bearing his last body; Would that monk, relying on conceit, say ‘I speak’, And say ‘They speak of me’?”
translations.sn1.25:4: “For one who has abandoned, there are no bonds, All bonds of conceit have been burnt up; He, the wise one, has gone beyond conceit, He might say ‘I speak’.
translations.sn1.25:5: He might say ‘They speak of me’, Knowing the convention in the world, He would speak merely by convention.”
translations.sn1.2:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain deity, in the far reach of the night, of stunning beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove, approached the Blessed One; having approached, she paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity said this to the Blessed One:
translations.sn1.2:5: “With the drying up of delight in existence, With the cessation of perception and consciousness; With the cessation of feelings and peace, Thus do I, friend, understand; The release and liberation of beings.”
translations.sn1.36:1: At one time the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then many deities fond of chatter, in the far reach of the night, of stunning beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, a certain deity spoke this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
translations.sn1.36:2: “Faith is second for a person, if he does not stand in unfaithfulness; Fame and praise are his, and he goes to heaven having left the body.”
translations.sn1.36:4: “Abandon anger, give up conceit, Overcome every fetter; Not clinging to name and form, No attachments follow the one with nothing.”
translations.sn1.36:5: “Fools, unwise people, engage in negligence, The wise one protects heedfulness as the best treasure.
translations.sn1.36:6: Do not engage in negligence, do not delight in intimacy with sensual pleasures; For one who is heedful, meditating, he attains the highest happiness.”
translations.sn1.38:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove at the Squirrels' Feeding Place. Now at that time the Buddha’s foot was injured by a splinter. Severe bodily feelings were arising in the Buddha—painful, sharp, severe, harsh, unpleasant, displeasing—and the Buddha was enduring them mindful and aware, without complaining. Then the Buddha, having arranged a fourfold robe, lay down on his right side in the lion’s posture, with one foot placed on top of the other, mindful and aware.
translations.sn1.38:10: Domineered by craving, bound by vows, practicing rough austerity for a hundred years; their minds are not truly released, they are of low nature and do not go beyond.
translations.sn1.38:11: There is no restraint for one who wants to be important, no calm for one who is not concentrated; living alone in the forest, negligent, one does not cross the flood of Death.”
translations.sn1.38:12: “Having abandoned conceit, well concentrated, clear-minded, fully released everywhere; living alone in the forest, not negligent, one crosses the flood of Death.”
translations.sn1.38:2: Then seven hundred deities of the Satullapa host, in the middle of the night, of stunning beauty, illuminating the entire Maddakucchi, approached the Buddha; having approached, they bowed to the Buddha and stood to one side. Standing to one side, one deity exclaimed this utterance in the presence of the Buddha: “Indeed, the ascetic Gotama is like an elephant; like an elephant, arisen bodily feelings—painful, sharp, severe, harsh, unpleasant, displeasing—are endured by him mindful and aware, without complaining.”
translations.sn1.38:3: Then another deity exclaimed this utterance in the presence of the Buddha: “Indeed, the ascetic Gotama is like a lion; like a lion, arisen bodily feelings—painful, sharp, severe, harsh, unpleasant, displeasing—are endured by him mindful and aware, without complaining.”
translations.sn1.38:8: Then another deity exclaimed this utterance in the presence of the Buddha: “See the concentration well developed, the mind well released, not constricted, not scattered, and gone beyond the confinement of formations. If one were to think that such a bull of a man, lion of a man, thoroughbred of a man, lord of men, hero of a man, tusked elephant of a man should be transgressed, what else if not by seeing?”
translations.sn1.38:9: “Five hundred ascetics, brahmins practicing; their minds are not truly released, they are of low nature and do not go beyond.
translations.sn1.41:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's park. Then a certain deity, in the middle of the night, of stunning beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove, approached the Buddha; having approached, she bowed to the Buddha and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity recited these verses in the presence of the Buddha:
translations.sn1.41:4: Giving bears the fruit of happiness, not giving does not bear that fruit; thieves steal it, kings take it, fire burns it, it perishes.
translations.sn1.41:5: Then one abandons the body with its acquisitions. Knowing this, the wise should enjoy and give. Having given and having become according to their nature, blameless they go to the heavenly place.”
translations.sn1.42:1: “What giving gives strength, what giving gives beauty; what giving gives happiness, what giving gives sight; and what is the giving that gives everything? Tell me this since I ask.”
translations.sn1.42:2: “Giving food gives strength, giving cloth gives beauty; giving a vehicle gives happiness, giving a lamp gives sight.
translations.sn1.42:3: And he who gives a dwelling gives everything; he who teaches the Dhamma gives the Deathless.”
translations.sn1.51:1: “What is good as long as old age, what is well established; what is the jewel of men, what is snatched away by thieves?”
translations.sn1.51:2: “Virtue is good as long as old age, faith is well established; wisdom is the jewel of men, merit is snatched away by thieves.”
translations.sn1.55:1: “What generates a man, what runs about for him; what does he attain in saṁsāra, what is his great fear?”
translations.sn1.55:2: “Craving generates a man, his mind runs about for him; a being attains saṁsāra, suffering is his great fear.”
translations.sn1.56:1: “What generates a man, what runs about for him; what does he attain in saṁsāra, by what is he not released?”
translations.sn1.56:2: “Craving generates a man, his mind runs about for him; a being attains saṁsāra, by suffering he is not released.”
translations.sn1.57:1: “What generates a man, what runs about for him; what does he attain in saṁsāra, what is his final resort?”
translations.sn1.57:2: “Craving generates a man, his mind runs about for him; a being attains saṁsāra, kamma is his final resort.”
translations.sn1.59:1: “What is a man's second, what binds him; for what, rejoicing, does a mortal release himself from all suffering?”
translations.sn1.59:2: “Faith is a man's second, wisdom binds him; rejoicing in Nibbāna, a mortal releases himself from all suffering.”
translations.sn1.62:1: “By what is the world led, by what does it drag along; for the sake of what one thing are all subject to control?”
translations.sn1.62:2: “By mind is the world led, by mind it is dragged along; for the sake of mind one thing are all subject to control.”
translations.sn1.63:2: “By craving is the world led, by craving it is dragged along; for the sake of craving one thing are all subject to control.”
translations.sn1.64:1: “What is the world's fetter, what is its wandering; by the abandoning of what is Nibbāna said?”
translations.sn1.64:2: “Delight is the world's fetter, wandering is thought; by the abandoning of craving Nibbāna is said.”
translations.sn1.65:1: “What is the world's bond, what is its wandering; by the abandoning of what does one cut all fetters?”
translations.sn1.65:2: “Delight is the world's bond, wandering is thought; by the abandoning of craving one cuts all fetters.”
translations.sn1.69:1: “By what is the world bound, by the abandoning of what is it released; by the abandoning of what does one cut all fetters?”
translations.sn1.69:2: “By desire is the world bound, by the abandoning of desire it is released; by the abandoning of desire one cuts all fetters.”
translations.sn1.71:2: “What, having cut, does one sleep happily, what, having cut, does one not grieve; for the sake of what one thing, Gotama, do you praise destruction?”
translations.sn1.71:3: “Having cut anger one sleeps happily, having cut anger one does not grieve; the noble praise the destruction of anger with its poisonous root and sweet tip; having cut that, one does not grieve.”
translations.sn1.73:1: “What indeed is the best wealth of a man, what, well practiced, brings happiness; what indeed is the sweetest of tastes, how is the best life said to be?”
translations.sn1.73:2: “Faith is indeed a man's best wealth,  A well-practiced Dhamma brings happiness;  Truth is said to be the sweetest of flavors,  Living by wisdom is called the best life.”
translations.sn1.7:2: “Those whose teachings are not well understood,  Are led into the doctrines of others;  The discourses do not wake them up,  It is time for them to awaken.”
translations.sn1.7:3: “Those whose teachings are well understood,  Are not led into the doctrines of others;  They, fully enlightened and right-knowing,  Wander in uneven places as recluses.”
translations.sn1.8:2: “Those whose teachings are confused,  Are led into the doctrines of others;  The discourses do not wake them up,  It is time for them to awaken.”
translations.sn1.8:3: “Those whose teachings are not confused,  Are not led into the doctrines of others;  They, fully enlightened and right-knowing,  Wander in uneven places as recluses.”
translations.sn11.14:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground.  There the Buddha addressed the monks:  “Monks.”  “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Buddha.  The Buddha said this:
translations.sn11.14:3: Then, monks, Sakka, king of the gods, addressed the gods of the Thirty-Three:  ‘Do not, dear friends, be angry with this young god.  For this young god, dear friends, when previously a human being, undertook faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom in the teaching and discipline made known by the Realized One.  Having undertaken faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom in the teaching and discipline made known by the Realized One, with the breakup of the body, after death, he was reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, in the company of the gods of the Thirty-Three.  He surpasses other gods in beauty and glory.’  Then, monks, Sakka, king of the gods, out of affection for the gods of the Thirty-Three, on that occasion spoke these verses:
translations.sn11.14:6: Therefore, one wise and energetic,  Should practice faith and virtue,  Confidence in the vision of the Dhamma,  Remembering the instruction of the Buddhas.”
translations.sn11.15:1: At Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove.  Then Sakka, king of the gods, approached the Buddha; having approached and bowed to the Buddha, he stood to one side.  Standing to one side, Sakka, king of the gods, said to the Buddha:  “What, venerable sir, is a pleasant resort for men?”
translations.sn11.15:2: “Parks and forests,  Lotus ponds beautifully made;  For a man's pleasant resort,  They do not exceed sixteen.”
translations.sn11.22:1: At Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove.  There … the Buddha said this:  “In the past, monks, a certain ugly, deformed ogre sat on Sakka's throne.  Then the gods of the Thirty-Three were annoyed, irritated, and resentful:  ‘It is wonderful, sir, it is marvelous, sir.  This ugly, deformed ogre is sitting on Sakka's throne.’  As the gods of the Thirty-Three became more and more annoyed, irritated, and resentful, that ogre became more and more beautiful to look at, attractive, and pleasing.
translations.sn11.22:3: Then, monks, Sakka, king of the gods, approached that anger-eating ogre; having approached, he arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, knelt on his right knee on the ground, raised his joined palms toward that anger-eating ogre, and announced his name three times:  ‘I am Sakka, friend, king of the gods; I am Sakka, friend, king of the gods.’  As Sakka, king of the gods, announced his name, that ogre became uglier and more deformed.  Having become uglier and more deformed, he vanished right there.  Then, monks, Sakka, king of the gods, having sat on his own throne, out of affection for the gods of the Thirty-Three, on that occasion spoke these verses:
translations.sn11.22:4: ‘I am not struck by anger,  Nor am I led astray by praise;  I do not get angry with you for long,  Anger does not persist in me.
translations.sn11.22:5: When angry I do not speak harshly,  Nor do I praise the Dhamma;  I restrain myself,  Reflecting on what is for my own good.’”
translations.sn11.24:2: “These two, monks, are fools.  Whoever does not see a transgression as a transgression, and whoever does not accept according to the Dhamma the one pointing out a transgression— these two, monks, are fools.  These two, monks, are wise.  Whoever sees a transgression as a transgression, and whoever accepts according to the Dhamma the one pointing out a transgression— these two, monks, are wise.
translations.sn11.24:3: In the past, monks, Sakka, king of the gods, out of affection for the gods of the Thirty-Three, on that occasion in the Sudhammā Hall spoke this verse:
translations.sn11.24:4: ‘Let anger be under your control,  And do not grow old with your friends;  Do not blame without blaming,  And do not speak slander;  For anger is a wicked thing,  Like a mountain crushing down.’”
translations.sn11.3:1: At Sāvatthī.  There the Buddha addressed the monks:  “Monks.”  “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Buddha.  The Buddha said this:
translations.sn11.3:10: If you do not recollect me, then you should recollect the Dhamma:  ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Buddha, visible in this very life, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally known by the wise.’  For if you, monks, were to recollect the Dhamma, any fear, terror, or gooseflesh that arises would be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:11: If you do not recollect the Dhamma, then you should recollect the Saṅgha:  ‘The Saṅgha of the Buddha's disciples is practicing the good way, the straight way, the true way, the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight kinds of individuals— this Saṅgha of the Buddha's disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.’  For if you, monks, were to recollect the Saṅgha, any fear, terror, or gooseflesh that arises would be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:12: For what reason?  Because the Tathāgata, monks, is worthy, fully enlightened, free from lust, free from hate, free from delusion, fearless, unshaken, undisturbed, and does not flee.’”  The Buddha said this.  Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this:
translations.sn11.3:13: “In the wilderness or at the root of a tree,  Or in an empty hut, monks,  Recollect the Awakened One,  And there will be no fear for you.
translations.sn11.3:14: If you do not recollect the Buddha,  The chief of the world, the bull among men,  Then recollect the Dhamma,  The leading teaching, well taught.
translations.sn11.3:15: If you do not recollect the Dhamma,  The leading teaching, well taught,  Then recollect the Saṅgha,  The unsurpassed field of merit.
translations.sn11.3:16: For those who recollect the Buddha,  The Dhamma and the Saṅgha, monks,  There will be no fear or terror,  Nor will there be gooseflesh.”
translations.sn11.3:2: “Formerly, monks, a battle between the devas and the asuras broke out. Then, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the devas of the Thirty-three:
translations.sn11.3:3: ‘If, gentlemen, fear, terror, or horripilation should arise in you when you have gone into battle, you should look upon my banner at that moment. When you look upon my banner, whatever fear, terror, or horripilation there is will vanish.
translations.sn11.3:4: If you do not look upon my banner, then look upon the banner of Pajāpati, the king of the devas. For when you look upon the banner of Pajāpati, the king of the devas, whatever fear, terror, or horripilation there is will vanish.
translations.sn11.3:8: For what reason? Because Sakka, lord of the devas, is not free from lust, not free from hatred, not free from delusion; he is frightened, terrified, and runs away.
translations.sn11.3:9: But I, monks, declare thus: ‘If, monks, when you have gone to the forest or to the foot of a tree or to an empty dwelling, fear, terror, or horripilation should arise in you, you should recollect me at that time: “The Blessed One is an Arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, awakened, blessed.” When you recollect me, monks, whatever fear, terror, or horripilation there is will vanish.
translations.sn11.5:12: He serves the good of both,  his own and that of another;  Knowing that the other is angry,  one who is mindful calms down.
translations.sn11.5:14: When the verses spoken by Sakka, lord of the devas, had been spoken, the devas were pleased, but the asuras were silent. Then, monks, the retinues of both the devas and the asuras said: ‘Verses were spoken by Vepacitti, lord of the asuras. They are accompanied by sticks and weapons, involving quarreling, strife, and dispute. Verses were spoken by Sakka, lord of the devas. They are unaccompanied by sticks and weapons, involving no quarreling, no strife, and no dispute. Sakka, lord of the devas, has won by his well-spoken words.’ Thus, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, won by his well-spoken words.”
translations.sn11.5:2: ‘Fools might increase more,  if there were no one to restrain them;  Therefore with a stick in due measure,  the wise should restrain the fool.’
translations.sn11.5:3: When the verse spoken by Vepacitti, lord of the asuras, had been spoken, the asuras were pleased, but the devas were silent. Then, monks, Vepacitti, lord of the asuras, said to Sakka, lord of the devas: ‘Speak, lord of devas, a verse.’ When this was said, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, spoke this verse:
translations.sn11.5:4: ‘This I consider to be,  the restraint of a fool;  Knowing that the other is angry,  one who is mindful calms down.’
translations.sn11.5:5: When the verse spoken by Sakka, lord of the devas, had been spoken, the devas were pleased, but the asuras were silent. Then, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, said to Vepacitti, lord of the asuras: ‘Speak, Vepacitti, a verse.’ When this was said, monks, Vepacitti, lord of the asuras, spoke this verse:
translations.sn11.5:6: ‘By this very endurance,  I see a fault, Vāsava;  When a fool thinks it is,  he endures out of fear;  The fool flares up,  like a cow running away more.’
translations.sn11.5:8: ‘Let him think it is or not,  he endures out of fear;  There is no benefit better than patience,  patience is not found more.’
translations.sn12.11:1: Thus I have heard— At one time the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's park. … “There are these four nutriments, monks, for the sustenance of beings who have come to be or for the assistance of those about to be born. What four? Edible food, coarse or fine; contact is the second; mental volition is the third; consciousness is the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the sustenance of beings who have come to be or for the assistance of those about to be born.
translations.sn12.12:1: He is living at Sāvatthī. “There are these four nutriments, monks, for the sustenance of beings who have come to be or for the assistance of those about to be born. What four? Edible food, coarse or fine; contact is the second; mental volition is the third; consciousness is the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the sustenance of beings who have come to be or for the assistance of those about to be born.”
translations.sn12.15:1: He is living at Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Kaccānagotta approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Kaccānagotta said to the Blessed One: “‘Right view, right view,’ it is said, venerable sir. In what way, venerable sir, is there right view?”
translations.sn12.15:2: “This world, Kaccāna, for the most part relies upon a duality—upon the notion of existence and the notion of non-existence. But for one who sees the origin of the world as it really is with right wisdom, the notion of non-existence in the world does not occur. For one who sees the cessation of the world as it really is with right wisdom, the notion of existence in the world does not occur. This world, Kaccāna, for the most part is bound by attachment, clinging, and adherence. But that attachment, clinging, and mental adherence—this underlying tendency to adherence—he does not approach, he does not cling, he does not adhere: ‘I am my self.’ He does not doubt or waver: ‘Suffering alone arises, suffering alone ceases.’ His knowledge here is independent of others. In this way, Kaccāna, there is right view.
translations.sn12.17:1: Thus I have heard— At one time the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and outer robe, entered Rājagaha for alms. The naked ascetic Kassapa saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Seeing him, he approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When they had exchanged greetings and courtesies, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, the naked ascetic Kassapa said to the Blessed One: “We would like to ask the Master Gotama about a certain point, if the Master Gotama would grant us the opportunity to ask a question and explain it.” “It is not the right time now, Kassapa, for questions; we have entered the inner dwelling.”
translations.sn12.17:5: “‘It is the same one who acts and the same one who feels,’ Kassapa: regarding this, holding to such a view, one declares the self to be the creator, and this leads to eternalism. ‘It is one who acts and another who feels,’ Kassapa: regarding this, driven by feeling, one declares suffering to be created by another, and this leads to annihilationism. Avoiding both extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: ‘With ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness … … thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. With the fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations comes cessation of consciousness … … thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’”
translations.sn12.17:6: When this was said, the naked ascetic Kassapa said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! The Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by the Blessed One, as if he were to raise up what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to point out the way to one who was lost, or to hold up a lamp in the dark so that those with eyes might see visible forms. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May I obtain going forth in the Blessed One’s presence, may I obtain full ordination.”
translations.sn12.17:7: “If anyone of another sect who was formerly of a different persuasion wishes to go forth or obtain full ordination in this Dhamma and Vinaya, they wait for four months. At the end of four months, the bhikkhus who are determined give them going forth and full ordination into the state of a bhikkhu. But I recognize individual differences in persons.”
translations.sn12.18:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the wanderer Timbaruka approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. After exchanging courteous greetings, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the wanderer Timbaruka said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn12.18:4: “‘It is the same feeling and the same one who feels,’ Timbaruka: regarding this, holding to such a view, I do not speak of ‘self-made pleasure and pain.’ ‘It is one feeling and another who feels,’ Timbaruka: regarding this, driven by feeling, I do not speak of ‘other-made pleasure and pain.’ Avoiding both extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: ‘With ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness … … thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. With the fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations comes cessation of consciousness … … thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’”
translations.sn12.19:1: At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, blocked by ignorance and bound by craving, this body has thus originated. Thus there is this body and external name-and-form; from these two comes contact; from the six sense fields contacted by which, the fool experiences pleasure and pain, or one or the other of these.
translations.sn12.19:2: Bhikkhus, blocked by ignorance and bound by craving, this body has thus originated. Thus there is this body and external name-and-form; from these two comes contact; from the six sense fields contacted by which, the wise person experiences pleasure and pain, or one or the other of these.
translations.sn12.19:3: Herein, bhikkhus, what is the distinction, what is the difference, what is the diversity between the wise person and the fool?” “Our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, take refuge in the Blessed One. It would be good if the Blessed One would explain the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.”
translations.sn12.25:10: When there is body, Ānanda, with bodily volition as cause, pleasure and pain arise internally. When there is speech, Ānanda, with verbal volition as cause, pleasure and pain arise internally. When there is mind, Ānanda, with mental volition as cause, pleasure and pain arise internally, and also due to ignorance as condition.
translations.sn12.23:7: Suppose, monks, that on a high mountain there is a large rock cleft. When the gods rain, the water flows down the slope and fills the cleft, the gullies, the creeks, the streams, the rivers, and finally the great ocean.
translations.sn12.25:1: He dwells at Sāvatthī. Then, in the evening, the Venerable Bhūmija, having risen from seclusion, approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta. After exchanging courteous and agreeable conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Bhūmija said to the Venerable Sāriputta:
translations.sn12.19:5: “For whom, monks, this body has originated, enveloped by ignorance and bound by craving, that ignorance of the fool is not abandoned and that craving is not exhausted.  For what reason?  The fool, monks, has not lived the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.  Therefore, with the breakup of the body, the fool goes to a body;  going to a body, he is not freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair.  I say he is not freed from suffering.”
translations.sn12.23:6: Thus, monks, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations;  with volitional formations as condition, consciousness;  with consciousness as condition, name-and-form;  with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases;  with the six sense bases as condition, contact;  with contact as condition, feeling;  with feeling as condition, craving;  with craving as condition, clinging;  with clinging as condition, becoming;  with becoming as condition, birth;  with birth as condition, suffering;  with suffering as condition, faith;  with faith as condition, joy;  with joy as condition, rapture;  with rapture as condition, tranquility;  with tranquility as condition, pleasure;  with pleasure as condition, concentration;  with concentration as condition, knowledge and vision of things as they are;  with knowledge and vision of things as they are as condition, disenchantment;  with disenchantment as condition, dispassion;  with dispassion as condition, liberation;  with liberation as condition, the knowledge of destruction.
translations.sn12.23:5: And what, monks, is the condition for craving?  ‘Feeling’ should be said …pe…  ‘Contact’ should be said …  ‘The six sense bases’ should be said …  ‘Name-and-form’ should be said …  ‘Consciousness’ should be said …  ‘Volitional formations’ should be said.  I say, monks, that volitional formations have a condition, they do not lack a condition.  And what, monks, is the condition for volitional formations?  ‘Ignorance’ should be said.
translations.sn12.25:11: They themselves, Ānanda, or others, Ānanda, or knowingly, Ānanda, or unknowingly, Ānanda, initiate bodily formations, because of which pleasure and pain arise internally.
translations.sn12.25:2: “There are, friend Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and who declare pleasure and pain to be self-made. There are, friend Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and who declare pleasure and pain to be made by another. There are, friend Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and who declare pleasure and pain to be both self-made and made by another. There are, friend Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and who declare pleasure and pain to be arisen without cause, neither self-made nor made by another. Here, friend Sāriputta, regarding what the Blessed One declares and says, how should we speak so that we would be speakers of his words and not misrepresent him with falsehood, explain the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, and so that no one who is a proponent of the Dhamma would incur a ground for blame?”
translations.sn12.25:3: “Dependent origination, friend, is how the Blessed One has declared pleasure and pain. Dependent on what? Contact. Speaking thus, one would be a speaker of his words and not misrepresent him with falsehood, explain the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, and so that no one who is a proponent of the Dhamma would incur a ground for blame.
translations.sn12.25:4: Herein, friend, those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare pleasure and pain to be self-made—that too is dependent on contact. Those ... those ... those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare pleasure and pain to be arisen without cause, neither self-made nor made by another—that too is dependent on contact.
translations.sn12.25:5: Herein, friend, those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare pleasure and pain to be self-made—would they experience it without contact? This is not found. Those ... those ... those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare pleasure and pain to be arisen without cause, neither self-made nor made by another—would they experience it without contact? This is not found.”
translations.sn12.25:6: Then Venerable Ānanda heard this conversation between Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Bhūmija. Then Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Ānanda reported to the Blessed One all the conversation that had taken place between Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Bhūmija.
translations.sn12.25:7: “Good, good, Ānanda, that Sāriputta should explain it correctly. Dependent origination, Ānanda, is how I have declared pleasure and pain. Dependent on what? Contact. Speaking thus, one would be a speaker of my words and not misrepresent me with falsehood, explain the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, and so that no one who is a proponent of the Dhamma would incur a ground for blame.
translations.sn12.2:11: And what, monks, is name-and-form? Feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention—this is called name. The four great elements, and form derived from the four great elements—this is called form. This, monks, is called name-and-form.
translations.sn12.2:12: And what, monks, is consciousness? These six, monks, are classes of consciousness—eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness. This, monks, is called consciousness.
translations.sn12.2:13: And what, monks, are formations? These three, monks, are formations—bodily formation, verbal formation, mental formation. These, monks, are called formations.
translations.sn12.2:14: And what, monks, is ignorance? Not knowing suffering, not knowing the origin of suffering, not knowing the cessation of suffering, not knowing the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, monks, is called ignorance.
translations.sn12.2:5: And what, monks, is existence? These three, monks, are existences—sense-sphere existence, form-sphere existence, formless-sphere existence. This, monks, is called existence.
translations.sn12.2:6: And what, monks, is grasping? These four, monks, are graspings—sense-grasping, view-grasping, precept-grasping, doctrine-of-self-grasping. This, monks, is called grasping.
translations.sn12.31:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One addressed Venerable Sāriputta: “Sāriputta, this was said in the Parāyana in the questions of Ajita:
translations.sn12.31:2: ‘Those who have conditioned things, and those who are in training here in many ways; Tell me their knowledge, O good one, when asked.’
translations.sn12.31:3: How, Sāriputta, should the meaning of this brief statement be seen in detail?” When this was said, Venerable Sāriputta remained silent.
translations.sn12.31:7: “Do you see, Sāriputta, that ‘It is existent’?” “‘It is existent’, venerable sir: one sees it as it really is with right wisdom. ‘It is existent’: having seen it as it really is with right wisdom, one practices for disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation towards the existent. ‘Born from nutriment’: one sees it as it really is with right wisdom. ‘Born from nutriment’: having seen it as it really is with right wisdom, one practices for disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation towards what is born from nutriment. ‘Due to the cessation of nutriment, that which is existent ceases’: one sees it as it really is with right wisdom. ‘Due to the cessation of nutriment, that which is existent ceases’: having seen it as it really is with right wisdom, one practices for disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation towards that which is of the nature of cessation. In this way, venerable sir, one is in training.
translations.sn12.31:8: And how, sir, is one who has understood the teaching? 'It is existent,' sir: they see what is real with right wisdom. Having seen what is real with right wisdom, they are freed without grasping through disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, regarding what is real. 'It is born from nutriment,' sir: they see what is real with right wisdom. Having seen what is real with right wisdom, they are freed without grasping through disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, regarding what is born from nutriment. 'When nutriment ceases, what is real is of the nature of cessation,' sir: they see what is real with right wisdom. Having seen what is real with right wisdom, they are freed without grasping through disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, regarding what is of the nature of cessation. Thus, sir, one is who has understood the teaching. Thus, sir, regarding what was said in the 'Questions of Ajita' in the Way to the Far Shore:
translations.sn12.35:1: He dwells at Sāvatthī. 'With ignorance as condition, mendicants, there are choices; with choices as condition, consciousness … … the origin of this whole mass of suffering occurs.' When this was said, a certain mendicant said to the Buddha: 'What, sir, is aging and death, and whose is this aging and death?' 'The question is not timely,' said the Buddha, 'Whether one says, "What is aging and death, and whose is this aging and death?" or whether one says, "Aging and death is one thing, and whose is this aging and death is another," both are merely a difference in phrasing, the meaning is one. When there is the view, "The soul and the body are the same," the holy life is not lived. When there is the view, "The soul is one thing and the body another," the holy life is not lived. Avoiding these two extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle way: "With birth as condition, aging and death."'
translations.sn12.35:2: 'What, sir, is birth, and whose is this birth?' 'The question is not timely,' said the Buddha, 'Whether one says, "What is birth, and whose is this birth?" or whether one says, "Birth is one thing, and whose is this birth is another," both are merely a difference in phrasing, the meaning is one. When there is the view, "The soul and the body are the same," the holy life is not lived. When there is the view, "The soul is one thing and the body another," the holy life is not lived. Avoiding these two extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle way: "With existence as condition, birth."'
translations.sn12.35:3: 'What, sir, is existence, and whose is this existence?' 'The question is not timely,' said the Buddha, 'Whether one says, "What is existence, and whose is this existence?" or whether one says, "Existence is one thing, and whose is this existence is another," both are merely a difference in phrasing, the meaning is one. When there is the view, "The soul and the body are the same," the holy life is not lived; when there is the view, "The soul is one thing and the body another," the holy life is not lived. Avoiding these two extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle way: "With grasping as condition, existence" … … "With craving as condition, grasping" … "With feeling as condition, craving" … "With contact as condition, feeling" … "With the six sense fields as condition, contact" … "With name and form as condition, the six sense fields" … "With consciousness as condition, name and form" … "With choices as condition, consciousness."'
translations.sn12.35:4: 'What, sir, are choices, and whose are these choices?' 'The question is not timely,' said the Buddha, 'Whether one says, "What are choices, and whose are these choices?" or whether one says, "Choices are one thing, and whose are these choices is another," both are merely a difference in phrasing, the meaning is one. When there is the view, "The soul and the body are the same," the holy life is not lived; when there is the view, "The soul is one thing and the body another," the holy life is not lived. Avoiding these two extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle way: "With ignorance as condition, choices."'
translations.sn12.35:5: With the fading away and cessation of ignorance without remainder, mendicant, whatever various speculative views, wanderings, and tremblings there are—whether one says, 'What is aging and death, and whose is this aging and death?' or 'Aging and death is one thing, and whose is this aging and death is another,' or 'The soul and the body are the same,' or 'The soul is one thing and the body another'—all those are abandoned, their root destroyed, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no longer subject to future arising.
translations.sn12.35:7: With the fading away and cessation of ignorance without remainder, mendicant, whatever various speculative views, wanderings, and tremblings there are—what is existence … … what is grasping … what is craving … what is feeling … what is contact … what is the six sense fields … what is name and form … what is consciousness … ….
translations.sn12.38:1: He dwells at Sāvatthī. 'Whatever one intends, whatever one plans, and whatever one has a latent tendency toward, this becomes a basis for the establishment of consciousness. When there is a basis, consciousness is established. When consciousness is established and has grown, there is the descent into a new womb. When there is a descent into a new womb, in the future there is birth, aging, and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. That is how the origin of this whole mass of suffering occurs.
translations.sn12.38:2: If one does not intend, if one does not plan, but one still has a latent tendency toward something, this becomes a basis for the establishment of consciousness. When there is a basis, consciousness is established. When consciousness is established and has grown, there is the descent into a new womb. When there is a descent into a new womb, in the future there is birth, aging, and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. That is how the origin of this whole mass of suffering occurs.
translations.sn12.44:1: He dwells at Sāvatthī. 'I will teach you the origin and the disappearance of the world, mendicants. Listen to that, attend closely, and I will speak.' 'Yes, sir,' those mendicants replied to the Buddha. The Buddha said this:
translations.sn12.44:2: “And what, monks, is the origin of the world? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. Dependent on contact is feeling; dependent on feeling is craving; dependent on craving is clinging; dependent on clinging is existence; dependent on existence is birth; dependent on birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. This is the origin of the world.
translations.sn12.44:3: Dependent on the ear and sounds … Dependent on the nose and odors … Dependent on the tongue and flavors … Dependent on the body and tactile objects … Dependent on the mind and phenomena, mind-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. Dependent on contact is feeling … Dependent on birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. This is the origin of the world.
translations.sn12.44:4: And what, monks, is the cessation of the world? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. Dependent on contact is feeling; dependent on feeling is craving. With the fading away and cessation of that very craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases … Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. This is the cessation of the world.
translations.sn12.46:1: He dwells at Sāvatthī. Then a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged courteous greetings with the Blessed One. After exchanging courteous greetings and memorable talk, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, that brahmin said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn12.46:2: “Does the same one act, Master Gotama, and the same one feel?” “‘The same one acts and the same one feels’—this, brahmin, is one extreme.
translations.sn12.46:3: “Then does one act, Master Gotama, and another feel?” “‘One acts and another feels’—this, brahmin, is the second extreme. Without approaching either of these two extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle way: ‘With ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness … Thus is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. But with the fading away and cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations … Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.’”
translations.sn12.51:10: If he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands that it is impermanent, that he is not infatuated with it, and that he does not delight in it. If he feels a painful feeling, he understands that it is impermanent, that he is not infatuated with it, and that he does not delight in it. If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands that it is impermanent, that he is not infatuated with it, and that he does not delight in it. If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it detached from it. If he feels a painful feeling, he feels it detached from it. If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it detached from it.
translations.sn12.51:11: While he feels feelings that are limited to the body, he understands: ‘I feel feelings that are limited to the body.’ While he feels feelings that are limited to life, he understands: ‘I feel feelings that are limited to life.’ He understands: ‘With the breakup of the body, following the exhaustion of life, all that was felt, not being delighted in, will become cool right here; bodily remains will be left behind.’
translations.sn12.51:12: Suppose, monks, a potter or a potter’s apprentice were to lift a hot pot out of a kiln and set it down on level ground. The heat in that pot would dissipate right there, and the potsherds would remain. So too, a monk, while feeling feelings that are limited to the body, understands: ‘I feel feelings that are limited to the body.’ While feeling feelings that are limited to life, he understands: ‘I feel feelings that are limited to life.’ He understands: ‘With the breakup of the body, following the exhaustion of life, all that was felt, not being delighted in, will become cool right here; bodily remains will be left behind.’
translations.sn12.51:13: What do you think, monks? Would a monk with taints destroyed still fabricate meritorious volitional formations, or demeritorious volitional formations, or imperturbable volitional formations?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn12.51:14: “But when, with the utter fading away and cessation of all volitional formations, would consciousness still be found?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn12.51:2: “To what extent, monks, does a monk examine so as to examine entirely for the complete ending of suffering?” “Our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, take refuge in the Blessed One. It would be good if the Blessed One would explain the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it.” “Then listen, monks, and attend closely, I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn12.51:3: “Here, monks, a monk examines: ‘What is the origin, source, birth, and condition of the various kinds of suffering that arise in the world—namely, aging-and-death? When what exists does aging-and-death occur; when what does not exist does aging-and-death not occur?’ Examining in this way, he understands: ‘The various kinds of suffering that arise in the world—namely, aging-and-death—have birth as their origin, birth as their source, birth as their birth, birth as their condition. When birth exists, aging-and-death occurs; when birth does not exist, aging-and-death does not occur.’
translations.sn12.51:4: He understands aging-and-death, its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation; and he practices in accordance with that way and does not deviate from it. This is called a monk who is practicing entirely for the complete ending of suffering, for the cessation of aging-and-death.
translations.sn12.51:5: Then, examining further, he examines: ‘What is the origin, source, birth, and condition of birth? When what exists does birth occur; when what does not exist does birth not occur?’ Examining in this way, he understands: ‘Birth has existence as its origin, existence as its source, existence as its birth, existence as its condition. When existence exists, birth occurs; when existence does not exist, birth does not occur.’
translations.sn12.51:6: They understand birth, its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation; and they practice in accordance with the Dhamma. This is called a mendicant who is practicing rightly for the complete ending of suffering, for the ending of birth.
translations.sn12.51:7: Then they examine it further: ‘What is the source of this existence? … What is the source of grasping? … What is the source of craving? … What is the source of feeling? … What is the source of contact? … What is the source of the six sense fields? … What is the source of name and form? … What is the source of consciousness? … What is the source, origin, birth, and source of conditions? When what exists do conditions exist? When what doesn’t exist do conditions not exist?’ Examining it further, they understand: ‘Conditions have ignorance as their source, ignorance as their origin, ignorance as their birth, and ignorance as their source. When ignorance exists, conditions exist; when ignorance doesn’t exist, conditions don’t exist.’
translations.sn12.51:8: They understand conditions, their origin, their cessation, and the practice that leads to their cessation; and they practice in accordance with the Dhamma. This is called a mendicant who is practicing rightly for the complete ending of suffering, for the ending of conditions.
translations.sn12.51:9: When a person has gone to ignorance, mendicants, if they create a meritorious formation, their consciousness tends toward merit. If they create a demeritorious formation, their consciousness tends toward demerit. If they create an imperturbable formation, their consciousness tends toward the imperturbable. When, mendicants, a mendicant’s ignorance has given way and true knowledge has arisen, then due to fading away of ignorance and the arising of true knowledge they don’t create a meritorious formation, a demeritorious formation, or an imperturbable formation. Not creating formations, not intending, they don’t grasp at anything in the world. Not grasping, they’re not anxious. Not anxious, they personally become extinguished. They understand: ‘Birth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is no return to any state of existence.’
translations.sn12.52:2: Suppose, mendicants, there was a great pile of firewood the size of ten, twenty, thirty, or forty cartloads. And a person would from time to time throw dry grass, dry cow dung, and dry wood into it. That great pile of fire burning with fuel and material would burn for a long time. In the same way, mendicants, when a mendicant lives seeing gratification in things that can be clung to, craving grows. Craving gives rise to grasping … and so the origin of this entire mass of suffering comes to be.
translations.sn12.52:3: When a mendicant lives seeing danger in things that can be clung to, craving ceases. When craving ceases, grasping ceases. When grasping ceases, existence ceases. When existence ceases, birth ceases. When birth ceases, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease. And so the cessation of this entire mass of suffering comes to be.
translations.sn12.55:1: At Sāvatthī. “When a mendicant lives seeing gratification in things that can be clung to, craving grows. Craving gives rise to grasping; grasping gives rise to existence … and so the origin of this entire mass of suffering comes to be.
translations.sn12.55:2: Suppose, mendicants, there was a great tree. Its roots growing downwards and across would all draw up sap. That great tree, standing with fuel and material, would stand for a long time. In the same way, mendicants, when a mendicant lives seeing gratification in things that can be clung to, craving grows. Craving gives rise to grasping … and so the origin of this entire mass of suffering comes to be.
translations.sn12.55:3: When a mendicant lives seeing danger in things that can be clung to, craving ceases. When craving ceases, grasping ceases. When grasping ceases, existence ceases … and so the cessation of this entire mass of suffering comes to be.
translations.sn12.61:1: Thus I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. … “An ordinary uninstructed person might grow disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding this body made of four elements. Why is that? Because the increase and decrease, taking up and letting go of this body made of four elements is visible. So an ordinary uninstructed person might grow disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding it.
translations.sn12.61:2: But as to that which is called mind, intellect, or consciousness, an ordinary uninstructed person is unable to grow disillusioned, dispassionate, or freed regarding it. Why is that? Because for a long time this has been held to by them, cherished, and grasped at: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self.’ So an ordinary uninstructed person is unable to grow disillusioned, dispassionate, or freed regarding it.
translations.sn12.61:3: It would be better, mendicants, for an ordinary uninstructed person to take this body made of four elements as their self, rather than the mind. Why is that? Because this body made of four elements is seen standing for one year, for two years, for three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or a hundred years, or even longer.
translations.sn12.61:5: Here, bhikkhus, a learned noble disciple carefully attends to dependent origination itself: ‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases—that is, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness … … thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. With the fading away and cessation of ignorance without remainder, there is the cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, the cessation of consciousness … … thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’
translations.sn12.62:3: Here, bhikkhus, a learned noble disciple carefully attends to dependent origination itself: ‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases.’ With pleasant contact as condition, bhikkhus, pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that very same pleasant contact, whatever pleasant feeling has arisen dependent on that pleasant contact ceases and subsides. With painful contact as condition, bhikkhus, painful feeling arises. With the cessation of that very same painful contact, whatever painful feeling has arisen dependent on that painful contact ceases and subsides. With neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact as condition, bhikkhus, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that very same neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact, whatever neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling has arisen dependent on that neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact ceases and subsides.
translations.sn12.62:4: Just as, bhikkhus, when two sticks are rubbed together, heat is generated and fire is produced; and when those two sticks are separated and laid apart, the heat generated by them ceases and subsides; so too, bhikkhus, with pleasant contact as condition, pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that very same pleasant contact, whatever pleasant feeling has arisen dependent on that pleasant contact ceases and subsides … … with painful contact as condition … with neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact as condition, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that very same neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact, whatever neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling has arisen dependent on that neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact ceases and subsides.
translations.sn12.63:3: What do you think, bhikkhus? Would you take food for the sake of beauty, or for the sake of intoxication, or for the sake of adornment, or for the sake of decoration?” “No, venerable sir.” “But would you not, bhikkhus, take food for the sake of crossing the wilderness?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “So too, bhikkhus, I say that edible food should be regarded. When edible food is fully understood, the lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure is fully understood. When the lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure is fully understood, there is no fetter by which a noble disciple would be bound that would cause them to return to this world again.
translations.sn12.63:4: And how, bhikkhus, should contact be regarded? Just as, bhikkhus, a cow with a young calf might stand depending on a thicket, or depending on a tree, or depending on water, or depending on an open space. Whatever she stands depending on, the creatures dependent on that would not eat her. So too, bhikkhus, I say that contact should be regarded. When contact is fully understood, the three feelings are fully understood. When the three feelings are fully understood, I say that there is nothing further for a noble disciple to do.
translations.sn12.63:5: And how, bhikkhus, should mental volition be regarded? Just as, bhikkhus, there might be a pit of glowing coals, deeper than a man’s height, full of glowing coals without flame and without smoke. Then a man might come along, wanting to live, not wanting to die, desiring happiness, averse to suffering. Then two strong men, each grabbing him by one arm, would drag him into the pit of glowing coals. Then, bhikkhus, that man would make an effort, a struggle, an exertion far away from that pit of glowing coals. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, that man would think: ‘I will fall into this pit of glowing coals, and because of that I will die or suffer deadly pain.’ So too, bhikkhus, I say that mental volition should be regarded. When mental volition is fully understood, the three cravings are fully understood. When the three cravings are fully understood, I say that there is nothing further for a noble disciple to do.
translations.sn12.64:2: If there is lust, delight, craving, and clinging in regard to edible food, bhikkhus, then consciousness is established and grows there. Where consciousness is established and grows, there is the descent of name-and-form. Where there is the descent of name-and-form, there is the growth of volitional formations. Where there is the growth of volitional formations, there is the production of future rebirth in the future. Where there is the production of future rebirth in the future, there is future birth, aging, and death. Where there is future birth, aging, and death, I say that there is sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair.
translations.sn12.64:4: Suppose, monks, a painter or a painter's apprentice, having dye, lac, yellow orpiment, indigo, or crimson, and a well-prepared board or cloth, or a piece of hide, would create the figure of a woman or a man, complete in all its parts. In the same way, monks, when there is lust, delight, and craving for nutriment, consciousness becomes established there and grows. Where consciousness is established and grows, there is the descent of name-and-form. Where there is the descent of name-and-form, there is the growth of volitional formations. Where there is the growth of volitional formations, there is the production of future rebirth in the future. Where there is the production of future rebirth in the future, there is future birth, aging, and death. Where there is future birth, aging, and death, I say there is sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair.
translations.sn12.64:6: When there is no lust, no delight, and no craving for nutriment, monks, consciousness is not established there and does not grow. Where consciousness is not established and does not grow, there is no descent of name-and-form. Where there is no descent of name-and-form, there is no growth of volitional formations. Where there is no growth of volitional formations, there is no production of future rebirth in the future. Where there is no production of future rebirth in the future, there is no future birth, aging, and death. Where there is no future birth, aging, and death, I say there is no sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, or despair.
translations.sn12.64:8: Suppose, monks, there is a storied building or a storied hall. When the sun rises in the east and a sunbeam enters through a window, where would it land? On the western wall, venerable sir. If there were no western wall, where would it land? On the ground, venerable sir. If there were no ground, where would it land? In the water, venerable sir. If there were no water, where would it land? It would not land, venerable sir. In the same way, monks, when there is no lust, no delight, and no craving for nutriment ….
translations.sn12.65:1: At Sāvatthī. Before my enlightenment, while I was still a bodhisatta, the thought occurred to me: 'This world has fallen into trouble; it is born, ages, dies, passes away, and is reborn. Yet it does not know the escape from this suffering, from aging and death. When will the escape from this suffering, from aging and death be known?' Then, monks, the thought occurred to me: 'What, being present, is aging and death? With what as condition is there aging and death?' Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in me knowledge and insight: 'When birth is present, aging and death is present; with birth as condition, there is aging and death.'
translations.sn12.65:3: Then, monks, the thought occurred to me— 'This consciousness turns back from name-and-form; it does not go beyond. To this extent, one is born, ages, dies, passes away, and is reborn, that is, with name-and-form as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact … In this way, the origin of this whole mass of suffering occurs.' 'Origin, origin,' monks, in teachings not heard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, understanding arose, light arose.
translations.sn12.65:5: Then, monks, the thought occurred to me: 'What, being absent, is consciousness not present; with the cessation of what is the cessation of consciousness?' Then, monks, through careful attention, there arose in me knowledge and insight: 'When name-and-form is absent, consciousness is not present; with the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of consciousness.'
