translations.sn12.65:6: Then, monks, the thought occurred to me— 'I have discovered the path to enlightenment, that is— with the cessation of name-and-form, the cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, the cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, the cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, the cessation of contact … In this way, the cessation of this whole mass of suffering occurs.' 'Cessation, cessation,' monks, in teachings not heard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, understanding arose, light arose.
translations.sn12.65:7: Suppose, monks, a man wandering in a forest would see an ancient path, an ancient road traveled by people of former times. He would follow it. Following it, he would see an ancient city, an ancient capital inhabited by people of former times, complete with parks, groves, ponds, ramparts, and delightful surroundings. Then that man, monks, would inform a king or a royal minister: 'Sir, you should know that I saw an ancient path, an ancient road traveled by people of former times in the forest. I followed it. Following it, I saw an ancient city, an ancient capital inhabited by people of former times, complete with parks, groves, ponds, ramparts, and delightful surroundings. Sir, restore that city.' Then that king or royal minister would restore the city. That city, sometime later, would become powerful and prosperous, well-populated, filled with people, and attained to growth and expansion. In the same way, monks, I saw an ancient path, an ancient road traveled by perfectly enlightened Buddhas of former times.
translations.sn12.66:1: Thus I have heard. At one time the Blessed One was living among the Kurus at a market town called Kammāsadhamma. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: 'Monks.' 'Venerable sir,' those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: 'Investigate, monks, whether there is an intermediate state.' When this was said, a certain monk said to the Blessed One: 'I, venerable sir, investigate whether there is an intermediate state.' 'How, monk, do you investigate whether there is an intermediate state?' Then that monk explained. As that monk explained, he did not please the Blessed One.
translations.sn12.66:2: When this was said, Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: 'It is time, Blessed One, it is time, Sugata, for the Blessed One to speak on the intermediate. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it.' 'Then listen, Ānanda, attend closely, I will speak.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' those monks answered the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn12.66:5: Then, examining the intermediate, he examines: 'But where, when arising, does craving arise? Where, when settling, does it settle?' Examining, he knows thus: Where in the world there is what is pleasant and agreeable, there this craving, when arising, arises; there, when settling, it settles. And what in the world is pleasant and agreeable? The eye in the world is pleasant and agreeable; there this craving, when arising, arises; there, when settling, it settles. The ear in the world is pleasant and agreeable … The nose in the world is pleasant and agreeable … The tongue in the world is pleasant and agreeable … The body in the world is pleasant and agreeable … The mind in the world is pleasant and agreeable; there this craving, when arising, arises; there, when settling, it settles.
translations.sn12.66:6: Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past, monks, saw what in the world is pleasant and agreeable as permanent, as pleasant, as self, as healthy, as secure—they increased craving. Those who increased craving increased attachment. Those who increased attachment increased suffering. Those who increased suffering did not escape from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair; I say they did not escape from suffering.
translations.sn12.66:7: Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future, monks, will see what in the world is pleasant and agreeable as permanent, as pleasant, as self, as healthy, as secure—they will increase craving. Those who increase craving will increase attachment. Those who increase attachment will increase suffering. Those who increase suffering will not escape from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair; I say they will not escape from suffering.
translations.sn12.66:8: Whatever ascetics or brahmins at present, monks, see what in the world is pleasant and agreeable as permanent, as pleasant, as self, as healthy, as secure—they increase craving. Those who increase craving increase attachment. Those who increase attachment increase suffering. Those who increase suffering do not escape from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair; I say they do not escape from suffering.
translations.sn12.67:1: At one time Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika were staying near Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika, in the evening, coming out of seclusion, approached Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Sāriputta. When they had concluded their friendly and agreeable conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika said to Venerable Sāriputta: 'Is aging and death self-made, friend Sāriputta, other-made, both self-made and other-made, or is aging and death arisen without cause, not made by self or other?' 'It is not, friend Koṭṭhika, that aging and death is self-made, nor other-made, nor both self-made and other-made, nor is aging and death arisen without cause, not made by self or other. But aging and death arises with birth as condition.'
translations.sn12.67:2: 'Is birth self-made, friend Sāriputta, other-made, both self-made and other-made, or is birth arisen without cause, not made by self or other?' 'It is not, friend Koṭṭhika, that birth is self-made, nor other-made, nor both self-made and other-made, nor is birth arisen without cause, not made by self or other. But birth arises with existence as condition.'
translations.sn12.67:4: 'Is consciousness self-made, friend Sāriputta, other-made, both self-made and other-made, or is consciousness arisen without cause, not made by self or other?' 'It is not, friend Koṭṭhika, that consciousness is self-made, nor other-made, nor both self-made and other-made, nor is consciousness arisen without cause, not made by self or other. But consciousness arises with name-and-form as condition.'
translations.sn12.67:5: 'Now we indeed know just what was said by Venerable Sāriputta thus: “It is not, friend Koṭṭhika, that name-and-form is self-made, nor other-made, nor both self-made and other-made, nor is name-and-form arisen without cause, not made by self or other. But name-and-form arises with consciousness as condition.”'
translations.sn12.67:7: “And how, friend Sāriputta, should the meaning of this statement be understood?” “I will give you a simile, friend. For by means of a simile some wise people understand the meaning of what is said. Suppose, friend, there were two sheaves of reeds, leaning one against the other. So too, friend, name-and-form is a condition for consciousness; consciousness is a condition for name-and-form; name-and-form is a condition for the six sense bases; the six sense bases are a condition for contact … … thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. If one were to pull away one of those sheaves of reeds, the other would fall; if one were to pull away the other, the first would fall. So too, friend, with the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact … … thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.”
translations.sn12.67:8: “It is wonderful, friend Sāriputta; it is marvelous, friend Sāriputta. This was well spoken by the Venerable Sāriputta. And we approve of what the Venerable Sāriputta said with these thirty-six subjects:
translations.sn12.68:13: “Is the Venerable Nāroda an arahant with taints destroyed?” “‘The cessation of becoming is Nibbāna’—this, friend, I have seen well with right wisdom as it really is, yet I am not an arahant with taints destroyed. Suppose, friend, there were a well in a wilderness road, but there was neither a rope nor a water bucket there. Then a man would come along, scorched and exhausted by the heat, tired and thirsty. He would look at that well. He would know that there is water, but he would not dwell having made contact with it physically. So too, friend, ‘the cessation of becoming is Nibbāna’—this I have seen well with right wisdom as it really is, yet I am not an arahant with taints destroyed.”
translations.sn12.68:6: “Is the Venerable Musila an arahant with taints destroyed?” When this was said, the Venerable Musila remained silent.
translations.sn12.69:1: Thus I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. There … … “Monks, the great ocean, having filled up, fills up the great rivers; the great rivers, having filled up, fill up the small rivers; the small rivers, having filled up, fill up the great lakes; the great lakes, having filled up, fill up the small lakes. So too, monks, ignorance, having filled up, fills up volitional formations; volitional formations, having filled up, fill up consciousness; consciousness, having filled up, fills up name-and-form; name-and-form, having filled up, fills up the six sense bases; the six sense bases, having filled up, fill up contact; contact, having filled up, fills up feeling; feeling, having filled up, fills up craving; craving, having filled up, fills up clinging; clinging, having filled up, fills up existence; existence, having filled up, fills up birth; birth, having filled up, fills up aging-and-death.
translations.sn12.70:1: Thus I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground. At that time the Buddha was respected, honored, revered, and venerated, and he was a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicines and requisites for the sick. The Saṅgha of monks too was respected, honored, revered, and venerated, and was a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicines and requisites for the sick. But the ascetics of other sects were not respected, honored, revered, or venerated, nor were they recipients of robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicines and requisites for the sick.
translations.sn12.70:10: “But do you, venerable sirs, knowing and seeing thus, dwell having made contact with those liberations that are peaceful and immaterial, transcending form?” “No, friend.”
translations.sn12.70:11: “In this case, venerable sirs, this explanation is given and there is no attainment of these states; how should this be understood?” “We are liberated by wisdom, friend Susīma.”
translations.sn12.70:12: “I do not understand the detailed meaning of this brief statement spoken by these venerable ones. It would be good if the venerable ones would speak in such a way that I might understand the detailed meaning of this brief statement spoken by these venerable ones.” “You may understand it, friend Susīma, or you may not understand it; but we are liberated by wisdom.”
translations.sn12.70:13: Then the Venerable Susīma rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and reported all the conversation he had had with those monks to the Buddha. “First, Susīma, there is knowledge of the establishment of the Dhamma; afterwards, there is knowledge of Nibbāna.”
translations.sn12.70:14: “I do not understand the detailed meaning of this brief statement spoken by the Blessed One, venerable sir. It would be good if the Blessed One would speak in such a way that I might understand the detailed meaning of this brief statement spoken by the Blessed One.” “You may understand it, Susīma, or you may not understand it; but first there is knowledge of the establishment of the Dhamma, afterwards there is knowledge of Nibbāna.
translations.sn12.70:16: “Therefore, Susīma, whatever form is past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or fine; inferior or superior; far or near: all form should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Whatever feeling is past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or fine; inferior or superior; far or near: all feeling should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Whatever perception … … whatever volitional formations are past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or fine; inferior or superior; far or near: all volitional formations should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Whatever consciousness is past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or fine; inferior or superior; far or near: all consciousness should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’
translations.sn12.70:17: Seeing thus, Susima, a learned noble disciple grows disenchanted with form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness. Being disenchanted, they become dispassionate; through dispassion, they are liberated. When liberated, there is the knowledge that they are liberated. They understand: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.’
translations.sn12.70:18: ‘With birth as condition, aging-and-death’—do you see this, Susima?” “Yes, Venerable Sir.” “‘With existence as condition, birth’—do you see this, Susima?” “Yes, Venerable Sir.” “‘With clinging as condition, existence’—do you see this, Susima?” “Yes, Venerable Sir.” “‘With craving as condition, clinging’—do you see this, Susima?” “Yes, Venerable Sir.” ‘With feeling as condition, craving’ … ‘With contact as condition, feeling’ … ‘With the six sense bases as condition, contact’ … ‘With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases’ … ‘With consciousness as condition, name-and-form’ … ‘With volitional formations as condition, consciousness’ … ‘With ignorance as condition, volitional formations’—do you see this, Susima?” “Yes, Venerable Sir.”
translations.sn12.70:2: Now at that time the wanderer Susima was staying at Rājagaha with a large company of wanderers. Then the wanderer Susima’s company said to the wanderer Susima: “Come, friend Susima, go forth in the holy life under the ascetic Gotama. Having learned the Dhamma, you should teach it to us. Having learned the Dhamma, we will speak to the householders. In this way we too will be respected, honored, esteemed, revered, and gain robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick.” “Yes, friends,” the wanderer Susima replied to his company. Then he approached Venerable Ānanda; having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Ānanda. After exchanging courteous and friendly talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the wanderer Susima said to Venerable Ānanda: “I wish, friend Ānanda, to lead the holy life in this Dhamma and Discipline.”
translations.sn12.70:21: “But do you, Susima, knowing and seeing in this way, hear with the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses human, both kinds of sounds, divine and human, whether far or near?” “That is not in my case, Venerable Sir.”
translations.sn12.70:25: “But do you, Susima, knowing and seeing in this way, dwell having touched with the body those peaceful liberations that are formless and transcend form?” “That is not in my case, Venerable Sir.”
translations.sn12.70:27: Then Venerable Susima fell at the Buddha’s feet with his head and said to the Buddha: “I have transgressed, Venerable Sir, I have done wrong, like a fool, a confused person, and an unskillful person, in that I went forth in this well-taught Dhamma and Discipline for the sake of a title. May the Buddha, Venerable Sir, acknowledge my transgression as a transgression for the sake of restraint in the future.”
translations.sn12.70:3: Then Venerable Ānanda, taking the wanderer Susima, approached the Buddha; having approached, he paid homage to the Buddha and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha: “This wanderer Susima, Venerable Sir, says this: ‘I wish, friend Ānanda, to lead the holy life in this Dhamma and Discipline.’” “Then, Ānanda, ordain Susima.” The wanderer Susima received the going forth under the Buddha, and he received the full admission.
translations.sn12.70:5: “But do you, venerable ones, knowing and seeing in this way, wield the many kinds of supernatural power—having been one, you become many; having been many, you become one; you appear and vanish; you go unhindered through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain as if through space; you dive in and out of the earth as if it were water; you walk on water without sinking as if it were earth; sitting cross-legged, you fly through the air like a bird; with your hand you touch and stroke the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; you exercise mastery with your body even as far as the Brahmā world?” “That is not in our case, friend.”
translations.sn12.70:6: “But do you, venerable ones, knowing and seeing in this way, hear with the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses human, both kinds of sounds, divine and human, whether far or near?” “That is not in our case, friend.”
translations.sn12.70:7: “But do you, venerable ones, knowing and seeing in this way, understand the minds of other beings, other individuals, having encompassed them with your own mind? You understand a mind with lust as a mind with lust; a mind free from lust as a mind free from lust; a mind with hate as a mind with hate; a mind free from hate as a mind free from hate; a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion; a mind free from delusion as a mind free from delusion; a constricted mind as a constricted mind; a scattered mind as a scattered mind; an expanded mind as an expanded mind; an unexpanded mind as an unexpanded mind; a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind; an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind; a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind; an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind; a liberated mind as a liberated mind; an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind?” “That is not in our case, friend.”
translations.sn12.70:8: “But do you, venerable ones, knowing and seeing in this way, recollect your many past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of contraction, many eons of expansion, many eons of contraction and expansion: ‘There I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life span; passing away from there, I reappeared here; and there too I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life span; passing away from there, I reappeared here.’ Thus with their aspects and particulars you recollect your many past lives?” “That is not in our case, friend.”
translations.sn12.70:9: “But do you, venerable sirs, knowing and seeing in this way, see beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—understanding how beings fare according to their deeds with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human: ‘These venerable beings are endowed with misconduct of body, speech, and mind; they revile the noble ones, hold wrong view, and undertake wrong view as their practice. With the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a realm of loss, a bad destination, the lower world, hell. Or these venerable beings are endowed with good conduct of body, speech, and mind; they do not revile the noble ones, hold right view, and undertake right view as their practice. With the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a good destination, a heavenly world’?” “No, friend.”
translations.sn16.11:1: At one time Venerable Mahākassapa was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground. Now at that time Venerable Ānanda was wandering in the Southern Hills with a large Saṅgha of monks.
translations.sn16.11:10: Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourselves thus: ‘My sense of moral dread and fear of wrongdoing will be firmly established towards elders, novices, and those of middle standing.’ Thus, Kassapa, you should train yourselves.
translations.sn16.11:11: Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourselves thus: ‘Whatever Dhamma I hear that is conducive to wholesomeness, I will listen to it with an attentive ear, attending to it with my whole mind.’ Thus, Kassapa, you should train yourselves.
translations.sn16.11:12: Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourselves thus: ‘Mindfulness of the body, accompanied by gladness, will not be neglected by me.’ Thus, Kassapa, you should train yourselves.’
translations.sn16.11:13: Then, friend, the Blessed One, having instructed me with this exhortation, rose from his seat and departed. For seven days, friend, I lived on almsfood as a refugee, and on the eighth day I attained realization.
translations.sn16.11:14: Then, friend, the Blessed One, leaving the road, approached a certain tree root. Then, friend, having arranged a fourfold robe of patchwork cloths, I said to the Blessed One: ‘Here, Bhante, let the Blessed One sit; it is for my long-term welfare and happiness.’ The Blessed One sat down on the seat prepared. Having sat down, friend, the Blessed One said to me: ‘This robe of patchwork cloths is soft, Kassapa.’ ‘Let the Blessed One accept this robe of patchwork cloths from me out of compassion.’ ‘But you, Kassapa, will wear rag-robes made of cast-off rags.’ ‘I will wear rag-robes made of cast-off rags, Bhante.’ I, friend, gave the robe of patchwork cloths to the Blessed One. But I wore the rag-robes made of cast-off rags of the Blessed One.
translations.sn16.11:17: I, friend, having destroyed the taints, realized for myself with direct knowledge the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and dwell having attained it in this very life; or one might think that a seven-gem elephant or an eight-gem elephant should be covered with a palm-leaf umbrella, but one might think that my six superknowledges should be covered with a palm-leaf umbrella.’
translations.sn16.11:2: Now at that time thirty of Venerable Ānanda’s monk pupils, having abandoned the training, reverted to the lower life, mostly while still young. Then Venerable Ānanda, having wandered in the Southern Hills as far as he wished, approached Rājagaha, the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground, and Venerable Mahākassapa; having approached, he bowed to Venerable Mahākassapa and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Mahākassapa said to Venerable Ānanda: “For what purpose, friend Ānanda, was the threefold meal in families allowed by the Blessed One?”
translations.sn16.11:3: “There are three purposes, friend Kassapa, for which the threefold meal in families was allowed by the Blessed One—for the restraint of wicked individuals, for the comfort of well-behaved monks, so that those with wicked desires do not split the Saṅgha by taking sides, and out of compassion for families. These, friend Kassapa, are the three purposes for which the threefold meal in families was allowed by the Blessed One.”
translations.sn16.11:4: “Then why, friend Ānanda, do you go on tour with these new monks who are unguarded in their faculties, not knowing the right amount in eating, and not devoted to wakefulness? I think you are destroying the crops, I think you are destroying the families. Your assembly is crumbling, friend Ānanda; your new shoots are crumbling. You are not acting like a mere child.”
translations.sn16.11:6: The nun Thullanandā heard: “It seems that the Venerable Mahākassapa has displeased the Venerable Ānanda, the Vedic sage, by speaking like a child.”
translations.sn16.11:7: Then the nun Thullanandā cried out in displeasure and spoke words of displeasure: “Why should the Venerable Mahākassapa, who was formerly a follower of another teaching, think that he should displeasure the Venerable Ānanda, the Vedic sage, by speaking like a child?” Venerable Mahākassapa heard the nun Thullanandā speaking these words.
translations.sn16.11:8: Then Venerable Mahākassapa said to Venerable Ānanda: 'It is indeed, friend Ānanda, that the nun Thullanandā has spoken suddenly without due reflection. For I, friend, having shaved off hair and beard, and putting on ochre robes, went forth from the home life into homelessness; I do not know another teacher designated, apart from that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. Formerly, friend, when I was a householder, this occurred to me: "Confined is household life, a path of dust; the going forth is open space. It is not easy while living at home to lead the holy life utterly complete and utterly pure, like a polished shell. Why should I not shave off hair and beard, and putting on ochre robes, go forth from the home life into homelessness?" So I, friend, at a later time, having made a patchwork robe, went forth from the home life into homelessness, having shaved off hair and beard and put on ochre robes, designating those Arahants in the world.'
translations.sn16.13:2: Just as, Kassapa, there is no disappearance of gold as long as no counterfeit gold has arisen in the world. But when, Kassapa, counterfeit gold has arisen in the world, then there is the disappearance of gold. So too, Kassapa, there is no disappearance of the true Dhamma as long as a counterfeit of the true Dhamma has not arisen in the world. But when, Kassapa, a counterfeit of the true Dhamma has arisen in the world, then there is the disappearance of the true Dhamma.
translations.sn16.13:4: There are, Kassapa, five factors that tend to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma. What five? Here, Kassapa, monks and nuns, male and female lay followers live without respect, without deference for the Teacher; they live without respect, without deference for the Dhamma; they live without respect, without deference for the Saṅgha; they live without respect, without deference for the training; they live without respect, without deference for concentration—these, Kassapa, are the five factors that tend to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.
translations.sn16.2:1: Thus have I heard. At one time Venerable Mahākassapa and Venerable Sāriputta were staying at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then Venerable Sāriputta, in the evening, coming out of seclusion, approached Venerable Mahākassapa; having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Mahākassapa. When they had concluded their friendly and agreeable conversation, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Sāriputta said to Venerable Mahākassapa: 'It is said, friend Kassapa, "One who is not ardent and not fearful is incapable of enlightenment, incapable of Nibbāna, incapable of attaining the unexcelled security from bondage; but one who is ardent and fearful is capable of enlightenment, capable of Nibbāna, capable of attaining the unexcelled security from bondage."'
translations.sn16.2:3: And how, friend, is one not fearful? Here, friend, a monk does not feel fear: 'Unarisen evil unwholesome states might arise in me to my harm'; he does not feel fear: 'Arisen evil unwholesome states might not be abandoned in me to my harm'; he does not feel fear: 'Unarisen wholesome states might not arise in me to my harm'; he does not feel fear: 'Arisen wholesome states might cease in me to my harm.' In this way, friend, one is not fearful. In this way, friend, one who is not ardent and not fearful is incapable of enlightenment, incapable of Nibbāna, incapable of attaining the unexcelled security from bondage.
translations.sn16.2:4: And how, friend, is one ardent? Here, friend, a monk makes an effort: 'Unarisen evil unwholesome states might arise in me to my harm'; he makes an effort: 'Arisen evil unwholesome states might not be abandoned in me to my harm'; unarisen wholesome states ... he makes an effort. In this way, friend, one is ardent.
translations.sn16.5:1: Thus have I heard ... at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove. Then Venerable Mahākassapa approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Blessed One said to Venerable Mahākassapa: 'You are now old, Kassapa, and these are your heavy hempen rag-robes. Therefore, Kassapa, you should wear lay robes too, accept invitations, and dwell near me.'
translations.sn21.10:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrel sanctuary. At that time a certain monk, named Elder, was a solitary dweller and a boaster about being a solitary dweller. He alone entered a village for alms, he alone returned, he alone sat in private, he alone paced back and forth. Then several monks approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One: 'Here, venerable sir, a certain monk, named Elder, is a solitary dweller and a boaster about being a solitary dweller.'
translations.sn21.10:3: 'This, elder, is not the solitary life, nor is there no solitary life; I do not say that. But, elder, listen to how the solitary life is fulfilled in detail; pay close attention; I will speak.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' ... 'And how, elder, is the solitary life fulfilled in detail? Here, elder, what is past is abandoned, what is future is relinquished, and desire and lust regarding acquisitions of self in the present are well subdued. In this way, elder, the solitary life is fulfilled in detail.'
translations.sn21.1:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. There Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the monks: 'Friends, monks.' 'Friends,' those monks replied to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
translations.sn21.1:2: Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this: 'Here, while I was in seclusion and withdrawn, this thought arose in my mind: “There is a noble silence, and it is called noble silence. What is the noble silence?” Then it occurred to me: “Here, a monk, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, enters upon and dwells in the second jhāna, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind, without applied thought and without sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. This is called noble silence.” So I, having entered upon and dwelt in the second jhāna—which has self-confidence and singleness of mind, without applied thought and without sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration—while dwelling in this way, perceptions and attentions accompanied by applied thought occurred to me.'
translations.sn21.2:1: At Sāvatthī. There the venerable Sāriputta addressed the monks: 'Friends, monks.' 'Yes, friend,' those monks replied to the venerable Sāriputta. The venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.sn21.2:2: 'Here, while I was in seclusion and withdrawn, this thought arose in my mind: “Is there anything in the world whose change and alteration would give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair?” Then it occurred to me: “There is nothing in the world whose change and alteration would give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair.”'
translations.sn21.3:1: Thus I have heard. At one time the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. At that time the venerable Sāriputta and the venerable Mahāmoggallāna were living at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground, in a single dwelling. Then the venerable Sāriputta, in the evening, came out of seclusion and approached the venerable Mahāmoggallāna; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the venerable Mahāmoggallāna. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the venerable Sāriputta said to the venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
translations.sn21.3:2: 'Your faculties are bright, friend Moggallāna; your complexion is clear and bright. Surely, friend Mahāmoggallāna, you must have been dwelling in some meditation today.' 'I dwelt today, friend, in a lowly meditation. But I had a Dhamma talk.' 'With whom, friend, did the venerable Mahāmoggallāna have a Dhamma talk?' 'I had a Dhamma talk, friend, with the Blessed One.' 'The Blessed One is far away, friend, living now at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Did the venerable Mahāmoggallāna approach the Blessed One by psychic power, or did the Blessed One approach the venerable Mahāmoggallāna by psychic power?' 'I did not, friend, approach the Blessed One by psychic power, nor did the Blessed One approach me by psychic power. But as far as the Blessed One is concerned, so far was my divine eye purified and the divine ear element. And as far as I am concerned, so far was the Blessed One's divine eye purified and the divine ear element.' 'How, friend, did the venerable Mahāmoggallāna have a Dhamma talk with the Blessed One?'
translations.sn21.3:3: 'Here, friend, I said this to the Blessed One: “It is said, 'One who has aroused energy, one who has aroused energy.' In what way, sir, is one one who has aroused energy?” When this was said, the Blessed One said to me: “Here, Moggallāna, a monk dwells having aroused energy—let only skin and sinew and bone remain, let the flesh and blood in the body dry up, but there shall be no letting go of one’s energy by means of manly strength, manly energy, manly striving, without attaining what is attainable by manly strength, manly energy, manly striving. In this way, Moggallāna, one is one who has aroused energy.” In this way, friend, I had a Dhamma talk with the Blessed One.'
translations.sn21.3:6: 'By wisdom and by virtue, and by calm as well, The monk who has gone to the beyond— He would be foremost of this kind.'
translations.sn21.6:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya approached the Blessed One. The Blessed One saw the venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya coming from afar. Seeing him, he addressed the monks: 'Do you see, monks, this monk coming, ugly to look at, unsightly, stunted, despised among monks?' 'Yes, sir.' 'This monk, monks, is of great psychic power and great might. And that attainment is not easy to attain which he has not previously attained. He has realized for himself with direct knowledge, right here and now, that unsurpassed culmination of the spiritual life, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness, and he is entering upon and dwelling in it.' Having said this, the Blessed One ... the Teacher said:
translations.sn21.6:2: 'Geese, cranes, and peacocks, Elephants, oxen, and deer; All fear the lion, There is no equality in the body.'
translations.sn21.8:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the venerable Nanda, the Buddha's maternal cousin, having dressed in robes that were patched and patched again, having arranged his eyes to look down, holding an alms bowl, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he bowed down to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Blessed One said to the venerable Nanda: 'It is not fitting, Nanda, for you, a clansman gone forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness, to dress in robes that are patched and patched again, to arrange your eyes to look down, and to carry an alms bowl. It is fitting, Nanda, for you, a clansman gone forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness, to dwell as a forest dweller, an alms-food eater, a rag-robe wearer, and to be without desire for sensual pleasures.' Having said this, the Blessed One ... the Teacher said:
translations.sn21.8:2: 'When shall I see Nanda, A forest dweller, a rag-robe wearer, Living on what others reject, Without desire for sensual pleasures?'
translations.sn21.9:1: He dwells at Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Tissa, the Buddha’s foster-son, approached the Buddha; having approached and bowed to the Buddha, he sat down to one side, sorrowful, distressed, and shedding tears. Then the Buddha said to Venerable Tissa: “Why, Tissa, do you sit to one side sorrowful, distressed, and shedding tears?” “For, sir, the monks surround me with verbal abuse and water.” “But you, Tissa, are a talker and not tolerant of speech. That is not fitting for you, Tissa, a clansman who has gone forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness, that you are a talker and not tolerant of speech. This is fitting for you, Tissa, a clansman who has gone forth out of faith from the home life into homelessness: ‘that you are a talker and also tolerant of speech.’”
translations.sn22.100:2: Have you seen, monks, a wandering mind called ‘mind’?” “Yes, sir.” “That very mind, monks, called ‘mind’ is intentioned by mind. By that very mind, monks, called ‘mind’, the mind is even more intentioned. Therefore, monks, you should frequently examine your own mind: ‘For a long time this mind has been defiled by lust, hatred, and delusion.’ Beings are defiled by the defilement of the mind, monks; beings are cleansed by the cleansing of the mind.
translations.sn22.100:3: I do not see, monks, even a single other class of beings with a mind like this, monks, as animals on the wrong path. Those very animals on the wrong path, monks, are intentioned by mind; by those very animals on the wrong path, monks, the mind is even more intentioned. Therefore, monks, you should frequently examine your own mind: ‘For a long time this mind has been defiled by lust, hatred, and delusion.’ Beings are defiled by the defilement of the mind, monks; beings are cleansed by the cleansing of the mind.
translations.sn22.101:1: At Sāvatthī. “I declare, monks, the destruction of the taints for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see. Knowing what, seeing what does the destruction of the taints occur? ‘This is form, this is the origin of form, this is the passing away of form; this is feeling … this is perception … these are mental formations … this is consciousness, this is the origin of consciousness, this is the passing away of consciousness’—in this way, monks, knowing and seeing thus, the destruction of the taints occurs.
translations.sn22.101:2: For a monk dwelling without devoted to cultivation, even if such a wish should arise: ‘Oh, may my mind be released from the taints without grasping,’ yet his mind is not released from the taints without grasping. Why is that? ‘Because it is not developed’ should be said. Not developed in what? Not developed in the four foundations of mindfulness, not developed in the four right strivings, not developed in the four bases of power, not developed in the five faculties, not developed in the five powers, not developed in the seven factors of enlightenment, not developed in the noble eightfold path.
translations.sn22.101:3: Suppose, monks, a hen has eight or ten or twelve eggs. They are not properly brooded, not properly incubated, not properly hatched by that hen. Even if that hen should have such a wish: ‘Oh, may my chicks break out of the eggshell with the point of their claw or the tip of their beak and hatch safely,’ yet those chicks are unable to break out of the eggshell with the point of their claw or the tip of their beak and hatch safely. Why is that? Because, monks, the hen has eight or ten or twelve eggs; they are not properly brooded, not properly incubated, not properly hatched by that hen. So too, monks, for a monk dwelling without devoted to cultivation, even if such a wish should arise: ‘Oh, may my mind be released from the taints without grasping,’ yet his mind is not released from the taints without grasping. Why is that? ‘Because it is not developed’ should be said. Not developed in what? Not developed in the four foundations of mindfulness … … the eightfold path.
translations.sn22.1:1: Thus I have heard. At one time the Buddha was dwelling among the Bhaggas at Suṃsumāra Hill, in the Deer Park at Bhesakalā. Then the householder Nakulapitā approached the Buddha; having approached and bowed to the Buddha, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Nakulapitā said to the Buddha:
translations.sn22.1:10: He regards feeling as self, or self as possessing feeling, or feeling as in self, or self as in feeling. He abides obsessed with the idea: ‘I am feeling, mine is feeling.’ For him, abiding obsessed with the idea: ‘I am feeling, mine is feeling,’ that feeling changes and becomes otherwise. From the change and alteration of feeling, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise.
translations.sn22.1:11: He regards perception as self, or self as possessing perception, or perception as in self, or self as in perception. He abides obsessed with the idea: ‘I am perception, mine is perception.’ For him, abiding obsessed with the idea: ‘I am perception, mine is perception,’ that perception changes and becomes otherwise. From the change and alteration of perception, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise.
translations.sn22.1:12: He regards mental formations as self, or self as possessing mental formations, or mental formations as in self, or self as in mental formations. He abides obsessed with the idea: ‘I am mental formations, mine are mental formations.’ For him, abiding obsessed with the idea: ‘I am mental formations, mine are mental formations,’ those mental formations change and become otherwise. From the change and alteration of mental formations, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise.
translations.sn22.1:13: He perceives consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness. He abides obsessed with the idea: ‘I am consciousness, this is my consciousness.’ As he abides obsessed with that idea, that consciousness changes and alters. With the change and alteration of consciousness, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise. Thus, householder, one is sick in body and sick in mind.
translations.sn22.1:14: And how, householder, is one sick in body but not sick in mind? Here, householder, a learned noble disciple has seen the noble ones, is expert on the teachings of the noble ones, and is well-trained in the doctrine of the noble ones; has seen good persons, is expert on the teachings of good persons, and is well-trained in the doctrine of good persons. He does not regard form as self, nor self as possessing form, nor form as in self, nor self as in form. He does not abide obsessed with the idea: ‘I am form, this is my form.’ As he does not abide obsessed with that idea, that form changes and alters. With the change and alteration of form, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair do not arise.
translations.sn22.1:2: “I am old, venerable sir, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, sick in body, and frequently in pain. I am a seer of impermanence, venerable sir, regarding the Blessed One and the monks whose minds are beautiful. Let the Blessed One admonish me, venerable sir; let the Blessed One instruct me, venerable sir; for what will be for my long-term welfare and happiness.”
translations.sn22.1:3: “So it is, householder, so it is, householder. This body is sick, householder, covered with a shell, tied up. Who, householder, caring for this body, would claim even a moment of health, except through foolishness? Therefore you should train yourself, householder: ‘While my body is sick, my mind will not be sick.’ Thus you should train yourself, householder.”
translations.sn22.1:4: Then the householder Nakulapita, having approved and agreed with the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, bowed down to the Blessed One, circled him to the right, and approached Venerable Sāriputta. Having approached, he bowed down to Venerable Sāriputta and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Sāriputta said to the householder Nakulapita: “Your faculties are bright, householder; your facial complexion is clear and pure. Did you get to hear a Dhamma talk in the presence of the Blessed One today?”
translations.sn22.1:7: “But did it not occur to you, householder, to ask the Blessed One a further question: ‘How, venerable sir, is one sick in body and sick in mind, and how is one sick in body but not sick in mind?’” “We might come from afar, venerable sir, to Venerable Sāriputta’s presence to understand the meaning of this statement. It would be good if Venerable Sāriputta himself would explain the meaning of this statement.”
translations.sn22.1:8: “Then listen, householder, attend closely, and I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” the householder Nakulapita replied to Venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.sn22.1:9: “And how, householder, is one sick in body and sick in mind? Here, householder, an unlearned ordinary person has not seen the noble ones, is not expert on the teachings of the noble ones, and is not well-trained in the doctrine of the noble ones; has not seen good persons, is not expert on the teachings of good persons, and is not well-trained in the doctrine of good persons. He regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. He abides obsessed with the idea: ‘I am form, this is my form.’ As he abides obsessed with that idea, that form changes and alters. With the change and alteration of form, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise.
translations.sn22.22:2: And who, monks, is the burden-bearer? The person, it should be said, that venerable of such and such name and clan. This is called, monks, the burden-bearer.
translations.sn22.22:3: And what, monks, is the picking up of the burden? That craving which leads to renewed becoming, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting here and there; that is, sensual craving, craving for existence, craving for non-existence. This is called, monks, the picking up of the burden.
translations.sn22.22:4: And what, monks, is the putting down of the burden? The fading away and cessation, giving up and relinquishing, release and letting go of that very craving. This is called, monks, the putting down of the burden.”
translations.sn22.22:6: “The five aggregates are the burden,  and the person is the burden-bearer;  Picking up the burden is suffering in the world,  putting down the burden is happiness.
translations.sn22.2:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was living among the Sakyans in the town of the Sakyans called Devadaha. Then several monks who were dwellers in the western country approached the Blessed One; having approached, they bowed down to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One: “We wish, venerable sir, to go to the western country, to dwell in the western country.”
translations.sn22.2:10: If, friends, dwelling having entered upon unwholesome states, there were happiness in the present life, free from trouble, distress, and fever, and a good destination could be expected after the breakup of the body, on death, the Blessed One would not praise the abandoning of unwholesome states. But since, friends, dwelling having entered upon unwholesome states, there is suffering in the present life, with trouble, distress, and fever, and a bad destination is to be expected after the breakup of the body, on death, therefore the Blessed One praises the abandoning of unwholesome states.
translations.sn22.2:2: “Has Sāriputta, monks, looked in on you?” “Venerable Sāriputta has not looked in on us, venerable sir.” “Look in on Sāriputta, monks. Sāriputta is wise, an assistant to the monks, a fellow practitioner.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
translations.sn22.2:3: Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta was sitting not far from the Buddha at the foot of a certain banyan tree. Then those monks, having approved and agreed to the Buddha’s statement, rose from their seats, bowed to the Buddha, circumambulated him, and approached Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, they exchanged greetings with Venerable Sāriputta. Having exchanged courteous and memorable talk, they sat down to one side. While sitting to one side, those monks said to Venerable Sāriputta: “We wish, friend Sāriputta, to go to the western country, to dwell in the western country. We have obtained leave from the Teacher.”
translations.sn22.2:5: “We would come even from afar, friend, to the presence of Venerable Sāriputta to understand the meaning of this statement. It would be good if Venerable Sāriputta himself would explain the meaning of this statement.” “Then listen, friend, and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to Venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.sn22.36:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain monk approached the Buddha … and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that monk said to the Buddha: “It would be good, venerable sir, if the Buddha would teach the Dhamma in brief so that I might hear the Dhamma from the Buddha and might dwell secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute.” “Whatever one frequents, that one cultivates; whatever one cultivates, that is the tendency one follows. Whatever one does not frequent, that one does not cultivate; whatever one does not cultivate, that is the tendency one does not follow.” “It is understood, Blessed One, it is understood, Sugata.”
translations.sn22.3:1: Thus have I heard. At one time Venerable Mahākaccāna was dwelling in Avantī at Kuraraghara on a steep mountain. Then the householder Hāliddikāni approached Venerable Mahākaccāna; having approached, he bowed to Venerable Mahākaccāna and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Hāliddikāni said to Venerable Mahākaccāna: “This was said, venerable sir, by the Blessed One in the Māgaṇḍiya’s Questions of the Group of Eight:
translations.sn22.3:10: And how, householder, is one plagued by sensual pleasures? Here, householder, some person has not abandoned lust, desire, affection, craving, fever, and thirst for sensual pleasures. Thus, householder, one is plagued by sensual pleasures.
translations.sn22.3:11: And how, householder, is one free from sensual pleasures? Here, householder, some person has abandoned lust, desire, affection, craving, fever, and thirst for sensual pleasures. Thus, householder, one is free from sensual pleasures.
translations.sn22.3:12: And how, householder, is one burdened with the future? Here, householder, it occurs to someone: ‘Such will be my form in the future, such will be my feeling, such my perception, such my mental formations, such my consciousness.’ Thus, householder, one is burdened with the future.
translations.sn22.3:14: And how, householder, is one a maker of quarrels after having analyzed a topic? Here, householder, some person is a maker of such talk as this: ‘You do not know this Dhamma and Vinaya; I know this Dhamma and Vinaya. How could you know this Dhamma and Vinaya? You are practicing wrongly; I am practicing rightly. What should be said first you say last; what should be said last you say first. What I have said is consistent; what you have said is inconsistent. Your statement has been overturned. You have been refuted; go on to rescue your statement if you can.’ Thus, householder, one is a maker of quarrels after having analyzed a topic.
translations.sn22.3:17: ‘Having gone forth from home, wandering without a home,  Not making ties with people in the village;  Free from sensual pleasures, not burdened with the future,  How could one make quarrels after analyzing a topic?’
translations.sn22.3:6: And how, householder, is one a wanderer with a home? Bound by the home of the sign of form, bound by the tether of the sign of form, householder, one is called ‘a wanderer with a home.’ Bound by the home of the sign of sound … bound by the home of the sign of odor … bound by the home of the sign of taste … bound by the home of the sign of touch … bound by the home of the sign of mind-objects, bound by the tether of the sign of mind-objects, householder, one is called ‘a wanderer with a home.’ Thus, householder, one is a wanderer with a home.
translations.sn22.3:8: And how, householder, is one one who has made ties in the village? Here, householder, some person dwells mixing with householders, rejoicing together, sorrowing together, happy when they are happy, unhappy when they are unhappy, and undertaking exertion himself in their business that has arisen. Thus, householder, one is one who has made ties in the village.
translations.sn22.3:9: And how, householder, is one one who has not made ties in the village? Here, householder, a monk dwells not mixing with householders, not rejoicing together, not sorrowing together, not happy when they are happy, not unhappy when they are unhappy, and not undertaking exertion himself in their business that has arisen. Thus, householder, one is one who has not made ties in the village.
translations.sn22.47:1: At Sāvatthī. “Whatever ascetics or brahmins, bhikkhus, regard the self in various ways, they all regard the five aggregates subject to clinging, or some one among them. What five? Here, bhikkhus, the uninstructed ordinary person, who has not seen the noble ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, untrained in the Dhamma of the noble ones, who has not seen good persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of good persons, untrained in the Dhamma of good persons, regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. He regards feeling as self … perception as self … mental formations as self … consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness.
translations.sn22.47:2: Thus this regard of ‘I am’ has not vanished for him. When, bhikkhus, the regard of ‘I am’ has not vanished, there is a descent of the five faculties— the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, the body faculty. There is mind, bhikkhus, there are phenomena, there is the element of ignorance. Touched by feeling born of ignorance, bhikkhus, for the uninstructed ordinary person there arises ‘I am’; there arises ‘I am this’; there arises ‘I will be’; there arises ‘I will not be’; there arises ‘I will be with form’; there arises ‘I will be formless’; there arises ‘I will be percipient’; there arises ‘I will be non-percipient’; there arises ‘I will be neither percipient nor non-percipient.’
translations.sn22.48:1: At Sāvatthī. 'I will teach the five aggregates, monks, and the five aggregates subject to clinging. Listen to that. And what, monks, are the five aggregates? Whatever form, monks, is past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: this is called the form aggregate. Whatever feeling … … whatever perception … whatever volitional formations are past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle … … this is called the volitional formations aggregate. Whatever consciousness, monks, is past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near: this is called the consciousness aggregate. These are called, monks, the five aggregates.
translations.sn22.53:1: At Sāvatthī. 'There is a means, monks, of not being released, and there is a means of being released. While consciousness remains established, relying on form, supported by form, with form as its object, delighting in it, it would grow, increase, and flourish. While consciousness remains established, relying on feeling … … relying on perception … … relying on volitional formations, monks, supported by volitional formations, with volitional formations as its object, delighting in them, it would grow, increase, and flourish.
translations.sn22.53:2: If anyone, monks, should say: “I will declare the coming, going, passing away, rebirth, growth, increase, or flourishing of consciousness apart from form, apart from feeling, apart from perception, and apart from volitional formations,” that is impossible.
translations.sn22.54:2: While consciousness remains established, monks, relying on form, supported by form, with form as its object, delighting in it, it would grow, increase, and flourish. While consciousness remains established, monks, relying on feeling … … while consciousness remains established, monks, relying on perception … … while consciousness remains established, monks, relying on volitional formations, supported by volitional formations, with volitional formations as its object, delighting in them, it would grow, increase, and flourish.
translations.sn22.55:1: At Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One uttered this solemn utterance: “‘I shall not be, and it shall not be mine; I will not exist, and it will not be mine’—a monk who thus resolves would cut off the lower fetters.” When this was said, a certain monk said to the Blessed One: “In what way, venerable sir, does a monk who thus resolves, ‘I shall not be, and it shall not be mine; I will not exist, and it will not be mine,’ cut off the lower fetters?”
translations.sn22.55:10: But how, venerable sir, does the destruction of the taints occur immediately for one who knows and sees?” “Here, monk, an unlearned ordinary person falls into those unsuitable places. For that monk, an unlearned ordinary person, it is: ‘I shall not be, and it shall not be mine; I will not exist, and it will not be mine.’
translations.sn22.55:4: He does not truly understand form as suffering, ‘form is suffering’; he does not truly understand feeling as suffering … perception as suffering … volitional formations as suffering … consciousness as suffering, ‘consciousness is suffering’.
translations.sn22.55:5: He does not truly understand form as not-self, ‘form is not-self’; he does not truly understand feeling as not-self, ‘feeling is not-self’; he does not truly understand perception as not-self, ‘perception is not-self’; he does not truly understand volitional formations as not-self, ‘volitional formations are not-self’; he does not truly understand consciousness as not-self, ‘consciousness is not-self’.
translations.sn22.55:6: He does not truly understand form as conditioned, ‘form is conditioned’; he does not truly understand feeling as conditioned … perception as conditioned … volitional formations as conditioned … consciousness as conditioned, ‘consciousness is conditioned’. He does not truly understand that form will vanish. Feeling will vanish … perception will vanish … volitional formations will vanish … consciousness will vanish.
translations.sn22.55:8: He truly understands form as impermanent, ‘form is impermanent’. He truly understands feeling as impermanent … perception as impermanent … volitional formations as impermanent … consciousness as impermanent, ‘consciousness is impermanent’. He truly understands form as suffering … … consciousness as suffering … form as not-self … … consciousness as not-self … form as conditioned … … consciousness as conditioned, ‘consciousness is conditioned’. He truly understands that form will vanish. Feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness will vanish.
translations.sn22.55:9: Because of the vanishing of form, the vanishing of feeling, the vanishing of perception, the vanishing of volitional formations, and the vanishing of consciousness, it is in this way, monk, that a monk who thus resolves, ‘I shall not be, and it shall not be mine; I will not exist, and it will not be mine,’ would cut off the lower fetters.” “‘Thus resolving,’ venerable sir, ‘a monk would cut off the lower fetters.’
translations.sn22.56:13: And what, monks, is consciousness? These six classes of consciousness, monks: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness. This is called consciousness, monks. With the arising of name-and-form comes the arising of consciousness; with the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of consciousness. This noble eightfold path is the way leading to the cessation of consciousness; that is, right view … … right concentration.
translations.sn22.56:14: Whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, who have directly known consciousness in this way, its origin in this way, its cessation in this way, and the way leading to its cessation in this way, and are practicing for disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding consciousness—they are well-practiced. Those who are well-practiced are established in this teaching and discipline.
translations.sn22.56:2: And what is the fourfold revolution? I directly understood form, its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation; feeling… perception… volitional formations… I directly understood consciousness, its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation.
translations.sn22.56:5: And whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, who have directly known form in this way … and have directly known the way leading to its cessation in this way, are released without grasping through the disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation of form—they are well released. Those who are well released are consummate ones. For those who are consummate ones, there is no need to point out the cycle.
translations.sn22.57:1: At Sāvatthī. “A monk who is skilled in the seven stations, monks, who has reviewed the threefold super-knowledge in this teaching and discipline, is called a consummate one who has lived the holy life, an unsurpassed person. And how, monks, is a monk skilled in the seven stations? Here, monks, a monk understands form, its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation; he understands the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to form; he understands feeling… perception… volitional formations… consciousness, its origin, its cessation, and the way leading to its cessation; he understands the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to consciousness.
translations.sn22.57:11: And what, monks, are volitional formations? There are these six classes of intention, monks: intention regarding form … intention regarding phenomena. These are called volitional formations, monks. With the arising of contact, volitional formations arise; with the cessation of contact, volitional formations cease. This noble eightfold path is the way leading to the cessation of volitional formations, that is to say: right view … right concentration.
translations.sn22.57:15: The pleasure and joy that arise dependent on consciousness: this is the gratification of consciousness. That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: this is the danger of consciousness. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for consciousness: this is the escape from consciousness.
translations.sn22.57:17: And whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, who have directly known consciousness in this way, its origin in this way, its cessation in this way, and the way leading to its cessation in this way; and have directly known the gratification of consciousness in this way, the danger of consciousness in this way, and the escape from consciousness in this way, are released without grasping through the disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation of consciousness—they are well released. Those who are well released are consummate ones. For those who are consummate ones, there is no need to point out the cycle. It is in this way, monks, that a monk is skilled in the seven stations.
translations.sn22.57:2: And what, monks, is form? The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements. This is called form, monks. With the arising of nutriment, form arises; with the cessation of nutriment, form ceases. This noble eightfold path is the way leading to the cessation of form, that is to say: right view … right concentration.
translations.sn22.57:5: And whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, who have directly known form in this way, its origin in this way, its cessation in this way, and the way leading to its cessation in this way; and have directly known the gratification of form in this way, the danger of form in this way, and the escape from form in this way, are released without grasping through the disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation of form—they are well released. Those who are well released are consummate ones. For those who are consummate ones, there is no need to point out the cycle.
translations.sn22.57:6: And what, monks, is feeling? There are these six classes of feeling, monks: feeling born of eye-contact … feeling born of mind-contact. This is called feeling, monks. With the arising of contact, feeling arises; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases. This noble eightfold path is the way leading to the cessation of feeling, that is to say: right view … right concentration.
translations.sn22.57:7: The pleasure and joy that arise dependent on feeling: this is the gratification of feeling. That feeling is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: this is the danger of feeling. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for feeling: this is the escape from feeling.
translations.sn22.58:1: At Sāvatthī. “The Realized One, monks, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is called a Perfectly Enlightened One because he is released without grasping through the disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation of form. A monk too, monks, who is released through wisdom, is called one released through wisdom because he is released without grasping through the disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation of form.
translations.sn22.58:3: The Realized One, monks, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is called a Perfectly Enlightened One because he is released without grasping through the disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation of perception … volitional formations … consciousness. A monk too, monks, who is released through wisdom, is called one released through wisdom because he is released without grasping through the disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation of consciousness.
translations.sn22.59:10: Whatever consciousness—past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—should all be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’
translations.sn22.59:7: “Therefore, bhikkhus, any form whatsoever—past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—should all be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’
translations.sn22.5:11: They do not delight in consciousness, do not welcome it, and do not remain holding to it. As they do not delight in consciousness, do not welcome it, and do not remain holding to it, the delight in consciousness ceases. With the cessation of delight comes cessation of clinging; with cessation of clinging, cessation of becoming … and thus the whole mass of suffering ceases.
translations.sn22.5:2: And what, bhikkhus, is the origin of form, the origin of feeling, the origin of perception, the origin of volitional formations, the origin of consciousness? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu delights, welcomes, and remains holding to.
translations.sn22.5:3: What do they delight in, welcome, and remain holding to? They delight in, welcome, and remain holding to form. As they delight in, welcome, and remain holding to form, delight arises. Whatever delight there is in form, that is clinging there. With clinging as condition, becoming; with becoming as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.5:4: They delight in feeling … they delight in perception … they delight in volitional formations … they delight in consciousness, welcome it, and remain holding to it. As they delight in, welcome, and remain holding to consciousness, delight arises. Whatever delight there is in consciousness, that is clinging there. With clinging as condition, becoming; with becoming as condition, birth; with birth as condition … thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.5:8: What do they not delight in, not welcome, and not remain holding to? They do not delight in, welcome, or remain holding to form. As they do not delight in, welcome, or remain holding to form, the delight in form ceases. With the cessation of delight comes cessation of clinging; with cessation of clinging, cessation of becoming … and thus the whole mass of suffering ceases.
translations.sn22.60:1: Thus I have heard. At one time the Blessed One was living near Vesālī in the Great Wood at the Gabled Hall. Then Mahāli the Licchavi approached the Blessed One … and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Mahāli the Licchavi said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn22.60:2: “Pūraṇa Kassapa, sir, says this: ‘There is no cause or condition for the defilement of beings; without cause or condition, beings become defiled. There is no cause or condition for the purification of beings; without cause or condition, beings become purified.’ What does the Blessed One say to this?”
translations.sn22.60:3: “There is, Mahāli, a cause and condition for the defilement of beings; with cause and condition, beings become defiled. There is, Mahāli, a cause and condition for the purification of beings; with cause and condition, beings become purified.”
translations.sn22.60:4: “But what, sir, is the cause and condition for the defilement of beings? How, with cause and condition, do beings become defiled?”
translations.sn22.60:5: “If, Mahāli, form were exclusively painful, steeped in pain, immersed in pain, not immersed in pleasure, beings would not become enamored of form. But because form is pleasurable, steeped in pleasure, immersed in pleasure, not immersed in pain, beings become enamored of form. Enamored, they become attached; through attachment, they become defiled. This, Mahāli, is the cause and condition for the defilement of beings; thus, with cause and condition, beings become defiled.
translations.sn22.60:8: If, Mahāli, consciousness were exclusively painful, steeped in pain, immersed in pain, not immersed in pleasure, beings would not become enamored of consciousness. But because consciousness is pleasurable, steeped in pleasure, immersed in pleasure, not immersed in pain, beings become enamored of consciousness. Enamored, they become attached; through attachment, they become defiled. This too, Mahāli, is the cause and condition for the defilement of beings. Thus, with cause and condition, beings become defiled.”
translations.sn22.60:9: “But what, sir, is the cause and condition for the purification of beings? How, with cause and condition, do beings become purified?” “If, Mahāli, form were exclusively pleasurable, steeped in pleasure, immersed in pleasure, not immersed in pain, beings would not become disenchanted with form. But because form is painful, steeped in pain, immersed in pain, not immersed in pleasure, beings become disenchanted with form. Disenchanted, they become dispassionate; through dispassion, they are purified. This, Mahāli, is the cause and condition for the purification of beings. Thus, with cause and condition, beings become purified.
translations.sn22.76:2: Seeing this, the learned noble disciple grows disenchanted with form, with feeling … with perception … with volitional formations … with consciousness. Disenchanted, they become dispassionate; through dispassion, they are freed. When freed, there is the knowledge: ‘I am freed.’ They understand: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.’ As far as, bhikkhus, the realm of sentient beings, as far as the plane of rebirth, these are the foremost, the best in the world: the Arahants.”
translations.sn22.76:4: “Happy are the Arahants, for in them craving is not found; The conceit ‘I am’ is cut off, and the net of delusion is destroyed.
translations.sn22.76:6: Having fully understood the five aggregates, seven are the wanderers in the true Dhamma; Good persons are to be praised, sons of the Buddha, close to him.
translations.sn22.76:7: Endowed with the seven treasures, trained in the three trainings; The great heroes wander on, having abandoned fear and dread.
translations.sn22.76:8: Possessing the ten factors, the great elephants are concentrated; These are the best in the world, in them craving is not found.
translations.sn22.76:9: The knowledge of the non-returner has arisen, this is the last body; The essence of the holy life, in them there is no further condition.
translations.sn22.79:1: At Sāvatthī. “Mendicants, whatever ascetics or brahmins recollect many kinds of past lives, they all recollect the five aggregates subject to clinging, or one of them. What five? ‘I was of such form in the past’—so recollecting, they recollect just form. ‘I was of such feeling in the past’—so recollecting, they recollect just feeling. ‘I was of such perception in the past’ … ‘I was of such choices in the past’ … ‘I was of such consciousness in the past’—so recollecting, they recollect just consciousness.
translations.sn22.79:10: ‘Right now, I feed on consciousness. In the past, too, I fed on consciousness in the same way I feed on present consciousness. If I were to enjoy future consciousness, in the future, too, I would feed on consciousness in the same way I feed on present consciousness.’ Reflecting on this, they grow uninterested in past consciousness; they do not enjoy future consciousness; and they practice for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present consciousness.
translations.sn22.79:7: There a learned noble disciple reflects like this: ‘Right now, I feed on form. In the past, too, I fed on form in the same way I feed on present form. If I were to enjoy future form, in the future, too, I would feed on form in the same way I feed on present form.’ Reflecting on this, they grow uninterested in past form; they do not enjoy future form; and they practice for disillusionment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present form.
translations.sn22.80:1: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sakyans, near Kapilavatthu in the Banyan Grove. Then the Buddha, having addressed the Saṅgha of mendicants on some matter, dressed in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Kapilavatthu for alms. Having walked for alms in Kapilavatthu and returned from the alms-round after the meal, he approached the Great Wood to spend the day. Having entered the Great Wood, he sat at the root of a banyan tree for the day’s meditation.
translations.sn22.80:4: The Buddha consented in silence. Then Brahmā Sahampati, knowing that the Buddha had consented, bowed to the Buddha, circumambulated him, and vanished right there.
translations.sn22.80:5: Then in the evening, the Buddha rose from seclusion and approached the Banyan Grove; having approached, he sat on the seat prepared. After sitting, the Buddha performed such a psychic feat that the mendicants, feeling uneasy, approached where he was. Those mendicants, feeling uneasy, approached the Buddha; having approached, they bowed to the Buddha and sat to one side. When those mendicants were seated to one side, the Buddha said to them:
translations.sn22.80:6: “Mendicants, this is the end of the life of a wanderer who lives on alms. In the world, a wanderer who lives on alms and carries a bowl is cursed. Yet, mendicants, gentlemen approach for the sake of benefit, relying on benefit; not forced by a king, nor by thieves, nor by debt, nor by fear, nor for livelihood. But we are stuck with birth, aging, and death; with sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress; we are burdened by suffering, overcome by suffering. It is to be expected that an end of this whole mass of suffering will be discerned.
translations.sn22.80:7: In this way, mendicants, this gentleman has gone forth. Yet he is greedy for sensual pleasures, fiercely lustful, of hateful mind, thinking of ill will, unmindful, lacking awareness, uncentered, with a scattered mind and uncontrolled faculties. Just as, mendicants, a piece of dry wood, burnt at both ends and with dung in the middle, serves neither as firewood in the village nor in the forest. So, mendicants, I make this comparison for this person: he has fallen away from the life of a householder and does not fulfill the ascetic life.
translations.sn22.80:9: There are two views, mendicants: the view of existence and the view of non-existence. There a learned noble disciple reflects like this: ‘Is there anything in the world that, if I were to cling to it, I would not be liable to fall into falsehood?’ They understand thus: ‘There is nothing in the world that, if I were to cling to it, I would not be liable to fall into falsehood. For if I were to cling to form alone, or feeling alone, or perception alone, or choices alone, or consciousness alone, then for me there would be existence due to clinging; due to existence, birth; due to birth, aging and death; and sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress would arise. That is how the origin of this whole mass of suffering would take place.’
translations.sn22.81:1: At one time the Buddha was staying in Kosambī at Ghosita’s Monastery. Then the Buddha, dressed in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Kosambī for alms. Having walked for alms in Kosambī and returned from the alms-round after the meal, he set his dwelling in order and, taking his bowl and robe, without informing the attendants or notifying the mendicant Saṅgha, set out wandering alone.
translations.sn22.81:10: He does not regard form as self, he does not regard feeling as self, he does not regard perception … he does not regard choices … he does not regard consciousness as self; but he has this view: ‘That self is that world; I will be after death, permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change.’ That view of permanence, mendicants, is a fabrication. And what is the origin of that fabrication? … Thus knowing and seeing, the taints are destroyed without delay.
translations.sn22.81:3: Then the Blessed One, walking tour little by little, eventually arrived at Pālileyyaka. There the Blessed One lived at Pālileyyaka at the root of a beautiful sala tree. Then several monks approached the Venerable Ānanda; having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Venerable Ānanda. Having exchanged courteous and memorable talk, they sat down to one side. While sitting to one side, those monks said to the Venerable Ānanda: “We have heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One for a long time, friend Ānanda; we wish to hear a Dhamma talk in the presence of the Blessed One, friend Ānanda.”
translations.sn22.82:1: At one time the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, the palace of Migāra’s mother, with a large Saṅgha of monks.
