At that time the Blessed One was sitting in the open air surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks on the fifteenth day, the full-moon night of the fortnight of theuposatha.
translations.sn22.82:10: “What, venerable sir, is the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to form? What is the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness?” “Whatever pleasure and joy arise dependent on form: that is the gratification in form. That form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: that is the danger in form. The removal and abandoning of desire and lust for form: that is the escape in regard to form. Whatever pleasure and joy arise dependent on feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness: that is the gratification in consciousness. That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: that is the danger in consciousness. The removal and abandoning of desire and lust for consciousness: that is the escape in regard to consciousness.” “It is good, venerable sir,” that monk said, and having approved and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s statement, he asked the Blessed One a further question:
translations.sn22.82:11: “How, venerable sir, does one know, how does one see so that in this conscious body and externally regarding all signs there are no conceit ‘I am,’ no conceit ‘I am this,’ no underlying tendency to ‘I am’?” “Whatever form is past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or fine; inferior or superior; far or near: all form is seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Whatever feeling is past, future, or present … Whatever perception is past, future, or present … Whatever volitional formations are past, future, or present … Whatever consciousness is past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or fine; inferior or superior; far or near: all consciousness is seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ It is in this way, monk, that one knows and sees so that in this conscious body and externally regarding all signs there are no conceit ‘I am,’ no conceit ‘I am this,’ no underlying tendency to ‘I am.’”
translations.sn22.82:12: Then at that time the following thought arose in a certain monk: “It is said that form is not-self, feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness is not-self; if actions are done by a not-self, how will they affect one?” Then the Blessed One, knowing with his mind the reflection in that monk’s mind, addressed the monks:
translations.sn22.82:13: “There is an occasion, monks, when some foolish person, unknowing, unwise, a victim of craving, with a mind dominated by craving, might think that the Teacher’s instruction should be exceeded. ‘It is said, friend, that form is not-self, feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness is not-self. If actions are done by a not-self, how will they affect one?’ You have been examined by me, monks, in those various Dhammas.
translations.sn22.82:4: “And what, venerable sir, is the root of these five aggregates subject to clinging?” “These five aggregates subject to clinging, monk, have desire as their root” … “Is it that very clinging that is the clinging of these five aggregates subject to clinging, or is there clinging apart from the five aggregates subject to clinging?” “It is not that very clinging that is the clinging of these five aggregates subject to clinging, nor is there clinging apart from the five aggregates subject to clinging, but rather whatever desire and lust is there, that is the clinging there.” “It is good, venerable sir,” that monk … asked a further question:
translations.sn22.82:5: “Could there be, venerable sir, variation in desire and lust regarding the five aggregates subject to clinging?” “There could be, monks,” the Blessed One said. “Here, monk, it occurs to someone: ‘May I be of such form in the future, may I have such feeling in the future, may I have such perception in the future, may I have such volitional formations in the future, may I have such consciousness in the future.’ It is in this way, monk, that there could be variation in desire and lust regarding the five aggregates subject to clinging.” “It is good, venerable sir,” that monk … asked a further question:
translations.sn22.82:7: “What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the condition for the designation of the form aggregate; what is the cause, what is the condition for the designation of the feeling aggregate; what is the cause, what is the condition for the designation of the perception aggregate; what is the cause, what is the condition for the designation of the volitional formations aggregate; what is the cause, what is the condition for the designation of the consciousness aggregate?” “The four great elements, monk, are the cause, the four great elements are the condition for the designation of the form aggregate. Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the designation of the feeling aggregate. Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the designation of the perception aggregate. Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the designation of the volitional formations aggregate. Name-and-form is the cause, name-and-form is the condition for the designation of the consciousness aggregate.” “It is good, venerable sir,” that monk … asked:
translations.sn22.82:8: "'How, friend, does identity view come to be?' 'Here, bhikkhu, an uninstructed ordinary person, who has not seen the noble ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, untrained in the Dhamma of the noble ones, who has not seen good persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of good persons, untrained in the Dhamma of good persons, regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. He regards feeling as self... perception as self... volitional formations as self... consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness. Thus, bhikkhu, identity view comes to be.' 'It is good, friend,' that bhikkhu ... asked:
translations.sn22.82:9: "'And how, friend, does identity view not come to be?' 'Here, bhikkhu, a well-instructed noble disciple, who has seen the noble ones, is skilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, trained in the Dhamma of the noble ones, who has seen good persons, is skilled in the Dhamma of good persons, trained in the Dhamma of good persons, does not regard form as self, nor self as possessing form, nor form as in self, nor self as in form. He does not regard feeling as self... perception as self... volitional formations as self... consciousness as self, nor self as possessing consciousness, nor consciousness as in self, nor self as in consciousness. Thus, bhikkhu, identity view does not come to be.' 'It is good, friend,' that bhikkhu ... asked:
translations.sn22.83:1: At Sāvatthī. There the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: 'Friends, bhikkhus.' 'Friend,' those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this:
translations.sn22.83:3: Suppose, friend Ānanda, a woman or man, young, youthful, and fond of ornaments, would look at their own facial reflection in a well-polished mirror or in a bowl of clear water; they would look at it depending on it, but not without depending on it; so too, friend Ānanda, depending on form, 'I am' comes to be; not without depending on it. Depending on feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness, 'I am' comes to be; not without depending on it.
translations.sn22.84:10: This simile, Tissa, has been created to explain the meaning. If there is meaning here: 'A person unskilled in the path,' Tissa, this is a designation for an ordinary person. 'A person skilled in the path,' Tissa, this is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. 'A forked road,' Tissa, this is a designation for doubt. 'The left path,' Tissa, this is a designation for the wrong eightfold path, that is to say—wrong view... wrong concentration. 'The right path,' Tissa, this is a designation for the noble eightfold path, that is to say—right view... right concentration. 'A dense thicket,' Tissa, this is a designation for ignorance. 'A great pit,' Tissa, this is a designation for sensual pleasures. 'A steep precipice,' Tissa, this is a designation for anger and malice. 'A level, pleasant ground,' Tissa, this is a designation for Nibbāna. Delight, Tissa, delight, Tissa. With my instruction, my support, my teaching.'
translations.sn22.84:5: "'Good, good, Tissa. So it is, Tissa. For one whose lust for volitional formations has not departed, whose lust for consciousness has not departed, whose desire, affection, thirst, fever, and craving have not departed, with the changing and alteration of that consciousness, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise.' 'So it is, venerable sir.'
translations.sn22.84:6: "'Good, good, Tissa. So it is, Tissa. For one whose lust for consciousness has not departed. What do you think, Tissa, for one whose lust for form has departed, whose desire, affection, thirst, fever, and craving have departed, with the changing and alteration of that form, do sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise?' 'No, venerable sir.'
translations.sn22.85:1: At one time the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. At that time the bhikkhu named Yamaka had such a bad view arisen: 'Thus I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One: that an arahant bhikkhu with the breakup of the body is annihilated and perishes, and does not exist after death.'
translations.sn22.85:10: "'What do you think, friend Yamaka, do you regard form... feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness as the Tathāgata?' 'No, friend.'
translations.sn22.85:11: "'What do you think, friend Yamaka, do you regard that which is formless... feelingless... perceptionless... without volitional formations... without consciousness as the Tathāgata?' 'No, friend.' 'Since here, friend Yamaka, the Tathāgata is not found in truth and reality, is it proper for you to declare: "Thus I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One: that an arahant bhikkhu with the breakup of the body is annihilated and perishes, and does not exist after death"?'
translations.sn22.85:12: "'I formerly had that bad view, friend Sāriputta, without knowing it; but having heard the Venerable Sāriputta's teaching of the Dhamma, that bad view has been abandoned in me, and I have realized the Dhamma.'
translations.sn22.85:16: He does not understand form as impermanent according to reality: 'Form is impermanent.' He does not understand feeling as impermanent according to reality: 'Feeling is impermanent.' He does not understand perception as impermanent according to reality: 'Perception is impermanent.' He does not understand volitional formations as impermanent according to reality: 'Volitional formations are impermanent.' He does not understand consciousness as impermanent according to reality: 'Consciousness is impermanent.'
translations.sn22.85:19: He does not understand conditioned form as conditioned according to reality: 'Form is conditioned.' He does not understand conditioned feeling... conditioned perception... conditioned volitional formations... conditioned consciousness as conditioned according to reality: 'Consciousness is conditioned.'
translations.sn22.85:20: They do not truly understand form as a butcher. They do not truly understand feeling as a butcher. They do not truly understand perception as a butcher. They do not truly understand volitional formations as butchers. They do not truly understand consciousness as a butcher.
translations.sn22.85:21: They approach form, grasp it, and insist: ‘This is mine.’ They approach feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness, grasp it, and insist: ‘This is mine.’ These five aggregates subject to clinging, having been approached and grasped, lead to what is unbeneficial and painful for a long time.
translations.sn22.85:23: They truly understand form as impermanent. They truly understand feeling as impermanent. They truly understand perception as impermanent. They truly understand volitional formations as impermanent. They truly understand consciousness as impermanent.
translations.sn22.85:25: They truly understand form as not-self. They truly understand feeling as not-self. They truly understand perception as not-self. They truly understand volitional formations as not-self. They truly understand consciousness as not-self.
translations.sn22.85:5: When the monks could not get the monk Yamaka to emerge from that wrong view, they rose from their seats and approached Venerable Sāriputta. Having approached, they said to Venerable Sāriputta: ‘The monk Yamaka has such a wrong view: “I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One such that an arahant monk, with the breakup of the body, is annihilated and perishes, and does not exist after death.” Please, Venerable Sāriputta, go to the monk Yamaka out of compassion.’ Venerable Sāriputta consented by silence. Then in the evening, Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and went to the monk Yamaka. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the monk Yamaka … and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Sāriputta said to the monk Yamaka:
translations.sn22.85:6: “Is it true, Yamaka, that you have such a wrong view: ‘I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One such that an arahant monk, with the breakup of the body, is annihilated and perishes, and does not exist after death’?” “Yes, friend, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One such that an arahant monk, with the breakup of the body, is annihilated and perishes, and does not exist after death.”
translations.sn22.85:9: “What do you think, Yamaka, do you regard the Tathāgata as form?” “No, friend.” “Do you regard the Tathāgata as apart from form?” “No, friend.” “Do you regard the Tathāgata as feeling … apart from feeling … perception … apart from perception … volitional formations … apart from volitional formations … consciousness?” “No, friend.” “Do you regard the Tathāgata as apart from consciousness?” “No, friend.”
translations.sn22.86:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying near Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall. At that time Venerable Anuruddha was staying in a forest hut not far from the Blessed One. Then several wanderers of other sects went to Venerable Anuruddha. Having approached, they exchanged greetings with Venerable Anuruddha. When they had exchanged courteous greetings, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those wanderers of other sects said to Venerable Anuruddha: “Friend Anuruddha, when the Tathāgata—the supreme person, the unsurpassed person, who has attained the supreme attainment—explains and declares, does he explain and declare regarding these four positions: ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’?”
translations.sn22.86:10: “What do you think, Anuruddha, do you regard form … feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness as the Tathāgata?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn22.86:11: “What do you think, Anuruddha, do you regard this formless … feelingless … perceptionless … formationless … consciousnessless one as the Tathāgata?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn22.86:12: “Since the Tathāgata is not found, in truth and reality, in the here and now, is it proper for you to declare: ‘That Tathāgata—the supreme person, the unsurpassed person, who has attained the supreme attainment—explains and declares apart from these four positions: “The Tathāgata exists after death” … “does not exist” … “both exists and does not exist” … “neither exists nor does not exist after death”’?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn22.86:2: When this was said, Venerable Anuruddha said to those wanderers of other sects: “That Tathāgata—the supreme person, the unsurpassed person, who has attained the supreme attainment—explains and declares apart from these four positions: ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘does not exist after death,’ or ‘both exists and does not exist after death,’ or ‘neither exists nor does not exist after death.’” When this was said, the wanderers of other sects said to Venerable Anuruddha: “This monk must be new, or he must be an elder who is foolish and incompetent.” Then the wanderers of other sects, having insulted Venerable Anuruddha as new and foolish, rose from their seats and left.
translations.sn22.86:3: Then soon after those wanderers of other sects had left, it occurred to Venerable Anuruddha: “If those wanderers of other sects were to ask me a further question, how should I answer so that I would be a speaker of the Blessed One’s words, not misrepresent him with what is false, explain the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, and so that no statement by those with reasonable grounds for censure would incur a ground for censure?”
translations.sn22.86:8: “What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard form as the Tathāgata?” “No, venerable sir.” “Do you regard feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness as the Tathāgata?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn22.86:9: “What do you think, Anurādha, do you regard the Tathāgata as in form?” “No, venerable sir.” “Do you regard the Tathāgata as apart from form?” “No, venerable sir.” “Do you regard the Tathāgata as in feeling … apart from feeling … in perception … apart from perception … in volitional formations … apart from volitional formations … in consciousness … apart from consciousness?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn22.89:10: Suppose, friend, there is the scent of a blue lotus, or a white lotus, or a red lotus. If someone were to say: ‘The scent of the petal’ or ‘the scent of the color’ or ‘the scent of the stamen’, would he be speaking correctly?” “No, friend.” “In what way, then, friend, would he be speaking correctly?” “He would be speaking correctly if he said: ‘The scent of the flower’, friend.” “So too, friend, I do not say that I am form, nor do I say that I am apart from form. I do not say that I am feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness, nor do I say that I am apart from consciousness. But, friend, with regard to the five aggregates subject to clinging, ‘I am’ is understood, yet I do not regard it as ‘I am this’.
translations.sn22.89:11: Even though, friend, a noble disciple has abandoned the five lower fetters, still there occurs in him: the conceit ‘I am’, the desire ‘I am’, the latent tendency ‘I am’ that has not been uprooted, which is accompanied by the five aggregates subject to clinging. At another time he dwells contemplating rise and fall in the five aggregates subject to clinging— ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the passing away of form; such is feeling … such is perception … such are volitional formations … such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.’ While he dwells contemplating rise and fall in these five aggregates subject to clinging, whatever conceit ‘I am’, desire ‘I am’, or latent tendency ‘I am’ that he has, accompanied by the five aggregates subject to clinging, that too is abandoned.
translations.sn22.89:12: Suppose, friend, a cloth is stained and dirty. The owner gives it to a washerman. The washerman scrubs it with salt-earth, lye, or cow-dung, and rinses it in clean water. Even though the cloth is clean and bright, still it has the smell of the salt-earth, lye, or cow-dung that has not been removed. The washerman gives it back to the owner. The owner puts it in a scented chest. Whatever smell of salt-earth, lye, or cow-dung it has that has not been removed, that too is abandoned. So too, friend, even though a noble disciple has abandoned the five lower fetters, still there occurs in him the conceit ‘I am’, desire ‘I am’, and latent tendency ‘I am’ that has not been uprooted, accompanied by the five aggregates subject to clinging. At another time he dwells contemplating rise and fall in the five aggregates subject to clinging. ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the passing away of form; such is feeling … such is perception … such are volitional formations … such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.’ While he dwells contemplating rise and fall in these five aggregates subject to clinging, whatever conceit ‘I am’, desire ‘I am’, or latent tendency ‘I am’ that he has, accompanied by the five aggregates subject to clinging, that too is abandoned.”
translations.sn22.89:13: When this was said, the elder monks said to Venerable Khemaka: “We did not question Venerable Khemaka out of a desire to trouble him, but Venerable Khemaka was able to explain, teach, point out, establish, disclose, analyze, and elucidate the Teacher’s instruction in detail. This has been explained, taught, pointed out, established, disclosed, analyzed, and elucidated in detail by Venerable Khemaka.”
translations.sn22.90:1: At one time several elder monks were staying at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then Venerable Channa, in the evening, having come out of seclusion, went to the monastery and approached the elder monks, and said to them: “Let the elder monks admonish me, let the elder monks instruct me, let the elder monks speak to me on Dhamma, so that I might see the Dhamma.”
translations.sn22.90:2: When this was said, the elder monks said to Venerable Channa: “Form, friend Channa, is impermanent; feeling is impermanent; perception is impermanent; volitional formations are impermanent; consciousness is impermanent. Form is not-self; feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness is not-self. All volitional formations are impermanent; all phenomena are not-self.”
translations.sn22.90:3: Then it occurred to Venerable Channa: “This is also how it is for me: ‘Form is impermanent, feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness is impermanent; form is not-self, feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness is not-self. All volitional formations are impermanent, all phenomena are not-self.’ But yet my mind does not leap forward, grow confident, settle down, or become established in Nibbāna, which is the cessation of craving, the fading away, the cessation, the giving up, the relinquishment of all volitional formations. Clinging arises; the mind wavers: ‘Then what is my self now?’ This does not happen when one sees the Dhamma. Who, then, would teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might see the Dhamma?”
translations.sn22.95:6: Suppose, monks, there were a magician or a magician’s apprentice at a crossroads who would display a magical illusion. A person with good sight would see it, examine it, and investigate it appropriately. To them, as it is seen, examined, and investigated appropriately, it would appear empty, void, and without substance. For what substance could there be in a magical illusion? So too, monks, whatever consciousness—past, future, or present … far or near—a monk sees, examines, and investigates appropriately. To them, as it is seen, examined, and investigated appropriately, it appears empty, void, and without substance. For what substance could there be in consciousness?
translations.sn22.95:7: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disenchanted with form, feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness. Disenchanted, they become dispassionate; through dispassion, they are liberated. When liberated, there is the knowledge that they are liberated. They understand: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming back to any state of existence.’
translations.sn22.95:9: “Form is like a lump of foam, feeling like a bubble; perception like a mirage, volitional formations like a plantain trunk; consciousness like a magic trick, so taught the Kinsman of the Sun.
translations.sn22.96:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain monk, sitting to one side, said to the Buddha: “Is there, sir, any form that is permanent, lasting, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same forever? Is there, sir, any feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness that is permanent, lasting, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same forever?” “There is not, monk, any form that is permanent, lasting, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same forever. There is not, monk, any feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness that is permanent, lasting, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same forever.”
translations.sn22.96:2: Then the Buddha, picking up a little bit of cow dung with his fingernails, said to that monk: “Even this small acquisition of self, monk, is not permanent, lasting, eternal, or not subject to change. If even this small acquisition of self were permanent, lasting, eternal, and not subject to change, this holy life would not be taught for the complete ending of suffering. But since even this small acquisition of self is not permanent, lasting, eternal, or not subject to change, this holy life is taught for the complete ending of suffering.
translations.sn22.96:3: In the past, monk, I was a king, a warrior monarch. I had, monk, eighty-four thousand cities, with Kusāvatī as the chief. I had, monk, eighty-four thousand palaces, with Dhamma Palace as the chief. I had, monk, eighty-four thousand chambered halls, with Great Canopy Hall as the chief. I had, monk, eighty-four thousand couches, made of ivory, reed, gold, covered with goat’s hair, woven strips, and strips of cloth, with antelope, deer, and leopard skins, with awnings above and red pillows at both ends. I had, monk, eighty-four thousand elephants, adorned with gold ornaments and gold banners, covered with gold nets, with Uposatha Hall as the chief. I had, monk, eighty-four thousand horses, adorned with gold ornaments and gold banners, covered with gold nets, with Valāhaka the king of horses as the chief. I had, monk, eighty-four thousand chariots, adorned with gold ornaments and gold banners, covered with gold nets, with Vejayanta the chariot as the chief. I had, monk, eighty-four thousand jewels, with the gem as the chief. I had, monk … eighty-four thousand women, with Subhaddā the goddess as the chief. I had, monk … eighty-four thousand warriors, with the counselors as the chief. I had, monk … eighty-four thousand cows, with fine linen covers and copper buckets. I had, monk … eighty-four thousand bundles of cloth, of fine linen, fine cotton, fine wool, and fine hemp. I had, monk … eighty-four thousand rice-cooking pots; morning and noon the food was distributed.
translations.sn22.97:2: Then the Buddha, placing a little bit of dust on the tip of his fingernail, said to that monk: “Even this small amount of form, monk, is not permanent, lasting, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same forever. If even this small amount of form were permanent, lasting, eternal, and not subject to change, this holy life would not be taught for the complete ending of suffering. But since even this small amount of form is not permanent, lasting, eternal, or not subject to change, this holy life is taught for the complete ending of suffering.”
translations.sn35.101:4: Suppose, monks, people were to take away, burn, or do whatever they liked with the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Jeta Grove. Would you think: ‘People are taking us away, burning us, or doing whatever they like with us’?”
translations.an3.62:4: These, monks, are the three fears that are common to mother and child, which the uninstructed ordinary person speaks of as fears not common to mother and child. What three? There is a time, monks, when a great fire blazes up. When a great fire blazes up, monks, villages are burned by it, towns are burned by it, cities are burned by it. While villages are being burned, towns are being burned, and cities are being burned, there is a time when at some point or other a mother finds her child, or a child finds its mother. This, monks, is the first fear that is common to mother and child, which the uninstructed ordinary person speaks of as a fear not common to mother and child.
translations.an3.62:5: Again, monks, there is a time when a great cloud bursts. When a great cloud bursts, monks, a great flood of water arises. When a great flood of water arises, monks, villages are swept away by it, towns are swept away by it, cities are swept away by it. While villages are being swept away, towns are being swept away, and cities are being swept away, there is a time when at some point or other a mother finds her child, or a child finds its mother. This, monks, is the second fear that is common to mother and child, which the uninstructed ordinary person speaks of as a fear not common to mother and child.
translations.an3.62:6: Again, monks, there is a time when there is a terror, a disturbance in the wilderness, and districts are raided by wheel-riding bandits. When there is a terror, monks, a disturbance in the wilderness, and districts are being raided by wheel-riding bandits, there is a time when at some point or other a mother finds her child, or a child finds its mother. This, monks, is the third fear that is common to mother and child, which the uninstructed ordinary person speaks of as a fear not common to mother and child. These, monks, are the three fears that are common to mother and child, which the uninstructed ordinary person speaks of as fears not common to mother and child.
translations.an3.62:7: There are, monks, three fears that are not common to mother and child. What three? The fear of aging, the fear of illness, the fear of death. A mother, monks, does not obtain her aging son thus: 'I am aging, let not my son age'; nor does a son obtain his aging mother thus: 'I am aging, let not my mother age'.
translations.an3.62:8: A mother, monks, does not obtain her sick son thus: 'I am sick, let not my son be sick'; nor does a son obtain his sick mother thus: 'I am sick, let not my mother be sick'.
translations.an3.62:9: A mother, monks, does not obtain her dying son thus: 'I am dying, let not my son die'; nor does a son obtain his dying mother thus: 'I am dying, let not my mother die'. These, monks, are the three fears that are not common to mother and child.
translations.an3.63:1: At one time the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosala country with a large community of monks when he arrived at a Brahmin village named Venāgapura. The Brahmin householders of Venāgapura heard: 'The ascetic Gotama of the Sakyans, who has gone forth from the Sakyan clan, has arrived at Venāgapura. Concerning that Blessed One Gotama, a good reputation has spread thus:
translations.an3.63:11: “It is wonderful, Master Gotama, it is marvelous, Master Gotama. Who else could attain such a noble high seat and great seat easily, without trouble, without difficulty, other than Master Gotama?
translations.an4.10:10: Beings wander in saṁsāra, going from birth to death; Those who, having understood sensual pleasures, and the bondage to existence entirely.
translations.an4.1:4: “Virtue, concentration, and wisdom, and the supreme liberation; These teachings have been realized by the famous Gotama.
translations.an4.24:2: Whatever, monks, in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its princes and men, has been seen, heard, sensed, known, reached, sought, and traversed by the mind—that I know.
translations.an4.18:1: “There are, monks, these four not going astray. What four? One does not go astray through desire, one does not go astray through hatred, one does not go astray through delusion, one does not go astray through fear— These, monks, are the four not going astray.
translations.an4.24:1: At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāketa in the Kāḷakārāma. There the Buddha addressed the monks: “Monks.” “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Buddha. The Buddha said this:
translations.an3.63:5: There are, brahmin, these three high seats and great seats which I have now attained easily, without trouble, without difficulty. What three? The divine high seat and great seat, the brahmā high seat and great seat, the noble high seat and great seat. These, brahmin, are the three high seats and great seats which I have now attained easily, without trouble, without difficulty.”
translations.an3.63:2: Then the brahmin householders of Veṇagapura approached the Buddha; having approached, some bowed down to the Buddha and sat down to one side, some exchanged greetings with the Buddha and, after exchanging courteous and friendly conversation, sat down to one side, some raised their joined palms in reverence to the Buddha and sat down to one side, some announced their name and clan and sat down to one side, and some sat down to one side in silence. When he had sat down to one side, the brahmin Vacchagotta of Veṇagapura said this to the Buddha:
translations.an4.1:1: Thus I have heard— At one time the Buddha was staying among the Vajjians at Bhaṇḍagāma. There the Buddha addressed the monks: “Monks.” “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Buddha. The Buddha said this:
translations.an4.10:9: Bound by the bond of craving, and by the bond of existence too; Bound by the bond of views, with ignorance as the chief cause.
translations.an5.43:7: It is not, householder, fitting for a noble disciple who desires fame to ask for fame or to delight in fame or to have a reason for fame.  A noble disciple who desires fame, householder, should practice a course of conduct conducive to fame.  Having practiced a course of conduct conducive to fame, it leads to the obtaining of fame.  They become a receiver of fame, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:9: Life, beauty, fame, and renown,  And high birth in a noble family;  For one who desires delights,  These are great, both present and future.
translations.an5.49:1: At one time the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.  Then King Pasenadi Kosala approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
translations.an5.49:2: Now at that time Queen Mallikā had died.  Then a certain man approached King Pasenadi Kosala; having approached, he announced into King Pasenadi Kosala's ear:  “Queen Mallikā, your majesty, has died.”  When this was said, King Pasenadi Kosala sat down sorrowful, dejected, with shoulders drooping and head down, glum, unable to respond.
translations.an5.51:3: It is impossible, monks, that a monk who has not abandoned these five hindrances, obstructions of the mind, weakenings of wisdom, while wisdom is weak and feeble, should know his own good, or the good of another, or the good of both, or realize a superior human state, the knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.  Suppose, monks, there were a river from the mountains, flowing far, swift-moving, carrying along everything.  A man would open breaches in both its banks.  Then, monks, the flow of the river in the middle would be dispersed, scattered, and spread out; it would no longer be far-flowing, nor swift-moving, nor carrying everything along.  So too, monks, it is impossible that a monk who has not abandoned these five hindrances, obstructions of the mind, weakenings of wisdom, while wisdom is weak and feeble, should know his own good, or the good of another, or the good of both, or realize a superior human state, the knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
translations.an5.56:1: Then a certain monk approached his preceptor; having approached, he said to his preceptor:  “Right now, venerable sir, my body is sluggish, the directions do not appear clear to me, the teachings do not resonate with me, my mind is overcome by sloth and drowsiness, I live the holy life without delight, and I have doubt in the teachings.”
translations.an5.56:3: “It is because of this, monk, that while living with unguarded sense doors, not knowing the right amount in food, not devoted to wakefulness, not discerning skillful qualities, and not devoted to the development of the factors leading to enlightenment, whether formerly, later, or now, one’s body is sluggish, the directions do not appear clear, the teachings do not resonate, one’s mind is overcome by sloth and drowsiness, one lives the holy life without delight, and one has doubt in the teachings.  Therefore, monk, you should train yourself thus:  ‘I will be one with guarded sense doors, knowing the right amount in food, devoted to wakefulness, discerning skillful qualities, and devoted to the development of the factors leading to enlightenment, whether formerly, later, or now.’  Thus, monk, should you train yourself.”
translations.an5.56:4: Then that monk, admonished by the Blessed One with this admonition, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him, and departed.  Then that monk, living alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute, before long—realizing for himself with direct knowledge what he was born for, the unsurpassed goal of the holy life—entered and dwelled in it.  He directly understood: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.”  That monk became one of the Arahants.
translations.an5.57:10: ‘It is not that I alone am separated and parted from all that is dear and pleasant, but that wherever beings come and go, pass away and are reborn, all beings are separated and parted from what is dear and pleasant.’  As he frequently reflects on that fact, a path arises.  He develops and cultivates that path.  As he develops and cultivates that path, the fetters are entirely abandoned and the underlying tendencies are eliminated.
translations.an5.57:11: ‘It is not that I alone am the owner of my actions, the heir of my actions, born of my actions, related to my actions, and have my actions as my refuge, and that whatever action I do—whether good or evil—I will be its heir;  but that wherever beings come and go, pass away and are reborn, all beings are the owners of their actions, heirs of their actions, born of their actions, related to their actions, and have their actions as their refuge, and that whatever action they do—whether good or evil—they will be its heirs.’  As he frequently reflects on that fact, a path arises.  He develops and cultivates that path.  As he develops and cultivates that path, the fetters are entirely abandoned and the underlying tendencies are eliminated.
translations.an5.57:15: I have overcome all intoxicants,  To see renunciation as safety;  That was my effort,  While looking towards Nibbāna.
translations.an5.57:7: That noble disciple, monks, reflects thus:  ‘It is not that I alone am subject to old age and have not gone beyond old age, but that wherever beings come and go, pass away and are reborn, all beings are subject to old age and have not gone beyond old age.’  As he frequently reflects on that fact, a path arises.  He develops and cultivates that path.  As he develops and cultivates that path, the fetters are entirely abandoned and the underlying tendencies are eliminated.
translations.an5.57:8: ‘It is not that I alone am subject to illness and have not gone beyond illness, but that wherever beings come and go, pass away and are reborn, all beings are subject to illness and have not gone beyond illness.’  As he frequently reflects on that fact, a path arises.  He develops and cultivates that path.  As he develops and cultivates that path, the fetters are entirely abandoned and the underlying tendencies are eliminated.
translations.mn52:12: Furthermore, householder, a monk, having completely passed beyond all perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, perceiving 'infinite space', enters and dwells in the base of infinite space. He reflects thus: 'This attainment of the base of infinite space is also constructed and willed. Whatever is constructed and willed is impermanent and subject to cessation.' He understands this. Standing firm there, he realizes the unexcelled relief from bondage.
translations.mn52:14: Furthermore, householder, a monk, having completely passed beyond the base of infinite consciousness, perceiving 'there is nothing', enters and dwells in the base of nothingness. He reflects thus: 'This attainment of the base of nothingness is also constructed and willed. Whatever is constructed and willed is impermanent and subject to cessation.' He understands this. Standing firm there, he realizes the destruction of the taints. If he does not realize the destruction of the taints, with that passion for the Dhamma, that delight in the Dhamma, he destroys the five lower fetters and, being spontaneously born, becomes fully extinguished there, not liable to return from that world. This too, householder, is that one thing declared by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Worthy One, fully enlightened Buddha, wherein a monk who is diligent, ardent, and resolute, while dwelling, the mind is released, and the taints, not yet exhausted, go to exhaustion, and the unexcelled relief from bondage, not yet attained, is attained.
translations.mn52:15: When this was said, the householder Dasama of Atthakanagara said to the Venerable Ananda:
translations.mn52:2: Then the householder Dasama of Atthakanagara went to the Gabled Hall and approached a certain monk; having approached and bowed to that monk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Dasama of Atthakanagara said to that monk:
translations.mn52:8: Furthermore, householder, a monk dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, and everywhere, and to all as to himself, he pervades the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, without ill will. He reflects thus: ‘This liberation of mind by loving-kindness is also fabricated and intentionally produced. Whatever is fabricated and intentionally produced is impermanent, subject to cessation.’ Standing firm there, he realizes the unexcelled relief from bondage.
translations.mn52:3: Then the householder Dasama of Atthakanagara, having attended to his business in Pataliputta, approached Verali, the Beluvagama, and the Venerable Ananda; having approached, he bowed to the Venerable Ananda and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Dasama of Atthakanagara said to the Venerable Ananda: 'Is there, Venerable Sir, one dhamma declared by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Worthy One, fully enlightened, wherein a monk who is diligent, ardent, and resolute, while dwelling, would have his mind released and not be bound, and the taints would be fully exhausted and come to an end, and he would attain the unexcelled relief from bondage that has not been attained before?' 'There is, householder, one dhamma declared by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Worthy One, fully enlightened, wherein a monk who is diligent, ardent, and resolute, while dwelling, would have his mind released and not be bound, and the taints would be fully exhausted and come to an end, and he would attain the unexcelled relief from bondage that has not been attained before.' 'What, then, Venerable Sir, is that one dhamma declared by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Worthy One, fully enlightened, wherein a monk who is diligent, ardent, and resolute, while dwelling, would have his mind released and not be bound, and the taints would be fully exhausted and come to an end, and he would attain the unexcelled relief from bondage that has not been attained before?'
translations.mn52:4: 'Here, householder, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhana, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. He reflects thus: ‘This first jhana is also fabricated and intentionally produced. Whatever is fabricated and intentionally produced is impermanent, subject to cessation.’ Standing firm there, he reaches the destruction of the taints. If he does not reach the destruction of the taints, then with that passion for the Dhamma, that delight in the Dhamma, by the destruction of the five lower fetters, he is one who is spontaneously born, and there he attains final Nibbana without returning from that world. This, householder, is that one dhamma declared by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Worthy One, fully enlightened, wherein a monk who is diligent, ardent, and resolute, while dwelling, would have his mind released and not be bound, and the taints would be fully exhausted and come to an end, and he would attain the unexcelled relief from bondage that has not been attained before.
translations.sn22.90:4: Then it occurred to Venerable Channa: 'The Venerable Ānando is staying at Kosambī in the Ghositārāma, praised and esteemed by the Teacher and by wise fellow practitioners. And Venerable Ānando is able to teach the Dhamma in such a way that I might see the Dhamma; and I have quite a lot of faith in Venerable Ānando. Why don't I go to Venerable Ānando?' Then Venerable Channa, having tidied up his dwelling and taking his bowl and robe, went to Kosambī, to the Ghositārāma, to Venerable Ānando. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Ānando … and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Channa said to Venerable Ānando:
translations.sn22.90:8: 'We are so pleased with Venerable Channa to this extent, yet Venerable Channa made a stake and cut it. Listen, friend Channa, open your ears; you are able to understand the Dhamma.' Then Venerable Channa felt such exquisite delight and joy: 'I am able to understand the Dhamma.'
translations.sn22.94:1: At Sāvatthī. 'I do not argue with the world, monks; the world argues with me. A speaker of the Dhamma does not argue with anyone in the world. What is not agreed to exist in the world by the wise, I also say "it does not exist." What is agreed to exist in the world by the wise, I also say "it exists.
translations.sn22.94:4: There is a worldly principle, monks, which the Tathāgata directly awakens to and realizes; having directly awakened to and realized it, he proclaims it, teaches it, sets it forth, establishes it, discloses it, analyzes it, and makes it clear.
translations.sn22.94:7: Whoever, monks, does not know and see when it is being proclaimed, taught, set forth, established, disclosed, analyzed, and made clear by the Tathāgata—what should I do with that foolish, uninstructed ordinary person who is blind, lacking vision, not knowing, not seeing?
translations.sn22.95:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Ayojjhā on the bank of the Ganges river. There the Buddha addressed the monks:
translations.sn22.95:10: However it is reflected upon, examined properly; It becomes void, hollow, for one who sees it properly.
translations.sn22.95:11: Taught by one of great wisdom, referring to this body; Abandoning the three things, you see form discarded.
translations.sn22.95:12: Life, heat, and consciousness, when they abandon this body; Then cast away, it lies there, like a log, unconscious.
translations.sn22.95:13: Such is this continuum, a conjuring trick of children; It is declared a killer, in this no essence is found.
translations.sn22.95:2: 'Suppose, monks, a large foam bubble were floating down this Ganges river. A man with good sight would see it, reflect on it, and examine it properly. As he reflects and examines it properly, it would appear to him empty, void, without substance. For what substance, monks, could there be in a foam bubble? So too, monks, whatever form is past, future, or present … far or near, a monk sees it, reflects on it, and examines it properly. As he reflects and examines it properly, it appears to him empty, void, without substance. For what substance, monks, could there be in form?'
translations.sn22.95:3: Suppose, monks, in the autumn, when the sky is raining, a water bubble appears on the water and vanishes again. A man with good sight would see it, reflect on it, and examine it properly. As he reflects and examines it properly, it would appear to him empty, void, without substance. For what substance, monks, could there be in a water bubble? So too, monks, whatever feeling is past, future, or present … far or near, a monk sees it, reflects on it, and examines it properly. As he reflects and examines it properly, it appears to him empty, void, without substance. For what substance, monks, could there be in feeling?
translations.sn22.95:4: Suppose, monks, at the end of the summer, in the last month of the hot season, a mirage shimmers. A man with good sight would see it, reflect on it, and examine it properly. As he reflects and examines it properly, it would appear to him empty, void, without substance. For what substance, monks, could there be in a mirage? So too, monks, whatever perception is past, future, or present … far or near, a monk sees it, reflects on it, and examines it properly. As he reflects and examines it properly, it appears to him empty, void, without substance. For what substance, monks, could there be in perception?
translations.sn22.95:5: Suppose, monks, a man seeking heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, would take a sharp ax and enter a forest. There he would see a large banana tree, straight, new, without knots. He would cut it at the root; having cut it at the root, he would cut it at the top; having cut it at the top, he would strip the outer layer. As he strips the outer layer, he would not even find the pith, much less the heartwood. A man with good sight would see it, reflect on it, and examine it properly. As he reflects and examines it properly, it would appear to him empty, void, without substance. For what substance, monks, could there be in a banana tree? So too, monks, whatever volitional formations are past, future, or present … far or near, a monk sees it, reflects on it, and examines it properly. As he reflects and examines it properly, it appears to him empty, void, without substance. For what substance, monks, could there be in volitional formations?
translations.sn35.116:2: Then it occurred to those monks: 'The Venerable Ānando is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by wise fellow practitioners. And Venerable Ānando is able to explain in detail the meaning of this brief summary given by the Blessed One, the meaning that has been stated but not distinguished in detail. Why don't we go to Venerable Ānando; having approached, we should ask Venerable Ānando about this matter.'
translations.sn22.94:3: And what, monks, is agreed upon in the world by the wise, that which I call 'exists'? Form, monks, is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change; this is agreed upon in the world by the wise, and I also call it 'exists'. Feeling is impermanent … Perception … Mental formations … Consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change; this is agreed upon in the world by the wise, and I also call it 'exists'. This, monks, is agreed upon in the world by the wise; I also call it 'exists'.
translations.sn35.116:3: Then those monks approached Venerable Ānanda; having approached, they exchanged greetings with Venerable Ānanda. Having exchanged courteous and friendly talk, they sat down to one side. While sitting to one side, those monks said to Venerable Ānanda:
translations.sn35.116:5: “Suppose, friend, a man seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, looking for heartwood, would pass over the root of a great standing tree that had heartwood, pass over the trunk, and seek heartwood among the branches and leaves; so too, now that the Teacher is present, it seems to us that we should ask the Blessed One about this matter, having passed him by. For the Blessed One knows and sees—he is the eye, knowledge, Dhamma, the Brahmā, the proclaimer, the bringer of the path, the guide for the purpose, the giver of the deathless, the master of Dhamma, the Tathāgata. And the time has come to ask the Blessed One himself about this matter. You should remember what the Blessed One declares.”
translations.sn35.116:6: “Indeed, friend Ānanda, the Blessed One knows and sees—he is the eye, knowledge, Dhamma, the Brahmā, the proclaimer, the bringer of the path, the guide for the purpose, the giver of the deathless, the master of Dhamma, the Tathāgata. And the time has come to ask the Blessed One himself about this matter. We should remember what the Blessed One declares. But Venerable Ānanda is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by wise fellow monks. And Venerable Ānanda is able to explain in detail the meaning of this brief teaching declared by the Blessed One without detailed explanation. Please explain, Venerable Ānanda, out of respect.”
translations.sn35.116:7: “Then listen, friends, and pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to Venerable Ānanda. Venerable Ānanda said this:
translations.sn35.116:9: “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to Venerable Ānanda. Then, rising from their seats, they approached the Blessed One; having approached, they bowed to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. While sitting to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn35.117:1: “Before my enlightenment, monks, while I was still a bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, this thought occurred to me: ‘When these five cords of sensual pleasure that have previously arisen and are past, ceased, and changed, my mind frequently goes to them, or to present ones, or to few future ones.’ Then it occurred to me: ‘When these five cords of sensual pleasure that have previously arisen and are past, ceased, and changed, I should establish non-negligence, mindfulness, and guard of the mind in that regard. Therefore, monks, you too, when these five cords of sensual pleasure that have previously arisen and are past, ceased, and changed, your mind should not frequently go to them, or to present ones, or to few future ones. Therefore, monks, you too, when these five cords of sensual pleasure that have previously arisen and are past, ceased, and changed, you should establish non-negligence, mindfulness, and guard of the mind in that regard. Therefore, monks, that base should be understood where the eye ceases and the perception of forms ceases; that base should be understood … where the tongue ceases and the perception of flavors ceases; that base should be understood … where the mind ceases and the perception of mental phenomena ceases.” Having said this, the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered the dwelling.
translations.sn35.118:1: At one time the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove. Then Sakka, lord of the gods, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he bowed to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of the gods, said to the Blessed One: “What, sir, is the cause, what is the reason why some beings here do not become fully extinguished in this visible life? And what, sir, is the cause, what is the reason why some beings here do become fully extinguished in this visible life?”
translations.sn35.118:2: “There are, lord of gods, forms cognizable by the eye, desirable, lovely, pleasing, agreeable, sensual, and arousing passion. If a monk welcomes them, persists in them, and remains clinging to them, then his consciousness becomes dependent on them and clings to them. With clinging, lord of gods, a monk does not become fully extinguished ….
translations.sn35.118:3: There are, lord of gods, flavors cognizable by the tongue … There are, lord of gods, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind, desirable, lovely, pleasing, agreeable, sensual, and arousing passion. If a monk welcomes them, persists in them, and remains clinging to them, then his consciousness becomes dependent on them and clings to them. With clinging, lord of gods, a monk does not become fully extinguished. This is the cause, this is the reason why some beings here do not become fully extinguished in this visible life.
translations.sn35.118:4: And there are, lord of gods, forms cognizable by the eye, desirable, lovely, pleasing, agreeable, sensual, and arousing passion. If a monk does not welcome them, does not persist in them, and does not remain clinging to them, then his consciousness does not become dependent on them and does not cling to them. Without clinging, lord of gods, a monk becomes fully extinguished ….
translations.sn35.127:1: At one time Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja was staying near Kosambī in the Ghosita Monastery. Then King Udena approached Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja; having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja. Having exchanged courteous and memorable talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, King Udena said to Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja: “What, Master Bhāradvāja, is the cause, what is the reason, that these young monks, with black hair, endowed with the blessings of youth, in the prime of life, have not indulged in sensual pleasures, and for the rest of their lives lead the complete and pure holy life, and bring it to completion?” “This has been stated, Great King, by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One: ‘Come, monks, establish the perception of a mother towards those who are mothers, establish the perception of a sister towards those who are sisters, establish the perception of a daughter towards those who are daughters.’ This, Great King, is the cause, this is the reason, that these young monks, with black hair, endowed with the blessings of youth, in the prime of life, have not indulged in sensual pleasures, and for the rest of their lives lead the complete and pure holy life, and bring it to completion.”
translations.sn35.127:2: “The mind, Master Bhāradvāja, is fickle. Sometimes states of greed arise even towards those who are mothers, sometimes states of greed arise even towards those who are sisters, sometimes states of greed arise even towards those who are daughters. Is there, Master Bhāradvāja, another cause, another reason, that these young monks, with black hair … [ellipsis in original] … bring it to completion?”
translations.sn35.127:3: “This has been stated, Great King, by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One: ‘Come, monks, reflect on this very body, from the soles of the feet up and from the crown of the head down, enclosed by skin, full of various impurities: ‘In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, membranes, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, snot, synovial fluid, urine.’ This too, Great King, is the cause, this is the reason, that these young monks, with black hair … [ellipsis in original] … bring it to completion.” “Those monks, Master Bhāradvāja, who are developed in body, developed in virtue, developed in mind, developed in wisdom; for them that is easy. But those monks, Master Bhāradvāja, who are undeveloped in body, undeveloped in virtue, undeveloped in mind, undeveloped in wisdom; for them that is difficult. Sometimes, Master Bhāradvāja, when I intend to consider the unattractive, the attractive comes instead. Is there, Master Bhāradvāja, another cause, another reason, that these young monks, with black hair … [ellipsis in original] … bring it to completion?”
translations.sn35.127:4: “This has been stated, Great King, by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One: ‘Come, monks, dwell with guarded sense doors. Having seen a form with the eye, do not grasp at its signs and features. Since, if one dwells with the eye faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and dejection might invade, practice its restraint. Guard the eye faculty; undertake restraint in the eye faculty. Having heard a sound with the ear … [ellipsis in original] … Having smelled an odor with the nose … Having tasted a flavor with the tongue … Having felt a touch with the body … Having known a mental phenomenon with the mind, do not grasp at its signs and features. Since, if one dwells with the mind faculty unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and dejection might invade, practice its restraint. Guard the mind faculty; undertake restraint in the mind faculty.’ This too, Great King, is the cause, this is the reason, that these young monks, with black hair, endowed with the blessings of youth, in the prime of life, have not indulged in sensual pleasures, and for the rest of their lives lead the complete and pure holy life, and bring it to completion.”
translations.sn35.136:2: “Forms, sounds, flavors, smells,  Touches and phenomena—only these;  Pleasing, charming, delightful,  These are called ‘worldly goods.’
translations.sn35.136:3: For the world with its gods,  These are agreed to be happiness;  But where these cease without remainder,  That is agreed by them to be suffering.
translations.sn35.136:4: The destruction of identity,  Seen by the noble ones as happiness;  This is contrary to the view  Of all the world looking on.
translations.sn35.136:5: What others say is happiness,  The noble ones say is suffering;  What others say is suffering,  The noble ones know as happiness.
translations.sn35.136:6: Look at this Dhamma hard to know,  By those who are muddled and unwise;  For those enveloped it is darkness,  Blind darkness for those who do not see.
translations.sn35.136:7: For those who see it is open,  Like light in the dark;  Being close they do not recognize,  The Dhamma’s path, the unwise.
translations.sn35.136:8: By those obsessed with existence,  Following the obsession with existence,  Attended by Māra’s domain,  This Dhamma is not well understood.
translations.sn35.63:1: At Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Migajāla approached the Blessed One … [ellipsis in original] … and sitting down to one side, Venerable Migajāla said to the Blessed One: “‘One who dwells alone, one who dwells alone,’ it is said, Venerable Sir. To what extent, Venerable Sir, is one a dweller alone, and to what extent is one a dweller with a companion?”
translations.sn35.69:1: At one time Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Upasena were staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, in the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground. At that time a snake had fallen on Venerable Upasena’s body. Then Venerable Upasena addressed the monks: “Lift this body of mine, friends, onto the couch and carry it outside. This body will scatter right here; like a heap of sand.”
translations.sn35.74:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain monk approached the Blessed One … [ellipsis in original] … and sitting down to one side, that monk said to the Blessed One: “In a certain dwelling, Venerable Sir, a certain monk, new, not well known, is sick, afflicted, and in severe pain. It would be good, Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One would approach that monk out of compassion.”
translations.sn35.74:12: “Good, good, monk. It is good that you, monk, understand that the Dhamma has been taught by me for the sake of dispassion. For the sake of dispassion, monk, the Dhamma has been taught by me. What do you think, monk, is the eye permanent or impermanent?”
translations.sn35.74:18: “What is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fit to regard it thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
translations.sn35.74:2: Then the Blessed One, having heard a report of newness and a report of illness, knowing, 'The monk is not well,' approached that monk. That monk saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Seeing him, he made a couch ready. Then the Blessed One said to that monk: 'Enough, monk, do not trouble yourself to make a couch. There are seats prepared; I will sit there.' The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat. Having sat, the Blessed One said to that monk: 'How is it for you, monk? Is it bearable? Is it supportable? Do painful feelings decrease and not increase, is a decrease evident and not an increase?'
translations.sn35.74:3: 'It is not bearable for me, venerable sir, not supportable. Painful feelings are increasing greatly for me, not decreasing; an increase is evident, not a decrease.'
translations.sn35.75:7: 'I understand, venerable sir, that the Dhamma has been taught by the Blessed One for the sake of final Nibbāna without clinging.'
translations.sn35.75:8: 'Good, good, monk. It is good that you, monk, understand that the Dhamma has been taught by me for the sake of final Nibbāna without clinging. For the sake of final Nibbāna without clinging, monk, the Dhamma has been taught by me.
translations.sn35.88:1: Then Venerable Puṇṇa approached the Blessed One; having approached... he sat down to one side. Then Venerable Puṇṇa said to the Blessed One: 'It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.'
translations.sn35.88:12: 'If the people of Sunāparanta should strike me with a staff, there will be in me this thought: "The people of Sunāparanta are good, the people of Sunāparanta are excellent, in that they do not strike me with a sword." It will be thus in this case, Blessed One; it will be thus in this case, Sugata.'
translations.sn35.88:14: 'If the people of Sunāparanta should strike me with a sword, there will be in me this thought: "The people of Sunāparanta are good, the people of Sunāparanta are excellent, in that they do not take my life with a sharp sword." It will be thus in this case, Blessed One; it will be thus in this case, Sugata.'
translations.sn35.88:16: 'If the people of Sunāparanta should take my life with a sharp sword, there will be in me this thought: "There are disciples of the Blessed One who, disgusted with the body and life, seeking an end to the body, have sought a weapon; this weapon of mine has been obtained without difficulty." It will be thus in this case, Blessed One; it will be thus in this case, Sugata.'
translations.sn35.88:17: 'Good, good, Puṇṇa. You will be able, Puṇṇa, endowed with this self-control, to dwell in the country of Sunāparanta. Go now, Puṇṇa, at the proper time.'
translations.sn35.88:18: Then Venerable Puṇṇa, delighting in and approving of the Blessed One's words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to the right, arranged his lodging, and taking his bowl and robe, set out on tour for the country of Sunāparanta. Wandering on tour by stages, he arrived at the country of Sunāparanta. There Venerable Puṇṇa lived in the country of Sunāparanta. Then in that very year Venerable Puṇṇa brought five hundred laymen to realization. In that very year he brought five hundred laywomen to realization. In that very year he realized the three knowledges. In that very year he attained final Nibbāna.
translations.sn35.88:19: Then several monks approached the Blessed One... sat down to one side. Then those monks said to the Blessed One: 'That layman Puṇṇa, venerable sir, who was admonished by the Blessed One with a brief admonition, has passed away. What is his destination? What is his future state?'
translations.sn35.88:4: 'In what country will you live, Puṇṇa, having been admonished by me with this brief admonition?' 'There is a country called Sunāparanta, venerable sir; there I will live.'
translations.sn35.88:5: 'The people of Sunāparanta are violent, Puṇṇa; the people of Sunāparanta are harsh. If the people of Sunāparanta abuse and insult you, Puṇṇa, what will occur to you then?'
translations.sn35.88:6: 'If the people of Sunāparanta abuse and insult me, there will be in me this thought: "The people of Sunāparanta are good, the people of Sunāparanta are excellent, in that they do not strike me with the hand." It will be thus in this case, Blessed One; it will be thus in this case, Sugata.'
translations.sn35.88:8: 'If the people of Sunāparanta should strike me with the hand, there will be in me this thought: "The people of Sunāparanta are good, the people of Sunāparanta are excellent, in that they do not strike me with a clod." It will be thus in this case, Blessed One; it will be thus in this case, Sugata.'
translations.sn35.95:1: Then Venerable Mālukyaputta approached the Blessed One... sat down to one side. Then Venerable Mālukyaputta said to the Blessed One: 'It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.'
translations.sn35.95:10: 'Herein for you, Mālukyaputta, in things to be seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, there will be only seen, only heard, only sensed, only cognized. When for you, Mālukyaputta, in things to be seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, there will be only seen, only heard, only sensed, only cognized; then you, Mālukyaputta, will not be by that. When you, Mālukyaputta, are not by that; then you, Mālukyaputta, will not be there. When you, Mālukyaputta, are not there; then you, Mālukyaputta, will be neither here nor beyond nor between the two. That is the end of suffering.'
translations.sn35.95:12: 'Seeing a form, mindfulness is lost,  One attends to a pleasing sign;  With a mind infatuated, one feels,  And clings fast to that.
translations.sn35.95:13: Feelings grow for him,  Many born of forms;  Craving and aversion,  The mind is harmed by them;  Thus accumulated suffering,  Is called a flood.
translations.sn35.95:14: Hearing a sound, mindfulness is lost,  One attends to a pleasing sign;  With a mind infatuated, one feels,  And clings fast to that.
translations.sn35.95:16: Smelling a scent, mindfulness is lost,  One attends to a pleasing sign;  With a mind infatuated, one feels,  And clings fast to that.
translations.sn35.95:18: Having tasted a flavor, one is deluded,  Fixing one’s mind on a pleasing sign;  With a mind that is entranced, one feels it,  And one clings to that.
translations.sn35.95:2: “What now shall we say to the monks, Mālukyaputta?  For you, monk, being aged, grown old, burdened with years, come to the last stage of life, ask for a brief teaching.”
translations.sn35.95:20: Having touched a contact, one is deluded,  Fixing one’s mind on a pleasing sign;  With a mind that is entranced, one feels it,  And one clings to that.
translations.sn35.95:22: Having known a phenomenon, one is deluded,  Fixing one’s mind on a pleasing sign;  With a mind that is entranced, one feels it,  And one clings to that.
translations.sn35.95:24: He does not lust after forms,  Seeing forms with mindfulness;  With a mind that is dispassionate, he feels it,  And he does not cling to that.
translations.sn35.95:25: Just as he sees forms,  And also experiences feelings;  It wastes away and does not grow,  Thus he lives mindful;  Thus suffering is retreated from,  Nibbāna is said to be near.
translations.sn35.95:26: He does not lust after sounds,  Hearing sounds with mindfulness;  With a mind that is dispassionate, he feels it,  And he does not cling to that.
translations.sn35.95:27: Just as he hears sounds,  And also experiences feelings;  It wastes away and does not grow,  Thus he lives mindful;  Thus suffering is retreated from,  Nibbāna is said to be near.
translations.sn35.95:28: He does not lust after smells,  Smelling smells with mindfulness;  With a mind that is dispassionate, he feels it,  And he does not cling to that.
translations.sn35.95:3: “Even though I, venerable sir, am aged, grown old, burdened with years, come to the last stage of life.  Let the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief, let the One-Well-Gone teach the Dhamma in brief; perhaps I might understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has said. Perhaps I might become an heir of the Blessed One’s teaching.”
translations.sn35.95:30: He does not lust after flavors,  Tasting flavors with mindfulness;  With a mind that is dispassionate, he feels it,  And he does not cling to that.
translations.sn35.95:35: Just as he knows phenomena,  And also experiences feelings;  It wastes away and does not grow,  Thus he lives mindful;  Thus suffering is retreated from,  Nibbāna is said to be near.”
translations.sn35.95:36: “Venerable sir, I understand the detailed meaning of what the Blessed One has said in brief in this way.”  “Good, good, Mālukyaputta.  It is good, Mālukyaputta, that you understand the detailed meaning of what I have said in brief:
translations.sn35.95:4: “What do you think, Mālukyaputta, regarding those forms cognizable by the eye that have not been seen, not seen before, and you do not see them, nor do you think that you will see them? Is there in you any desire or lust or affection?”?  “No, venerable sir”.
translations.sn35.95:9: “Regarding those phenomena cognizable by the mind that have not been known, not known before, and you do not know them, nor do you think that you will know them? Is there in you any desire or lust or affection?”?  “No, venerable sir”.
translations.sn36.19:12: What, Ānanda, is another pleasure that is more exalted and superior than this pleasure?  Here, Ānanda, a monk, having entirely transcended the base of infinite space, enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.  This, Ānanda, is another pleasure that is more exalted and superior than this pleasure.  If, Ānanda, anyone should say: ‘This is the highest peace, pleasure, and happiness that sentient beings experience’— I do not grant them that.  For what reason?  Because, Ānanda, there is another pleasure that is more exalted and superior than this pleasure.
translations.sn36.19:15: What, Ānanda, is another pleasure that is more exalted and superior than this pleasure?  Here, Ānanda, a monk, having entirely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling.  This, Ānanda, is another pleasure that is more exalted and superior than this pleasure.
translations.sn36.19:7: What, Ānanda, is another pleasure that is more exalted and superior than this pleasure?  Here, Ānanda, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.  This, Ānanda, is another pleasure that is more exalted and superior than this pleasure.  If, Ānanda, anyone should say: ‘This is the highest peace, pleasure, and happiness that sentient beings experience’— I do not grant them that.  For what reason?  Because, Ānanda, there is another pleasure that is more exalted and superior than this pleasure.
translations.sn36.19:8: What, Ānanda, is another pleasure that is more exalted and superior than this pleasure?  Here, Ānanda, a monk, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, entering and dwelling in the second jhāna, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind without applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration.  This, Ānanda, is another pleasure that is more exalted and superior than this pleasure.  If, Ānanda, anyone should say: ‘This is the highest peace, pleasure, and happiness that sentient beings experience’— I do not grant them that.  For what reason?  Because, Ānanda, there is another pleasure that is more exalted and superior than this pleasure.
translations.sn36.19:9: What, Ānanda, is another pleasure that is more exalted and superior than this pleasure?  Here, Ānanda, a monk, with the fading away of rapture, dwells equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing pleasure with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘Equanimous and mindful, one dwells in pleasure.’  This, Ānanda, is another pleasure that is more exalted and superior than this pleasure.  If, Ānanda, anyone should say: ‘This is the highest peace, pleasure, and happiness that sentient beings experience’— I do not grant them that.  For what reason?  Because, Ānanda, there is another pleasure that is more exalted and superior than this pleasure.
translations.sn36.21:1: At one time the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground.  Then Moḷiyasīvaka the wanderer went up to the Blessed One; having gone up, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.  When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side.  Seated to one side, Moḷiyasīvaka the wanderer said to the Blessed One:  “There are, Master Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and view as this:  ‘Whatever this person feels—pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is caused by past deeds.’  What does Master Gotama say to this?”
translations.sn36.21:2: “Some feelings, Sīvaka, arise born of bile. This, too, Sīvaka, should be understood by oneself: that some feelings arise born of bile. This, too, Sīvaka, is acknowledged as true in the world: that some feelings arise born of bile. Those ascetics and brahmins, Sīvaka, who hold such views and such opinions: ‘Whatever feeling this person experiences—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—all that is caused by past deeds’—they go beyond what is known by oneself and what is acknowledged as true in the world. Therefore, I say that those ascetics and brahmins are wrong.
translations.sn36.21:4: When this was said, the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka said to the Blessed One: “Excellent, Master Gotama, excellent, Master Gotama …pe… Let Master Gotama consider me a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward.”
translations.sn36.23:1: Then a certain monk approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that monk said to the Blessed One: “What, venerable sir, is feeling? What is the origin of feeling? What is the practice leading to the origin of feeling? What is the cessation of feeling? What is the practice leading to the cessation of feeling? What is the gratification in feeling, what is the danger, and what is the escape?”
translations.sn36.31:2: And what, bhikkhus, is non-carnal rapture? Here, bhikkhus, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought and consists of rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind without applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. This is called non-carnal rapture, bhikkhus.
translations.sn36.31:3: And what, bhikkhus, is non-carnal and more non-carnal rapture? When, bhikkhus, a monk who is an arahant reflects on his mind liberated from lust, liberated from hatred, and liberated from delusion, rapture arises. This is called non-carnal and more non-carnal rapture, bhikkhus.
translations.sn36.31:5: And what, bhikkhus, is non-carnal pleasure?
