Here, bhikkhus, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought and consists of rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind without applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. He dwells equanimous and mindful, experiencing pleasure with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘Equanimous and mindful, he dwells in pleasure.’ This is called non-carnal pleasure, bhikkhus.
translations.sn36.31:6: And what, bhikkhus, is non-carnal and more non-carnal pleasure? When, bhikkhus, a monk who is an arahant reflects on his mind liberated from lust, liberated from hatred, and liberated from delusion, pleasure and gladness arise. This is called non-carnal and more non-carnal pleasure, bhikkhus.
translations.sn36.31:8: And what, bhikkhus, is non-carnal equanimity? Here, bhikkhus, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and displeasure, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes mindfulness purified by equanimity. This is called non-carnal equanimity, bhikkhus.
translations.sn36.31:9: And what, bhikkhus, is non-carnal and more non-carnal equanimity? When, bhikkhus, a monk who is an arahant reflects on his mind liberated from lust, liberated from hatred, and liberated from delusion, equanimity arises. This is called non-carnal and more non-carnal equanimity, bhikkhus.
translations.sn36.4:2: If one does not endure these, arisen feelings are painful; Physical, life-consuming, by which, when struck, one trembles.
translations.sn36.4:3: He cries and laments, weak and without self-control; He did not rise from the underworld, nor did he escape from the deep pit.
translations.sn36.6:2: When struck by a painful feeling, a noble disciple who has heard the teaching does not sorrow, does not lament, does not grieve, does not weep beating his breast, and does not become confused. He feels one feeling—a bodily one, not a mental one.
translations.sn36.6:4: The wise person does not feel a feeling, even though learned, whether pleasant or painful; This is the great difference between the wise one and the uninstructed worldling in skillfulness.
translations.sn36.6:5: For one who has heard much, who understands the conditioned nature, Who contemplates this world and the next; Likable states do not disturb his mind, nor does he react with aversion to unlikable states.
translations.sn36.7:3: And how, bhikkhus, is a monk mindful? Here, bhikkhus, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings …pe… he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind …pe… he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. Thus, bhikkhus, a monk is mindful.
translations.sn36.7:4: And how, bhikkhus, is a monk clearly comprehending? Here, bhikkhus, a monk acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; when looking ahead and looking away; when bending and stretching; when wearing the outer robe, the upper robe, and the bowl; when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; when defecating and urinating; when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, speaking, and remaining silent. Thus, bhikkhus, a monk acts with clear comprehension. A mindful monk, bhikkhus, should live with clear comprehension. This is our instruction to you.
translations.sn36.7:5: When a monk lives mindful, aware, diligent, resolute, and a pleasant feeling arises in him, he understands thus: ‘This pleasant feeling has arisen in me. It is dependent, not independent. Dependent on what? Dependent on this very body. But this body is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen. How can a pleasant feeling that has arisen dependent on an impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen body be permanent?’ He dwells contemplating impermanence in the body and in that pleasant feeling, contemplating fading away, contemplating cessation, and contemplating relinquishment. As he dwells contemplating impermanence, fading away, cessation, and relinquishment in the body and in that pleasant feeling, the underlying tendency to lust for the body and for that pleasant feeling is abandoned.
translations.sn36.7:8: When he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands it as impermanent; he understands it as not to be clung to; he understands it as not to be relished. When he feels a painful feeling … When he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands it as impermanent; he understands it as not to be clung to; he understands it as not to be relished. When he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it detached from it; when he feels a painful feeling, he feels it detached from it; when he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it detached from it. Feeling a feeling that has the body as its limit, he understands: ‘I am feeling a feeling that has the body as its limit.’ Feeling a feeling that has life as its limit, he understands: ‘I am feeling a feeling that has life as its limit.’ He understands: ‘With the breakup of the body and the exhaustion of life, all that is felt here, not being delighted in, will become cool.’
translations.sn4.13:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove. At that time the Blessed One’s foot was injured by a splinter; severe physical pains arose in the Blessed One—painful, sharp, harsh, disagreeable, unpleasant. The Blessed One endured them mindful and clearly comprehending, without being distressed. Then the Blessed One, having arranged his fourfold robe and lying down on his right side in the lion’s posture, with one foot placed on the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
translations.sn4.13:2: “Are you slumbering now, or are you intoxicated? Have you attained your goal, and are there no more left? All alone in a secluded resting place, Why are you sleeping now, this sleeper?”
translations.sn4.13:3: “I am not slumbering, nor am I intoxicated; I have attained my goal and am free from sorrow. All alone in a secluded resting place, I sleep, compassionate towards all beings.
translations.sn4.13:4: “For those in whose chest a barb is stuck, With heart trembling again and again, They too can obtain sleep with the barb; Therefore I do not sleep, having cast out the barb.
translations.sn4.13:5: “I do not fear a swamp, nor do I fear a precipice; Day and night do not burn me. I do not see any decline in the world; Therefore I sleep, compassionate towards all beings.”
translations.sn4.18:1: At one time the Blessed One was living in Magadha at the brahmin village of Pañcasāla. At that time the girls of Pañcasāla had reached marriageable age. Then the Blessed One, dressing in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, entered Pañcasāla brahmin village for alms. At that time the brahmin householders of Pañcasāla were obsessed by Māra the Evil One: “Let the ascetic Gotama not get alms.”
translations.sn4.18:2: Then the Blessed One entered Pañcasāla brahmin village for alms with a bowl as if washed by oil, and returned with a bowl as if washed by oil. Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said to the Blessed One: “Did you get alms, ascetic?” “Did you make it so, Evil One, that I would not get alms?” “In that case, venerable sir, let the Blessed One enter Pañcasāla brahmin village for alms a second time. I will make it so that the Blessed One gets alms.”
translations.sn4.19:4: “Whatever they say is mine, And those who say ‘it is mine’; If you have any intention about this, You will not escape from the ascetic.”
translations.sn4.19:5: “Whatever they say is not mine, And those who say ‘it is mine’ are not I; Know thus, Evil One, You did not even see my path.”
translations.sn4.1:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was living at Uruvelā on the bank of the Nerañjarā River at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree, just after his enlightenment. Then, while the Blessed One was alone and in seclusion, a reflection arose in his mind thus: “I am released from that difficult task. It is good that I am released from that difficult task, which was not beneficial. It is good that I have attained enlightenment after striving.”
translations.sn4.1:2: Then Māra the Evil One, knowing the reflection in the Blessed One’s mind, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
translations.sn4.1:3: “Having given up the austerity, By which young men purify themselves; You think you are pure though impure, You have not deviated from the path of purity.”
translations.sn4.1:6: “Virtue, concentration, and wisdom, The path leading to enlightenment I have developed; I have attained the highest purity, You are destroyed, O terminator.”
translations.sn4.1:7: Then Māra the Evil One, realizing “The Blessed One knows me, the Well-Gone One knows me,” sad and disappointed, vanished right there.
translations.sn4.20:1: At one time the Blessed One was living in Kosala in a forest hut in the Himalayan region. Then, while the Blessed One was alone and in seclusion, a reflection arose in his mind thus: “Is it possible to exercise sovereignty lawfully without killing, causing to kill, conquering, causing to conquer, sorrowing, or causing sorrow?”
translations.sn4.20:3: “Of a golden mountain, entirely of jātarūpa; There are only two crests of a single nāla tree, Knowing this, wander like a rhinoceros.
translations.sn4.20:4: “One who has seen suffering and its origin, How could that being delight in sensual pleasures? Having understood the substrate, he wanders in the world; Let him learn for the abandoning of that very being.”
translations.sn4.21:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakkas at Sīlavatī. At that time several monks were dwelling near the Blessed One, ardent, energetic, resolute. Then Māra the Evil One, having created the appearance of a brahmin, with a massive topknot, dressed in an antelope skin, aged, carrying a water pot, breathing heavily, holding a club of udumbara wood, approached those monks; approaching, he said this to those monks: “You have gone forth young, with black hair, endowed with the beauty of youth, in the prime of life, without having indulged in sensual pleasures. Enjoy, sirs, human sensual pleasures. Do not run after the temporal, having abandoned what is visible here and now.” “We do not, brahmin, run after the temporal, having abandoned what is visible here and now. We, brahmin, abandon the temporal and run after what is visible here and now. For sensual pleasures, brahmin, have been declared by the Blessed One to be suffering with much distress, much tribulation, and there is more danger in this. This Dhamma is visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be known by the wise for themselves.” When this was said, Māra the Evil One, shaking his head, sticking out his tongue, raising his eyebrows, leaning on his staff, went away.
translations.sn4.24:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā on the bank of the Nerañjarā River at the Goatherd’s Banyan Tree. At that time Māra the Evil One was following the Blessed One for seven years, looking for an opening but finding none. Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; approaching, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
translations.sn4.24:10: Having found no flavor there, the bird departs; Like a crow pecking at a stone, we will leave Gotama.”
translations.sn4.24:2: “Are you meditating in the forest overwhelmed by sorrow? Have you lost your wealth while desiring it? Have you done something in the village? Why do you not make yourself known to people? No one becomes your witness.”
translations.sn4.24:3: “Having pulled up the root of sorrow entirely, I meditate without sorrow, unaging. Having cut off all delight in existence, I meditate without defilements, with relatives in negligence.”
translations.sn4.24:6: “If you have understood the path, secure, leading to the Deathless; Go there alone, why do you instruct others?”
translations.sn4.24:7: “Those who have gone to the far shore ask for the unconditioned; Asked by them, I proclaim that truth which is without cause.”
translations.sn4.24:8: “Suppose, sir, there is a lotus pond near a village or town. There is a crab in it. Then, sir, several boys or girls, having left that village or town, might approach that lotus pond; approaching, they might pull that crab out of the water and place it on the ground. Whatever limb of that crab, sir, it might insert into a crevice, those boys or girls would cut it off with a stick or a stone splinter. In that way, sir, that crab, with all its limbs cut off, broken, and shattered, would be unable to dive into that lotus pond. So too, sir, whatever writhing and shaking tendencies, all of them have been cut off, broken, and shattered by the Blessed One. Now, sir, I am unable to approach the Blessed One again, looking for an opening.” Then Māra the Evil One spoke these stinging verses in the presence of the Blessed One:
translations.sn4.24:9: “A stone honey-colored, birds fly around it; We find nothing soft here, nor would there be any flavor.
translations.sn4.25:10: ‘The Worthy One, the Well-Gone One in the world, is not tied by greed; He has crossed over the realm of Māra, therefore I grieve abundantly.’
translations.sn4.25:12: Then Craving, Discontent, and Passion, Māra’s daughters, approached the Blessed One; approaching, they stood to one side. Standing to one side, Craving, Māra’s daughter, addressed the Blessed One in verse:
translations.sn4.25:14: “Having conquered the army of desire with an agreeable appearance, having attained the peace of the heart, the attainment of the goal; I meditate alone, having understood happiness; therefore I do not make myself known to people; no one becomes my witness.”
translations.sn4.25:16: “In what way does a monk dwell often, having crossed the flood of five and the sixth? How does one meditate often on the perception of sensual pleasures? Those who have not obtained it are surrounded.”
translations.sn4.25:17: “With a body tranquil, mind well released, unshaken, mindful, without a support; Having known the Dhamma, he meditates without thought; He does not get angry, does not remember, is not torpid.
translations.sn4.25:2: “Why are you sorrowful, dear? For what man are you grieving? We will bring that man, bound by a net of greed, like an elephant into the forest; he will be your servant.”
translations.sn4.25:20: “Having cut off craving, who goes with the multitude, many faithful ones will go for a long time; Many people here, he without a support, having cut off, will cross the domain of the King of Death.”
translations.sn4.25:23: “Fools, with lotus stalks, attacked the mountain; Dig the mountain with a fingernail, chew iron with teeth.
translations.sn4.25:24: Enter the abyss like a snake splitting the head; Having joined the chest to a stump, make Gotama suffer.”
translations.sn4.25:4: Then Craving, Discontent, and Passion, Māra’s daughters, approached the Blessed One; approaching, they said this to the Blessed One: “We will serve you, ascetic, by your feet.” Then the Blessed One did not pay attention to them, as he was released from the unsurpassed fetter.
translations.sn4.25:5: Then Craving, Discontent, and Passion, Māra’s daughters, having gone to one side, thought thus: “The inclinations of men are high and low. Suppose we create a hundred, a hundred forms of maidens.” Then Craving, Discontent, and Passion, Māra’s daughters, having created a hundred, a hundred forms of maidens, approached the Blessed One; approaching, they said this to the Blessed One: “We will serve you, ascetic, by your feet.” The Blessed One did not pay attention to them either, as he was released from the unsurpassed fetter.
translations.sn4.8:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; approaching, he spoke this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
translations.sn4.8:2: “The father of sons delights in his sons, just as a cowherd delights in his cows. Men’s delights are acquisitions; one who has no acquisitions does not delight.”
translations.sn4.8:3: “A father grieves for his children,  a cowherd grieves for his cows just so;  A person’s grief is for attachments,  for one without attachments does not grieve.”
translations.sn44.1:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s park.  Now at that time the nun Khemā, while touring Kosala, had gone to stay at Toraṇavatthu between Sāvatthī and Sāketa.  Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, while going from Sāketa to Sāvatthī, went to stay for a single night at Toraṇavatthu between Sāketa and Sāvatthī.  Then King Pasenadi of Kosala addressed a certain man:  “Come here, man, find out if there is a mendicant or brahmin of such kind at Toraṇavatthu that I might pay respects to today.”
translations.sn44.1:2: “Yes, your majesty,” replied that man to King Pasenadi of Kosala. He searched all of Toraṇavatthu but did not see a mendicant or brahmin of such kind that King Pasenadi of Kosala might pay respects to.  That man saw the nun Khemā staying at Toraṇavatthu.  Seeing her, he approached King Pasenadi of Kosala; having approached, he said this to King Pasenadi of Kosala:
translations.sn44.1:3: “There is no mendicant or brahmin of such kind at Toraṇavatthu that your majesty might pay respects to.  But there is, your majesty, a nun named Khemā, a female disciple of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the perfectly enlightened Buddha.  And a good report of that lady has spread about:  ‘She is wise, capable, clever, learned, of good speech, and ready to answer.’  Your majesty should pay respects to her.”
translations.sn44.1:6: “In that case, great king, I will ask you about this very point. Answer as it seems right to you.  What do you think, great king?  Is there any accountant or calculator or mathematician who could count the grains of sand in the Ganges— saying: ‘There are this many grains of sand, or this many hundreds, or this many thousands, or this many hundreds of thousands’?”  “No, lady.”  “But is there any accountant or calculator or mathematician who could count the water in the great ocean— saying: ‘There are this many gallons of water, or this many hundreds, or this many thousands, or this many hundreds of thousands’?”  “No, lady.”  “Why is that?”  “Lady, the ocean is deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom.”  “So too, great king, the form by which one would designate a Tathāgata has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising.  The Tathāgata is freed from the designation of form, great king— deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom— like the ocean.  He does not apply the view ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ nor does he apply the view ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ nor does he apply the view ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ nor does he apply the view ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.’
translations.sn44.1:9: The consciousness by which one would designate a Tathāgata has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising.  The Tathāgata is freed from the designation of consciousness, great king— deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom— like the ocean.  He does not apply the view ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ nor does he apply the view ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ nor does he apply the view ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ nor does he apply the view ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.’ Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, pleased and approving of the nun Khemā’s words, got up from his seat, bowed to the nun Khemā, circled her to the right, and departed.
translations.sn45.1:2: “Ignorance, monks, precedes unwholesome states and is followed by lack of conscience and lack of regard.  For an ignorant person who has not seen the truth, wrong view arises;  for one with wrong view, wrong intention arises;  for one with wrong intention, wrong speech arises;  for one with wrong speech, wrong action arises;  for one with wrong action, wrong livelihood arises;  for one with wrong livelihood, wrong effort arises;  for one with wrong effort, wrong mindfulness arises;  for one with wrong mindfulness, wrong immersion arises.
translations.sn45.2:1: Thus I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying among the Sakyans in a town of the Sakyans called Nagaraka.  Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:  “This spiritual life is half of it, sir— that is, good friendship, good companionship, good comradeship.”
translations.sn45.2:2: “Not so, Ānanda! Not so, Ānanda!  This is the entire spiritual life, Ānanda— that is, good friendship, good companionship, good comradeship.  It is to be expected that a monk with good friends, good companions, and good comrades will develop and cultivate the noble eightfold path.
translations.sn45.2:3: And how does a monk with good friends, good companions, and good comrades develop and cultivate the noble eightfold path?  Here, Ānanda, a monk develops right view that relies on seclusion, fading away, cessation, and ripening as letting go.  He develops right intention that relies on seclusion …  He develops right speech …  He develops right action …  He develops right livelihood …  He develops right effort …  He develops right mindfulness …  He develops right immersion that relies on seclusion, fading away, cessation, and ripening as letting go.  That is how a monk with good friends, good companions, and good comrades develops and cultivates the noble eightfold path.
translations.sn45.4:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and outer robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. The Venerable Ānanda saw the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi leaving Sāvatthī in a white carriage covered entirely with white. The horses are white, adorned with white trappings; the carriage is white, the retinue is white, the canopy is white, the goad is white, the umbrella is white, the turban is white, the clothes are white, the sandals are white, and even the whip is white with a white handle. Seeing him, the people said: “It is a brahma vehicle, sir. It looks like a brahma vehicle, sir.”
translations.sn45.4:10: Non-ill will and non-harming, seclusion is his weapon; endurance is his leather armor, it proceeds for the sake of liberation from bondage.
translations.sn45.4:2: Then the Venerable Ānanda, having walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from the alms round after the meal, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. While seated to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn45.4:4: “It is possible, Ānanda,” the Blessed One said. “For this very noble eightfold path, the designation is: ‘Brahma Vehicle’, and also ‘Dhamma Vehicle’, and also ‘Unsurpassed Victory in Battle’.”
translations.sn45.4:8: “For one who has faith and wisdom, and the Dhammas well fitted, always bearing the burden; shame and dread harnessed in the mind, mindfulness is the guarding charioteer.
translations.sn45.4:9: The chariot furnished with virtue, with the axle of jhāna and the wheels of energy; Equanimity is the yoke of concentration, non-craving is the retinue.
translations.sn45.8:1: At Sāvatthī. “I will teach you the noble eightfold path, bhikkhus, and I will analyze it. Listen to that, pay close attention, and I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn45.8:3: And what, bhikkhus, is right view? Knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of suffering—this is called right view, bhikkhus.
translations.sn45.8:4: And what, bhikkhus, is right intention? The intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, the intention of non-harming—this is called right intention, bhikkhus.
translations.sn45.8:5: And what, bhikkhus, is right speech? Abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from idle chatter—this is called right speech, bhikkhus.
translations.sn45.8:6: And what, bhikkhus, is right action? Abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct—this is called right action, bhikkhus.
translations.sn45.8:7: And what, bhikkhus, is right livelihood? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, makes his living by right livelihood—this is called right livelihood, bhikkhus.
translations.sn45.8:8: And what, bhikkhus, is right effort? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu generates desire, endeavors, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states... for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome states... for the arising of unarisen wholesome states... for the maintenance, preservation, increase, maturity, development, and completion of arisen wholesome states by generating desire, endeavoring, arousing energy, exerting his mind, and striving—this is called right effort, bhikkhus.
translations.sn45.8:9: And what, bhikkhus, is right mindfulness? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world—this is called right mindfulness, bhikkhus.
translations.sn46.11:1: “Just as, bhikkhus, all beings that move on four paths—walking at times, standing at times, sitting at times, lying down at times—all do so relying on the earth, grounded on the earth; so too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops and cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment relying on virtue, grounded on virtue.
translations.sn46.14:1: At one time the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground. Now at that time the Venerable Mahākassapa was living at the Pipphali Cave, sick, afflicted, and gravely ill. Then the Blessed One, in the evening, having come out of seclusion, approached the Venerable Mahākassapa; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Mahākassapa:
translations.sn46.14:2: “How are you, Kassapa? Are you bearing up? Are you managing? Do your painful feelings decrease, not increase; do they decrease, not increase?” “I am not bearing up, venerable sir, I am not managing. My painful feelings are increasing greatly, not decreasing; I see an increase, not a decrease.”
translations.sn46.29:2: Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness dependent on seclusion... he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, maturing in relinquishment. When developed and cultivated in this way, bhikkhus, the seven factors of enlightenment lead to the abandoning of fetters.
translations.sn46.30:1: At one time the Blessed One was living among the Sumbhas in a town of the Sumbhas called Setaka. Then the Venerable Udāyī approached the Blessed One... sat down to one side. While seated to one side, the Venerable Udāyī said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn46.30:2: “It is wonderful, sir, it is marvelous, sir. For I have much love and respect, conscience and dread for the Blessed One. For formerly, sir, while I was a householder, I had little contact with the Dhamma and little contact with the Saṅgha. So, sir, perceiving love and respect, conscience and dread for the Blessed One, I went forth from the home life into homelessness. The Blessed One taught me the Dhamma: ‘This is material form, this is the origin of material form, this is the cessation of material form; this is feeling … this is perception … this are choices … this is consciousness, this is the origin of consciousness, this is the cessation of consciousness.’
translations.sn46.30:3: So, sir, having gone to an empty dwelling, I turned over and over these five aggregates subject to clinging. I truly understood ‘This is suffering’, I truly understood ‘This is the origin of suffering’, I truly understood ‘This is the cessation of suffering’, I truly understood ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering’. The Dhamma has been realized by me, sir, and the path has been attained; which, when developed and cultivated, will lead to dwelling in that state, such that I will know: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.’
translations.sn46.38:1: At the time, monks, when a noble disciple makes an effort, applies their mind, and brings their whole heart to bear, and listens to the Dhamma with an eager ear, the five hindrances are not present at that time. The seven factors of enlightenment at that time reach full development.
translations.sn46.3:1: “Those monks, monks, who are virtuous, concentrated, wise, liberated, and possess liberation-knowledge and vision—I declare that seeing them is of great benefit; I declare that hearing them is of great benefit; I declare that approaching them is of great benefit; I declare that attending on them is of great benefit; I declare that recollecting them is of great benefit; I declare that going forth under them is of great benefit. For what reason? When such monks hear the Dhamma, they dwell considering it in two ways—by way of the body and by way of the mind. Dwelling thus considering it, they recollect that Dhamma and examine it.
translations.sn46.3:2: At the time when a monk, dwelling thus considering it, recollects that Dhamma and examines it, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness is aroused in that monk; the enlightenment factor of mindfulness is developed by that monk at that time; the enlightenment factor of mindfulness reaches full development by that monk at that time. Dwelling thus mindful, that monk scrutinizes, examines, and investigates that Dhamma with wisdom.
translations.sn46.51:20: And what, monks, is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of energy, or for the fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of energy? There is, monks, the element of initiative, the element of exertion, the element of effort. Non-attention to that—this is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of energy, or for the fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of energy.
translations.sn46.51:21: And what, monks, is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of rapture, or for the fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of rapture? There are, monks, things that are bases for rapture. Non-attention to that—this is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of rapture, or for the fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of rapture.
translations.sn46.51:22: And what, monks, is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of tranquility, or for the fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of tranquility? There is, monks, tranquility of body and tranquility of mind. Non-attention to that—this is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of tranquility, or for the fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of tranquility.
translations.sn46.51:23: And what, monks, is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of concentration, or for the fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of concentration? There is, monks, a sign of serenity and a sign of non-distraction. Non-attention to that—this is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of concentration, or for the fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of concentration.
translations.sn46.52:1: Then several monks, having dressed in the morning and taking their bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Then it occurred to those monks: “It is rather too early to go for alms in Sāvatthī. Why don't we go to the monastery of the wanderers of other sects?”
translations.sn46.52:10: And what, monks, is the method, by which method the seven factors of enlightenment become fourteen? Whatever mindfulness regarding phenomena internally, that is the enlightenment factor of mindfulness; whatever mindfulness regarding phenomena externally, that is the enlightenment factor of mindfulness. ‘Enlightenment factor of mindfulness’—thus goes the description. In this way there are two by this method.
translations.sn46.52:11: Whatever, monks, scrutiny, examination, and investigation of phenomena internally with wisdom, that is the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena; whatever scrutiny, examination, and investigation of phenomena externally with wisdom, that is the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena. ‘Enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena’—thus goes the description. In this way there are two by this method.
translations.sn46.52:12: Whatever, monks, physical energy, that is the enlightenment factor of energy; whatever mental energy, that is the enlightenment factor of energy. ‘Enlightenment factor of energy’—thus goes the description. In this way there are two by this method.
translations.sn46.52:13: Whatever, monks, rapture with applied and sustained thought, that is the enlightenment factor of rapture; whatever rapture without applied and sustained thought, that is the enlightenment factor of rapture. ‘Enlightenment factor of rapture’—thus goes the description. In this way there are two by this method.
translations.sn46.52:14: Whatever, monks, physical tranquility, that is the enlightenment factor of tranquility; whatever mental tranquility, that is the enlightenment factor of tranquility. ‘Enlightenment factor of tranquility’—thus goes the description. In this way there are two by this method.
translations.sn46.52:15: Whatever concentration, monks, that is with applied thought and sustained thought, that too is the concentration awakening factor; whatever concentration that is without applied thought and sustained thought, that too is the concentration awakening factor. It goes by the designation 'concentration awakening factor'. In this way, it is twofold by way of this method.
translations.sn46.52:2: Then those monks approached the dwelling of the wanderers of other sects; having approached, they exchanged greetings with the wanderers of other sects. Having exchanged courteous greetings and talk, they sat down to one side. While sitting to one side, those wanderers of other sects said to those monks:
translations.sn46.52:3: “The ascetic Gotama, friends, teaches the Dhamma to his disciples thus: 'Come, monks, having abandoned the five hindrances, the corruptions of the mind that weaken wisdom, develop the seven factors of enlightenment as they really are.' We too, friends, teach the Dhamma to our disciples thus: 'Come, friends, having abandoned the five hindrances, the corruptions of the mind that weaken wisdom, develop the seven factors of enlightenment as they really are.' In this case, friends, what is the difference, what is the distinction, what is the diversity between the ascetic Gotama and us, that is—in the teaching of the Dhamma or the instruction?”
translations.sn46.52:4: Then those monks neither delighted in nor rejected the statement of those wanderers of other sects; without delighting and without rejecting, they rose from their seats and departed: “We will learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One.” Then those monks, having gone for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from the alms-round after the meal, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. While sitting to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn46.52:8: “Wanderers of other sects of such views, monks, should be answered thus: 'Is there, friend, a method by which, relying on that method, the five hindrances become ten and the seven factors of enlightenment become fourteen?' When asked thus, monks, wanderers of other sects will not be able to answer and will fall into confusion. For what reason? Because that, monks, is not their domain. I do not see, monks, anyone in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, who would satisfy their mind with an explanation of these questions, other than a Tathāgata or a disciple of a Tathāgata, or one who has heard it from them.
translations.sn46.52:9: And what, monks, is the method by which, relying on that method, the five hindrances become ten? Whatever internal sensual desire, monks, that too is a hindrance; whatever external sensual desire, that too is a hindrance. It goes by the designation 'sensual desire hindrance'. In this way, it is twofold by way of this method. Whatever internal ill will, monks, that too is a hindrance; whatever external ill will, that too is a hindrance. It goes by the designation 'ill will hindrance'. In this way, it is twofold by way of this method. Whatever sloth, monks, that too is a hindrance; whatever torpor, that too is a hindrance. It goes by the designation 'sloth-and-torpor hindrance'. In this way, it is twofold by way of this method. Whatever restlessness, monks, that too is a hindrance; whatever remorse, that too is a hindrance. It goes by the designation 'restlessness-and-remorse hindrance'. In this way, it is twofold by way of this method. Whatever internal doubt about phenomena, monks, that too is a hindrance; whatever external doubt about phenomena, that too is a hindrance. It goes by the designation 'doubt hindrance'. In this way, it is twofold by way of this method. This, monks, is the method by which, relying on that method, the five hindrances become ten.
translations.sn46.53:10: At a time, monks, when the mind is restless, it is not the right time to develop the investigation of phenomena awakening factor, it is not the right time to develop the energy awakening factor, it is not the right time to develop the rapture awakening factor. For what reason? Because a restless mind, monks, is hard to calm with those states.
translations.sn46.53:11: Suppose, monks, a person wanted to extinguish a large mass of fire. He would throw dry grass there, dry cow dung, and dry wood; he would give it a mouthful of air and would not scatter dust with his hand. Would that person be able to extinguish that large mass of fire?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn46.53:13: But at a time, monks, when the mind is restless, it is the right time to develop the tranquility awakening factor, it is the right time to develop the concentration awakening factor, it is the right time to develop the equanimity awakening factor. For what reason? Because a restless mind, monks, is easy to calm with those states.
translations.sn46.53:14: Suppose, monks, a person wanted to extinguish a large mass of fire. He would throw wet grass there, wet cow dung, and wet wood; he would give it a mouthful of water and would scatter dust with his hand. Would that person be able to extinguish that large mass of fire?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.sn46.53:2: “Wanderers of other sects of such views, monks, should be answered thus: 'At a time, friend, when the mind is sluggish, for which awakening factors is it not the right time to develop, and for which awakening factors is it the right time to develop? And at a time, friend, when the mind is restless, for which awakening factors is it not the right time to develop, and for which awakening factors is it the right time to develop?' When asked thus, monks, wanderers of other sects will not be able to answer and will fall into confusion. For what reason? Because that, monks, is not their domain.
translations.sn46.53:3: I do not see, monks, anyone in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, who would satisfy their mind with an explanation of these questions, other than a Tathāgata or a disciple of a Tathāgata, or one who has heard it from them.
translations.sn46.53:4: At a time when the mind is sluggish, monks, it is not the right time to develop the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the enlightenment factor of concentration, or the enlightenment factor of equanimity. Why is that? Because the mind is sluggish, and it is difficult to rouse it with these qualities.
translations.sn46.53:5: Suppose, monks, a person wanted to make a small fire flare up. He would put damp grass on it, damp cow dung, and damp wood; he would give it water and cover it with dust. Would that person be able to make the small fire flare up? "No, venerable sir."
translations.sn46.53:7: But at a time when the mind is sluggish, monks, it is the right time to develop the enlightenment factor of investigation of qualities, the enlightenment factor of energy, and the enlightenment factor of rapture. Why is that? Because the mind is sluggish, and it is easy to rouse it with these qualities.
translations.sn46.53:8: Suppose, monks, a person wanted to make a small fire flare up. He would put dry grass on it, dry cow dung, and dry wood; he would give it a mouthful of wind and not cover it with dust. Would that person be able to make the small fire flare up? "Yes, venerable sir."
translations.sn46.54:1: At one time the Buddha was staying among the Koliyans in the Koliyan town named Haliddavasana. Then several monks, dressing in the morning and taking their bowls and robes, entered Haliddavasana for alms. Then it occurred to those monks: "It is rather far to walk for alms in Haliddavasana. Why don't we go to the park of the wanderers of other sects?"
translations.sn46.54:11: "Wanderers of other sects who speak thus, monks, should be questioned like this: 'But, friend, when developed, what is the liberation of mind by loving-kindness grounded in, what is its pinnacle, what is its fruit, and what is its final goal? When developed, what is the liberation of mind by compassion grounded in, what is its pinnacle, what is its fruit, and what is its final goal? When developed, what is the liberation of mind by empathetic joy grounded in, what is its pinnacle, what is its fruit, and what is its final goal? When developed, what is the liberation of mind by equanimity grounded in, what is its pinnacle, what is its fruit, and what is its final goal?' When questioned thus, monks, wanderers of other sects will not be able to answer and will fall into confusion. Why is that? Because that is not their domain, monks. I do not see anyone in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its princes and men, who could satisfy their minds with an answer to these questions, except the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, or one who has heard it from them.
translations.sn46.54:12: And when developed, monks, what is the liberation of mind by loving-kindness grounded in, what is its pinnacle, what is its fruit, and what is its final goal? Here, monks, a monk develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness accompanied by loving-kindness ... he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity accompanied by loving-kindness, dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, resulting in letting go. If he wishes, he dwells perceiving the repulsive in the not repulsive. If he wishes, he dwells perceiving the not repulsive in the repulsive. If he wishes, he dwells perceiving the repulsive in both the repulsive and the not repulsive. If he wishes, he dwells perceiving the not repulsive in both the repulsive and the not repulsive. If he wishes, avoiding both the repulsive and the not repulsive, he dwells equanimous, mindful and fully aware. Or he enters upon and dwells in the beautiful deliverance. I call the liberation of mind by loving-kindness beautiful in its pinnacle, for a wise monk who has not penetrated to a higher deliverance.
translations.sn46.54:13: And when developed, monks, what is the liberation of mind by compassion grounded in, what is its pinnacle, what is its fruit, and what is its final goal? Here, monks, a monk develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness accompanied by compassion ... he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity accompanied by compassion, dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, resulting in letting go. If he wishes, he dwells perceiving the repulsive in the not repulsive ... If he wishes, avoiding both the repulsive and the not repulsive, he dwells equanimous, mindful and fully aware. Or, completely transcending all perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, perceiving 'infinite space,' he enters upon and dwells in the base of infinite space. I call the liberation of mind by compassion the base of infinite space in its pinnacle, for a wise monk who has not penetrated to a higher deliverance.
translations.sn46.54:14: And when developed, monks, what is the liberation of mind by empathetic joy grounded in, what is its pinnacle, what is its fruit, and what is its final goal? Here, monks, a monk develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness accompanied by empathetic joy ... he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity accompanied by empathetic joy, dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, resulting in letting go. If he wishes, he dwells perceiving the repulsive in the not repulsive ... If he wishes, avoiding both the repulsive and the not repulsive, he dwells equanimous, mindful and fully aware. Or, completely transcending the base of infinite space, perceiving 'infinite consciousness,' he enters upon and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness. I call the liberation of mind by empathetic joy the base of infinite consciousness in its pinnacle, for a wise monk who has not penetrated to a higher deliverance.
translations.sn46.54:3: “The ascetic Gotama, friends, teaches such a Dhamma to his disciples:  ‘Come, monks, having abandoned the five hindrances, mental corruptions that weaken wisdom, dwell pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; and so above, below, across, everywhere, in all ways, the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from ill will and free from affliction—dwell pervading it.  Dwell pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with compassion, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; and so above, below, across, everywhere, in all ways, the entire world with a mind imbued with compassion—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from ill will and free from affliction—dwell pervading it.  Dwell pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with empathetic joy, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; and so above, below, across, everywhere, in all ways, the entire world with a mind imbued with empathetic joy—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from ill will and free from affliction—dwell pervading it.  Dwell pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with equanimity, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; and so above, below, across, everywhere, in all ways, the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from ill will and free from affliction—dwell pervading it.’”
translations.sn46.8:1: At one time Venerable Upavāna and Venerable Sāriputta were staying at Kosambī in the Ghosita Monastery.  Then Venerable Sāriputta, in the evening, came out of seclusion and approached Venerable Upavāna; having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Upavāna.  After exchanging courteous and agreeable conversation, he sat down to one side.  When he had sat down to one side, Venerable Sāriputta said to Venerable Upavāna:
translations.sn46.8:2: “Would a monk know, friend Upavāna, that ‘my seven factors of enlightenment are well developed for comfortable dwelling due to proper attention in this way’?”  “A monk would know, friend Sāriputta, that ‘my seven factors of enlightenment are well developed for comfortable dwelling due to proper attention in this way.’”
translations.sn47.10:1: Then Venerable Ānanda, dressing in the morning and taking his bowl and outer robe, approached a certain monks’ dwelling; having approached, he sat down on the appointed seat.  Then several bhikkhunīs approached Venerable Ānanda; having approached, they paid homage to Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side.  When they had sat down to one side, those bhikkhunīs said to Venerable Ānanda:
translations.sn47.10:2: “Here, venerable sir, several bhikkhunīs dwell with well-established minds in the four foundations of mindfulness, experiencing a distinction superior to before and after.”  “It is so, sisters, it is so.  For whoever, sisters, a monk or a bhikkhunī, dwells with a well-established mind in the four foundations of mindfulness, it is to be expected of them:  ‘they will experience a distinction superior to before and after.’”
translations.sn47.10:7: Furthermore, Ānanda, a monk dwells contemplating feelings in feelings … mind in mind … phenomena in phenomena, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world.  While he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, based on phenomena, physical fever arises in the body, or mental listlessness, or the mind becomes agitated externally.  Therefore, Ānanda, the monk should fix his mind on some inspiring sign.  When he fixes his mind on some inspiring sign, joy arises.  Being joyful, rapture arises.  When the mind is full of rapture, the body becomes tranquil.  When the body is tranquil, one experiences pleasure.  With pleasure, the mind becomes concentrated.  He reflects thus:  ‘The purpose for which I fixed my mind has been achieved.  Let me now withdraw.’  So he withdraws and does not think about it or examine it.  He understands:  ‘I am not thinking or examining; internally mindful, I am happy.’  Thus, Ānanda, development occurs with a basis.
translations.sn47.10:9: Thus, Ānanda, I have taught development with a basis, and I have taught development without a basis.  What should be done by a teacher out of compassion for his disciples, seeking their welfare, that has been done by me for you.  These are the roots of trees, these are empty huts.  Meditate, Ānanda, do not be negligent; do not regret it later.  This is our instruction to you.”
translations.sn47.13:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.  At that time Venerable Sāriputta was staying in Magadha in the village of Nālaka, sick, afflicted, and severely ill.  The novice monk Cunda was Venerable Sāriputta’s attendant.
translations.sn47.13:2: Then Venerable Sāriputta passed away due to that very illness.  Then the novice monk Cunda, taking Venerable Sāriputta’s bowl and outer robe, approached Sāvatthī, Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, and approached Venerable Ānanda; having approached, he paid homage to Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side.  When he had sat down to one side, the novice monk Cunda said to Venerable Ānanda:  “Venerable sir, Sāriputta has passed away.  This is his bowl and outer robe.”
translations.sn47.13:3: “There is an opportunity, friend Cunda, to see the Blessed One.  Come, friend Cunda, let us approach the Blessed One; having approached, we will report this matter to the Blessed One.”  “Yes, venerable sir,” the novice monk Cunda replied to Venerable Ānanda.
translations.sn47.13:4: Then Venerable Ānanda and the novice monk Cunda approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.  When he had sat down to one side, Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:  “This novice monk Cunda, venerable sir, says:  ‘Venerable sir, Sāriputta has passed away;  this is his bowl and outer robe.’  And, venerable sir, my body feels as if drugged, the directions do not appear clear to me, and the Dhamma does not occur to me when I hear that ‘Venerable Sāriputta has passed away.’”
translations.sn47.19:1: At one time the Buddha was staying in the Sumbha country, a market town named Sedaka. There the Buddha addressed the monks: 'Monks, formerly a trainer of elephants, having roused an elephant, addressed his apprentice: 'Come, good apprentice Medakathālika, mount the elephant and stand behind me.' 'Yes, teacher,' replied the apprentice Medakathālika to the elephant trainer. Having mounted the elephant, he stood behind the teacher. Then the elephant trainer addressed the apprentice Medakathālika: 'You, good apprentice Medakathālika, protect me, and I will protect you. Thus, being protected and guarding each other, we will display our skills, earn a living, and safely bring down the elephant.' When this was said, the apprentice Medakathālika addressed the elephant trainer: 'That will not be so, teacher. You, teacher, protect yourself, and I will protect myself. Thus, being self-protected and self-guarded, we will display our skills, earn a living, and safely bring down the elephant.'
translations.sn47.19:2: 'In this case, the principle,' the Buddha said, 'is as the apprentice Medakathālika said to the teacher. Monks, the establishment of mindfulness should be practiced thinking:
translations.sn47.20:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying in the Sumbha country, a market town named Sedaka. There the Buddha addressed the monks: 'Monks.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' those monks replied to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
translations.sn47.20:2: 'Suppose, monks, a crowd of people might gather, saying:
translations.sn47.25:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. Then a certain brahmin approached the Buddha; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Buddha. When the courteous and agreeable conversation was finished, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that brahmin said to the Buddha: 'What is the cause, Master Gotama, what is the reason why, when a Tathāgata has passed away, the true teaching does not last long? And what is the cause, Master Gotama, what is the reason why, when a Tathāgata has passed away, the true teaching lasts long?'
translations.sn47.25:2: 'Because the four establishments of mindfulness have not been developed and cultivated, brahmin, when a Tathāgata has passed away, the true teaching does not last long. But because the four establishments of mindfulness have been developed and cultivated, brahmin, when a Tathāgata has passed away, the true teaching lasts long.
translations.sn47.29:2: Then Venerable Ānanda, dressing in the morning and taking his bowl and outer robe, approached the house of the householder Sirivaḍḍha; having approached, he sat down on the seat made ready. Having sat down, Venerable Ānanda said to the householder Sirivaḍḍha: 'Householder, is it bearable, is it endurable? Do painful feelings subside and not increase? Is their subsiding evident, not their increase?' 'It is not bearable for me, venerable sir, nor endurable. Painful feelings are increasing greatly, not subsiding; their increase is evident, not their subsiding.'
translations.sn47.29:3: 'Therefore, householder, you should train yourself thus:
translations.sn47.33:1: 'For whomever, monks, the four establishments of mindfulness are not developed, for them the noble path is not developed for the complete ending of suffering. For whomever, monks, the four establishments of mindfulness are developed, for them the noble path is developed for the complete ending of suffering.
translations.sn47.37:1: 'Monks, there are four establishments of mindfulness. What four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. For him dwelling contemplating the body in the body, any desire regarding the body is abandoned. With the abandoning of desire, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.37:2: He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. For him dwelling contemplating feelings in feelings, any desire regarding feelings is abandoned. With the abandoning of desire, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.37:3: He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. For him dwelling contemplating the mind in the mind, any desire regarding the mind is abandoned. With the abandoning of desire, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.38:1: 'Monks, there are four establishments of mindfulness. What four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. For him dwelling contemplating the body in the body, the body is fully understood. Because the body is fully understood, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.38:2: He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. For him dwelling contemplating feelings in feelings, feelings are fully understood. Because feelings are fully understood, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.38:3: They dwell contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. As they dwell contemplating the mind in the mind, the mind is fully understood. Because the mind is fully understood, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.40:1: “Monks, I will teach you the establishment of mindfulness and the development of the establishment of mindfulness, and the practice that leads to the development of the establishment of mindfulness. Listen to that. And what, monks, is the establishment of mindfulness? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world; they dwell contemplating feelings in feelings … they dwell contemplating the mind in the mind … they dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. This is called the establishment of mindfulness, monks.
translations.sn47.40:2: And what, monks, is the development of the establishment of mindfulness? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body as subject to arising, as subject to passing away, as subject to both arising and passing away, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. They dwell contemplating feelings in feelings as subject to arising … they dwell contemplating the mind in the mind as subject to arising … they dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena as subject to arising, as subject to passing away, as subject to both arising and passing away, ardent, fully aware, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. This is called the development of the establishment of mindfulness, monks.
translations.sn47.4:1: At one time the Buddha was staying in the Kosalan country in the brahmin village of Sālā. There the Buddha addressed the monks … and said:
translations.sn47.4:2: “Those monks, monks, who are new, not long gone forth, who have recently arrived at this Dhamma and discipline—those monks, you should encourage, settle, and establish in the development of the four establishments of mindfulness. Which four? Come, friends, dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, fully aware, unified, with clear minds, concentrated, with one-pointed minds, for the knowledge of the body as it really is; dwell contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, fully aware, unified, with clear minds, concentrated, with one-pointed minds, for the knowledge of feelings as they really are; dwell contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, fully aware, unified, with clear minds, concentrated, with one-pointed minds, for the knowledge of the mind as it really is; dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, fully aware, unified, with clear minds, concentrated, with one-pointed minds, for the knowledge of phenomena as they really are.
translations.sn47.4:3: Those monks, monks, who are in training, whose minds have not yet reached the goal, who are desiring the unsurpassed security from bondage, they also dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, fully aware, unified, with clear minds, concentrated, with one-pointed minds, for the full understanding of the body; they dwell contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, fully aware, unified, with clear minds, concentrated, with one-pointed minds, for the full understanding of feelings; they dwell contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, fully aware, unified, with clear minds, concentrated, with one-pointed minds, for the full understanding of the mind; they dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, fully aware, unified, with clear minds, concentrated, with one-pointed minds, for the full understanding of phenomena.
translations.sn47.4:4: Those monks, monks, who are arahants, with taints destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of becoming, and are liberated by right knowledge, they also dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, fully aware, unified, with clear minds, concentrated, with one-pointed minds, detached from the body; they dwell contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, fully aware, unified, with clear minds, concentrated, with one-pointed minds, detached from feelings; they dwell contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, fully aware, unified, with clear minds, concentrated, with one-pointed minds, detached from the mind; they dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, fully aware, unified, with clear minds, concentrated, with one-pointed minds, detached from phenomena.
translations.sn47.6:1: “Once upon a time, monks, a hawk suddenly seized a quail. Then the quail, while being carried off by the hawk, lamented thus: ‘We are unlucky, we have little merit, in that we wandered in an inappropriate place, in another’s domain. If we today were to wander in our own ancestral domain, you would not get me, hawk, for a fight.’ ‘And what, quail, is your own ancestral domain?’ ‘A clod of earth turned up by a plow.’ Then the hawk, not letting go of the quail, not arguing with his own strength, released the quail: ‘Go then, quail, even if you go there, you won’t escape me.’
translations.sn47.6:2: Then the quail, monks, went to the clod of earth turned up by a plow, and standing on top of a large clod, addressed the hawk: ‘Come now for me, hawk, come now for me, hawk.’ Then the hawk, monks, not letting go of his own strength, not arguing with his own strength, swooped down on both sides and suddenly seized the quail. When the quail, monks, realized that the hawk had come in great numbers, he slipped inside that very clod. Then the hawk, monks, smashed his beak right there. So it is, monks, for one who wanders in an inappropriate place, in another’s domain.
translations.sn47.6:3: Therefore, monks, do not wander in an inappropriate place, in another’s domain. One who wanders, monks, in an inappropriate place, in another’s domain, Māra gets an opportunity, Māra gets a basis. And what, monks, is a monk’s inappropriate place, another’s domain? The five cords of sensual pleasure. Which five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, charming, beautiful, arousing of passion—sounds cognizable by the ear … odors cognizable by the nose … flavors cognizable by the tongue … tactile objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, charming, beautiful, arousing of passion—this, monks, is a monk’s inappropriate place, another’s domain.
translations.sn47.7:1: “There are, monks, in the Himalayas, the king of mountains, difficult, uneven regions where neither monkeys nor humans go. There are, monks, in the Himalayas, the king of mountains, difficult, uneven regions where monkeys go, but humans do not. There are, monks, in the Himalayas, the king of mountains, level, pleasant regions where both monkeys and humans go. There, monks, hunters lay sticky traps in the monkeys’ paths to catch monkeys.
translations.sn47.8:2: That foolish, unskilled, bad cook, monks, does not pick up the sign of his own master: ‘Today this curry pleases my master, or he praises this, or he takes a lot of this, or he speaks highly of this. Today this sour curry pleases my master, or he praises the sour one, or he takes a lot of the sour one, or he speaks highly of the sour one. Today this bitter curry pleases my master … Today this pungent curry pleases my master … Today this sweet curry pleases my master … Today this dry curry pleases my master … Today this non-dry curry pleases my master … Today this salty curry pleases my master … Today this unsalty curry pleases my master, or he praises the unsalty one, or he takes a lot of the unsalty one, or he speaks highly of the unsalty one.’
translations.sn47.8:4: That foolish, unskilled, bad monk, monks, is neither a recipient of pleasant abiding in the here and now, nor a recipient of mindfulness and right awareness. For what reason? Because that foolish, unskilled, bad monk does not pick up the sign of his own mind.
translations.sn47.8:5: Suppose, monks, a wise, skilled, good cook were to wait upon a king or a king’s minister with various curries—sour ones, bitter ones, pungent ones, sweet ones, dry ones, non-dry ones, salty ones, unsalty ones.
translations.sn5.10:1: At Sāvatthī. Then, in the morning, the nun Vajirā dressed and, taking her bowl and outer robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from the alms round after the meal, she approached the Andhavana forest for day’s abiding. Having entered the Andhavana, she sat down at the root of a tree for day’s abiding. Then Māra the Wicked, wanting to arouse fear, terror, and gooseflesh in the nun Vajirā, wanting to make her abandon concentration, approached her. Having approached, he addressed the nun Vajirā with a verse:
translations.sn5.10:2: “By whom has this being been created? Where is the maker of the being? Where has the being arisen? Where does the being cease?”
translations.sn5.10:3: Then it occurred to the nun Vajirā: “Who is this reciting a verse—a human or a non-human?” Then it occurred to the nun Vajirā: “This is Māra the Wicked, wanting to arouse fear, terror, and gooseflesh in me, wanting to make me abandon concentration, reciting a verse.” Then the nun Vajirā, knowing “This is Māra the Wicked,” replied to Māra the Wicked with verses:
translations.sn5.10:4: “Why now do you assume a ‘being’? Māra, is this your view? This is a heap of pure fabrications; here no being is found.
translations.sn5.10:5: For just as, when the parts are assembled, there occurs the word ‘chariot’; so, when the aggregates are present, there occurs the convention ‘a being’.
translations.sn5.10:6: For only suffering arises, suffering stands firm, and only suffering ceases; apart from suffering, no arising; apart from suffering, no ceasing.”
translations.sn5.1:1: Thus I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then, in the morning, the nun Āḷavikā dressed and, taking her bowl and outer robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from the alms round after the meal, she approached the Andhavana forest desiring seclusion. Then Māra the Wicked, wanting to arouse fear, terror, and gooseflesh in the nun Āḷavikā, wanting to make her abandon seclusion, approached the nun Āḷavikā. Having approached, he addressed the nun Āḷavikā with a verse:
translations.sn5.1:2: “There is no escape in the world; why do you speak of seclusion? Enjoy sensual pleasures; do not be remorseful afterwards.”
translations.sn5.1:3: Then it occurred to the nun Āḷavikā: “Who is this reciting a verse—a human or a non-human?” Then it occurred to the nun Āḷavikā: “This is Māra the Wicked, wanting to arouse fear, terror, and gooseflesh in me, wanting to make me abandon seclusion, reciting a verse.” Then the nun Āḷavikā, knowing “This is Māra the Wicked,” replied to Māra the Wicked with verses:
translations.sn5.1:4: “There is an escape in the world, which I have well cultivated by wisdom. Friend Māra, companion of the negligent, you do not know that state.
translations.sn5.1:5: Sensual pleasures are like a stake of spears, the aggregates are their chopping block. What you call sensual pleasure is for me displeasure.”
translations.sn5.1:6: Then Māra the Wicked, sad and dejected, “The nun Āḷavikā knows me,” vanished right there.
translations.sn5.2:2: “That state to be attained by the sages, a place hard to gain; that cannot be reached by two-fingered wisdom, by a woman.”
translations.sn5.2:4: “What is the use of being a woman, when the mind is well concentrated, when knowledge is arising, rightly contemplating the Dhamma?
translations.sn5.2:5: For whoever it might be thus: ‘I am a woman’ or ‘I am a man’; or anything else I am, Māra is not fit to speak of that.”
translations.sn5.3:2: “Are you, with a tearful face, searching for a man alone, having gone into the middle of the forest?”
translations.sn5.3:3: Then it occurred to the nun Kisāgotamī: “Who is this reciting a verse—a human or a non-human?” Then it occurred to the nun Kisāgotamī: “This is Māra the Wicked, wanting to arouse fear, terror, and gooseflesh in me, wanting to make me abandon concentration, reciting a verse.”
translations.sn5.3:5: “I am utterly done with mother and father, men are near at hand. I do not sorrow, I do not weep, I am not afraid of you, friend.
translations.sn5.3:6: Craving is destroyed everywhere, the mass of darkness is shattered. Having vanquished the army of Death, I dwell without taints.”
translations.sn5.3:7: Then Māra the Wicked, sad and dejected, “The nun Kisāgotamī knows me,” vanished right there.
translations.sn5.4:1: At Sāvatthī. Then, in the morning, the nun Vijayā dressed and, taking her bowl and outer robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from the alms round after the meal, she approached the Andhavana forest for day’s abiding. Having entered the Andhavana, she sat down at the root of a tree for day’s abiding. Then Māra the Wicked, wanting to arouse fear, terror, and gooseflesh in the nun Vijayā, wanting to make her abandon concentration, approached the nun Vijayā. Having approached, he addressed the nun Vijayā with a verse:
translations.sn5.4:2: “You are young and beautiful, and I am young and very handsome. Let us enjoy ourselves with the five-stringed lute.”
translations.sn5.4:4: “Forms, sounds, tastes, smells, touches, and delightful thoughts: I give them up to you, Māra; I am not one for those.”
translations.sn5.4:5: With this foul, rotting body, fragile and breaking apart; I am weary and disgusted, craving for sensual pleasures has been destroyed.
translations.sn5.4:6: Those beings who resort to form, and those who stand on the formless; Whatever attainments of serenity there are, everywhere darkness is vanquished.”
translations.sn5.5:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the nun Uppalavaṇṇā, having dressed in the morning… taking her seat… at the root of a sala tree in full bloom. Then Māra the Evil One, wanting to arouse fear, terror, and gooseflesh in the nun Uppalavaṇṇā, wanting to make her fall away from concentration, approached Uppalavaṇṇā the nun; having approached, he addressed Uppalavaṇṇā the nun with a verse:
translations.sn5.5:2: “Having approached a sala tree in full bloom, nun, You stand alone at the root of the sala tree; There is no second element of beauty for you, Fool, are you not afraid of rascals?”
translations.sn5.5:4: “Even if a hundred thousand rascals, Like that should come here; My hair does not stand on end, nor do I tremble, I do not fear you, Māra, even a bit.
translations.sn5.5:6: I am master of my mind, the bases of power are well developed; I am freed from all fetters, I do not fear you, friend.”
translations.sn5.5:7: Then Māra the Evil One, thinking “Uppalavaṇṇā the nun knows me,” sad and disappointed, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.6:2: “Why do you not delight in birth, one born enjoys sensual pleasures? Who has taught you this, nun, do not delight in birth.”
translations.sn5.6:3: “For one born there is death, one born encounters suffering; Bondage, destruction, and distress, therefore I do not delight in birth.
translations.sn5.6:4: The Buddha taught the Dhamma, the surmounting of birth; For the removal of all suffering, He established me in the truth.
translations.sn5.6:5: Those beings who resort to form, and those who stand on the formless; Not knowing cessation, they come again to repeated becoming.”
translations.sn5.7:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the nun Upacālā, having dressed in the morning… taking her seat… at the root of a certain tree for day’s abiding. Then Māra the Evil One approached Upacālā the nun; having approached, he said this to Upacālā the nun: “Where, nun, do you wish to be born?” “I do not, friend, wish to be born anywhere.”
translations.sn5.7:2: “The Thirty-three gods and the Yāmā gods, And the Tusita gods too, The gods who create by mind, and the gods who wield power over others; Fix your mind there, and enjoy the delights.”
translations.sn5.7:3: “The Thirty-three gods and the Yāmā gods, And the Tusita gods too, The gods who create by mind, and the gods who wield power over others; They are bound by the bond of sensual pleasure, they go again to Māra’s domain.
translations.sn5.7:4: The whole world is ablaze, the whole world is smoke-covered; The whole world is burning, the whole world is quaking.
translations.sn5.7:5: Unquaking, unburning, not frequented by fools; Where there is no going for Māra, there my mind is inclined.”
translations.sn5.7:6: Then Māra the Evil One, thinking “Upacālā the nun knows me,” sad and disappointed, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.8:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the nun Sīsupacālā, having dressed in the morning… taking her seat… at the root of a certain tree for day’s abiding. Then Māra the Evil One approached Sīsupacālā the nun; having approached, he said this to Sīsupacālā the nun: “In whose doctrine, nun, do you delight?” “I do not, friend, delight in anyone’s doctrine.”
translations.sn5.8:2: “For whose sake are you shaven, You appear like a recluse; But you do not delight in a doctrine, Like a fool you behave.”
translations.sn5.8:3: “Outside here are doctrines, Those who delight in views; I do not delight in their Dhamma, They are unknowing of the Dhamma.
translations.sn5.8:5: Freed everywhere, unattached, the one with eyes sees everything; Having reached the ending of all kamma, freed from the clinging to existence; That Blessed One is my teacher, I delight in his teaching.”
translations.sn5.9:2: “By whom is this image made, Who is the maker of the image? Where has the image arisen, Where does the image perish?”
translations.sn5.9:4: “This image is not made by self, this trouble is not made by another; Arisen dependent on a cause, it perishes with the breaking of the cause.
translations.sn5.9:6: Thus the aggregates and the elements, and these six sense bases; Arisen dependent on a cause, they perish with the breaking of the cause.”
translations.sn56.11:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. There the Blessed One addressed the group of five monks:
translations.sn56.11:10: When, monks, in these four noble truths my knowledge-and-vision—threefold, twelvefold, purified as to its components—was thoroughly realized, then I, monks, in the world with its devas, māras, and Brahmās, with its generations of ascetics and brahmins, with its princes and men, knew that I had attained the unexcelled right self-awakening. And knowledge-and-vision arose in me: ‘My liberation is unshakable. This is the last birth. There is no more renewed existence.’ This is what the Blessed One said. Gratified, the group of five monks delighted in the Blessed One’s statement.
translations.sn56.11:11: And while this exposition was being spoken, the dust-free, stainless vision of the Dhamma arose in Venerable Koṇḍañña: “Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.”
translations.sn56.11:13: Then, at that moment, at that instant, at that second, the cry spread as far as the Brahmā world. And this ten-thousandfold world-system shook, quaked, and trembled, and an immeasurable glorious radiance appeared in the world surpassing the divine majesty of the devas.
translations.sn56.11:2: “These two extremes, monks, should not be followed by one who has gone forth. What two? The pursuit of sensual pleasure in sensual pleasures, which is low, vulgar, common, ignoble, and unbeneficial; and the pursuit of self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial. Without veering towards either of these extremes, the Tathāgata has awakened to the middle way, which gives vision, which gives knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, awakening, and Nibbāna.
translations.sn56.11:3: And what, monks, is that middle way awakened to by the Tathāgata, which gives vision, which gives knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, awakening, and Nibbāna? It is this noble eightfold path; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. This, monks, is that middle way awakened to by the Tathāgata, which gives vision, which gives knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, awakening, and Nibbāna.
translations.sn56.11:4: Now this, monks, is the noble truth of suffering—birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering, association with the disliked is suffering, separation from the liked is suffering, not getting what one wishes is suffering—in brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering. Now this, monks, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering—that craving which produces rebirth, is accompanied by delight and lust, and delights here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence.
