Now this, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering—the fading away and cessation of that very craving, the giving up and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, non-reliance on it. Now this, monks, is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering—this very noble eightfold path; that is, right view … right concentration.
translations.sn56.11:5: ‘This is the noble truth of suffering’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. ‘That this noble truth of suffering is to be fully understood’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before … arose. ‘That this noble truth of suffering has been fully understood’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.
translations.sn56.11:6: ‘This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. ‘That this noble truth of the origin of suffering is to be abandoned’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before … arose. ‘That this noble truth of the origin of suffering has been abandoned’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.
translations.sn56.11:7: ‘This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. ‘That this noble truth of the cessation of suffering is to be realized’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before … arose. ‘That this noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.
translations.sn56.11:8: ‘This is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. ‘That this noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering is to be developed’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before … arose. ‘That this noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering has been developed’—in me, monks, regarding things not heard before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.
translations.sn56.11:9: As long as, monks, my knowledge and vision of these four noble truths in their three phases and twelve aspects was not thoroughly purified in this way, I did not claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, maras, and brahmas, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans.
translations.sn56.20:1: “These four things, monks, are true, not otherwise, and not otherwise. What four? ‘This is suffering,’ monks, this is true, not otherwise, and not otherwise; ‘this is the origin of suffering,’ this is true, not otherwise, and not otherwise; ‘this is the cessation of suffering,’ this is true, not otherwise, and not otherwise; ‘this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering,’ this is true, not otherwise, and not otherwise—these four, monks, are true, not otherwise, and not otherwise.
translations.sn56.26:1: “Whoever, monks, you might have compassion for, or whoever you might consider worthy of listening—friends or colleagues or relatives or kin—you should urge them, establish them, and settle them in the realization of the four noble truths as they really are.
translations.sn56.26:2: In which four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Whoever, monks, you might have compassion for, or whoever you might consider worthy of listening—friends or colleagues or relatives or kin—you should urge them, establish them, and settle them in the realization of these four noble truths as they really are.
translations.sn56.27:1: “These four, monks, are noble truths. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering—these four, monks, are noble truths, true, not otherwise, and not otherwise; therefore they are called ‘noble truths’.
translations.sn56.28:1: “These four, monks, are noble truths. What four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. The Tathagata is noble in this world with its devas, maras, and brahmas, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans; therefore they are called ‘noble truths’.
translations.sn56.30:1: At one time several elder monks were dwelling in the Ceti country with a large retinue. Then, on that occasion, when the several elder monks had returned from their alms round after the meal, they sat down together in the pavilion hall and this discussion arose among them: “Who, friends, sees suffering sees also the origin of suffering, sees also the cessation of suffering, sees also the way leading to the cessation of suffering.”
translations.sn56.31:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Kosambī in the Sīsapāvana. Then the Buddha, having taken a few Sīsapā leaves in his hand, addressed the mendicants: 'What do you think, mendicants, which is more numerous—these few Sīsapā leaves that I have taken in my hand, or those in the grove above?' 'Few are the Sīsapā leaves that the Blessed One has taken in his hand, sir; but those in the grove above are far more numerous.' 'So too, mendicants, the things I have directly known but not declared are far more numerous. And why have I not declared them? Because they are not beneficial, they do not belong to the fundamentals of the holy life, they do not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to awakening, to nibbāna. That is why I have not declared them.
translations.sn56.31:2: And what have I declared? 'This is suffering'—I have declared this, 'this is the origin of suffering'—I have declared this, 'this is the cessation of suffering'—I have declared this, 'this is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering'—I have declared this.
translations.sn56.31:3: And why have I declared them? Because they are beneficial, they belong to the fundamentals of the holy life, they lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to awakening, to nibbāna. That is why I have declared them.
translations.sn56.35:1: 'Suppose, mendicants, a man were to live for a hundred years, a hundred years long. They might say to him: 'Come here, man! In the morning they will stab you with a hundred spears; at noon they will stab you with a hundred spears; in the evening they will stab you with a hundred spears.' Being stabbed by three hundred spears each day, that man—living for a hundred years, a hundred years long—would, upon the passing of a hundred years, realize the four noble truths.'
translations.sn56.35:2: It is enough, mendicants, for a clansman intent on his good to go forth. Why is that? This cycle of rebirth has no known beginning, mendicants. No first point is found of living beings hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving. If this were the case, I would not speak of the realization of the four noble truths together with suffering and dejection. But I do speak of the realization of the four noble truths together with happiness and joy. Which four? The noble truth of suffering ... the noble truth of the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.
translations.sn56.36:1: 'Suppose, mendicants, a man were to gather all the grass, sticks, branches, and foliage in this Jambudīpa and, having gathered them together, make a spike. Having made the spike, he would impale the large creatures in the great ocean on large spikes, the medium-sized creatures on medium-sized spikes, and the small creatures on small spikes. Yet the large creatures in the great ocean would not be exhausted.
translations.sn56.36:2: But here in this Jambudīpa the grass, sticks, branches, and foliage would be exhausted and used up. There are far more small creatures in the great ocean, mendicants, that are not easy to impale on spikes. Why is that? Because of the fineness of their physical size. So great is the plane of deprivation, mendicants. So great is the plane of deprivation that a person endowed with right view who has escaped from it understands suffering as it really is ... understands the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering as it really is.
translations.sn56.42:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove. Then the Buddha addressed the mendicants: 'Come, mendicants, let's go to the Paṭibhānakūṭa for the day's abode.' 'Yes, sir,' those mendicants replied to the Buddha. Then the Buddha, together with a large number of mendicants, went to the Paṭibhānakūṭa. A certain mendicant saw a great precipice at the Paṭibhānakūṭa. Seeing this, he said to the Buddha: 'Sir, this precipice is great, sir, this precipice is terrifying. Is there, sir, another precipice more great and terrifying than this one?' 'There is, mendicant, another precipice more great and terrifying than this one.'
translations.sn56.42:2: 'But what, sir, is that other precipice more great and terrifying than this one?' 'Those ascetics and brahmins who do not understand suffering as it really is, do not understand the origin of suffering as it really is, do not understand the cessation of suffering as it really is, do not understand the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering as it really is—they delight in volitional formations that lead to rebirth, in volitional formations that lead to aging, in volitional formations that lead to death, in volitional formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. Delighting in volitional formations that lead to rebirth ... they generate volitional formations that lead to rebirth ... they fall down the precipice of rebirth, the precipice of aging, the precipice of death, the precipice of sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They are not freed from rebirth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. I say they are not freed from suffering.'
translations.sn56.45:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī in the Great Wood at the Gabled Hall. Then, in the morning, Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Vesālī for alms. He saw many Licchavi youths practicing archery in the hall, shooting through a small keyhole from a distance with a fine arrow, hitting a target without missing. Seeing this, he thought: 'These Licchavi youths are well trained, very well trained; that they can shoot through a small keyhole from a distance with a fine arrow and hit a target without missing.'
translations.sn56.45:3: 'What do you think, Ānanda, which is more difficult and harder to achieve—shooting through a small keyhole from a distance with a fine arrow and hitting a target without missing, or piercing the tip of a hair seven times with the tip of another hair?' 'The latter, sir, is more difficult and harder to achieve: piercing the tip of a hair seven times with the tip of another hair.' 'Yet, Ānanda, they pierce something even harder to pierce when they truly understand “this is suffering” … and truly understand “this is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.”'
translations.sn56.46:1: 'There is, mendicants, an inter-cosmic void, an abyss of darkness, pitch-black darkness, where even the mighty sun and moon, so powerful and majestic, cannot make their light felt.'
translations.sn56.46:2: When this was said, a certain mendicant said to the Buddha: 'That is a great darkness, sir, a very great darkness, sir. Is there, sir, another darkness greater and more terrifying than this darkness?' 'There is, mendicant, another darkness greater and more terrifying than this darkness.'
translations.sn56.48:1: 'Suppose, mendicants, this great earth were one single mass of water. A man would throw a single yoke in there. The easterly wind would drive it west, the westerly wind would drive it east, the northerly wind would drive it south, and the southerly wind would drive it north. And there is a blind turtle. It comes up to the surface once every hundred years. What do you think, mendicants? Would that blind turtle, coming up to the surface once every hundred years, put its neck into that single yoke?' 'It would be very unlikely, sir, that the blind turtle, coming up to the surface once every hundred years, would put its neck into that single yoke.'
translations.sn56.48:2: 'It is just as unlikely, mendicants, to obtain a human state. It is just as unlikely, mendicants, that a Realized One arises in the world—a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha. It is just as unlikely, mendicants, that the teaching and discipline proclaimed by a Realized One shines in the world. Therefore, mendicants, you have obtained a human state, a Realized One has arisen in the world—a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha—and the teaching and discipline proclaimed by a Realized One shines in the world.
